Its dancing builds static electricity in its feathers, which it can discharge against opponents, and Scarlet describes it approaching with nimble steps before striking with electrically charged attacks. This Style is friendly toward people and is known to dance in an effort to encourage Trainers or other people who are feeling down. Its energetic, cheerful performances are especially popular with children in Paldea, even though wild Pom-Pom Oricorio are not considered common throughout the region.

pokemon.name: Oricorio
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Pa'u Style Oricorio is associated with Akala Island and, in the modern Terarium, the Coastal Biome; Pink Nectar produces its pink coloration and Psychic/Flying state. Its temperament is comparatively laid-back and can make it difficult to handle, and it may become so absorbed in dancing that it ignores its Trainer's instructions. The dance itself focuses Oricorio's mind and increases its psychic power, and Alolan tradition describes the performance as an offering of thanks to a guardian deity. In Paldea, the airy dance is practiced or admired as a means of maintaining health, extending the form's cultural role beyond battle.

pokemon.name: Oricorio
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Sensu Style Oricorio is associated with Poni Island and southwest Kitakami and assumes its purple Ghost/Flying form after drinking Purple Nectar. It has a calm, collected temperament and performs an elegant fan-like dance that draws nearby spirits to it so that it can borrow their power in battle. Some Pokédex accounts go further and describe it calling forth the spirits of the dead, then using their power to curse opponents. Its dance reminds people who migrated from Kanto of their homeland, making the form culturally significant as well as supernatural. In Paldea its graceful performances are particularly popular with adults, while wild Sensu Oricorio are more commonly encountered in Kitakami.

playthrough: Cutiefly is obtainable very early in Alola and evolves into Ribombee at level 25, giving the line a favorable combination of early availability and a reasonably timed final evolution. The line is built around Speed rather than durability: Cutiefly is already quick, and Ribombee's base 124 Speed is exceptional for an ordinary story Pokémon, letting it move first against a large portion of in-game opponents. Bug/Fairy provides a Dragon immunity, a 4× Fighting resistance, and additional useful resistances, while Moonblast becomes the line's most dependable high-value STAB and Bug moves add secondary coverage; the tradeoff is weakness to Fire, Flying, Poison, Rock, and Steel. Ribombee's base 95 Special Attack is good rather than overwhelming, so its value comes from attacking first, exploiting super-effective matchups, and using its unusually broad support movepool rather than simply overpowering every neutral target. Quiver Dance can turn favorable matchups into sweeps, while Pollen Puff is particularly useful in doubles because it can damage enemies or heal an ally; Sticky Web, Stun Spore, Tailwind, and other support options vary by generation and can give Ribombee value even when raw damage is insufficient. Timid is the most consistently useful Nature when maximizing Ribombee's signature Speed matters, though Modest can be reasonable in ordinary play when the extra damage is more valuable than winning the narrowest Speed ties.
competitive: Ribombee has had a much better competitive career than its frail appearance suggests because base 124 Speed and an exceptional support movepool give it jobs that bulkier Bug-types cannot easily replicate. In Generation VII it was an RU Pokémon capable of acting as a very fast special attacker or Quiver Dance sweeper while also providing Sticky Web, Tailwind, or Defog, though mediocre base 95 Special Attack and very poor physical durability prevented it from becoming a premier conventional sweeper. Its hazard-setting identity became even more important in Generation VIII: despite a nominal PU tier placement, Smogon's UU analysis described Ribombee as a cornerstone of Sticky Web teams because its Speed, Shield Dust, offensive pressure, and access to tools such as Skill Swap let it establish Webs against many attempts to deny them. In Scarlet and Violet it currently sits in RU and continues to function as one of the game's fastest practical Sticky Web leads, using Moonblast, Stun Spore, Trick, or other disruption to make hazard removal difficult. Its utility is specialized enough that Ribombee has also received analyses in formats far above its usage tier, including Ubers, where a fast Focus Sash Sticky Web lead can be worthwhile even though Ribombee itself is obviously not an Ubers-level combatant by raw stats. Shield Dust is often the preferred singles Ability because blocking secondary effects prevents flinches and other incidental disruption from stopping its job, while Sweet Veil has more obvious team value in doubles.
nuzlocke: Ribombee is a high-value but low-margin Nuzlocke Pokémon: it can outspeed and cleanly remove many threats, but its 60/60/70 defensive profile gives little room for an incorrect damage estimate. The line's early availability and level-25 evolution are major positives because the player does not have to protect a weak first stage until the late game. Its Dragon immunity and very strong Fighting resistance can create safe entries when enemy movesets are known, but five weaknesses and low physical bulk make blind switching dangerous, especially against opponents carrying priority or coverage. Shield Dust is excellent for permadeath play because it removes secondary-effect variance from incoming damaging moves, preventing events such as an unexpected flinch or status proc from turning a planned sequence into a death. Moonblast is reliable and accurate, whereas Stun Spore is useful but should never be treated as guaranteed speed control because its imperfect accuracy can fail at the worst possible moment. Quiver Dance is safest when Ribombee already walls or strongly threatens the opposing Pokémon; attempting to stack multiple boosts against a foe that can land meaningful neutral damage creates unnecessary critical-hit exposure.

pokemon.name: Cutiefly
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Cutiefly can perceive the aura of living things, including plants, people, and Pokémon, and uses differences in aura color and brightness to locate flowers and even anticipate an opponent's movements. It feeds on nectar and pollen through its long proboscis and stores unfinished pollen in its body fur. Strong excitement makes a person's or Pokémon's aura resemble a flower in full bloom, so Cutiefly may gather around emotionally excited beings and then painfully prod them with its proboscis after approaching. Although common in fields and meadows, this sensitivity to emotion can draw it toward towns and buildings as well. It competes with Butterfree for nectar and pollen, is attracted by sources such as Fomantis's scent and Gossifleur's pollen, and is preyed upon by Spinarak and Pineco.

pokemon.name: Ribombee
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Ribombee stores collected pollen in its fluffy body hair, but rain makes both its fur dirty and its pollen damp, so it avoids fields unless clear weather is expected. It can predict approaching weather by sensing moisture levels and wind direction; before storms it hides in hollow trees and waits motionless. The nectar and pollen it gathers are fashioned into Pollen Puffs with different properties, including edible varieties and soothing versions that relieve fatigue. Alolan people sell especially nutritious Pollen Puffs as valuable supplements, and later accounts describe Ribombee making puffs to cheer sad humans or Pokémon. Recent animation has also shown that Ribombee can sometimes live inside the cells of a Vespiquen's abdomen in places normally occupied by Combee, adding an unusual documented association between the species.

playthrough: Rockruff evolves beginning at level 25, but the desired Lycanroc form must be planned around both time and Ability: ordinary Rockruff becomes Midday Form during the day or Midnight Form at night, while only the separate Own Tempo Rockruff can become Dusk Form during the evening. Generation VII adds version restrictions—Sun and Ultra Sun naturally produce Midday while Moon and Ultra Moon produce Midnight—and Own Tempo Rockruff was originally event-exclusive in Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon, whereas later games make the form easier to obtain. All three evolutions remain pure Rock physical attackers, but their stat distributions and Abilities create clearly different roles: Midday is fastest at base 112 Speed and can use Sand Rush, Midnight trades Speed for greater bulk and can use No Guard for perfectly accurate Stone Edge, and Dusk combines base 117 Attack with base 110 Speed and Tough Claws. Midday and Dusk also have access to Accelerock, a reliable Rock-type priority attack that is particularly useful for finishing faster weakened foes, while Dusk's Tough Claws boosts many of the contact coverage moves it already wants to use. Pure Rock typing supplies useful Fire, Flying, Normal, and Poison resistances but leaves all forms weak to Fighting, Grass, Ground, Steel, and Water, and none has the bulk to ignore strong super-effective attacks. Jolly is excellent for Midday and Dusk when preserving their natural Speed is important, while Adamant is a legitimate damage-focused alternative; Midnight is more comfortable with Adamant because its lower Speed makes raw power and No Guard reliability more central to its role.
competitive: The three Lycanroc forms have never been competitively equivalent despite sharing a species and pure Rock typing. Midday Form was PU in Generation VII, where base 112 Speed, Swords Dance, Accelerock, and the Lycanium Z-powered Splintered Stormshards gave it a respectable late-game sweeping role, and it continues to find lower-tier value as a fast attacker, hazard lead, or Sand Rush cleaner. Midnight Form has historically been the weakest of the three in singles: it was ZU in Generation VII and remains a lower-tier option, with No Guard granting the genuinely useful niche of perfectly accurate Stone Edge but not compensating fully for base 82 Speed, common weaknesses, and competition from faster Rock attackers. Dusk Form immediately occupied a stronger position, landing in RU in Generation VII because Tough Claws, base 117 Attack, base 110 Speed, Swords Dance, Accelerock, and its exclusive Z-Move made it an imposing wallbreaker; in Sword and Shield it rose to UU and remained valued as a fast revenge killer. In Scarlet and Violet, Dusk is currently NUBL and receives RU analysis, with Tough Claws-boosted coverage plus Accelerock and Sucker Punch preserving its role as a wallbreaker, cleaner, or setup sweeper, while Midday and Midnight reside much lower. The line illustrates how a small stat redistribution and one excellent Ability can matter more competitively than a shared typing: Dusk's Tough Claws and offensive stat line consistently give it the most serious singles presence, Midday's Speed grants a real niche, and Midnight's No Guard Stone Edge is useful but comparatively narrow.
nuzlocke: Rockruff's level-25 evolution is early enough to be practical, but the safest form depends on what the run values more: natural Speed, reliable Rock STAB, or stronger priority. Midday Form's base 112 Speed and Accelerock make it the easiest form to use for clean revenge kills, reducing the number of turns in which it must absorb damage; Dusk offers similar Speed, more Attack, Tough Claws, and the same priority, making it especially strong when Own Tempo Rockruff is legitimately obtainable. Midnight Form's No Guard removes Stone Edge's dangerous accuracy variance, a real Nuzlocke advantage, but No Guard also means opposing attacks cannot miss, and its base 82 Speed forces it to take more hits than the other forms. All three are pure Rock and share five weaknesses, so none should be treated as a general-purpose tank even when resisting the opponent's primary STAB; Water, Ground, Fighting, Steel, and Grass coverage must be checked carefully. Accelerock is one of the line's best permadeath tools because priority can remove a weakened threat without risking a Speed tie or an unexpected Choice Scarf, while Sucker Punch on appropriate sets is useful but less deterministic because it can fail against status moves. Swords Dance can enable sweeps from a genuinely safe matchup, but the forms' modest defenses make greedy setup dangerous, and recoil or Defense-dropping coverage should be avoided when a safer move still secures the knockout.

pokemon.name: Rockruff
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Rockruff is a canine Pokémon with small rocks embedded in the fur around its neck, and it has an exceptionally strong sense of smell that allows it to remember an odor permanently. Stories describe Rockruff following a faint remembered scent to reunite with a Trainer after becoming separated, and the species has lived alongside humans since ancient times. Young Rockruff are friendly and bond readily, but as evolution approaches they become increasingly unruly and independent, begin howling at sunset, and may disappear from their Trainer before later returning as Lycanroc. Wild Rockruff travel in packs until they evolve, and their persistent temperament is expressed by repeatedly attacking even much stronger opponents. They strike the ground with the stones in their neck ruff to intimidate enemies and have territorial conflicts with Growlithe.

pokemon.name: Lycanroc
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Midday Form Lycanroc has a calm, cautious temperament and normally lives alone rather than forming packs with others of its species. It becomes fiercely loyal to Trainers who accepted Rockruff during its difficult pre-evolution stage and will also protect Rockruff in its care with its claws and rocky mane. In battle it uses swift movement to slip past and corner opponents, striking weak points with its fangs or the razor-sharp stones projecting from its mane. Fragments broken from those mane stones are traditionally considered good-luck charms. Lycanroc are also used by people as field guards to protect crops from Deerling, providing a documented working relationship between the species and humans.

pokemon.name: Lycanroc
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Midnight Form Lycanroc is also solitary, but its temperament is almost the reverse of Midday Form: it is reckless, vicious in battle, and becomes increasingly excited when facing a stronger opponent. Its eyes glow as that battle excitement rises, and it deliberately closes distance and provokes an opponent into attacking so that it can answer with a devastating counterblow. A full-force headbutt is powerful enough to shatter giant boulders, and Pokédex accounts emphasize that it may charge without concern for injuries it receives in return. It respects Trainers capable of drawing out its strength but despises people with whom it disagrees or those who try to force it to fight. This combination of pain tolerance, counterattacking behavior, and selective trust gives Midnight Form a distinctly more confrontational ecology and temperament than its Midday counterpart.

pokemon.name: Lycanroc
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Dusk Form Lycanroc combines behavioral traits of the other two forms: it normally displays Midday Form's calm demeanor and loyalty, but its eyes turn red and it exhibits Midnight Form's ferocious fighting spirit once battle begins. It relentlessly drives opponents into a corner, blending the swift stance and movement associated with Midday Form with the aggression of Midnight Form. Because Rockruff can assume this form only during the brief evening period and only when it has Own Tempo, Dusk Form is regarded as the rarest Lycanroc form. It is also described as temperamental and unusually difficult to raise despite its normally quiet demeanor. Unlike Midday and Midnight Lycanroc, Dusk Form normally does not bark.

playthrough: Wishiwashi is mechanically unusual because it never evolves, but from level 20 onward its Schooling Ability can transform it into School Form whenever it enters battle or ends a turn above 25% of its maximum HP. That transformation is the entire reason to use it: Solo Form has extremely poor combat stats, while School Form jumps to base 140 Attack, 140 Special Attack, 130 Defense, and 135 Special Defense, giving it extraordinary offensive and defensive numbers for the point at which the mechanic becomes available. The tradeoff is that School Form still has only base 45 HP and base 30 Speed, so Wishiwashi usually takes a hit before attacking and can abruptly collapse back into its extremely frail Solo Form if its HP falls to 25% or lower. Its equal physical and special attacking stats make either Waterfall or Liquidation and Surf or Hydro Pump legitimate STAB approaches, while Ice Beam and U-turn can provide useful coverage or momentum where available. Pure Water typing is straightforward but effective, leaving only Grass and Electric weaknesses while resisting Fire, Ice, Steel, and Water, and its huge School Form defenses often allow it to absorb strong neutral attacks despite its low HP. A Brave or Quiet Nature can suit deliberately slow physical or special sets, while mixed playthrough sets often benefit more from keeping both attacking stats usable than from forcing a single specialized Nature.
competitive: Wishiwashi never became a high-tier singles staple, but its School Form has repeatedly supported a real lower-tier niche because its enormous mixed bulk and attacking stats make it function more like a slow heavyweight than its tiny Solo Form suggests. In Generation VII it was placed in ZU, where defensive RestTalk and slow-pivot sets used Scald and U-turn to exploit School Form's bulk while minimizing the risk of dropping below the Schooling threshold. Generation VIII was considerably kinder to it: Wishiwashi rose to PU, and Smogon described it as one of the tier's best bulky pivots because it could absorb attacks from common threats, threaten them with strong Water moves, and use a very slow U-turn to bring frailer teammates in safely. Its greatest competitive flaw has always been the Schooling threshold itself; once Wishiwashi falls to 25% HP or less, its defenses and offenses collapse so severely that the opponent can often force it out immediately. It also lacks dependable instant recovery and is vulnerable to common Grass- and Electric-types, so repeated switching, entry hazards, and chip damage can undermine the very bulk that gives it a niche. Wishiwashi is not available in standard Scarlet and Violet play, so it has no ordinary Generation IX usage-tier history there; its established competitive reputation remains primarily that of a specialized slow pivot and tank from Generations VII and VIII.
nuzlocke: Wishiwashi can be extremely powerful in a Nuzlocke once it reaches level 20, but it must be managed around the 25% HP threshold rather than treated like a conventional bulky Water-type. Above the threshold, School Form's enormous defenses give it substantial margin for error against neutral attacks, while its huge Attack and Special Attack let it retaliate without needing setup. The danger is that a strong hit can push it to 25% HP or lower at the end of the turn, immediately returning it to Solo Form with drastically worse defenses and leaving it exposed to a follow-up attack if it cannot be healed or switched safely. Its low Speed means it often has to absorb damage before acting, so blind matchups against Grass- or Electric-type coverage are particularly dangerous even when School Form appears healthy. A slow U-turn can be valuable because Wishiwashi can take the opponent's attack first and then bring in a teammate without exposing that teammate to the same hit, provided Wishiwashi remains above the Schooling threshold. Reliable Water STAB and only two type weaknesses make it a strong Nuzlocke asset, but the run should always track its current HP percentage rather than judging safety only by how impressive School Form's defensive stats look.

pokemon.name: Wishiwashi
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: An individual Wishiwashi is exceptionally small and weak and is described as notably tasty, making it prey for numerous species including Dewgong, Wailmer, Wailord, Wingull, Pelipper, and even humans. Although Wishiwashi often travel in schools, individuals may also be found alone after straying from the group. When threatened, a Wishiwashi's eyes tear up and shine brightly, producing an SOS signal visible from nearly 25 miles away that summons others of its species. This response turns a species that is individually easy prey into one whose predators risk attracting an entire defensive school.

pokemon.name: Wishiwashi
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: School Form is not a single enlarged individual but a coordinated formation of many Wishiwashi that assemble when one of their kind is endangered. The combined formation is feared in Alola as the 'demon of the sea,' and even Gyarados are said to flee from its appearance. The school concentrates enough power that its combined Water Gun has been described as exceeding the power of Hydro Pump. This strength depends on the group remaining intact: when the Wishiwashi are sufficiently injured and their numbers dwindle, the formation disperses back into ordinary individuals. New Pokémon Snap further depicts School Form producing an enormous Illumina energy reading, reinforcing the degree to which many individually weak Wishiwashi can become something dramatically more powerful through collective behavior.

playthrough: Mareanie evolves into Toxapex at level 38, which is a fairly late evolution for a Pokémon whose main strength lies in the final stage's defenses rather than immediate offensive power. In Sun, Moon, Ultra Sun, and Ultra Moon, Mareanie is also awkward to obtain because it appears through SOS Battles called by wild Corsola rather than as an ordinary encounter, so acquiring one can require deliberate hunting; Sword, Shield, and Scarlet/Violet make the species much easier to encounter directly. Toxapex has only base 50 HP but enormous base 152 Defense and 142 Special Defense, and Poison/Water grants eight resistances while leaving only Electric, Ground, and Psychic weaknesses, making it one of the most dependable defensive Pokémon available in games that permit it. Its drawback is extremely poor offense and base 35 Speed, so ordinary trainer battles can become slow unless status, stronger teammates, or favorable super-effective attacks are used to make progress. Recover, Toxic or Toxic Spikes, Haze, and Baneful Bunker give it excellent defensive utility depending on the generation, while Regenerator is its outstanding Hidden Ability because switching restores one third of its maximum HP; in Alola, however, obtaining the Hidden Ability requires more effort than simply catching the first Mareanie that appears. Bold and Calm are both genuinely useful Natures for emphasizing physical or special walling respectively, but a normal story playthrough does not require perfect optimization for Toxapex to be extraordinarily difficult for most neutral attackers to break.
competitive: Toxapex was one of the defining defensive Pokémon of both Generation VII and Generation VIII singles, immediately establishing itself in OU rather than slowly climbing from the lower tiers. Its success came from an unusually complete defensive package: immense mixed defenses, excellent Poison/Water typing, Regenerator, Recover, Haze, Toxic Spikes, Scald, Toxic, and historically Knock Off allowed it to wall or scout large portions of the metagame while continually generating chip damage or removing resources. In Sun and Moon OU it was among the most splashable defensive Pokémon in the tier, checking threats such as Ash-Greninja, Volcarona, and Mega Charizard Y while also absorbing opposing Toxic Spikes; Sword and Shield preserved that status, where Regenerator pivoting, Knock Off, Scald burns, and Haze made it extraordinarily difficult to wear down cleanly. Generation IX finally reduced that dominance: Recover's base PP was cut from 10 to 5 and standard Scarlet/Violet Toxapex lost the old combination of Scald and Knock Off that had allowed it to punish so many switch-ins, making it substantially more passive. That decline is reflected in its current Scarlet/Violet placement in UU, even though its raw bulk, Regenerator, Toxic Spikes, Haze, and defensive typing still give it serious value on slower teams. Pokémon Champions has produced a new, very recent chapter: as of 2026 Smogon's Champions dex lists Toxapex in OU, where the format's different item and threat environment again rewards its ability to repeatedly wall attackers and regenerate health, but that result is too new to treat as the same kind of long-established reputation it earned in Generations VII and VIII.
nuzlocke: Toxapex is one of the safest defensive Pokémon a Nuzlocke can offer once it is obtained and evolved, but the line's acquisition and slow development matter much more in permadeath play than they do in competitive analysis. In the Alola games, Mareanie's SOS-only appearance through Corsola makes the encounter unreliable and potentially costly in time or resources, and level 38 leaves a long period in which the player must protect the much less impressive first stage. Once evolved, Poison/Water typing, huge mixed defenses, Recover, and especially Regenerator when available create enormous switching safety and let Toxapex scout movesets without being permanently worn down by every neutral hit. Haze is valuable insurance against enemy setup, Baneful Bunker can safely scout contact moves while potentially poisoning attackers, and immunity to poison prevents one common form of long-term attrition. The major danger is that Toxapex's terrible offensive stats make battles last longer, exposing it to more critical hits, status attempts, and unexpected coverage than a faster Pokémon that simply secures the knockout; strong Ground, Electric, and Psychic attacks therefore still need to be respected. Generation IX's reduced Recover PP lowers its long-battle margin somewhat, but Regenerator remains excellent for conserving recovery resources when switching is safe.

pokemon.name: Mareanie
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Mareanie lives on beaches and seafloors in groups and hunts by poisoning prey with the spike on top of its head before trapping or finishing it with its ten tentacles. Its most famous prey is Corsola: the coral branches on Corsola's head are described as a delicacy, and Alolan Mareanie are hated by craftsmen who value naturally shed Corsola branches. The ecological relationship is mechanically reflected in the Alola games, where Mareanie can appear when Corsola calls for help in an SOS Battle and may attack the Corsola that summoned it instead of the player's Pokémon. Nearly every part of Mareanie except its head can regenerate overnight after being severed, although the regenerated or detached limbs have an intensely bitter, astringent taste and are unsuitable as food. Mareanie will also attempt to eat broken Pincurchin spines despite sometimes receiving electric shocks, while Bruxish is itself a predator of Mareanie. Its venom causes numbness followed by severe itching, giving the species a well-defined predatory and defensive ecology rather than merely a generic Poison-type theme.

pokemon.name: Toxapex
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Toxapex walks along the ocean floor on twelve long, spiny legs and continues the line's predation on Corsola. Those legs can be arranged into a dome-like shelter that protects its central body from tides and, in colder regions, helps trap body heat. The spines can sense the flow of ocean currents and tides, providing environmental information while Toxapex moves across the seafloor. They can also be fired as poisonous projectiles; the venom is described as causing intense pain for three days even in a Pokémon as large as Wailord, with lingering aftereffects after the immediate poisoning subsides. If an opponent gets through the spines, Toxapex attacks with the claws on its legs instead. Bruxish is a natural enemy, and the two species compete in warm ocean currents despite those confrontations tending to favor Bruxish.

playthrough: Mudbray evolves into Mudsdale at level 30, giving the line a practical evolution point and making it a strong midgame-to-endgame Ground-type in every region where it is obtainable during the main story. Mudsdale's base 125 Attack, 100 HP, and 100 Defense combine well with Ground STAB such as High Horsepower or Earthquake, while Rock, Steel, and Fighting coverage can handle many Pokémon that resist or avoid Ground attacks. Stamina is generally its most valuable Ability because every damaging hit raises Defense by one stage, allowing Mudsdale to become progressively harder for physical opponents to break; later-generation Body Press can convert those Defense boosts directly into stronger Fighting-type damage. Own Tempo and Inner Focus have also improved in later generations because both now protect against Intimidate in addition to their original effects, which can matter against physical teams, although they usually lack Stamina's broad defensive value in ordinary play. The major drawback is base 35 Speed, meaning Mudsdale almost always takes a hit before attacking, and Ground typing leaves common Water-, Grass-, and Ice-type attacks as serious threats despite its excellent physical bulk. Adamant maximizes its already high physical damage, while Impish is a legitimate choice for players emphasizing Stamina, Body Press, and a more defensive role.
competitive: Mudsdale has never been an OU singles mainstay, but it has remained a legitimate lower-tier defensive Ground-type across several generations because Stamina, strong physical bulk, and base 125 Attack give it more presence than a passive wall. In Generation VII it was a notable PU Stealth Rock setter that checked physical attackers such as Lycanroc, Stoutland, and Aggron while threatening meaningful damage with Earthquake; Choice Band sets also existed, although low Speed and a shallow movepool limited its wallbreaking ceiling. Its official-format history was stronger than a PU label alone suggests: Mudsdale saw meaningful VGC 2017 use, including top-cut appearances and a place on Andrew Nowak's Athens-winning team, where Assault Vest and its naturally low Speed made it useful both inside and outside Trick Room structures. Sword and Shield placed it in NU, while Scarlet and Violet currently place it in PU, preserving essentially the same identity as a physically bulky Ground-type, Stealth Rock user, and Stamina-based check to contact-heavy attackers. Body Press became an especially natural later-generation addition because Stamina boosts the Defense stat that Body Press uses for damage, allowing defensive momentum to become offensive pressure. Its long-term limitations are also consistent: no dependable recovery outside Rest or items, very low Speed, common Water/Grass/Ice weaknesses, and predictable coverage mean it can be worn down even while repeatedly increasing its Defense.
nuzlocke: Mudsdale is exceptionally valuable in Nuzlockes because Stamina directly rewards surviving hits, and unlike many defensive strategies it does not require setup turns before beginning to work. Its Electric immunity provides free switches when enemy movesets are known, while Rock and Poison resistances and strong natural physical bulk give it additional safe entry points. Against physical opponents, every damaging move can make the next one weaker by raising Mudsdale's Defense, and Body Press in later games lets those boosts contribute to damage as well as survival. The Ability does nothing to increase Special Defense, however, so strong special Water-, Grass-, and Ice-type moves remain dangerous and should not be challenged simply because Mudsdale has accumulated several Stamina boosts. Base 35 Speed means it usually has to take damage before attacking, and the lack of reliable healing makes repeated neutral hits, status, and route attrition more important than its impressive one-battle bulk initially suggests. Accurate Ground moves are generally preferable to riskier alternatives in permadeath play, and recoil-heavy options such as Double-Edge rarely justify shortening the lifespan of such a useful defensive Pokémon.

pokemon.name: Mudbray
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Mudbray eats dirt in order to produce mud, then regurgitates that mud and coats its body and hooves with it. The material does not readily dry out even under prolonged sunlight, and access to mud is behaviorally important: a Mudbray denied opportunities to play in and consume mud becomes stressed and may disobey its Trainer. Mud around its hooves improves traction and power, allowing it to cross rough terrain without slipping. Despite its small size, Mudbray can drag or carry loads weighing as much as fifty times its own body weight. The species was once hunted nearly to extinction across much of its former range and was for a time believed to survive wild only in Alola, but later populations in Galar and Paldea indicate a broader recovery.

pokemon.name: Mudsdale
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Mudsdale mixes dirt with saliva to create an exceptionally durable mud that resists both wind and water and can become harder than stone. That material has direct human uses: old houses have been coated with Mudsdale's mud, and the species is valued both for heavy labor and for pottery made from its unusually high-quality mud. The mud packed around its legs also amplifies its kicks; a single kick is said to reduce a car or large truck to scrap, while its hooves can gouge holes into asphalt as it gallops. Mudsdale is not fast, but its stamina is extraordinary, with accounts describing it dragging loads exceeding ten tons continuously for three days and three nights. In Alola, people use Mudsdale as a Ride Pokémon to cross rough, rocky terrain, giving the species an established transportation role in addition to its agricultural and construction value.

playthrough: Dewpider evolves into Araquanid at level 22, making this one of the fastest-developing Alola lines and allowing the final evolution to contribute for most of a normal playthrough. Araquanid's defining trait is Water Bubble: it doubles the power of its Water-type attacks, prevents burns, and halves incoming Fire-type damage, so its modest base 70 Attack produces Water damage far beyond what the raw stat suggests. Liquidation is therefore exceptionally strong and reliable STAB, while Leech Life provides secondary Bug STAB and useful recovery; Sticky Web, Lunge, Mirror Coat, Wide Guard, and other support options can add value depending on the game and format. Its base 132 Special Defense is outstanding and base 92 Defense is respectable, but base 68 HP and especially base 42 Speed mean Araquanid tends to absorb an attack before responding. Water/Bug gives useful resistances to Fighting, Ground, Ice, Steel, and Water and only three weaknesses—Electric, Flying, and Rock—while Water Bubble further reduces Fire damage despite Bug's normal weakness to that type. Adamant is the clearest Nature for maximizing physical Water Bubble attacks in a standard playthrough, while Brave is a genuine alternative on deliberately slow or Trick Room teams.
competitive: Araquanid's competitive niche has always been much stronger than base 70 Attack would imply because Water Bubble effectively doubles the strength of its Water STAB while also preventing burns and improving its defensive matchup against Fire attacks. In Generation VII it was an RU Pokémon and one of the tier's better Sticky Web setters, combining real offensive pressure from Liquidation with enough special bulk to set Webs more than once rather than functioning only as a suicide lead. It also had a documented VGC 2017 niche as a slow Trick Room attacker: Water Bubble made Hydro Vortex exceptionally powerful, burn immunity protected its physical offense, and Wide Guard or other support let it contribute beyond raw damage. In Sword and Shield it was PUBL but retained useful NU and Monotype roles as a specially bulky Water attacker and Sticky Web user, while Scarlet and Violet currently place it in PU, where Choice Band, Sticky Web, and Water Bubble remain the core reasons to use it. Its persistent flaws are low Speed, a Stealth Rock weakness, no reliable full recovery, and extremely one-dimensional offense outside Water attacks; Grass- or Water-resistant opponents can often exploit the weakness of its non-Water coverage. Pokémon Champions has created a striking but very recent change: Smogon's current Champions dex lists Araquanid in OU with a Sticky Web set, so it presently has much higher placement in that young format than it ever sustained in traditional singles, although that result should be treated as developing history rather than proof of a long-term OU reputation.
nuzlocke: Araquanid is a strong Nuzlocke Pokémon because it evolves early, has unusually good special bulk, and gains several forms of risk reduction from Water Bubble without requiring any setup. Burn immunity prevents one of the most dangerous long-term status conditions for physical attackers, while the Ability's Fire-damage reduction turns a matchup that would otherwise be neutral from Water/Bug's combined typing into a much safer one. Its Fighting, Ground, Ice, Steel, and Water resistances give it numerous switch opportunities when movesets are known, and Leech Life can recover health while dealing damage instead of forcing a completely passive healing turn. The major danger is Speed: base 42 means Araquanid commonly has to absorb an attack first, so an unexpected Electric-, Flying-, or Rock-type coverage move can be lethal before it gets the chance to retaliate. Liquidation is especially attractive for permadeath play because it is accurate, very strong after Water Bubble, and does not impose recoil or defensive drops. Water Absorb can create a true Water immunity if the Hidden Ability is obtained, but Water Bubble is usually the safer all-purpose Nuzlocke Ability because it combines burn immunity, Fire mitigation, and the enormous Water-STAB boost in a single package.

pokemon.name: Dewpider
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Dewpider normally lives underwater but can breathe only oxygen dissolved in water, so when it ventures onto land in search of food it carries a water bubble around its head. Sticky silk produced by the species helps form a durable bubble that rarely bursts, and Dewpider supports it with three of its six legs, sometimes secretly switching which legs perform the task. The bubble protects Dewpider's soft head but also functions as a weapon, allowing it to slam its water-covered head into prey or enemies. When two Dewpider meet, they compare the size of their bubbles, and the individual with the smaller bubble yields and moves aside. Animation has also shown the species producing both silk and water bubbles from its spinneret, reinforcing that maintaining the portable aquatic environment is an active biological behavior rather than a passive feature.

pokemon.name: Araquanid
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Araquanid uses the large water bubble surrounding its head as a weapon, storage chamber, protective enclosure, and nursery. It can launch sticky water bubbles from its legs to trap prey; small Pokémon may drown inside, and recent Pokédex material describes unconscious prey being torn apart by Araquanid's jaws after capture. When it is not hungry, Araquanid may store subdued prey in the head bubble for later instead of consuming it immediately. The same structure is also used benevolently: Araquanid brings vulnerable Pokémon and valued objects into the bubble for protection, and adults carry Dewpider children inside while sharing leftover food with them. This combination of predatory behavior and direct parental care makes Araquanid unusually complex ecologically, using the same adaptation both to kill prey and to shelter weaker members of its environment.

playthrough: Fomantis evolves into Lurantis at level 34 only when it levels up during the daytime, so the evolution is not especially late but can be delayed accidentally if the player reaches the required level at night. Lurantis is a slow physical-leaning Grass-type with base 105 Attack, respectable 70/90/90 bulk, and only base 45 Speed; Leaf Blade is usually a safer everyday STAB than the more dramatic two-turn Solar Blade unless sun support is already part of the team. Pure Grass grants useful Water, Ground, Electric, and Grass resistances but also five weaknesses to Bug, Fire, Flying, Ice, and Poison, so Lurantis benefits from deliberate matchup selection rather than simply relying on its decent defenses. Its ordinary Ability Leaf Guard prevents status in harsh sunlight, but the line becomes mechanically much more interesting with its Hidden Ability Contrary, which reverses stat changes and turns normally self-debilitating moves such as Leaf Storm and Superpower into boosting attacks when those moves are available. Contrary is not something every normal playthrough Lurantis will naturally possess, especially in Alola where the Hidden Ability requires special acquisition through SOS mechanics, so ordinary physical sets should not be evaluated as though every Lurantis automatically has access to that strategy. Adamant is useful for straightforward Leaf Blade and physical coverage sets, while slower Contrary-oriented builds can justify defensive or mixed Natures depending on whether the team is leaning on Leaf Storm, Superpower, or utility.
competitive: Lurantis has remained a lower-tier Pokémon throughout its competitive history, but Contrary prevents it from being completely generic and has repeatedly given it a specialized role on bulky teams. In Generation VII it was PU, where Defog, Synthesis, Aromatherapy, solid mixed defenses, and a pure Grass typing let it switch into many Ground- and Water-types while clearing hazards; Contrary Leaf Storm and Superpower also meant it could increase its own stats while attacking instead of becoming completely passive. It faced heavy competition from faster or more flexible hazard removers and suffered from common Fire- and Flying-type weaknesses, low Speed, and low-PP key moves, which kept it from establishing a higher-tier presence. Sword and Shield dropped it to ZU but preserved essentially the same identity: a bulky Contrary user capable of Defogging while threatening to snowball through Leaf Storm and Superpower. Scarlet and Violet currently also list Lurantis in ZU, where Terastallization can patch its poor defensive typing or provide better coverage, but its base 45 Speed and dependence on a narrow set of Contrary-compatible attacks remain major restrictions. Historically, therefore, Lurantis is best described as a legitimate low-tier utility Pokémon with a unique self-boosting mechanic, not as an overlooked high-tier sweeper.
nuzlocke: Lurantis is useful in a Nuzlocke when its favorable resistances can be planned around, but its five weaknesses and low Speed make it much less forgiving than its balanced defensive stats first suggest. The level-34 daytime evolution is manageable as long as the player remembers the time requirement, and Fomantis can be protected more easily than species that remain unevolved into the late 30s or 40s. Accurate physical Grass STAB such as Leaf Blade is generally safer than relying on Solar Blade's charge turn or Leaf Storm's imperfect accuracy, particularly when a missed or interrupted attack could expose Lurantis to a second hit. Synthesis provides valuable recovery in generations where it is available, though weather affects the amount healed and later games reduce the move's PP, so it should not be treated as unlimited sustain. Contrary can be excellent if the Hidden Ability is legitimately obtained because Leaf Storm can raise Special Attack and Superpower can raise Attack and Defense, but attempting to accumulate boosts against an opponent carrying super-effective coverage still creates unnecessary critical-hit exposure. Against Water- and Ground-type opponents Lurantis can be a sturdy answer, but Fire, Flying, Ice, Poison, and Bug coverage should be checked carefully because base 45 Speed rarely allows it to escape a bad matchup by simply moving first.

pokemon.name: Fomantis
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Fomantis is nocturnal but performs the photosynthesis needed for growth while sleeping during the day, spreading its leaves wide to collect sunlight. It does not remain in the same daytime resting place for more than one day because staying put would be dangerous, so each night it searches for a new location in which to sleep and gather light. Photosynthetic energy is essential to its evolution and vivid coloration, and Fomantis becomes fiercely aggressive toward anything that interrupts this process. Although it can use powerful long-range attacks, it is reluctant to expend the energy stored through photosynthesis on moves such as Solar Beam unless necessary. Its body releases a sweet, refreshing scent that attracts Bug Pokémon such as Cutiefly, and Trainers often provide potted plants or flowerpots so a captive Fomantis can sunbathe undisturbed.

pokemon.name: Lurantis
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Lurantis reverses the usual relationship between flower and insect mimicry: although it is a Grass-type plant Pokémon, it resembles a mantis and uses its flowerlike appearance and sweet aroma to lure actual Bug Pokémon into lowering their guard before attacking them with its scythes. Its brilliant coloration and elegant movements have led to it being described as one of the most beautiful Grass-type Pokémon, but maintaining that appearance requires meticulous grooming. This care affects its relationship with people: Lurantis is said to trust a Trainer who diligently maintains it, while having difficulty bonding with a lazy caretaker. Its scythe-like arms can channel Solar Blade, producing a cutting beam sharp enough in official descriptions to slice rock in half. The species therefore combines visual mimicry, active predation, dependence on careful physical maintenance, and powerful sunlight-based attacks rather than behaving merely as a decorative flower Pokémon.

playthrough: Morelull evolves into Shiinotic at level 24, so the line reaches its final stage early enough to contribute through most of an Alola playthrough rather than requiring a prolonged weak middle stage. Shiinotic is a very slow special attacker and support Pokémon with base 30 Speed, but its 90 Special Attack, 100 Special Defense, and Grass/Fairy typing give it useful matchups against Water-, Ground-, Fighting-, Dark-, and Dragon-type opponents. Its most valuable tools are often defensive rather than purely offensive: Spore provides perfectly accurate sleep against targets that are not immune, Strength Sap heals Shiinotic while lowering the target's Attack, and Giga Drain can restore additional HP while dealing damage. Effect Spore is generally more useful in battle than Illuminate in the generations where Shiinotic is normally available, since contact can inflict sleep, paralysis, or poison, while Rain Dish is a more specialized Hidden Ability for rain teams. The typing also carries a severe 4× Poison weakness along with weaknesses to Fire, Flying, Ice, and Steel, and Shiinotic's low HP and Speed mean it can be overwhelmed quickly if it is sent into the wrong matchup. A Calm or Bold Nature can reinforce its special or physical defensive role, while Modest is reasonable when a normal playthrough values stronger Moonblast and Giga Drain damage over further bulk.
competitive: Shiinotic has historically been a lower-tier defensive specialist rather than a broadly successful competitive Pokémon, with its most clearly established singles role appearing in Generation VII ZU and occasional PU use. Grass/Fairy typing, Spore, Strength Sap, Moonblast, and Giga Drain gave it a real niche against Water-, Ground-, and Fighting-types, while Effect Spore could punish physical contact and add another layer of status pressure. Morelull itself also had a small Little Cup niche for similar reasons, using Spore, Strength Sap, respectable special bulk, and Fairy typing as a defensive pivot, though Foongus and other bulky Grass-types usually outclassed it. Shiinotic's limitations are substantial: base 30 Speed forces it to take hits first, base 60 HP makes its defenses less impressive than the raw Defense and Special Defense numbers suggest, and a 4× Poison weakness is especially troublesome in tiers where Poison-types are common. Its modest base 90 Special Attack can pressure frailer targets but does not prevent dedicated special walls from exploiting it, and faster Grass-types often offer more immediate offensive value. As a result, Shiinotic is best understood historically as a legitimate low-tier sleep-and-recovery specialist rather than an overlooked high-tier threat.
nuzlocke: Shiinotic can be excellent in a Nuzlocke when used deliberately because Spore and Strength Sap directly reduce battle variance instead of requiring risky offensive setup. A successful Spore can create a safe healing or switching turn, while Strength Sap simultaneously restores HP and lowers a physical opponent's Attack, allowing Shiinotic to become progressively safer against many physical enemies. Its Grass/Fairy typing also supplies a Dragon immunity and useful resistances to Fighting, Ground, Water, Electric, Dark, and Grass, creating several good switch opportunities when the opponent's moveset is known. The major warning is its 4× weakness to Poison; even moderate Poison coverage can be fatal, and weaknesses to Fire, Flying, Ice, and Steel are also dangerous because Shiinotic's base 30 Speed rarely lets it escape by attacking first. Effect Spore can provide valuable emergency status against contact moves, but the random status should be treated as a bonus rather than part of a guaranteed plan. Because its offensive damage is only moderate, long fights can expose Shiinotic to additional critical hits, so using sleep, Attack reduction, and recovery to control the battle is usually safer than simply trading neutral attacks.

pokemon.name: Morelull
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Morelull inhabits dark, damp places such as dense forests and jungles, but it changes its sleeping location every night so that it does not drain too many nutrients from the plants in any one area. Its root-like feet are used both for movement and for communication with other Morelull. At night, spores stored in the mushroom caps on its head can glow and pulse with light; when threatened, Morelull releases these glittering spores, whose flickering illumination can induce drowsiness. A mass release of spores by disturbed Morelull was once said to have nearly caused an accident involving an aircraft passing overhead. The mushroom caps themselves are eaten by forest Pokémon, but they can grow back overnight.

pokemon.name: Shiinotic
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Shiinotic lives in dark forests and produces strange light from its mushroom cap and gills, confusing travelers and causing them to lose their way. Its flickering spores induce sleep, after which Shiinotic drains vitality from sleeping prey through the tips of its arms. The same structures can also transfer energy in the opposite direction, allowing Shiinotic to restore weakened members of its own species or provide vitality to other Pokémon, humans, and even vegetation. Shiinotic competes with Parasect for forest territory, and conflicts between the two species can leave the surrounding area completely coated in spores. These behaviors make its bioluminescence both a hunting adaptation and a means of manipulating energy within its forest environment.

playthrough: Salandit is available early enough in Alola to become a useful Fire/Poison attacker, but only female Salandit can evolve into Salazzle at level 33, and females make up only one eighth of ordinary Salandit encounters. That gender restriction is the line's largest practical drawback during a normal playthrough: a male Salandit permanently remains the much weaker first stage unless the player replaces it. Salazzle rewards the effort with base 117 Speed and 111 Special Attack, excellent special STAB from moves such as Flamethrower and Sludge Bomb, and a typing that strongly resists Bug, Fairy, and Grass while also resisting Fighting, Fire, Ice, Poison, and Steel. Its Corrosion Ability is unique strategically because it allows Salazzle to poison even Poison- and Steel-type targets, while Nasty Plot can turn its already strong Special Attack into genuine sweeping power; from Generation VIII onward, Oblivious also blocks Intimidate in addition to preventing infatuation and Taunt. The line is extremely frail, however, and Salazzle has a crippling 4× Ground weakness along with weaknesses to Water, Rock, and Psychic, so it performs far better when attacking first than when asked to switch into neutral damage. Timid is usually the safest beneficial Nature because preserving Salazzle's exceptional Speed is central to its role, while Modest can be justified in ordinary play when the additional damage matters more than the narrowest Speed benchmarks.
competitive: Salazzle has maintained a respectable lower-tier competitive career because very high Speed, strong Fire/Poison STAB, Nasty Plot, and Corrosion give it tools that most other frail Fire-types lack. In Generation VII it was an important RU threat, where base 117 Speed let it outrun much of the unboosted metagame and Z-Moves could help Nasty Plot sets break specially bulky answers that would otherwise survive its attacks. Corrosion also supported specialized Toxic sets by allowing Salazzle to badly poison Steel- and Poison-types that normally ignore Toxic, creating a stallbreaking niche distinct from its direct offensive sets. In Sword and Shield it fell to NU but remained dangerous as a fast Nasty Plot sweeper and utility attacker; Heavy-Duty Boots also reduced the cost of repeatedly switching a Fire-type through Stealth Rock. Scarlet and Violet currently place Salazzle in PU, where the same combination of Speed, Nasty Plot, Fire/Poison coverage, and disruptive status remains effective but its terrible physical bulk, 4× Ground weakness, and difficulty breaking some specially bulky opponents keep it from sustaining higher usage. Salazzle therefore has real competitive history across several generations, but its career is that of a dangerous specialized lower-tier attacker rather than a stable OU presence.
nuzlocke: The first Nuzlocke challenge with this family is obtaining the correct individual: because only female Salandit evolve and females are uncommon, a ruleset that permits only the first encounter in an area may leave the player with a permanently unevolved male. A female that reaches level 33 becomes much more useful, as Salazzle's base 117 Speed lets it avoid many hits entirely by securing the knockout first. Its numerous resistances and Poison immunity create safe entries against known Bug-, Fairy-, Grass-, Fighting-, Fire-, Ice-, Poison-, or Steel-type moves, but its low defensive stats mean even resisted damage should not be treated casually over a long battle. The 4× Ground weakness is the critical danger: an unexpected Earthquake, High Horsepower, or similar coverage move can erase Salazzle before its Speed matters. Flamethrower and Sludge Bomb provide reliable, accurate STAB, while Corrosion-backed Toxic can safely wear down certain defensive enemies that Salazzle cannot overpower directly. Nasty Plot is best used only when the opposing Pokémon is genuinely unable to threaten Salazzle, because spending a turn setting up with such frail defenses creates much less margin for an incorrect damage estimate than simply attacking.

pokemon.name: Salandit
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Salandit inhabits volcanic and dry rocky environments and can produce both flames and poisonous gas from markings near the base of its tail. The gas is created by burning bodily fluids and has a sweet odor that causes dizziness; Bug Pokémon are attracted to the smell and become common prey. Female Salandit additionally release powerful pheromones capable of attracting males of their own species and even affecting other species, including humans. Male Salandit surrender much of their food to females under this influence, leaving them malnourished enough that they do not develop into Salazzle. Although physically unimpressive compared with its evolution, Salandit compensates with deceptive movement, poison, and other tactics intended to unbalance opponents before attacking.

pokemon.name: Salazzle
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Salazzle is an exclusively female evolved stage that lives deep in caves surrounded by groups of male Salandit attracted by its pheromone-laced poisonous gas. It compels those males to gather food and serve it, punishing individuals that fail with blows from its flame-producing palms. When two Salazzle meet, they compete over the males in their groups using pheromone gas, and the individual with the larger following is treated as the winner. The gas has enough fragrance that diluted forms are used by humans in perfume production. Salazzle can also cling to vertical or inverted surfaces with its feet, giving it considerable mobility inside the caves and rocky environments it inhabits.

playthrough: Stufful evolves into Bewear at level 27, giving the line an accessible final evolution and a major jump in HP and Attack before the late game. Bewear has base 120 HP and 125 Attack and combines Normal/Fighting STAB with coverage for Ghost-, Psychic-, Flying-, and other troublesome types depending on the generation, making it a powerful physical attacker without requiring complicated setup. Fluffy is its defining Ability: contact moves deal only half their normal damage, allowing Bewear to absorb many physical attacks far better than its base 80 Defense suggests, but Fire-type moves deal double damage to it, creating a major matchup-specific weakness. Drain Punch is particularly useful in a story playthrough because it provides reliable Fighting damage and converts Bewear's high Attack into recovery, while moves such as Double-Edge hit extremely hard but impose recoil that can become costly over multiple battles. Its base 60 Speed and 60 Special Defense are important weaknesses, so fast special attackers can bypass much of the physical safety created by Fluffy. Adamant is the most straightforward Nature for maximizing Bewear's wallbreaking power, while Impish can be useful on a deliberately physical-tank-oriented Fluffy set.
competitive: Bewear established itself as a serious lower-tier wallbreaker immediately in Generation VII, where it was an RU Pokémon distinguished from other Fighting-types by the unusual defensive utility of Fluffy. Fluffy allowed it to switch into many contact-based physical attackers that would normally pressure an offensive Fighting-type, while base 125 Attack, Swords Dance, Choice Band, and powerful Normal/Fighting STAB let it punish the opponent heavily in return. Drain Punch could offset accumulated damage, whereas Double-Edge supplied enormous neutral power at the cost of recoil; Ghost coverage such as Shadow Claw or Darkest Lariat was important because Ghost-types were immune to both of Bewear's STAB types. In Sword and Shield it was classified NUBL while receiving substantial RU use, again functioning as a wallbreaker that exploited contact moves from Pokémon such as Golisopod, Steelix, and Registeel. Its flaws consistently prevented higher-tier stability: base 60 Speed is poor for an attacker, Special Defense is only base 60, and Fluffy effectively creates an additional Fire weakness, allowing fast special attackers to revenge kill it even when physical attackers struggle. Bewear is absent from standard Scarlet and Violet, so its established singles history currently ends with Generation VIII rather than extending into the ordinary Generation IX usage tiers.
nuzlocke: Bewear can be outstanding in a Nuzlocke if Fluffy is understood precisely rather than treated as a generic physical-defense boost. The Ability halves damage from contact moves, making many punches, bites, tackles, and other contact attacks remarkably safe, but it does not reduce every physical move and it doubles incoming Fire-type damage, so identifying the actual move being used matters more than simply identifying whether the opponent is physical. Its Normal typing also grants a valuable Ghost immunity, while Fighting adds resistances to Bug, Dark, and Rock, giving Bewear several reliable switch opportunities when coverage is known. High HP and Drain Punch provide excellent staying power, but base 60 Special Defense means strong special attacks can still cut through it quickly, especially because its low Speed commonly forces it to take the first hit. Double-Edge and other recoil attacks may secure impressive knockouts but are less attractive in permadeath play than slightly weaker options that preserve Bewear's long-term health. If Fluffy is unavailable, Bewear loses much of the safety that defines the species, so the Ability should be treated as an important part of its Nuzlocke evaluation rather than a minor bonus.

pokemon.name: Stufful
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Stufful resembles a harmless plush toy, but the tag-like structure beneath its tail is actually an organ that releases an odor used to communicate with other members of its species. Its cute appearance and soft fur make it popular with people, yet Stufful strongly dislikes being touched or hugged. When restrained, it flails its arms with enough force to break thick tree trunks and can knock out even trained Pokémon that underestimate it. Pokémon Sleep material likewise depicts the species moving and flailing even while asleep, emphasizing that its unusual physical strength is present from an early stage rather than appearing only after evolution.

pokemon.name: Bewear
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Bewear is regarded as one of Alola's most dangerous Pokémon despite its friendly appearance, largely because it has difficulty controlling its extraordinary physical strength. It shows affection through embraces powerful enough to crush or seriously injure a recipient, so Trainers are specifically warned that a Bewear must be taught to restrain itself. Even the apparently friendly motion of swinging its arms can function as a warning display and should not be interpreted as an invitation to approach. Bewear can snap trees and heavy logs with ease, sometimes accidentally destroying objects after mistaking them for companions. Animated portrayals additionally show highly developed intelligence and problem solving, including tool construction and remarkable locomotion, while also depicting Bewear as intensely protective of Stufful. It feeds on foods such as Berries and Combee-produced Honey.

playthrough: Bounsweet evolves into Steenee at level 18, then becomes Tsareena after leveling up while knowing Stomp, making the line's final evolution dependent more on understanding the move requirement than on reaching an unusually high level. Tsareena is a physical Grass-type attacker with base 120 Attack and balanced base 98 Defense and Special Defense, allowing it to hit hard without being as fragile as many offensive Grass-types. Queenly Majesty is usually its most valuable Ability because it prevents opposing priority moves from striking Tsareena or its allies, protecting it from moves such as Quick Attack, Aqua Jet, Bullet Punch, and Sucker Punch and becoming particularly useful in doubles. Trop Kick is a distinctive playthrough move because it combines accurate Grass-type damage with a guaranteed Attack reduction, while stronger options such as Power Whip trade reliability for raw power; High Jump Kick offers valuable Fighting coverage but its crash damage creates an unnecessary risk when safer coverage is sufficient. Rapid Spin gives Tsareena useful field support in games where entry hazards matter, and from Generation VIII onward Rapid Spin also raises the user's Speed, making the move more valuable than it was at Tsareena's debut. Adamant suits maximum physical damage, while Jolly is equally legitimate when preserving Speed against nearby benchmarks is more important.
competitive: Tsareena has maintained a consistent lower-tier competitive niche because it combines real physical power with utility that most offensive Grass-types do not provide. It was an RU Pokémon in Generation VII, where base 120 Attack, Power Whip, Knock Off, High Jump Kick, Rapid Spin, Synthesis, and Queenly Majesty allowed it to function as both a wallbreaker and an offensive hazard remover. Queenly Majesty was especially useful against revenge-killing priority, while Knock Off punished Ghost-types trying to block Rapid Spin and Synthesis could keep Tsareena healthy enough to remove hazards repeatedly. Sword and Shield placed Tsareena in NU, but Rapid Spin's Generation VIII buff to 50 base power and a +1 Speed boost made successful spinning substantially more rewarding; Queenly Majesty also gave Tsareena a meaningful doubles niche by protecting partners from Fake Out and priority such as Grassy Glide. Scarlet and Violet currently keep Tsareena in NU, where it remains an offensive spinner and pivot with strong Grass STAB and coverage but competes against faster Grass-types and struggles with common Fire-, Flying-, Ice-, Poison-, and Bug-type pressure. Its historical reputation is therefore one of dependable role compression rather than dominance: Tsareena attacks, removes hazards, blocks priority, and can pivot or recover, but middling base 72 Speed and pure Grass typing prevent those tools from carrying it into the highest singles tiers.
nuzlocke: Tsareena is a strong Nuzlocke Pokémon because it combines respectable bulk, high Attack, recovery or utility options, and an Ability that directly removes one common source of surprise deaths. Queenly Majesty blocks opposing priority directed at Tsareena or its allies, preventing a weakened Pokémon from being unexpectedly finished by moves such as Sucker Punch, Aqua Jet, or Bullet Punch when the player would otherwise expect to move first. Trop Kick is particularly safe because it is accurate and always lowers the target's Attack, allowing Tsareena to weaken physical opponents while still dealing damage instead of spending a separate turn on setup. The line's evolution is reasonably accessible, but the player must remember that Steenee evolves only after leveling while it knows Stomp; overlooking or replacing the move can delay Tsareena unnecessarily. Power Whip and High Jump Kick are competitively powerful but introduce accuracy or crash-damage risks that may not be justified in a permadeath run when Trop Kick, Seed Bomb, Low Kick, or other safer options can secure the required result. Tsareena's five weaknesses still demand caution, especially against faster Fire-, Flying-, Ice-, Poison-, and Bug-type attackers, because base 72 Speed does not reliably let it escape poor matchups before being hit.

pokemon.name: Bounsweet
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Bounsweet releases a strong sweet fragrance from its entire body, and Alolan households have kept the species because the scent has a calming effect and works like a living air freshener. Its sweat is excessively sweet on its own but can be diluted into a pleasantly flavored juice, and Bounsweet were especially valued by humans in eras when sweets were difficult to obtain. The same scent creates serious ecological danger by attracting predators and collectors, particularly Toucannon and Greedent; Toucannon have been known to swallow Bounsweet whole. Bounsweet attempts to defend itself by spinning the leafy calyx on its head, but this often makes it dizzy, and its skipping motion while fleeing can look so carefree that others fail to realize it is in danger.

pokemon.name: Steenee
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: After evolution, Steenee's calyx becomes hard enough that it can play with other Pokémon without being damaged as easily as Bounsweet. It uses both the hardened calyx and its equally strong legs in battle, first striking with the spinning leaves and then following with kicks. Those legs also protect it against natural predators such as Corvisquire. Steenee produces a pleasant fragrance used by humans in antiperspirant products, while its peeled rind has been used as a remedy for stomach pain. Its lively movements can send the calyx striking nearby objects, and Steenee appears largely unconcerned by the collateral contact as it bounces through its forest habitat.

pokemon.name: Tsareena
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Tsareena is a powerful, aggressive Pokémon whose fighting style centers on highly refined kicks and graceful movements, and it is known to laugh or cackle as its attacks connect. It may continue kicking or stepping on a defeated opponent, giving the species a notably domineering battle temperament. Only particularly capable Steenee are described as reaching this stage, and Tsareena uses its strength to protect Bounsweet and Steenee. Its crown-like growth is an unusual vulnerability: touching it can immediately calm Tsareena and leave it defenseless. Tsareena may ignore or resent commands it considers improper, even from its own Trainer, while its sweet fragrance can distract opponents during combat. Its highly developed kicking style has also produced a documented rivalry with Quaquaval.

playthrough: Comfey does not evolve and arrives with its full support-oriented stat spread immediately: base 100 Speed, 110 Special Defense, and 90 Defense are good, but base 51 HP and only 82 Special Attack limit how much punishment or raw damage it can produce without assistance. Its signature Ability Triage is the main reason to use it, increasing the priority of HP-restoring moves by three stages; this allows attacks such as Draining Kiss and Giga Drain to function as unusually fast sources of both damage and recovery and also gives Floral Healing extremely high priority in doubles. Pure Fairy typing provides a Dragon immunity and resistances to Fighting, Dark, and Bug while leaving only Poison and Steel weaknesses, making Comfey surprisingly easy to position against the right enemies. Calm Mind can increase both Special Attack and Special Defense before Comfey begins recovering through priority attacks, while support options such as Leech Seed, Taunt, Helping Hand, or screens vary by game and can make it useful even when its damage is modest. The principal danger is its low HP and mediocre physical staying power despite base 90 Defense, so strong neutral physical attackers can overpower it before its recovery becomes decisive. Modest is a strong Nature for Triage-based offensive sets because priority reduces the need to maximize natural Speed, while Bold can make sense when the goal is to improve Comfey's weaker physical resilience.
competitive: Comfey has enjoyed a persistent competitive niche because Triage fundamentally changes how its otherwise modest offensive stats behave, giving priority +3 to eligible healing moves such as Draining Kiss and Giga Drain. In Generation VII it was an NU Pokémon and a legitimate Calm Mind sweeper: after boosting, priority Draining Kiss could revenge kill faster attackers and simultaneously restore health, while Giga Drain punished bulky Water- and Ground-types. Its weaknesses were equally clear, as base 82 Special Attack often required setup before it could break defensive teams and Steel-, Poison-, and certain Fire-types could withstand its attacks and threaten it in return. Later generations preserved the same basic identity while expanding some of its utility, and Scarlet/Violet currently place Comfey in RU, where Calm Mind or Growth, Draining Kiss, Stored Power, Taunt, and Terastallization can support late-game sweeping roles. Triage is also strategically important in doubles because it applies to Floral Healing and other qualifying recovery moves, allowing Comfey to restore a teammate before many opposing attacks occur. Comfey has never been defined by raw base-stat dominance; its competitive value comes from exploiting an exceptionally strong priority mechanic, good defensive typing, and recovery to perform jobs that faster but more conventional Fairy-types cannot reproduce.
nuzlocke: Comfey is a useful Nuzlocke support Pokémon because Triage turns recovery into a form of speed control, often allowing it to heal through Draining Kiss or Giga Drain before a faster opponent can finish it. Its Dragon immunity and resistances to Fighting, Dark, and Bug provide safe switch opportunities when the enemy's moveset is known, and only Poison and Steel hit its pure Fairy typing super effectively. The combination of Calm Mind and priority Draining Kiss can stabilize favorable special matchups, but base 51 HP means Comfey should not be mistaken for a true high-HP wall merely because its Defense and Special Defense stats are respectable. Strong physical neutral attacks remain dangerous, and repeatedly setting up Calm Mind exposes it to critical hits that ignore the accumulated defensive boosts. In doubles-oriented challenge formats, Triage-boosted Floral Healing can rescue a damaged partner before ordinary attacks resolve, giving Comfey a survival role that goes beyond its own HP. Accurate draining attacks are especially valuable in permadeath play because they combine damage and recovery without recoil, defensive drops, or a separate vulnerable healing turn.

pokemon.name: Comfey
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Comfey uses sticky vine-like tendrils extending from its head to gather flowers and arrange them into the ring it carries around its body, and it may present these flower rings to individuals it likes. Oil produced by Comfey is spread over the gathered flowers, causing them to emit a soothing fragrance; the treated flowers retain their individual scents and do not wither. That aroma has practical medicinal value, and Comfey have been used in hospitals and Pokémon Centers to help treat or comfort both people and Pokémon. Comfey becomes uneasy when deprived of its flowers but can throw them at an attacker to create an opening to flee or counterattack. New Pokémon Snap describes the vine itself as nutrient-rich enough to revitalize attached flowers, and Comfey living in the nature park spend time among the flowers cultivated by Florges. Pokémon Sleep further depicts Comfey sleeping contentedly with fragrant flowers close to its face, suggesting it also uses soothing floral scents for its own comfort.

playthrough: Oranguru does not evolve, so any one obtained arrives with its full 90 HP, 90 Special Attack, and 110 Special Defense immediately, although base 60 Speed means it rarely functions as a conventional fast attacker. Normal/Psychic is an unusual defensive typing that grants a Ghost immunity, a Psychic resistance, and only Bug and Dark weaknesses, while Fighting becomes neutral rather than super effective because Psychic offsets Normal's weakness. Its broad special and support movepool can support Psychic STAB, coverage, Calm Mind, screens, Trick Room, and status or utility depending on the game, giving it considerably more flexibility than its modest offensive stats initially suggest. Instruct is the line's defining move but is primarily relevant in doubles, where it orders an ally to repeat its most recent move; Telepathy likewise becomes much more useful in doubles because it protects Oranguru from damaging moves used by its partner. Inner Focus was improved in Generation VIII to block Intimidate as well as flinching, which gives it a small but meaningful advantage against common doubles disruption. Oranguru is version-exclusive in several of its main-series appearances, including Moon/Ultra Moon, Shield, and Scarlet, so availability can be more restrictive than its lack of an evolution requirement would imply; Calm or Modest are reasonable Natures for defensive support or stronger special offense respectively.
competitive: Oranguru's competitive reputation is much more significant in doubles than its low singles usage suggests. In Generation VII singles it was a ZU Pokémon with occasional PU relevance, where its good special bulk, broad movepool, and setup options were undermined by middling Speed, only moderate immediate power, and competition from more efficient Psychic-types. VGC 2017 gave Oranguru its clearest historical role: it could set Trick Room and then use its signature Instruct to make a slow partner such as Torkoal, Alolan Marowak, or another heavy attacker execute a powerful move a second time in the same turn. Telepathy was especially useful on such teams because spread attacks from its own partner could be used without damaging Oranguru, while Inner Focus protected it from flinching and later generations added Intimidate immunity to that Ability. In Sword/Shield singles it remained in ZU and could experiment with Nasty Plot or bulky setup, while Scarlet/Violet also currently lists Oranguru in ZU, confirming that its unusual tools have never translated into sustained high-tier singles usage. Its historical identity is therefore best described as a specialized Trick Room and Instruct enabler in doubles and a niche bulky Psychic-type in lower-tier singles rather than a generally dominant competitive Pokémon.
nuzlocke: Oranguru can be a dependable Nuzlocke support Pokémon because its solid mixed bulk, Ghost immunity, and only two type weaknesses give it more safe switching opportunities than many Psychic-types. Its low Speed means it often has to take a hit before acting, however, so strong physical Dark- or Bug-type attacks are dangerous despite its respectable HP and Defense. Calm Mind can make it difficult for special attackers to break, but repeated setup creates unnecessary critical-hit exposure when a direct attack, screen, or switch would already secure the matchup. In single battles, Instruct and Telepathy provide little or no value, so a Nuzlocke should judge Oranguru primarily by its bulk, coverage, status options, and Psychic STAB rather than by the doubles gimmicks that define its competitive reputation. Trick Room can be excellent on deliberately slow teams but also changes turn order for the opponent, so it is safest when the opposing roster and Speed relationships are well understood. Inner Focus becomes especially useful from Generation VIII onward because immunity to both flinching and Intimidate removes two common forms of battle variance and disruption.

pokemon.name: Oranguru
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Oranguru is a solitary forest-dwelling Pokémon that spends long periods meditating high in trees and becomes increasingly long-furred with age. Despite its aloof behavior, it gives food to hungry Pokémon and medicine to injured ones, and its intelligence is high enough that it has been observed using human tools and even Poké Balls. Ancient people regarded Oranguru as people of the forest, while modern accounts emphasize that it often gives orders to other Pokémon and may be difficult for a Trainer to command. Members of its own species do not readily cooperate; Oranguru instead challenge one another in contests of intelligence to establish superiority. It also travels to beaches to match wits with Slowking, providing a rare documented intellectual rivalry between two Pokémon species. The fan it carries is constructed from leaves woven together with strands of its own purple fur.
