playthrough: Passimian does not evolve and brings strong physical performance immediately, with base 120 Attack, 100 HP, 90 Defense, and a workable base 80 Speed making it far more straightforward in ordinary battles than its counterpart Oranguru. Pure Fighting STAB gives it powerful options such as Close Combat, while Knock Off, U-turn, Earthquake, Rock coverage, and Poison coverage in appropriate generations help it avoid being completely stopped by Psychic-, Ghost-, Flying-, and Fairy-type opponents. Receiver is designed for doubles because it copies the Ability of a fainted ally and consequently contributes little in an ordinary single-player battle, whereas the Hidden Ability Defiant is much more generally useful because opposing stat reductions can sharply raise Passimian's Attack. Defiant is particularly valuable against Intimidate and against opponents that try to lower Attack or other stats, although obtaining the Hidden Ability may require more effort than simply catching a normal Passimian. Its main weakness is special durability: base 60 Special Defense is much less reliable than its physical bulk, and pure Fighting leaves it vulnerable to Fairy-, Flying-, and Psychic-type attacks. Jolly is excellent for preserving useful Speed advantages and works especially well with an offensive pivoting role, while Adamant is a legitimate alternative when maximizing the damage of its already high Attack matters more.
competitive: Passimian has built a respectable competitive history as a physical pivot and revenge killer, with U-turn and Defiant distinguishing it from many other Fighting-types. In Generation VII its official usage tier was NU, but it also had meaningful RU use because Choice Scarf let it revenge kill faster threats while U-turn preserved momentum and Knock Off punished common Psychic- and Ghost-type switch-ins. Defiant added strategic value by turning Defog, Sticky Web, Intimidate, and other opponent-induced stat drops into a two-stage Attack boost, making careless forms of hazard control or stat manipulation dangerous. Its physical bulk and Fighting resistance profile also let it switch into some Rock-, Dark-, and Bug-type attackers rather than functioning only as a fragile Choice user. Scarlet/Violet currently places Passimian in ZU, where Choice Scarf remains its characteristic set, showing that power creep and competition have reduced its usage even though the basic pivoting toolkit remains effective. The very new Pokémon Champions metagame currently lists Passimian in UU, but that placement is still developing and should not be treated as equivalent to its much longer established Generation VII singles history.
nuzlocke: Passimian's high Attack, good HP, and respectable physical Defense make it a useful Nuzlocke attacker with more margin for error than many offensive Fighting-types. U-turn is particularly valuable because it can deal damage while moving Passimian out of an unfavorable matchup, although using it safely still depends on knowing that Passimian can survive the incoming hit if the opponent moves first. Defiant is excellent when legitimately obtainable because it discourages Intimidate and can turn an enemy stat-lowering move into an immediate offensive advantage without spending a setup turn. Close Combat is powerful and accurate but lowers both Defense and Special Defense, so repeatedly using it can leave Passimian vulnerable to a follow-up attack even after scoring a knockout; safer Fighting moves may be preferable when maximum power is unnecessary. Its base 60 Special Defense is the largest defensive warning, and strong special Fairy-, Flying-, or Psychic-type attacks should rarely be challenged directly. Receiver is generally much less valuable in standard Nuzlocke singles and should not be treated as equivalent to Defiant merely because it is Passimian's signature Ability.

pokemon.name: Passimian
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Passimian live in organized troops of roughly 20 to 30 individuals led by a dominant member, which selects about ten of the strongest troop members to search for food. The leader also determines the color and placement of the leaves worn by the group, creating visible markings that distinguish one troop from another. Troops train rigorously to improve coordination and Berry handling, and individuals unable to tolerate the training may abandon the group. Passimian fight by throwing hard Berries for impact, softer Berries to obscure an opponent's vision, and passes between troop members that confuse enemies about where the next attack will originate; the troop leader is the individual capable of throwing Berries the farthest. They compete with Ambipom over desirable trees and are described as winning roughly half of those territorial disputes. A Trainer effectively replaces the troop leader for a captive Passimian, and the species is so attentive to throwing technique that it may refuse to obey a Trainer whose Poké Ball throwing form it considers poor.

playthrough: Wimpod evolves into Golisopod at level 30, producing one of the largest practical transformations in Alola: Wimpod has extremely poor battle stats, while Golisopod immediately gains base 125 Attack, 140 Defense, and 90 Special Defense. Catching and training Wimpod can itself be awkward because Wimp Out forces it to flee or switch when its HP falls to half or lower, mirroring the behavior of Emergency Exit after evolution and making careless weakening during capture counterproductive. Golisopod's Bug/Water typing provides useful resistances to Fighting, Ground, Ice, Steel, and Water and only three weaknesses to Electric, Flying, and Rock, while First Impression gives it exceptionally strong priority on the first turn it enters battle and Aqua Jet can finish other weakened targets. Liquidation, Leech Life, Knock Off, and other physical coverage make good use of its enormous Attack, and Leech Life can recover health while attacking, but base 40 Speed means Golisopod depends heavily on priority or bulk. Emergency Exit is a genuine drawback as well as an occasional pivoting tool: falling to half HP or lower can force Golisopod out before it gets to perform the action the player intended, making HP management unusually important. Mega Golisopod, introduced in Pokémon Legends: Z-A – Mega Dimension, changes to Bug/Steel and reaches base 150 Attack, 175 Defense, and 120 Special Defense while retaining base 40 Speed; it gains many resistances and a Poison immunity but acquires a severe 4× Fire weakness, making it an extraordinarily bulky slow attacker rather than a faster version of the base form. Adamant is usually the clearest Nature for maximizing Golisopod's physical damage, while Brave can be appropriate on deliberately slow or Trick Room-oriented builds.
competitive: Golisopod established a genuine competitive niche immediately in Generation VII and was an RU Pokémon rather than merely a novelty built around First Impression. Its base 125 Attack, strong physical bulk, STAB First Impression, Aqua Jet, Liquidation, and access to Spikes made it one of RU's better revenge killers and an effective source of offensive hazard pressure. Emergency Exit was the central limitation: although a forced switch could occasionally recreate the opportunity to use First Impression, it more often removed Golisopod from the field before it wanted to leave and compounded its vulnerability to Stealth Rock and chip damage. Sword and Shield kept Golisopod in RU, but Heavy-Duty Boots materially improved its ability to switch repeatedly, while Knock Off and Spikes strengthened its role as an offensive supporter as well as a revenge killer. Base Golisopod is absent from standard Scarlet/Violet play, so it does not have a normal SV usage-tier career comparable to its Generation VII and VIII history. Mega Golisopod is a very recent addition from Legends: Z-A's Mega Dimension content: it becomes Bug/Steel with 630 total base stats, including 150 Attack and 175 Defense, but its long-term traditional singles or doubles reputation is not yet established enough to describe as historical fact.
nuzlocke: The Wimpod stage is the largest Nuzlocke obstacle in this family because its extremely poor stats must survive until level 30, and Wimp Out can force an unwanted switch as soon as Wimpod falls to half HP. After evolution, Golisopod becomes dramatically safer against physical attacks thanks to base 140 Defense and several useful resistances, while First Impression and Aqua Jet allow it to remove dangerous opponents without relying on its very low Speed. Emergency Exit remains a mixed blessing: automatically leaving at half HP can save Golisopod from a follow-up attack, but it can also expose a teammate unexpectedly or interrupt a planned healing, knockout, or setup sequence. Leech Life is valuable because it combines accurate Bug STAB with recovery, whereas repeated hazard damage from switching can undermine both Golisopod's bulk and the exact HP thresholds that control Emergency Exit. Electric-, Flying-, and Rock-type moves require care, especially special attacks that bypass Golisopod's enormous physical Defense, and the player should never assume that high raw defenses make a forced switch harmless. If Mega Golisopod is available under the ruleset being played, its huge defensive gains and numerous Bug/Steel resistances provide substantially more survival margin, but the new 4× Fire weakness creates an obvious catastrophic matchup that must be avoided.

pokemon.name: Wimpod
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Wimpod is naturally cowardly and reacts to loud noises or sudden movement by fleeing almost instantly, though curiosity can make it approach humans or Pokémon that remain completely still. It lives from beaches to the seafloor in swarms whose members constantly watch for danger and scatter together as soon as an enemy is detected. When threatened it spits a foul-smelling poisonous liquid, and the odor acts as a warning signal to nearby Wimpod. The species is also an important scavenger, consuming and storing almost anything it finds—including rotting material and garbage from the sea—and its many rapidly moving legs leave surfaces unusually clean behind it. Because of this behavior, Wimpod are valued as natural cleaners rather than treated only as pests. They sometimes accompany Golisopod, and coins collected during scavenging can attract opportunistic Murkrow and Meowth.

pokemon.name: Golisopod
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Golisopod is covered in armor described as hard as diamond and possesses retractable claws sharp enough to cleave seawater in two. Despite its intimidating appearance and willingness to exploit any opening in combat, it often spends long periods meditating peacefully in deep seaside caves or on the ocean floor, sometimes accompanied by Wimpod. When an opponent is vulnerable, Golisopod uses the smaller claws on its forward limbs to deliver a finishing attack rather than relying only on its largest arms. New Pokémon Snap depicts Golisopod training with companions and becoming strong enough to cut stone in half with one stroke. In Galarian waters it has a direct predator-prey relationship with Grapploct: when the two species fight, the loser becomes food for the winner.

pokemon.name: Golisopod
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Mega Evolution radically alters Golisopod's armor and body plan, turning much of its plating dark silver and purple and giving it additional functional limbs derived from structures along its back. Several black claws can be launched as projectiles, while other arms remain concealed behind its waist armor until they are needed. Its documented fighting style is deliberately deceptive: Mega Golisopod attacks fiercely with four primary arms, pushes the opponent close to defeat, and then reveals the hidden arms to deliver the finishing blow. The form also changes from Bug/Water to Bug/Steel, emphasizing the increased armor and producing one of the most heavily armored Bug-type stat profiles currently known.

playthrough: Sandygast evolves into Palossand at level 42, which is relatively late for a two-stage line and leaves the player using the weaker first stage for a substantial part of the game if it is caught early. Palossand becomes a slow but sturdy Ghost/Ground special attacker and wall with base 85 HP, 110 Defense, 100 Special Attack, and only 35 Speed, while its typing grants complete immunities to Normal, Fighting, and Electric attacks. Shore Up provides reliable recovery and becomes even stronger during sandstorm, while Earth Power and Shadow Ball offer accurate dual STAB and Stealth Rock can add long-term team support where available. Water Compaction sharply raises Defense when Palossand is hit by a Water-type move, but it does not reduce or negate the Water damage itself; because Water is super effective and many Water attacks are special, intentionally absorbing a strong Water move can still be extremely dangerous. Its other weaknesses to Grass, Ice, Ghost, and Dark and mediocre base 75 Special Defense mean its physical bulk is much more reliable than its special durability. Bold is a natural Nature for maximizing the physical-wall role, while Modest can be useful in a conventional playthrough when stronger Earth Power and Shadow Ball damage is preferable to still more Defense.
competitive: Palossand has consistently occupied a lower-tier defensive niche built around the rare combination of Ghost/Ground typing, Stealth Rock, reliable recovery, and meaningful Special Attack. In Generation VII it was an NU Pokémon that checked several physical Fighting-types, blocked Rapid Spin through its Ghost typing, and used Shore Up to remain healthy while setting Stealth Rock. Unlike many passive hazard setters, base 100 Special Attack and STAB Earth Power and Shadow Ball allowed Palossand to threaten certain opposing setters and Magic Bounce users rather than conceding momentum automatically. Water Compaction could make already strong physical bulk even more extreme after weak Water attacks such as priority Aqua Jet, but the Ability never removed Palossand's underlying Water weakness and was therefore not a universal defensive solution. Scarlet/Violet currently places Palossand in PU, where it still functions as a physically defensive Stealth Rock setter and spinblocker with Shore Up, showing remarkable continuity in its basic role despite generational power creep. Its ceiling has always been limited by very low Speed, only moderate special bulk, common Dark/Ghost/Grass/Ice/Water weaknesses, and the fact that stronger special attackers can bypass the Defense advantages that define its niche.
nuzlocke: Palossand can be an excellent Nuzlocke defensive specialist because three immunities—Normal, Fighting, and Electric—create completely safe switch opportunities when enemy movesets are known. Its high physical Defense, Shore Up, and resistance to Bug and Rock also make it reliable against many physical opponents, while accurate Earth Power and Shadow Ball allow it to contribute without depending entirely on status or stall. The late level-42 evolution is the main developmental drawback, since Sandygast is much less durable and base 15 Speed leaves it exposed while the player waits for the final stage. Water Compaction should never be mistaken for a Water immunity: the Defense boost occurs after Palossand is damaged, and a strong special Water move may simply knock it out before that physical Defense increase becomes useful. Dark, Ghost, Grass, Ice, and Water coverage therefore need to be checked carefully, and its low Speed means an unexpected super-effective attack often lands before Palossand can heal or retaliate. Shore Up significantly improves long-term survival, but conserving its PP is important in extended routes or challenge rulesets because Palossand often wins through repeated defensive exchanges rather than quick sweeps.

pokemon.name: Sandygast
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Sandygast is formed when grudges associated with the dead or with Pokémon defeated in battle possess a mound of sand, giving the apparently simple sand pile an explicitly supernatural origin. It can drain life force through its mouth, and anyone who grabs its shovel or puts a hand inside that mouth may fall under its control. Sandygast uses this influence to force children and other victims to pile more sand onto its body so that it can grow larger. The shovel itself is extremely important to the species: if it loses the object, it may temporarily substitute a branch, flag, or similar item but continues searching for the original shovel. It attacks prey by flinging sand into their eyes and trying to approach while they are blinded, although its extreme slowness often allows the target to escape. Alolan tradition even treats putting one's hand into Sandygast's mouth as a test of courage despite the obvious danger.

pokemon.name: Palossand
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Palossand can control the sand making up its body, with Pokédex material describing every grain as possessing a will of its own, and unlike Sandygast it can replenish lost sand without forcing others to rebuild it. It nevertheless curses and controls humans and Pokémon to gather additional sand, while the shovel on its tower rotates when searching for prey and is believed to function like a radar. Smaller Pokémon can be dragged beneath its body and have their vitality drained until only dried bones remain; Palossand can then fire those bones from openings in its arms. The lingering ill will of its victims is said to seep into surrounding sand and become the origin of new Sandygast, creating a direct supernatural life-cycle connection between predation by Palossand and the appearance of its pre-evolution. Although it inhabits beaches, Palossand hates water and loses the ability to maintain its castle structure under heavy rain. Animated material shows that it can greatly increase its apparent size and generate sandstorms, reinforcing the degree of control it exercises over the material surrounding its body.

playthrough: Pyukumuku does not evolve and is almost completely unlike a conventional story Pokémon: it has base 130 Defense and 130 Special Defense but only 55 HP, base 5 Speed, negligible special offense, and an extremely limited supply of direct damaging moves. Pure Water typing leaves only Grass and Electric weaknesses while resisting Fire, Ice, Steel, and Water, so its raw defensive profile can be impressive when the opponent lacks Taunt, setup-breaking tools, or super-effective coverage. Its Hidden Ability Unaware is usually far more useful for sustained play than Innards Out because Unaware ignores the opponent's offensive stat boosts, allowing Pyukumuku to stand in front of certain setup sweepers that would overwhelm ordinary walls. Recover, Toxic in generations where it can use it, Block, Soak, Counter, Mirror Coat, and other utility moves can create elaborate stall strategies, but they are dramatically slower and less convenient during a normal playthrough than simply using a Pokémon capable of reliable direct damage. Innards Out only activates when Pyukumuku is knocked out, so although it can punish the attacker in ordinary battles, it is obviously undesirable as a planned strategy in any playthrough where keeping the Pokémon alive matters. Bold or Calm can strengthen one side of its already excellent defenses, but for most story teams Pyukumuku is a specialized defensive choice rather than an efficient general-purpose party member.
competitive: Pyukumuku is one of the clearest examples of a Pokémon whose competitive usefulness comes from a narrow defensive mechanic rather than offensive statistics. In Generation VII it was officially ZU, but Unaware, base 130 Defense and Special Defense, Recover, Block, Toxic, Spite, and Soak gave it legitimate niches even in much higher formats, including dedicated OU stall teams. Unaware let it ignore the Attack and Special Attack boosts of setup sweepers, while Block plus Toxic or Spite could trap and slowly remove passive targets that other Unaware users merely forced out. The cost of this specialization was extreme passivity: Pyukumuku had essentially no conventional offensive presence, allowing Taunt users, Substitute users, certain Mold Breaker attackers, and many strong wallbreakers to exploit it. Sword and Shield again placed Pyukumuku in ZU, where Unaware stall and Counter/Mirror Coat strategies in specialized formats preserved its niche without changing its fundamental limitations. It is unavailable in standard Scarlet/Violet and therefore has no ordinary SV usage-tier career; historically, its significance lies in being an unusually pure stall Pokémon that could appear above its nominal tier when a team specifically needed its version of Unaware.
nuzlocke: Pyukumuku can wall certain opponents extremely safely in a Nuzlocke, but its lack of conventional offense means every matchup must be evaluated for how the battle will actually end rather than merely whether Pyukumuku can survive. Unaware is the preferred Ability when available because it prevents setup sweepers from simply boosting past its defenses, while Recover gives it genuine long-term staying power. Counter and Mirror Coat can produce large retaliatory damage, but both require Pyukumuku to absorb the opponent's attack first and therefore become dangerous if the damage range, attacking category, critical-hit possibility, or coverage move is misread. Innards Out should never be considered a desirable Nuzlocke strategy because its effect requires Pyukumuku to faint, directly conflicting with the purpose of preserving the encounter. Likewise, Memento is normally inappropriate because it deliberately sacrifices the user, even if the resulting stat drops would help another teammate. Against opponents without Taunt, Substitute, strong Grass/Electric coverage, or overwhelming wallbreaking power, Unaware plus Recover can provide exceptional insurance, but Pyukumuku's extreme passivity makes blind battles significantly less predictable than its raw defensive numbers imply.

pokemon.name: Pyukumuku
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Pyukumuku selects a favored spot and may remain there indefinitely, returning to the same location even after being physically moved; after exhausting the available food, it can stubbornly remain until it begins to starve. Its body is coated in a viscous fluid that prevents it from drying out for roughly a week on land, and humans use the same substance as a moisturizing skin treatment. Pyukumuku can expel its internal organs through its mouth and shape them into structures such as a fist, which it uses to strike anyone who steps on it; it particularly dislikes having its mouth or dorsal spikes touched. Tourists often regard stranded Pyukumuku as unsightly or accidentally step on them, creating paid beach work in Alola centered on throwing them back into the sea. Local people also deliberately return thin individuals to the water so that they can find food rather than starve in the spots they refuse to abandon. Pyukumuku has a documented symbiotic relationship with Pelipper, which may scoop it from the water and carry it.

playthrough: Type: Null and Silvally are unusual to evaluate for a normal playthrough because Type: Null is only given to the player after becoming Champion in Sun, Moon, Ultra Sun, Ultra Moon, and Sword/Shield, so the family is effectively postgame-only unless it is traded in from elsewhere. Type: Null has an exceptional 95/95/95 defensive profile and Battle Armor prevents critical hits, but its heavy control mask leaves it with only base 59 Speed; because it can still evolve, Eviolite can make the unevolved form dramatically bulkier than Silvally and genuinely preferable for a defensive role. It evolves after leveling up with high friendship, and Silvally raises Speed to 95 while leaving every other base stat at 95, creating an unusually balanced 570-BST attacker, pivot, or utility Pokémon. RKS System lets Silvally become any one of the eighteen types by holding the corresponding Memory, while Multi-Attack changes to match that type, so the same individual can be reconfigured around the team's current weaknesses rather than being locked into a single matchup profile. Multi-Attack was only 90 base power in Generation VII but rose to 120 in Generation VIII, making physical Memory sets substantially stronger in Sword and Shield. Silvally can also use Swords Dance, U-turn or Parting Shot, and broad physical or special coverage depending on the game; Jolly is a strong default for physical sets that want to exploit base 95 Speed, while Adamant can be justified when maximum Multi-Attack damage is more important.
competitive: The Type: Null family developed two distinct competitive identities: unevolved Type: Null became a specialized Eviolite wall and slow pivot, while Silvally's eighteen type forms filled a large number of offensive and utility niches across the lower tiers. In Generation VII, Type: Null was classified ZUBL and received substantial PU use because Eviolite multiplied its already excellent mixed defenses, Battle Armor removed critical-hit variance, and slow U-turn, Rest, Sleep Talk, Iron Defense, or Swords Dance let it compress several defensive jobs into one slot. Silvally's base Normal form was only ZU, but individual Memory forms could be much more valuable because typing determined both defensive utility and the type of Multi-Attack; Fighting, Dark, Fairy, Water, and other forms found different niches as Defog users, pivots, or setup sweepers. Generation VIII materially strengthened the entire Silvally concept by increasing Multi-Attack from 90 to 120 power, and PU in particular featured strong Silvally-Fairy, Silvally-Ghost, and Silvally-Steel variants, with Steel serving as an especially useful hazard remover and glue Pokémon. The Memory requirement is also a built-in competitive cost: every typed Silvally must devote its item slot to the Memory, preventing Heavy-Duty Boots, Leftovers, Choice items, or other conventional equipment even when those would otherwise fit the set. Neither Type: Null nor Silvally is available in standard Generation IX play, so their established competitive history currently ends with the Generation VIII and National Dex ecosystems rather than extending into ordinary Scarlet/Violet usage tiers.
nuzlocke: This family is rarely relevant to a standard main-story Nuzlocke because every ordinary core-series gift of Type: Null is obtained after the Champion, but it becomes interesting in postgame or traded-in challenge rulesets. Type: Null is extraordinarily safe with Eviolite because its 95 HP and balanced 95 defenses are further amplified and Battle Armor completely eliminates critical hits, one of the most dangerous sources of unexpected permadeath variance. The tradeoff is low Speed and dependence on Rest for substantial self-healing, so battles can become long and expose it to status, Knock Off, strong Fighting attacks, and repeated damage while it waits to act. Evolving to Silvally sacrifices Eviolite bulk but raises Speed from 59 to 95 and gives access to RKS System, allowing the player to choose a type specifically suited to an upcoming boss and potentially create useful resistances or immunities on demand. Parting Shot or U-turn can reduce switching risk by generating momentum, while accurate 120-power Multi-Attack in Generation VIII is particularly attractive because it combines strong damage with no recoil, defensive drop, or accuracy gamble. For survival-focused runs, there is a legitimate decision between keeping Type: Null as an Eviolite tank or evolving into the faster and far more adaptable Silvally rather than assuming evolution is automatically the safer option.

pokemon.name: Type: Null
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Type: Null is an artificial chimeric Pokémon created by the Aether Foundation as part of the Beast Killer project, an attempt to produce an anti-Ultra Beast life-form using cells associated with all known Pokémon types. Its original design, called Type: Full, was intended to shift between types through the RKS System, a mechanism inspired by a mythical Pokémon described in research connected with Canalave Library. The three original specimens rejected the system and went berserk, so heavy control helmets were fitted to suppress their power and agility, after which the project was declared a failure and the creatures were renamed Type: Null. The helmet is therefore not a natural anatomical structure but an artificial limiter physically restraining the creature's senses and movement. Gladion freed one of the Alolan specimens, while Sword and Shield reveal that another Type: Null was later created in Galar from stolen research notes, showing that the technology did not remain unique to the original Aether Foundation project. Type: Null has also been depicted sensing the appearance of Ultra Beasts and the opening of Ultra Wormholes, consistent with the purpose for which it was engineered.

pokemon.name: Silvally
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Silvally is the liberated form of Type: Null: after developing a strong bond with a trusted partner, Type: Null gains enough strength and will to destroy its control mask and reactivate the RKS System. The removal of the mask restores greater speed and sensory freedom, while Memories inserted into its drive allow its body to assume any of the eighteen elemental types. This type-changing system was deliberately modeled on the power of a mythical Pokémon, reflecting the artificial project's attempt to reproduce a legendary biological capability through engineered means. Silvally retains its chimeric body—combining mammalian, reptilian, insect-like, and aquatic traits—but is described as returning to a more natural temperament after the limiter is removed. It becomes intensely loyal to the Trainer whose bond allowed it to evolve and is willing to risk its own life to protect that partner. Gladion coined the name Silvally for his evolved partner; the project's original designation for this unrestricted state had been Type: Full.

playthrough: Minior does not evolve, but Shields Down makes it function almost like two different Pokémon during battle: above half HP it is in Meteor Form with base 100 Defense and Special Defense, while at half HP or below its shell breaks and Core Form shifts those strengths into base 100 Attack and Special Attack plus base 120 Speed. Meteor Form is also immune to non-volatile status conditions and Yawn-induced drowsiness, making it much easier to find a safe setup opportunity than its 60 HP might otherwise suggest. Shell Smash is the line's defining offensive tool because one turn can raise both attacking stats and Speed by two stages, after which Core Form becomes extremely fast and can sweep with Acrobatics, Rock STAB, Earthquake, or special alternatives. A White Herb pairs naturally with Shell Smash by removing the defensive drops and then disappearing, which simultaneously activates Acrobatics' doubled power if the move is being used. Rock/Flying gives Minior a Ground immunity and useful resistances to Normal, Fire, Flying, Bug, and Poison, but weaknesses to Water, Electric, Ice, Rock, and Steel can force the transformation at unsafe times or simply knock it out before it capitalizes on Core Form. Adamant is useful for maximizing physical Shell Smash sets, while Jolly is genuinely beneficial when the player wants better unboosted Speed or additional insurance before Shields Down activates.
competitive: Minior has consistently been a specialized Shell Smash sweeper whose value comes from the interaction between Shields Down, White Herb, Acrobatics, and its dramatic stat redistribution rather than from broadly useful defensive utility. In Generation VII it appeared in RU and NU analyses as a late-game cleaner: Meteor Form's 100/100 defenses and status immunity created setup opportunities, Shell Smash doubled its offenses and Speed, and dropping below half HP activated a 120-Speed Core Form that could clean weakened teams. White Herb was particularly synergistic because it erased Shell Smash's defensive penalties and was then consumed, turning Acrobatics into a 110-power Flying STAB without requiring another item-management step. The strategy has always been fragile, however, because Core Form falls to only base 60 Defense and Special Defense and is susceptible to priority, Stealth Rock, and bulky opponents that can survive its boosted attacks. After being absent from Sword and Shield, Minior returned in Scarlet/Violet's Blueberry Academy content and is currently classified ZU, although it has received PU analysis using essentially the same Shell Smash, Acrobatics, Earthquake, and White Herb formula. Terastallization gives modern Minior additional ways to alter defensive matchups or strengthen coverage, but it has not changed the species' fundamental identity as a dangerous yet matchup-dependent late-game setup sweeper.
nuzlocke: Minior is inherently risky in a Nuzlocke because its offensive transformation requires reaching half HP or lower, exactly the range in which an unexpected critical hit, priority attack, or damage roll becomes much more threatening. Meteor Form is the safer state for entering battle: its defenses are substantially higher and Shields Down prevents ordinary status conditions and Yawn, removing several forms of disruptive variance. Shell Smash can create enormous offensive momentum, but lowering both defenses while deliberately moving toward Core Form compounds the consequences of a mistake, so it is safest against an opponent that cannot meaningfully damage Minior or while using White Herb to cancel the drops. Once Core Form is active, base 120 Speed can let Minior finish encounters without taking another hit, but its defenses fall to base 60 and common priority attacks can bypass that Speed advantage entirely. Accurate moves such as Acrobatics and Earthquake are preferable to relying on Stone Edge when the additional Rock damage is unnecessary, because an 80% accurate attack is a significant permadeath risk. Explosion is normally inappropriate despite its competitive utility, since sacrificing Minior directly contradicts the objective of preserving the encounter.

pokemon.name: Minior
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Minior originate in the stratosphere from aggregations of mutated nanoparticles and feed on atmospheric dust, gradually accumulating particulate matter into both a central core and a durable rocky outer shell. As the shell becomes heavier, Minior eventually fall toward the planet, and Alola is one of relatively few places where these falls commonly occur. While they remain in the ozone layer, stronger Pokémon prey upon them, so the shell functions as protection as well as the structure whose increasing mass eventually forces them downward. Meteor Form Minior slowly spin even while apparently resting and react when touched or called, though Pokédex material explicitly leaves uncertain whether those responses indicate true consciousness. A sufficiently strong impact can shatter the outer shell, revealing the much lighter Core Form inside.

pokemon.name: Minior
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Once its shell breaks, Minior's extremely light core is exposed and becomes capable of much faster movement, matching the dramatic Speed increase represented by Shields Down. The core occurs naturally in seven colors—red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet—and the color is determined by the composition of the atmospheric dust the Minior consumed; these colors are otherwise cosmetic rather than separate biological forms. Its visible eyes and mouth are made of energy floating in front of the core rather than ordinary facial structures, and the face remains level even as the rest of the body spins. An exposed Minior cannot survive for long outside its shell and may fade away if it is not placed inside a Poké Ball quickly enough. Fallen Minior nevertheless attempt to return to space after losing their shells even though they are unable to complete that journey, making their time on the surface naturally brief. The pastel colors of exposed cores have become culturally popular enough to inspire human clothing and accessory designs.

playthrough: Komala does not evolve and is available around the middle of the Alola story on Route 11, while Scarlet and Violet make it available much earlier in several Paldean areas. Its base 115 Attack and 95 Special Defense are strong for a single-stage Pokémon, but base 65 HP, Defense, and Speed mean it is noticeably less comfortable against fast physical attackers than against special damage. Comatose is its defining Ability and keeps Komala permanently treated as asleep while preventing other major status conditions from being inflicted, so burn cannot halve its Attack and paralysis cannot undermine its already modest Speed. Strong Normal STAB, Earthquake, Knock Off, U-turn, Rapid Spin, and setup or recovery options have varied by generation and allow Komala to act as much more than a simple one-move physical attacker. Normal typing provides a useful Ghost immunity and only one weakness, Fighting, but offers no ordinary resistances, so Komala's good special bulk should not be confused with a large number of safe switch-in opportunities. Adamant is the most straightforward beneficial Nature for maximizing its 115 Attack, while Careful can be reasonable when emphasizing its naturally stronger special-defense profile.
competitive: Komala has remained a low-tier Pokémon, but Comatose and a surprisingly deep utility movepool have repeatedly given it more competitive value than its ZU labels alone imply. In Generation VII it was ZU and one of that tier's more versatile Normal-types, combining base 115 Attack with Return, Earthquake, Knock Off, U-turn, Rapid Spin, Toxic, Wish, Bulk Up, or Swords Dance depending on the team's needs. Comatose is strategically excellent because Komala cannot be burned, poisoned, paralyzed, frozen, or put to sleep by an opponent while still counting as asleep for specific move interactions, making conventional status-based counterplay ineffective. Its main restrictions are physical fragility, base 65 Speed, and the lack of super-effective Normal STAB, which often force it to rely on coverage instead of overpowering bulky opponents directly. Komala was absent from Sword and Shield but returned in Scarlet/Violet, where it is currently listed in ZU and remains a niche physical attacker and utility option rather than a major usage-tier force. Its competitive history is therefore modest but coherent: good Attack, status immunity, and role compression have kept it useful in the lowest tiers without ever overcoming its mediocre physical bulk and Speed enough to establish a higher-tier career.
nuzlocke: Komala's permanent Comatose state is extremely valuable in a Nuzlocke because the usual dangers of poison, paralysis, burn, freeze, and enemy sleep strategies are effectively removed from consideration. Burn immunity is especially important for a physical attacker, since Komala never has to worry about its base 115 Attack being cut in half by an unexpected burn. Its Ghost immunity can create completely safe switches when the opponent's move is known, and its respectable Special Defense gives it decent margin against many neutral special attacks. The weakness is physical combat: base 65 HP and Defense provide much less room for a bad damage estimate, while base 65 Speed means Komala often takes the hit before it can retaliate. U-turn can be useful for escaping unfavorable situations and Rapid Spin can remove hazards in games where Komala has access to it, but recoil-heavy moves such as Double-Edge should be evaluated carefully because Komala lacks enormous HP reserves. Comatose makes Komala unusually predictable from a status-management perspective, which is a genuine safety advantage in blind or semi-blind challenge runs even though its raw defensive stats remain only moderate.

pokemon.name: Komala
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Komala spends its entire life asleep, yet it can eat, travel, battle, and react to its surroundings without waking; apparent changes in expression are described as manifestations of whatever it is dreaming. The permanent sleep state results from its diet of particular leaves containing toxins that Komala alone can break down, producing sedative compounds inside its body. Each Komala receives a wooden log from its parents at birth and clings to it continuously; removing the log prevents restful sleep and causes the Pokémon to thrash violently, although a Komala may substitute the arm of a Trainer it deeply trusts. Its saliva inherits strong sedative properties from its diet, and diluted Komala drool was historically used both as a sleep aid and as an anesthetic during surgery. Hypno are known predators of Komala in Alola and are described as preferring them over humans, giving the otherwise sleepy species a documented place in the region's food web.

playthrough: Turtonator is a single-stage Fire/Dragon Pokémon with excellent base 135 Defense and useful base 91 Special Attack, but only 60 HP and 36 Speed, making it much better at absorbing physical hits than moving before opponents. Its typing is defensively valuable, strongly resisting Fire and Grass and also resisting Bug, Electric, and Steel while leaving only Dragon, Ground, and Rock weaknesses; however, the Rock weakness also makes entry hazards more troublesome in formats or playthroughs where Stealth Rock is common. Shell Armor is outstanding for consistency because Turtonator cannot be struck by critical hits, giving defensive calculations much more reliability than most Pokémon enjoy. Shell Smash can transform its poor Speed and moderate Special Attack into sweeping power by raising both offenses and Speed two stages, while Dragon Pulse and reliable Fire moves are safer ordinary STAB options than relying constantly on Draco Meteor or Fire Blast. Its signature Shell Trap reaches enormous power if Turtonator is struck by a physical attack after setting the trap, but it fails if the opponent does not trigger it, making it more situational in a normal playthrough than its 150 base power suggests. Turtonator is also version-restricted in its main appearances—wild in Sun/Ultra Sun and Sword but not their paired versions—so availability can determine whether it is practical at all; Timid is useful on Shell Smash sets, while Modest is reasonable when prioritizing damage over post-boost Speed.
competitive: Turtonator has been a specialized lower-tier Shell Smash sweeper rather than a broadly dominant Fire- or Dragon-type. In Generation VII it was classified ZUBL but received PU analysis, where Fire/Dragon STAB was exceptionally difficult for the tier to resist and base 135 Defense gave it setup opportunities against weaker physical attackers. Shell Smash was essential because base 36 Speed is otherwise crippling, and Z-Moves could turn Draco Meteor into a one-time Dragon attack capable of breaking defensive checks without suffering the usual Special Attack drop on the Z-Move itself. Even after a Shell Smash, however, common Choice Scarf users could revenge kill it, while Stealth Rock, the defensive drops from Shell Smash, and competition from Fire- or Dragon-types with stronger immediate pressure limited its consistency. Sword and Shield preserved essentially the same role: Turtonator remained ZUBL with PU usage as a niche hyper-offense sweeper, using Shell Smash, Fire Blast, Dragon STAB, and coverage such as Flash Cannon. It is unavailable in standard Scarlet/Violet, so its competitive history remains centered on Generations VII and VIII and has not developed a normal Generation IX usage-tier chapter.
nuzlocke: Turtonator has one of the best variance-control Abilities available for a Nuzlocke because Shell Armor completely prevents critical hits, allowing its enormous physical Defense to function without the usual fear that one unlucky crit will bypass accumulated defensive advantages. Fire/Dragon also provides several useful resistances and only three weaknesses, making Turtonator a strong physical switch-in when the opponent's Ground-, Rock-, and Dragon-type coverage has been ruled out. The danger is low Speed and only average Special Defense, so a strong special attacker can damage Turtonator heavily before it acts even when the matchup looks favorable on typing alone. Shell Smash is powerful but explicitly lowers Defense and Special Defense, sacrificing part of the reliability that makes Shell Armor so attractive; in permadeath play it is best reserved for an opponent that cannot punish the setup turn. Shell Trap is even more prediction-dependent because it requires Turtonator to prepare the move and then be struck physically, so it should not be treated as guaranteed 150-power damage when a straightforward Fire or Dragon attack would safely secure the knockout. Accurate Dragon Pulse or Flamethrower-style options are usually preferable to unnecessary reliance on Draco Meteor or Fire Blast when the extra power is not required.

pokemon.name: Turtonator
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Turtonator lives in volcanic environments, where its rocky appearance lets it camouflage itself while waiting for prey and where it consumes sulfur and other minerals as part of its normal diet. Compounds derived from that mineral-rich food accumulate in its shell as unstable explosive material, and even its feces become dangerously explosive enough to have practical uses. When prey steps on the shell, Turtonator can strike itself with its own tail, creating sparks at the shell spikes and detonating the explosive coating outward through the opening on its chest. That chest opening is also its anatomical weak point, so the shell combines an extremely dangerous defensive weapon with a specific vulnerable region. Moisture interferes with the shell's explosive properties; on rainy days Turtonator retreats quietly into caves rather than remaining exposed on the volcano. It can additionally expel flame and poisonous gases through its nostrils, making its volcanic diet responsible for several different offensive adaptations rather than only its signature shell explosions.

playthrough: Togedemaru does not evolve and is obtainable at Blush Mountain in the Alola games, giving it a useful midgame arrival without requiring the player to protect a weaker pre-evolution. Electric/Steel is one of its greatest strengths: it provides an Electric immunity with Lightning Rod or at minimum an Electric resistance with another Ability, a Poison immunity from Steel typing, numerous resistances, and only three weaknesses—Fire, Fighting, and a severe 4× weakness to Ground. Base 96 Speed and 98 Attack make Togedemaru a quick physical utility attacker rather than a conventional special Electric-type, with Zing Zap, Iron Head, U-turn, Nuzzle, and Spiky Shield providing offense, momentum, paralysis, and scouting. Lightning Rod is especially useful in doubles or on teams containing Water- or Flying-types because it redirects Electric attacks and makes Togedemaru itself immune, while Iron Barbs punishes contact and Sturdy can provide emergency survival from full HP. Its actual defensive stats are mediocre, so the impressive resistance list should not be mistaken for true wall-level bulk, and any Ground coverage is especially dangerous because of the 4× weakness. Jolly is usually the most useful Nature for preserving its strong base-96 Speed and maximizing the chance to attack, pivot, or paralyze before the opponent.
competitive: Togedemaru has had a stronger lower-tier competitive career than many regional electric rodents because Electric/Steel typing, good Speed, U-turn, Nuzzle, Wish, and several excellent Abilities give it substantial role compression. In Generation VII it was an NU Pokémon and an effective pivot, using U-turn to maintain momentum while Lightning Rod let it block opposing Volt Switch and Nuzzle supplied reliable paralysis support; offensive sets also exploited Zing Zap and Iron Head. Its typing allowed it to check numerous Flying-, Fairy-, Ice-, Psychic-, and Electric-type threats, but base 65 HP and mediocre defenses limited how often it could repeatedly absorb even resisted attacks. Sword and Shield placed Togedemaru in PU, where it became a notable Choice Scarf user and also supported bulkier teams with Wish, Spiky Shield, U-turn, and Iron Barbs; Smogon's SS PU viability rankings placed it among the tier's stronger options. Sturdy has additionally enabled specialized 1v1 and Endeavor strategies, while Lightning Rod is more valuable in doubles because redirecting Electric attacks can directly protect a partner. Togedemaru is unavailable in standard Scarlet/Violet, so its established history currently ends with Generation VIII rather than extending into the ordinary SV singles tiers.
nuzlocke: Togedemaru offers excellent Nuzlocke utility because Electric/Steel supplies a huge number of resistances, a Poison immunity, and—with Lightning Rod—a complete Electric immunity that can create free switches for a correctly predicted move. Nuzzle is particularly valuable because it combines perfect accuracy with guaranteed paralysis, reducing enemy Speed without relying on the lower accuracy of Thunder Wave and dealing enough damage to bypass certain purely status-based countermeasures. U-turn can move Togedemaru out of dangerous matchups while maintaining momentum, and Spiky Shield can safely scout an opponent's move while punishing contact. Sturdy is an alternative source of emergency insurance if Togedemaru is at full HP, but entry hazards or prior chip damage can silently remove that protection, while Iron Barbs is useful only when the opponent makes contact. The overwhelming danger is the 4× Ground weakness: Earthquake, High Horsepower, or unexpected Ground coverage can easily knock it out despite the otherwise impressive resistance profile, and mediocre raw bulk means strong neutral attacks also deserve respect. Because its best attacks and support moves are generally accurate and non-recoil, Togedemaru can be played conservatively without sacrificing most of the utility that makes it valuable.

pokemon.name: Togedemaru
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Togedemaru's back carries fourteen specialized fur spikes that normally lie flat but rise involuntarily when the Pokémon is surprised, agitated, or defending itself, turning its rounded body into a much more dangerous contact surface. The long needle on its head functions as a lightning rod used to gather electricity, which is then stored in an internal electric sac. Because Togedemaru's own electrical capacity is limited, groups gather during storms with their needles pointed upward and deliberately wait to be struck by lightning so they can replenish their stored energy. Trainers can exploit the same adaptation by baiting an opponent into using an Electric attack and having Togedemaru absorb the energy before turning it back against the attacker. When pleased, Togedemaru curls into a ball and rolls around with little control, while sleeping individuals normally keep their spines relaxed but can raise them defensively if disturbed. Togedemaru also competes directly with Elekid over electricity, and encounters between the two species are described as generally ending evenly.

playthrough: Mimikyu does not evolve, so it is immediately usable at full strength once obtained, although in the Alola games it appears relatively late around the abandoned Thrifty Megamart rather than serving as an early-game Fairy- or Ghost-type. Ghost/Fairy is an excellent offensive and defensive combination, giving Mimikyu immunities to Normal, Fighting, and Dragon, a 4× resistance to Bug, and only Ghost and Steel weaknesses under normal conditions. Its base 90 Attack and 96 Speed are merely good rather than exceptional, so Swords Dance is important when Mimikyu needs to break bulky opponents; Play Rough, Shadow Claw, and priority Shadow Sneak provide strong coverage between its two STAB types. Disguise is the defining advantage: in Generation VII the first damaging hit was completely negated, while from Generation VIII onward the attack is still blocked but Mimikyu loses one eighth of its maximum HP when the disguise breaks, reducing how freely it can exploit the mechanic. Pokémon Legends: Z-A does not use conventional Abilities, but Mimikyu still preserves a version of this identity by taking reduced damage from the first attack before shifting into Busted Form. Jolly is usually the safest Nature for preserving its useful Speed tier, while Adamant is also beneficial when the player values stronger Swords Dance and Shadow Sneak damage over narrower Speed benchmarks.
competitive: Mimikyu has maintained a meaningful competitive niche across several generations because Disguise gives it something most frail setup sweepers cannot guarantee: a highly reliable opportunity to survive the first damaging attack. In Generation VII it was a UU Pokémon with legitimate OU use, while Battle Spot Singles valued it even more highly as a revenge killer capable of stopping boosted sweepers, setting Swords Dance behind Disguise, and using its exclusive Mimikium Z move, Let's Snuggle Forever, for a one-time burst of Fairy damage. Its raw Attack is not especially high, so it has historically depended on Swords Dance, Z-Moves, Life Orb, or prior team damage to break bulky Steel-types and defensive walls, with Shadow Sneak compensating for opponents faster than base 96 Speed. Generation VIII nerfed Disguise by adding the one-eighth HP penalty when it breaks, but Mimikyu still became an important RU setup sweeper because a protected setup turn and priority remained valuable even after the nerf. Scarlet and Violet currently also place Mimikyu in RU, where the same core formula of Swords Dance, Play Rough, Ghost STAB, Shadow Sneak, and Disguise remains relevant despite substantial power creep. Its historical strength therefore comes less from overwhelming base stats than from compressing revenge killing, emergency checking, setup, and late-game cleaning into a single Pokémon.
nuzlocke: Mimikyu is unusually valuable in a Nuzlocke because Disguise can function as emergency insurance against one incorrectly estimated damaging attack, giving the player a margin for error that most offensive Pokémon lack. Its three immunities create additional safe-switch opportunities when movesets are known, and Shadow Sneak can finish a weakened threat without risking a Speed tie or exposing Mimikyu to another normal-priority attack. Disguise is not absolute protection: Mold Breaker-style effects and moves that ignore Abilities can bypass it in games where those mechanics apply, and multi-hit moves can break the disguise with the first hit before later hits continue damaging Mimikyu. From Generation VIII onward, breaking Disguise also costs one eighth of Mimikyu's maximum HP, so repeated hazard damage, Life Orb recoil, or other chip can leave it much closer to a lethal threshold than the free-hit concept initially suggests. Swords Dance is safest when Disguise is intact and the opponent cannot exploit the setup turn with status or multi-hit pressure, while Play Rough's imperfect accuracy should be considered before relying on it for a survival-critical knockout. Because Disguise refreshes between battles but not repeatedly within the same battle, preserving it until the most dangerous opposing Pokémon appears is often more valuable than spending it casually against an ordinary trainer.

pokemon.name: Mimikyu
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Mimikyu is a tiny Ghost-type whose true body remains almost entirely concealed beneath an old cloth fashioned to resemble Pikachu, complete with a crudely drawn face and a stick used as a fake tail. It is a quiet, lonely species that adopted the disguise in hopes of becoming more approachable after Pikachu merchandise became enormously popular, although the imitation often frightens people instead of attracting them. Mimikyu lives in dark places and becomes ill when exposed to sunlight, so its covering may serve a protective purpose as well as a social one. Its actual appearance is still unknown; only parts such as its eyes, lower body, and a long claw-like appendage have been seen, and Pokédex accounts repeatedly warn that seeing what lies beneath the cloth can cause mysterious illness, extreme terror, or death. Because of that danger and its own fear of exposure, Mimikyu reacts violently when someone attempts to look under the disguise. It imitates Pikachu closely enough that Pokémon Sleep even depicts it copying Pikachu-like sleeping behavior.

pokemon.name: Mimikyu
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Busted Form occurs when an attack damages Mimikyu's cloth disguise and the false Pikachu head can no longer remain upright. The damage is primarily to the disguise rather than evidence that Mimikyu itself has suffered a broken neck, but Mimikyu becomes deeply distressed because the failure increases the risk that its true body will be exposed. It attempts to keep the imitation going even while the rag is damaged and may spend the entire night repairing the costume in front of a mirror. Repairing the cloth correctly is difficult, and accounts describe Mimikyu as inwardly crying while it works. Its distress can become obsessive retaliation: it remembers whoever damaged the disguise and may pursue revenge for the rest of its life, even at the risk of its own death.

playthrough: Bruxish is a single-stage Water/Psychic physical attacker with base 105 Attack and 92 Speed, making it immediately functional once caught without requiring an evolution investment. In Alola it is obtained by fishing on the western side of Ula'ula Island and surrounding waters, while Scarlet and Violet make it more directly available in the East and West Paldean Seas, so its usefulness depends substantially on when the player chooses to explore aquatic areas. Strong Jaw is usually the most straightforward offensive Ability because it boosts biting moves by 50%, turning STAB Psychic Fangs into an unusually strong physical Psychic attack and also strengthening coverage such as Crunch and Ice Fang. Dazzling trades that raw damage for protection from opposing priority moves, which can be valuable for preserving Bruxish against revenge kills, while Wonder Skin is a more situational Hidden Ability that reduces the reliability of many status moves used against it. Water STAB such as Liquidation provides reliable damage, and later games add options such as Wave Crash and Flip Turn, although Wave Crash's recoil is often unnecessary during a long story route when Liquidation already secures the knockout. Its 68/70/70 bulk is mediocre and Water/Psychic leaves weaknesses to Bug, Dark, Electric, Ghost, and Grass, so Jolly is useful for maximizing its decent Speed while Adamant is a legitimate alternative for stronger Strong Jaw attacks.
competitive: Bruxish entered competitive play with a surprisingly dangerous offensive niche built around Strong Jaw-boosted Psychic Fangs, Swords Dance, and enough Speed to threaten slower balance teams. In Generation VII it was classified NUBL while receiving RU analysis, where boosted Psychic Fangs could overwhelm many neutral targets and Aqua Jet let it finish faster weakened opponents; Crunch or Liquidation handled different defensive answers. Dazzling provided an alternate niche by shutting off opposing priority, but Strong Jaw was generally more important to dedicated wallbreaking because Bruxish's average bulk made immediate damage essential. Bruxish was unavailable in Sword and Shield, interrupting its singles history for a generation. It returned in Scarlet and Violet and is currently placed in PU, where stronger Water tools such as Wave Crash and pivoting through Flip Turn let it function as a wallbreaker, Choice user, or offensive pivot even though the overall power level around it has increased. Its recurring shortcomings are limited defensive utility, middling bulk, and a Speed tier that is good but not exceptional, so it has remained a threatening specialized attacker rather than a consistent high-tier staple.
nuzlocke: Bruxish can be effective in a Nuzlocke because it combines respectable Speed with strong physical Water and Psychic attacks, allowing it to end favorable matchups before its mediocre bulk becomes relevant. Dazzling is particularly attractive for survival-focused runs because opposing priority moves cannot unexpectedly finish Bruxish or its allies, removing a common way that a weakened fast Pokémon dies despite appearing to have the Speed advantage. Strong Jaw is usually better when the safest plan is simply to secure a knockout with Psychic Fangs or another biting move, and Psychic Fangs itself is accurate while also removing Reflect, Light Screen, and Aurora Veil when those effects matter. Bruxish should not be switched blindly into neutral attacks because base 68 HP and 70 defenses leave relatively little margin for an unexpected critical hit or coverage move. Wave Crash is powerful in later games but its recoil creates avoidable permadeath risk, so Liquidation is generally preferable when the extra power is unnecessary. Wonder Skin can reduce the chance of certain status moves connecting, but because it introduces probability rather than certainty, it is less dependable as a Nuzlocke safety plan than Dazzling's guaranteed priority protection.

pokemon.name: Bruxish
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Bruxish buries most of its body in the seafloor and leaves the colorful growth on its head exposed, using low-level psychic emissions from that organ like radar to detect nearby prey. When it attacks, grinding its teeth stimulates its brain and produces much stronger psychic energy; the sound is unpleasant enough that nearby Pokémon flee, while direct exposure to the psychic power can cause severe headaches and unconsciousness. Its prey includes Shellder and Mareanie, which Bruxish crushes into mush with its powerful teeth before eating. It competes with Toxapex in warm ocean currents, creating a direct ecological rivalry between two Alolan reef predators. Alolan lifeguards deliberately tolerate Bruxish near swimming areas because the noise and psychic activity drive away other dangerous Water-type Pokémon, giving the species an unusual protective role around humans. Sunlight reflecting through the ripples created by its psychic organ can also make the surrounding water glitter brightly.

playthrough: Drampa is a single-stage Normal/Dragon special attacker with enormous base 135 Special Attack, solid 78/85/91 bulk, and only base 36 Speed, so it plays much more naturally as a slow wallbreaker or Trick Room attacker than as a sweeper that expects to move first. In the Alola games it is a late, version-exclusive encounter in Moon and Ultra Moon around Mount Lanakila, and it is likewise associated with Shield rather than Sword, meaning that availability is one of the largest practical limits on using it during an ordinary story. Its Normal/Dragon typing provides a Ghost immunity and resistances to Fire, Water, Grass, and Electric while leaving weaknesses to Fighting, Ice, Dragon, and Fairy. Berserk raises Special Attack when Drampa drops to half HP or below, Sap Sipper provides a complete Grass immunity even though the accompanying Attack boost is usually less useful, and Cloud Nine can neutralize dangerous weather effects for the entire field. Draco Meteor provides extreme burst damage but lowers Special Attack, while Dragon Pulse, Hyper Voice, Flamethrower, and broad special coverage are generally safer for repeated story battles; Roost also improves its staying power where available. Mega Drampa, introduced in Pokémon Legends: Z-A, keeps Normal/Dragon typing and base 36 Speed but rises to 160 Special Attack, 110 Defense, and 116 Special Defense, making it a much stronger slow tank and special breaker rather than changing its fundamental pace. Modest is usually the clearest beneficial Nature for ordinary special offense, while Quiet is especially appropriate on deliberate Trick Room teams.
competitive: Drampa has historically been a lower-tier wallbreaker whose threat level is much greater than its Speed or usage tier might suggest because base 135 Special Attack and unusually broad coverage leave few completely safe switch-ins. In Generation VII it was a PU Pokémon, where Choice Specs or other offensive sets used Draco Meteor, Hyper Voice, Fire coverage, and Focus Blast or Energy Ball to punish defensive cores while Sap Sipper supplied a useful Grass immunity. Sword and Shield classified it PUBL while giving it an NU analysis, where it remained a potent anti-metagame breaker and could also exploit Calm Mind and Roost against slower teams. Its greatest historical limitation is base 36 Speed: even when Drampa wins the prediction battle, opponents can often bring in a faster Fairy-, Fighting-, Ice-, or Dragon-type and force it out before it attacks again. Mega Drampa is a genuinely new 2025–2026 competitive development rather than an established historical archetype; in Pokémon Champions, Smogon's current dex lists both Drampa and Mega Drampa in UU, with the Mega reaching 160 Special Attack and gaining substantial defensive bulk while retaining Berserk. Because the Mega form has existed for only a short period, its long-term tier stability and defining tournament role are still developing and should not be treated as equivalent to Drampa's established PU/NU history.
nuzlocke: Drampa is most useful in a Nuzlocke when its excellent special damage and defensive resistances are paired with careful planning around its extremely low Speed. A Ghost immunity and Fire, Water, Grass, and Electric resistances give it several predictable switch opportunities, while Sap Sipper can add a true Grass immunity and Cloud Nine can remove the benefits of threatening weather teams. Berserk rewards surviving a hit that takes Drampa below half HP, but intentionally hovering near that threshold is risky in permadeath play because a critical hit or unexpected coverage move can turn the desired boost into a death. Draco Meteor's Special Attack drop can leave Drampa unable to finish a second opponent, so accurate repeatable attacks such as Dragon Pulse, Hyper Voice, and Flamethrower are often safer when maximum power is not required. Roost can greatly improve long-term survival where available, but base 36 Speed means Drampa usually needs to survive the incoming attack before it gets the chance to heal. Mega Drampa's large increases to both defenses provide much more margin for a slightly incorrect damage estimate, yet it remains just as slow and retains the same Fighting, Ice, Dragon, and Fairy weaknesses, so Mega Evolution does not make careless matchups safe.

pokemon.name: Drampa
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Drampa lives high in the mountains but descends toward lower elevations around dawn because the Berries it eats do not grow at its normal altitude. It has a famously gentle disposition and actively seeks interaction with people and Pokémon, especially children, often visiting schools and parks where parents are comfortable allowing it to play with them. That kindness becomes extreme protectiveness when a child is harmed: Pokédex accounts state that an enraged Drampa may seek out the bully and burn the offender's house, while its rampages generate gales and Dragon Breath powerful enough to damage buildings. Despite its elderly appearance and very low battle Speed, Drampa is capable of flight. Pokémon Sleep depicts it resting with its head laid across its back and suggests that sleeping Drampa may dream about protecting exhausted children after playing with them.

pokemon.name: Drampa
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Mega Evolution reinvigorates Drampa's cells and restores much of its youthful vitality, causing it to hold its long neck upright and adopt a visibly more vigorous posture. Its normally pale fur becomes dark gray and much spikier, its claws become more exposed, and its beard and facial hair become longer and more elaborate. Mega Drampa continually floats above the ground rather than merely resting its body on the surface. Most importantly, its rejuvenated body can manipulate the atmosphere strongly enough to summon storms, extending Drampa's existing association with wind into direct control of severe weather. Its eyes glow and its fur rises when it attacks or becomes enraged, making the normally gentle dragon's emotional change much more visually pronounced in this form.

playthrough: Dhelmise is a single-stage Ghost/Grass physical attacker with base 131 Attack, 100 Defense, and 90 Special Defense, but only base 40 Speed, making it a slow powerhouse rather than a conventional cleaner. In Sun and Moon it is found very late by fishing in Seafolk Village and has only a 1% ordinary fishing rate, though bubbling spots raise the chance; Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon improve the bubbling-spot rate substantially, while Sword and Shield make the species easier to encounter on Route 9 and through later fishing or raid areas. Ghost/Grass grants immunities to Normal and Fighting and resistances to Water, Electric, Grass, and Ground, while weaknesses to Fire, Ice, Flying, Ghost, and Dark mean it still requires thoughtful switching despite its strong bulk. Steelworker increases the power of Steel-type attacks by 50%, effectively giving Dhelmise a third STAB-like attacking type without actually granting Steel's defensive resistances; Anchor Shot therefore complements physical Ghost and Grass attacks unusually well. Rapid Spin gives it hazard-removal utility and became stronger from Generation VIII onward when the move was raised to 50 power and began increasing Speed, while Synthesis can provide recovery in generations where available. Power Whip is extremely strong but its 85% accuracy creates more variance than a normal playthrough always needs, so safer Grass options can be preferable when the extra damage is unnecessary; Adamant maximizes Dhelmise's huge Attack, while Brave is natural on Trick Room teams.
competitive: Dhelmise carved out a durable lower-tier competitive niche because it combines hazard removal, spinblocking, strong natural bulk, and genuine offensive pressure in a single slot. In Generation VII it was an NU Pokémon capable of switching into many common Stealth Rock setters, using Rapid Spin to remove hazards while its Ghost typing simultaneously prevented opposing Rapid Spin, and threatening bulky targets with base 131 Attack. Steelworker made Anchor Shot and other Steel attacks hit with pseudo-STAB power, while Choice Band sets could punish even dedicated physical walls rather than allowing opponents to treat Dhelmise as a passive utility spinner. Sword and Shield again placed Dhelmise in NU, where Synthesis, Rapid Spin, Poltergeist or other Ghost STAB, Power Whip, and Steelworker coverage preserved the same core identity; Rapid Spin's Speed boost gave the otherwise base-40 Pokémon an additional reward for successfully clearing hazards. Its weaknesses have also remained consistent: poor Speed, several common weaknesses, vulnerability to Knock Off and strong special attackers, and competition from faster or more reliable hazard removers keep it from becoming a higher-tier staple. Dhelmise is unavailable in standard Scarlet and Violet, so it has no ordinary Generation IX usage-tier chapter outside National Dex formats.
nuzlocke: Dhelmise is valuable in a Nuzlocke because its Normal and Fighting immunities can create completely safe switches, while base 100 Defense and 90 Special Defense give it enough bulk to survive many neutral attacks. Steelworker is purely offensive and does not make Dhelmise a Steel-type defensively, so expecting Steel resistances against Fairy, Flying, Ice, or other attacks can lead to a fatal matchup error. Anchor Shot is reliable physical coverage and can trap an opponent, while Rapid Spin can remove entry hazards that would otherwise accumulate dangerous chip damage across the entire team. Power Whip's enormous damage is attractive but its 85% accuracy is a significant permadeath risk, especially when a lower-power accurate Grass move would still secure the knockout. Synthesis provides useful recovery where available, although weather and PP limitations can affect how dependable that healing is over a long route. Base 40 Speed means Dhelmise normally takes the first hit, so strong Fire-, Ice-, Flying-, Ghost-, and Dark-type coverage should be identified before committing it to battle despite its generally good raw defenses.

pokemon.name: Dhelmise
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: The anchor and ship's wheel associated with Dhelmise are not its true body; the living Pokémon is the ghostly mass of green seaweed wrapped through and around the wreckage. Pokédex accounts describe seaweed adrift in the ocean becoming reborn as this Ghost-type after merging with debris from a sunken ship, and Dhelmise continually maintains itself by incorporating new seaweed and seabed detritus. It actively hunts very large prey such as Wailmer and Wailord, swinging the attached anchor with enough force to knock out even Wailord before wrapping the victim in seaweed and draining its life force. The chain-like seaweed can stretch for hundreds of yards, giving the otherwise heavy-looking species an enormous effective reach. Despite this predatory behavior, Dhelmise is specifically known to get along well with Skrelp and Dragalge.

playthrough: Jangmo-o evolves into Hakamo-o at level 35 and then Kommo-o at level 45, but in the original Alola games the family is found very late in Vast Poni Canyon at levels already close to those thresholds, so the weak first stage usually does not need to be protected for long. Hakamo-o gains Fighting typing, and Kommo-o finishes with an unusually balanced offensive and defensive spread of 110 Attack, 100 Special Attack, 125 Defense, 105 Special Defense, and 85 Speed, supporting physical, special, mixed, setup, or defensive roles. Dragon/Fighting supplies seven useful resistances but carries weaknesses to Dragon, Flying, Ice, and Psychic and an especially dangerous 4× Fairy weakness, making Fairy coverage the defining matchup concern in every generation before Terastallization can alter its typing. Bulletproof, Soundproof, and the Hidden Ability Overcoat each create different immunities to specific move classes or environmental effects, so the best Ability depends heavily on the opponents and game being played rather than one option being universally superior. Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon gave Kommo-o its defining Kommonium Z strategy through Clanging Scales and Clangorous Soulblaze, a damaging Dragon Z-Move that also raised all five combat stats; from Generation VIII onward the family instead has Clangorous Soul, which gives the same one-stage omniboost at the cost of one third of maximum HP. Dragon Dance, Iron Defense plus Body Press, Drain Punch, Close Combat, Clanging Scales, Boomburst, and extensive coverage allow very different playthrough sets, but moves such as Clangorous Soul, Clanging Scales, Close Combat, and Belly Drum all impose defensive or HP costs that matter more in a long story run than in a single competitive calculation. Jolly suits fast physical setup sets, Timid supports special Clangorous Soul builds, and Hasty or Naive can be useful on established mixed sets that need both attacking stats.
competitive: Kommo-o has one of the strongest competitive histories among Alola's non-legendary families because its broad movepool, three useful Abilities, mixed offenses, and excellent physical bulk allow it to change roles dramatically between teams and generations. In the mature Generation VII metagame it was an OU Pokémon, with Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon's Kommonium Z transforming Clangorous Soulblaze into a powerful damaging omniboost that enabled frightening late-game mixed sweeps; Dragon Dance, Stealth Rock, specially defensive, and even Belly Drum variants prevented opponents from assuming one set from team preview. Fairy-types were the most important structural answer because Dragon/Fighting leaves Kommo-o 4× weak to Fairy and Fairy immunity could prevent Clangorous Soulblaze from functioning as intended, forcing coverage such as Poison Jab or substantial team support. Sword and Shield removed Z-Moves but introduced Clangorous Soul and expanded defensive possibilities such as Body Press, leaving Kommo-o classified UUBL while still seeing OU use as a versatile setup sweeper, rocker, or bulky attacker. Scarlet and Violet currently also place Kommo-o in UUBL, where Clangorous Soul, Dragon Dance, Iron Defense plus Body Press, special sound-based sets, and Terastallization allow it to patch its Fairy weakness or create unexpected offensive matchups. Kommo-o has also remained relevant in doubles and VGC-style play, where Clangorous Soul and spread Clanging Scales can become dangerous with redirection or defensive Tera support, but its strongest historical reputation remains its versatility in singles rather than one fixed tournament-defining doubles role.
nuzlocke: The Kommo-o family can be extremely strong in a Nuzlocke because Jangmo-o is encountered late in Alola at levels close to its evolution thresholds, allowing the player to reach the much safer final stage without a long period protecting a 300-BST first stage. Kommo-o's excellent Defense and solid Special Defense create real margin against neutral attacks, while Dragon/Fighting resistances to Fire, Water, Grass, Electric, Rock, Bug, and Dark generate many useful switch opportunities. The 4× Fairy weakness is nevertheless catastrophic and should be treated as a hard warning: even weak Fairy coverage can invalidate Kommo-o's bulk, and a blind switch into an unknown moveset can result in an immediate death. Bulletproof can create safe entries against specific ball- and bomb-based moves, Soundproof can nullify sound attacks and phazing such as Roar where applicable, and Overcoat protects against powder moves and damaging weather, making Ability knowledge unusually useful for planning boss fights. Drain Punch is one of its safest Fighting options because it restores HP, whereas Close Combat lowers both defenses, Clanging Scales lowers Defense, and Clangorous Soul deliberately consumes one third of maximum HP; Belly Drum is even more dangerous despite its enormous offensive ceiling. In a permadeath run, Kommo-o is often better used as a bulky attacker that takes one controlled setup opportunity than as a sweeper repeatedly trading away HP and defensive stages for maximum damage.

pokemon.name: Jangmo-o
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Jangmo-o lives and trains with others of its species in remote, harsh environments far from most people and other Pokémon. Its scales are actually fur hardened until it behaves like metal, and the large scale on its forehead serves both offensive and defensive functions. Jangmo-o refuses to show its back to an opponent, a behavior ancient warriors admired as evidence of courage and pride. It strikes its scales against rocks, the ground, or other Jangmo-o during training, strengthening both fighting ability and spirit. The metallic sounds created by those scales also express emotion, communicate with allies, and intimidate opponents, and a whole group of Jangmo-o can create a considerable racket.

pokemon.name: Hakamo-o
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: After evolving, Hakamo-o leaves its companions and begins a solitary period of intense training, traveling wherever it expects to find strong opponents.
