It announces a challenge with a ritualized dance, clanging the scales on its body before ending the display with a forceful war cry. Because its scales function as armor, Hakamo-o attacks aggressively without prioritizing self-protection, often breaking or tearing away parts of that armor during combat. Rather than treating the damage as a weakness, it wears exposed areas and broken scales as evidence of a worthwhile battle; replacement scales immediately begin growing and are said to return harder and sharper. The discarded scales conduct heat effectively enough that people mold them into pots and pans, giving Hakamo-o's normal growth and combat cycle a direct human material use.

pokemon.name: Kommo-o
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Kommo-o completes the family's harsh training cycle and returns to its birthplace, where it watches over young Jangmo-o from a distance rather than directly joining their training groups. Its body is protected by scales described as hard as steel, and historically those scales were processed by humans into armor, weapons, and other useful objects. Kommo-o seeks strong opponents and warns weaker ones away by clanging its scales, apparently preferring not to waste effort fighting foes that cannot challenge it; the scales also generate powerful offensive sound waves. Its uppercuts are strong enough to launch opponents away, while the heavy scales on its tail are swung as a threat before combat and comrades answer a successful hunt with metallic celebration after its victory howl. According to Alolan legend, the brilliance of Kommo-o's scales exists to drive away a great darkness, and its constant search for strength is connected to becoming powerful enough to defeat that darkness. Modern game depictions also show that despite its bipedal combat posture, Kommo-o often prefers knuckle-walking when moving normally.

playthrough: Tapu Koko is a single-stage Electric/Fairy Legendary Pokémon whose main-story usefulness is limited in the Alola games because it is normally caught only after the player becomes Champion, although Sword and Shield's Crown Tundra can make it available through Dynamax Adventures. Its defining strengths are base 130 Speed, a strong base 115 Attack, useful base 95 Special Attack, and Electric Surge, which automatically creates Electric Terrain and strengthens grounded Electric-type attacks while preventing grounded Pokémon from falling asleep. Thunderbolt and Volt Switch make special sets easy to use despite the lower Special Attack, while Wild Charge can exploit the higher Attack at the cost of recoil; U-turn, Roost, Taunt, and broad coverage give Tapu Koko excellent utility beyond raw damage. Electric/Fairy is also excellent defensively for a fast attacker, providing a Dragon immunity and resistances to Bug, Dark, Electric, Fighting, and Flying while leaving only Ground and Poison weaknesses. Generation VIII weakened Electric Terrain's same-type damage boost from 50% to 30%, so Tapu Koko's terrain-boosted attacks are less overwhelming than they were at debut, but Heavy-Duty Boots and its still-exceptional Speed help compensate. Timid is usually the safest Nature for special or pivoting sets because preserving base 130 Speed is central to Tapu Koko's role, while Jolly is appropriate for physical sets built around Wild Charge and U-turn.
competitive: Tapu Koko was one of Generation VII's defining OU Pokémon and remained OU in Sword and Shield, with its combination of Electric Surge, base 130 Speed, and access to both Volt Switch and U-turn making it one of the premier offensive pivots of both generations. In Sun and Moon, Electric Terrain boosted grounded Electric moves by 50%, allowing even Tapu Koko's merely base 95 Special Attack to produce frightening Thunderbolt and Volt Switch damage while enabling teammates such as Hawlucha through terrain-dependent strategies. Choice Specs, Z-Move, Life Orb, utility, and later Calm Mind sets all existed, while Roost and a useful defensive typing let Tapu Koko check selected Flying-, Fighting-, and Dark-type threats instead of functioning only as a frail attacker. It was also highly important in VGC 2017, where its Speed made it one of the fastest relevant Pokémon in the format and Electric Terrain simultaneously boosted offense, blocked sleep, and contested the other island guardians' Terrains. Generation VIII reduced Electric Terrain's damage multiplier to 1.3×, but Tapu Koko still remained OU because Heavy-Duty Boots, reliable pivoting, Calm Mind, and the ability to pressure common Water- and Flying-types preserved its role. Its recurring weaknesses are mediocre raw special power outside terrain, vulnerability to Ground-types, and relatively modest bulk, but historically few Pokémon have matched its combination of speed, terrain control, and momentum.
nuzlocke: Tapu Koko is extremely strong in a Nuzlocke if the ruleset allows postgame or transferred Legendary Pokémon, primarily because base 130 Speed dramatically reduces the number of opponents that can attack it before it acts. Its Dragon immunity and five resistances create several safe switch opportunities, while Electric Terrain prevents sleep for grounded allies and can remove an entire category of status-based danger during its five-turn duration. Volt Switch and U-turn are valuable for escaping unfavorable matchups while maintaining momentum, but Volt Switch fails against Ground-types and Wild Charge recoil is usually unnecessary risk when Thunderbolt or another non-recoil option can accomplish the same objective. Tapu Koko's defenses are only moderate, so an unexpected Earthquake or Poison attack can still be lethal despite its Legendary status, and its Speed should not encourage blind switching into unknown coverage. Nature's Madness can safely remove half of a bulky opponent's current HP without depending on Tapu Koko's offensive stats, though its 90% accuracy introduces a small amount of variance. Timid sets that attack first with accurate moves are usually the safest way to use it, while physical recoil-heavy sets trade some of that reliability for maximum damage.

pokemon.name: Tapu Koko
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Tapu Koko is the guardian deity of Melemele Island and resides at the Ruins of Conflict, where it is revered by the island's people despite a temperament that makes its protection unpredictable. It is intensely curious and may appear before people or Pokémon that interest it, but it has a hair-trigger temper and can become violently hostile when provoked; just as unusually, it may forget the source of its anger almost immediately. Tapu Koko summons thunderclouds and stores their electricity by closing the shell-like structures around its body, while its extraordinary movement speed can make it difficult for an opponent to follow visually. Its shells close into the appearance of a stylized rooster, linking its anatomy to the totem-like visual language shared by all four Alolan guardian deities. Although it does not automatically help every person in danger, it is known to defend Melemele from Ultra Beasts and has cooperated with the other tapu in events involving Cosmog, Z-Power Rings, and Ultra Space.

playthrough: Tapu Lele is a single-stage Psychic/Fairy Legendary whose ordinary Alola availability is postgame, so like the other guardian deities it is generally more relevant to optional content, rematches, or transferred playthroughs than to the initial island challenge. Base 130 Special Attack and 115 Special Defense make it an exceptionally powerful special attacker, while Psychic Surge automatically creates Psychic Terrain, strengthening grounded Psychic-type attacks and protecting grounded Pokémon from opposing priority moves. Psychic or Psyshock and Moonblast provide outstanding dual STAB, with Focus Blast commonly supplying coverage against Steel-types that resist both; Calm Mind can turn Tapu Lele into a setup sweeper, while Choice Specs or Choice Scarf offer immediate power or speed control. Its base 95 Speed is good but not elite, and base 70 HP with 75 Defense means strong physical attackers can overwhelm it if it does not move first. Generation VIII reduced Psychic Terrain's power boost from 50% to 30%, lowering the absurd peak of its Psychic attacks without removing the priority-blocking utility that makes the terrain so valuable. Timid is useful when maximizing Speed matters, while Modest is genuinely valuable on Choice Scarf or wallbreaking sets because Tapu Lele's terrain-enhanced special attacks benefit enormously from additional raw power.
competitive: Tapu Lele was an elite OU wallbreaker in both Generation VII and Sword and Shield, with Psychic Surge turning already enormous base 130 Special Attack into one of the most punishing offensive packages available outside the restricted Legendary tiers. In Sun and Moon, terrain-boosted Psychic or Psyshock combined with Moonblast forced defensive teams to rely heavily on Steel-types and specially prepared checks, while Choice Specs could 2HKO many otherwise sturdy neutral targets. Psychic Terrain also blocked opposing priority against grounded Pokémon, making Tapu Lele itself harder to revenge kill and supporting fragile offensive teammates that feared moves such as Bullet Punch, Extreme Speed, or Sucker Punch. Choice Scarf traded some wallbreaking force for speed control, while Calm Mind and Z-Move sets added further set diversity and made scouting its item important. Generation VIII reduced Psychic Terrain's offensive multiplier from 1.5× to 1.3×, but Tapu Lele remained OU because Choice Specs, Choice Scarf, Future Sight, Psyshock, and its nearly unresisted Psychic/Fairy pressure still made it one of the generation's most feared special attackers. Its consistent flaws are only average physical bulk, a Speed tier that requires a Scarf against the fastest offensive teams, and imperfect Focus Blast as its most direct answer to several Steel-types.
nuzlocke: Tapu Lele is extremely powerful but less forgiving than its Special Defense suggests because its physical bulk is only moderate and base 95 Speed does not guarantee the first move against every dangerous opponent. Psychic Terrain provides valuable safety by preventing opposing priority moves from striking grounded Pokémon, eliminating many surprise revenge kills while it remains active. Psychic/Fairy also grants a Dragon immunity, a 4× Fighting resistance, and a Psychic resistance, creating excellent entries against correctly identified attacks, although Ghost-, Poison-, and Steel-type coverage remains dangerous. Psyshock and Psychic are both accurate and reliable, while Moonblast provides dependable Fairy damage; Focus Blast should be avoided as a survival-critical answer whenever a safer move can accomplish the same job because its 70% accuracy creates substantial variance. Calm Mind can make Tapu Lele extremely difficult for special attackers to stop, but setting up repeatedly against physical opponents creates unnecessary critical-hit exposure. A Choice Scarf set is often safer for permadeath play than a pure wallbreaking set because it converts more matchups into guaranteed first attacks rather than relying on Tapu Lele to absorb physical damage.

pokemon.name: Tapu Lele
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Tapu Lele is the guardian deity of Akala Island and resides at the Ruins of Life, drawing strength from both the vital energy stored within its shell and the fragrance of flowers. It scatters glowing scales that stimulate the bodies of people and Pokémon and can rapidly heal wounds or restore health, but exposure to too many of the scales is dangerous rather than purely beneficial. This dual nature contributes to Tapu Lele's reputation for guileless cruelty: it may weaken others with its scales for amusement and is described as acting without guilt, leading some Alolan accounts to portray it as nature itself rather than a conventionally benevolent guardian. An old story credits Tapu Lele with ending a war between Alola's islands by healing exhausted warriors, although other traditions imply that the true events may have been less gentle than the popular version suggests. Its closed shell resembles an insect-like head, and like the other tapu it is known to defend its island from Ultra Beasts and participate in the guardianship surrounding Cosmog.

playthrough: Tapu Bulu is a single-stage Grass/Fairy Legendary that is normally obtained only after the Alola League, so its excellent battle statistics are generally reserved for postgame use in its debut games rather than the initial story. Base 130 Attack, 115 Defense, and 95 Special Defense make it a powerful physical tank and wallbreaker, while Grassy Surge automatically creates Grassy Terrain to strengthen grounded Grass-type attacks, restore grounded Pokémon's HP each turn, and halve the power of Earthquake, Bulldoze, and Magnitude. Horn Leech is particularly valuable because terrain boosts its damage while the move heals Tapu Bulu, creating unusually efficient offense and recovery; Wood Hammer offers far greater damage at the cost of recoil, while Superpower, Stone Edge, and other coverage handle resistant targets. Grass/Fairy provides a Dragon immunity and six useful resistances, but it also carries weaknesses to Fire, Flying, Ice, and Steel and a dangerous 4× Poison weakness. Generation VIII reduced Grassy Terrain's Grass-type damage boost from 50% to 30%, and Tapu Bulu did not receive Grassy Glide, meaning later competition from Rillaboom is mechanically important rather than merely a matter of popularity. Adamant maximizes its already enormous physical power, while Careful or Impish can be justified on slower defensive builds that emphasize Grassy Terrain recovery, Horn Leech, and its natural bulk.
competitive: Tapu Bulu was an OU Pokémon in Generation VII, where Grassy Surge, base 130 Attack, strong bulk, and recovery from both Horn Leech and terrain let it operate as either a devastating wallbreaker or a surprisingly persistent defensive check. Grassy Terrain did much more than empower Wood Hammer and Horn Leech: it restored grounded teammates every turn and weakened Earthquake, allowing Tapu Bulu to support Steel-types and other partners that normally feared Ground coverage. Swords Dance, Choice Band, specially defensive, and mixed utility sets all saw use, with Superpower and Stone Edge punishing several common Grass resists that otherwise appeared safe. Its Generation VIII standing declined to UU because Grassy Terrain's offensive boost was reduced to 1.3×, Z-Moves disappeared, and Rillaboom became an alternative Grassy Surge user with higher Speed and access to priority Grassy Glide, a move Tapu Bulu notably did not receive. Tapu Bulu nevertheless remained a strong UU wallbreaker and defensive Grass-type, with excellent bulk, Horn Leech, Synthesis, and terrain support preserving legitimate value despite that competition. Its long-term weaknesses are middling base 75 Speed, a 4× Poison weakness, and susceptibility to common Steel- and Flying-types, which make it more matchup-dependent than Koko, Lele, or Fini at their competitive peaks.
nuzlocke: Tapu Bulu can be extremely safe against the right opponents because Grassy Terrain provides passive recovery every turn while also weakening Earthquake, one of the most common high-power physical moves in the series. Its Dragon immunity and resistances to Dark, Electric, Fighting, Grass, Ground, and Water create many useful switch opportunities, and base 115 Defense plus 95 Special Defense give it substantial margin against neutral attacks. Horn Leech is one of its best Nuzlocke attacks because it is accurate, receives terrain and STAB bonuses, and restores HP without requiring a separate recovery turn. Wood Hammer is much less attractive in permadeath play because recoil can erase the health advantage gained from Grassy Terrain, while Superpower's stat drops and Stone Edge's imperfect accuracy introduce additional risk. The critical warning is the 4× Poison weakness: even a Pokémon that Tapu Bulu otherwise walls can become lethal if it carries Sludge Bomb, Poison Jab, or another strong Poison move. Because base 75 Speed is only moderate, the safest approach is to exploit known resistances and healing rather than assuming Tapu Bulu can simply attack before every threatening coverage move.

pokemon.name: Tapu Bulu
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Tapu Bulu is the guardian deity of Ula'ula Island and resides at the Ruins of Abundance, with the ability to make vegetation grow and reshape it at will. It can pull entire trees from the ground and wield them as clubs, then absorb energy from the vegetation it has caused to flourish. Despite this enormous physical power, Tapu Bulu is generally inactive and avoids unnecessary conflict, ringing the bell-like structure on its tail to warn others of its presence so that fights do not begin accidentally. Its restraint has clear limits: it is merciless toward those it judges to be enemies, and Alolan tradition associates ruined settlements and defeated thieves with its wrath. The shell closes into the form of a stylized bull, and like the other guardian deities Tapu Bulu protects its island against Ultra Beasts and participates in safeguarding Cosmog.

playthrough: Tapu Fini is a single-stage Water/Fairy Legendary obtained after the Alola League in its debut games, but when available it functions as the most defensively oriented of the four guardian deities. Its base 115 Defense and 130 Special Defense combine with an excellent Water/Fairy typing that grants a Dragon immunity and resistances to Bug, Dark, Fighting, Fire, Ice, and Water, leaving only Electric, Grass, and Poison weaknesses. Misty Surge automatically creates Misty Terrain, preventing grounded Pokémon from receiving major status conditions and halving Dragon-type damage against them, which can make entire boss strategies substantially safer. Moonblast and Surf provide accurate STAB, while Calm Mind can compensate for its merely base 95 Special Attack; Taunt, Haze, Defog, Nature's Madness, and other utility allow it to solve problems that cannot be handled by damage alone. Its most important practical flaw is the absence of strong reliable recovery: Leftovers, Draining Kiss, Aqua Ring, or Rest-based strategies are much less convenient than Recover, and Misty Terrain itself prevents grounded Tapu Fini from using Rest successfully while the terrain is active. Bold and Calm are both excellent Natures depending on whether the team wants to emphasize physical or special durability, while Modest can be reasonable for a more straightforward story attacker.
competitive: Tapu Fini was an OU staple in both Generation VII and Sword and Shield and was also one of the defining defensive Water-types of VGC 2017, giving it arguably the broadest combination of singles and doubles success among the guardian deities. Misty Terrain made it exceptional team support by shielding grounded allies from burn, poison, paralysis, sleep, and confusion while also weakening incoming Dragon attacks, and Water/Fairy typing let Tapu Fini check prominent Dark-, Fighting-, Fire-, and Dragon-type threats. In Generation VII OU, Defog, Taunt, Nature's Madness, Calm Mind, and Choice sets all saw use, allowing it to remove hazards, break passive walls, or become a win condition rather than acting as a single-purpose tank. VGC 2017 prominently featured Calm Mind and bulky support variants, with Misty Terrain contesting the other tapu's terrains and protecting entire teams from disruptive status strategies. Sword and Shield preserved Tapu Fini's OU status, where it checked threats such as Urshifu-R and Weavile and used Taunt, Trick, Calm Mind, or Whirlpool, although the lack of reliable recovery made Knock Off and accumulated chip especially troublesome. Unlike Koko, Lele, and Bulu, its signature terrain was not defined by a same-type damage multiplier, so the Generation VIII terrain-power nerf did not directly reduce Tapu Fini's principal defensive function.
nuzlocke: Tapu Fini is one of the safest defensive Pokémon available to a permissive Nuzlocke because its excellent mixed defenses, Dragon immunity, six resistances, and Misty Terrain collectively remove many common sources of unexpected loss. Misty Terrain prevents major status conditions on grounded Pokémon, so burns, poison, sleep, paralysis, and confusion cannot derail a planned sequence while the terrain is active, and Dragon attacks are simultaneously weakened. Moonblast and Surf are accurate STAB options, while Haze can erase dangerous enemy setup and Taunt can prevent recovery or status strategies without exposing Tapu Fini to unreliable accuracy. Its main endurance problem is the lack of Recover or a comparable immediate healing move; once Leftovers are removed or repeated neutral hits accumulate, even Tapu Fini's excellent defenses can be worn down across a long route. Misty Terrain also prevents grounded Tapu Fini from falling asleep, so Rest cannot simply be used as a conventional recovery button while its own terrain remains active. Electric-, Grass-, and Poison-type attacks still require careful respect, but compared with many defensive Pokémon Tapu Fini provides unusually strong protection against both direct damage and status-based variance.

pokemon.name: Tapu Fini
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Tapu Fini is the guardian deity of Poni Island and resides at the Ruins of Hope, drawing energy from ocean currents and exercising direct control over water. It creates a mysterious mist that can disorient opponents so severely that they attack themselves, allowing Tapu Fini to avoid exposing its own body unnecessarily in battle. The same mist protects access to special water said to cleanse anything unclean, and Tapu Fini tests people who seek that water rather than granting it freely; repeated attempts by selfish humans have left the guardian deeply distrustful of people. Accounts nevertheless describe it helping those who prove worthy, making its relationship with humans selective rather than purely hostile. In animation, Tapu Fini's mist can bridge the world of the living with the dead, allowing people to encounter deceased loved ones, but remaining in that mist too long risks trapping a person there permanently. Like the other guardian deities, it protects its island from Ultra Beasts and participates in Alola's larger spiritual and cosmological traditions.

playthrough: The Cosmog family is unique among Legendary Pokémon because it contains two genuine evolution stages and then branches into one of two box Legendary final forms: Cosmog evolves into Cosmoem at level 43, and Cosmoem evolves at level 53 into Solgaleo in Sun, Ultra Sun, Sword, and Scarlet or Lunala in Moon, Ultra Moon, Shield, and Violet. Training the early stages normally is extremely impractical because Cosmog has extraordinarily low battle stats and almost no offensive presence, while Cosmoem has enormous 131 Defense and Special Defense but still cannot contribute meaningful damage; in Sun and Moon, the player's usable Cosmog is also obtained after the main story, although the story itself provides the corresponding Solgaleo or Lunala before the League. Solgaleo becomes a 680-BST Psychic/Steel physical powerhouse with base 137 Attack, 137 HP, and 107 Defense; Sunsteel Strike is accurate, strong, and ignores the target's Ability, while Full Metal Body prevents opposing effects from lowering Solgaleo's stats. Lunala instead becomes a Psychic/Ghost special attacker with base 137 Special Attack, 137 HP, and 107 Special Defense; Moongeist Beam likewise ignores the target's Ability, while Shadow Shield halves damage from attacks taken at full HP. Solgaleo has ten resistances or immunities but weaknesses to Fire, Ground, Ghost, and Dark, while Lunala has useful Normal and Fighting immunities but disastrous 4× weaknesses to Ghost and Dark, so the two branches demand very different defensive planning despite nearly mirrored statistics. Adamant or Jolly are strong Solgaleo Natures depending on whether power or Speed is more valuable, while Modest or Timid perform the corresponding roles for Lunala; neither final evolution needs elaborate optimization to overwhelm ordinary story opponents once legally obtained.
competitive: Cosmog and Cosmoem have essentially no conventional competitive role because their developmental movepools and offensive statistics make them incapable of meaningful pressure, so the family's competitive history belongs almost entirely to Solgaleo and Lunala. Both final evolutions have always been classified as Ubers-level Pokémon, but their historical success is not equal: Generation VII Solgaleo struggled to distinguish itself because Necrozma-Dusk-Mane performed many Steel-type roles more efficiently, leaving Solgaleo with niches such as Choice Scarf speed control and specific checks to threats including Xerneas. Lunala was much more individually distinctive in Generation VII Ubers because Shadow Shield gave it an exceptionally safe first hit and Moongeist Beam, Calm Mind, Roost, broad coverage, and Lunalium Z supported both wallbreaking and defensive sets. Sword and Shield improved Solgaleo's utility through tools such as Teleport and Future Sight, giving it a defined defensive-pivot niche even though Necrozma-DM still competed heavily for the Steel-type slot. Lunala remained an Ubers mainstay in Generation VIII, where Shadow Shield and enormous mixed stats allowed it to participate in sturdy defensive cores while still threatening major damage; both Solgaleo and Lunala also appeared in restricted VGC formats such as 2019 and 2022. Their signature Abilities are especially valuable in high-power formats: Full Metal Body prevents stat reductions from effects such as Intimidate and Sticky Web, while Shadow Shield can halve otherwise enormous damage at full HP, although hazards and chip damage are therefore especially important against Lunala.
nuzlocke: If a ruleset actually requires the player to raise Cosmog from its first stage, the family presents an unusually dangerous development period because Cosmog is almost incapable of fighting and Cosmoem, while extraordinarily bulky, remains effectively unable to defeat normal opponents on its own. Cosmoem's huge defenses can survive attacks far better than Cosmog, but its extreme passivity means experience sharing or carefully controlled switch training is far safer than expecting it to battle directly until level 53. Solgaleo is generally the safer final form for blind physical combat because Psychic/Steel supplies numerous resistances and an immunity to poison, while Full Metal Body prevents enemy stat drops and Sunsteel Strike is accurate without recoil or defensive penalties. Lunala's Shadow Shield is outstanding emergency insurance at full HP because the first damaging attack is halved, but maintaining that protection requires avoiding hazards and chip, and its 4× Dark and Ghost weaknesses can still turn an unexpected coverage move into catastrophic damage once Shadow Shield is broken. Moongeist Beam and Sunsteel Strike are both excellent Nuzlocke attacks because they are accurate and ignore defensive Abilities without imposing recoil or self-debuffs, while more extreme options such as Draco Meteor or risky coverage should be used only when the extra power is required. The family is therefore extraordinarily strong once fully evolved but has one of the least practical pre-evolution periods in the series, making the route from Cosmog to level 53 far more dangerous than the final Legendary statistics imply.

pokemon.name: Cosmog
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Cosmog is an extremely light, gaseous Pokémon resembling a small nebula, and its fragile body can be blown away by ordinary winds without appearing to trouble it very much. It gradually grows by collecting dust from the atmosphere and is naturally curious, trusting, and dangerously incautious, quickly becoming attached to anyone who shows it kindness even when that individual has harmful intentions. Cosmog can teleport itself and nearby companions, and under severe stress it can open Ultra Wormholes; using that power is extremely taxing and can leave it immobile for long periods or even kill it if forced too far. The Aether Foundation studied Cosmog closely and theorized that it might be related to Ultra Beasts, although it is not formally classified as one. Ancient Alolans called it the 'child of the stars,' and Alolan tradition holds that Solgaleo and Lunala can create Cosmog and entrust the young Pokémon to the guardian deities until it matures and returns to Ultra Space.

pokemon.name: Cosmoem
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Cosmoem is an immobile cocoon-like stage in which Cosmog's diffuse body becomes enclosed within a shell said to be harder than any known material. It cannot move or even eat normally, instead continuing to develop by absorbing starlight and atmospheric dust while remaining warm to the touch. Despite being one of the smallest Pokémon by physical dimensions, it weighs 999.9 kilograms, tying the maximum standard Pokédex weight recorded for a Pokémon and creating an extraordinary contrast with the nearly weightless Cosmog stage. The people of ancient Alola called it the 'cocoon of the stars,' reflecting its role as a transitional celestial body rather than a conventional active animal. Its evolution culminates in either Solgaleo or Lunala, with the two outcomes represented even during the transformation by different solar or lunar coloration.

pokemon.name: Solgaleo
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Solgaleo is a lion-like being associated with the sun and was known in ancient Alola as 'the beast that devours the sun,' while also being honored as an emissary of the sun. Its body can store enormous quantities of energy and radiate light intense enough to make nighttime appear like midday, and its solar energy is capable of influencing Rockruff toward Midday Form Lycanroc. A third eye-like structure becomes visible when Solgaleo enters its radiant state, and it can create Ultra Wormholes to travel between the Pokémon world and Ultra Space; the Ultra Recon Squad has used it as a Ride Pokémon for this purpose. Solgaleo and Lunala are beings strongly associated with light and can create Cosmog, produce Z-Crystals, and help restore stolen light to Necrozma. That enormous reserve of light also makes Solgaleo prey for Necrozma, which seeks to absorb its energy and can possess it to become Dusk Mane Necrozma. Alolan legend therefore treats Solgaleo not simply as a powerful predator-shaped Pokémon but as part of a continuing cosmic cycle involving Cosmog, Ultra Space, the guardian deities, and Necrozma.

pokemon.name: Lunala
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Lunala is a vast bat-like being associated with the moon and was known in ancient Alola as 'the beast that calls the moon,' while being revered as an emissary of the moon. It constantly absorbs surrounding light and converts it into energy; with its wings fully spread, its body resembles a luminous crescent and star-filled night sky, and its power can darken an otherwise bright daytime environment. Its lunar energy can influence Rockruff toward Midnight Form Lycanroc, providing a direct biological link between this Legendary and one of Alola's ordinary species. Lunala can open Ultra Wormholes and travel through Ultra Space, and the Ultra Recon Squad uses it as a Ride Pokémon for interdimensional travel. Alongside Solgaleo it can create Cosmog, generate Z-Crystals, and restore Necrozma's lost light, but this same luminous nature causes Necrozma to hunt it relentlessly and possess it as Dawn Wings Necrozma when successful. Its relationship to Cosmog, the guardian deities, Ultra Space, and Necrozma places Lunala within the same recurring celestial life cycle as Solgaleo rather than treating the two box Legendaries as unrelated counterparts.

playthrough: Nihilego is a single-stage Rock/Poison Ultra Beast whose usefulness in a conventional story run is limited mainly by availability: in Sun and Moon it is obtained through the postgame Ultra Beast missions, while Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon make repeat encounters possible through Ultra Warp Ride only after the story has already reached its late climax. When it is available, base 127 Special Attack, 131 Special Defense, and 103 Speed make it a strong special attacker with considerably more special resilience than its jellyfish-like appearance suggests. Rock/Poison provides useful resistances to Normal, Fire, Flying, Bug, Fairy, and especially Poison, but its base 47 Defense is extremely poor and the typing carries a catastrophic 4× Ground weakness in addition to Water, Psychic, and Steel weaknesses. Power Gem and Sludge Bomb or Sludge Wave provide accurate dual STAB, while Grass Knot and Thunderbolt can punish several Water- and Ground-type answers and Stealth Rock adds team utility. Beast Boost raises Nihilego's highest stat after it scores a knockout; depending on Nature and investment, this can reinforce either Special Attack or Speed and let it snowball through weakened teams. Generation VIII added Meteor Beam as an especially strong option when paired with Power Herb, granting a Special Attack boost before a one-time powerful Rock attack; Timid is normally the safest Nature for preserving Nihilego's good Speed, while Modest is a legitimate choice when maximum special damage matters more.
competitive: Nihilego has maintained a respectable competitive career without ever becoming a permanent OU staple, occupying UU in both Generation VII and Sword and Shield while repeatedly finding niches above its nominal tier. In Sun and Moon UU, its uncommon Rock/Poison STAB combination, base 127 Special Attack, base 103 Speed, Stealth Rock, and broad special coverage made it a highly customizable offensive utility Pokémon rather than a single-purpose sweeper. Choice Scarf and offensive Stealth Rock sets exploited Beast Boost differently, and Nihilego also had relevant VGC 2017 and doubles use because Rock coverage punished common Fire- and Flying-types while its high Special Defense helped it survive many special attacks. Sword and Shield significantly improved its offensive ceiling through Power Herb Meteor Beam: the move immediately raised Special Attack before dealing heavy Rock damage, and a subsequent Beast Boost could allow Nihilego to compound boosts after securing a knockout. Heavy-Duty Boots and Knock Off also improved its utility options in Generation VIII, while carefully chosen EV spreads could make Speed the Beast Boost target rather than Special Attack and turn it into a late-game cleaner. Its limitations have remained consistent across generations: base 47 Defense makes physical priority and strong contact attackers dangerous, Steel-types resist both STAB types, and the 4× Ground weakness allows common Ground attacks to force it out regardless of its excellent special bulk. Nihilego is unavailable in standard Scarlet and Violet, so its ordinary usage-tier history currently ends with Generation VIII rather than continuing into the main Generation IX metagame.
nuzlocke: Nihilego is extremely effective against the right special opponents in a Nuzlocke but has unusually little margin for error against physical coverage because its defensive stats are so lopsided. Base 131 Special Defense and useful resistances allow it to absorb many neutral or resisted special attacks, while base 103 Speed means it can often remove threats before they move rather than relying entirely on tanking damage. The 4× Ground weakness is the critical danger: even comparatively modest physical Ground coverage can be fatal, and base 47 Defense means strong neutral physical moves deserve respect as well. Power Gem and Sludge Bomb are safer everyday attacks than relying on lower-accuracy options, while Grass Knot can provide an important answer to heavy Ground- and Water-types that would otherwise threaten it. Meteor Beam can create a powerful sweep in Generation VIII but normally depends on a single-use Power Herb and still has imperfect accuracy, so it should not be the only plan for a survival-critical matchup. Beast Boost can turn one safe knockout into momentum against an entire opposing team, but it is better treated as a reward for an already favorable matchup than as justification for leaving Nihilego exposed to physical revenge killers.

pokemon.name: Nihilego
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Nihilego is a jellyfish-like Ultra Beast native to Ultra Deep Sea whose translucent body is described in concept material as being composed of several kinds of glass. Its most remarkable adaptation is parasitism: it can attach itself over the head of a human or Pokémon and inject a highly stimulating neurotoxin into the host. Rather than simply controlling the host like a puppet, the toxin suppresses inhibition and drives the victim's existing abilities, emotions, and impulses to unusually extreme levels, apparently helping Nihilego protect itself through the empowered host. Aether Foundation research describes the species as acting largely from self-preservation instinct, with uncertain intelligence and little obvious emotion or will, although its changing silhouette can resemble a young human girl. The toxin may remain in a victim after separation and cause continuing illness that requires treatment, making the effects of parasitism potentially longer-lasting than the physical attachment itself. Nihilego was among the first Ultra Beasts studied by Professor Mohn, making it central to the Aether Foundation's early discovery of Ultra Space and Ultra Beast biology.

playthrough: Buzzwole is a single-stage Bug/Fighting Ultra Beast with extraordinary physical statistics: base 107 HP, 139 Attack, and 139 Defense make it both a powerful physical attacker and one of the most naturally durable physical tanks available when Ultra Beasts are permitted. Its availability is normally late or postgame in Alola, with Buzzwole specifically associated with Sun and Ultra Sun, so its story usefulness is much greater in optional content or transferred/DLC-assisted play than during the ordinary island challenge. Bug/Fighting resists Bug, Dark, Fighting, Grass, and Ground, but its very low base 53 Special Defense creates a sharp defensive split and the typing carries a dangerous 4× Flying weakness along with Fire, Psychic, and Fairy weaknesses. Drain Punch is particularly valuable because Buzzwole's enormous Attack turns it into meaningful recovery, while Leech Life can provide a second draining STAB and Ice Punch, Earthquake, or other coverage can punish common answers. Roost gives it reliable recovery in generations where available, and Bulk Up can amplify both Attack and its already exceptional Defense, but Beast Boost can also raise Attack automatically after a knockout without spending a setup turn. Impish is excellent for a physical-wall role, Adamant maximizes wallbreaking and draining-move recovery, and Careful can be justified when a player specifically wants to patch Buzzwole's weak special side.
competitive: Buzzwole's competitive history is defined less by sweeping than by the rare combination of elite physical bulk and enough offensive power to prevent most physical attackers from exploiting it. In Generation VII it was UUBL rather than a consistent OU usage staple, but it found serious niches in both OU and even Ubers because base 107 HP and 139 Defense, Roost, and resistances to Fighting and Ground allowed it to answer extremely strong physical threats. It also had a legitimate VGC 2017 role as one of the format's useful Fighting-types, checking bulky Normal-types such as Porygon2 and Snorlax while threatening heavy physical damage. Sword and Shield was Buzzwole's strongest standard-singles generation: it became a major OU defensive presence and was valued for checking threats such as Urshifu-Rapid-Strike, Garchomp, Landorus-T, Kartana, and other physically oriented attackers in a single team slot. Drain Punch and Roost made it difficult to wear down through ordinary physical attacks, while Ice Punch, Earthquake, Toxic, and coverage choices kept common switch-ins from being completely safe. Its enormous physical specialization is also its main weakness: base 53 Special Defense, a 4× Flying weakness, and vulnerabilities to Fire, Psychic, and Fairy mean special attackers can force it out very easily, and Future Sight support became an especially effective way to overwhelm it in Sword/Shield OU. Buzzwole is unavailable in standard Scarlet and Violet, so that strong Generation VIII OU period remains the latest ordinary main-series singles chapter of its competitive history.
nuzlocke: Buzzwole is exceptionally safe against known physical attackers because few Pokémon combine this level of HP, Defense, Attack, and access to healing through Drain Punch or Roost. Its resistances to Fighting, Ground, Dark, Grass, and Bug provide strong switch opportunities, and Beast Boost can raise Attack after a knockout so that later opponents are removed more quickly without requiring a risky setup turn. The line's greatest Nuzlocke trap is assuming its physical invulnerability extends to special damage: base 53 Special Defense is poor, and an unexpected special Fire, Psychic, or Fairy attack can deal enormous damage before Buzzwole has time to heal. Flying attacks are even more dangerous because Bug/Fighting creates a 4× weakness, making even non-STAB coverage potentially lethal. Drain Punch and Leech Life are especially attractive because they combine accurate damage and recovery without recoil, whereas Close Combat's defensive drops can undermine the very durability that makes Buzzwole valuable. Bulk Up can make favorable physical matchups nearly unwinnable for the opponent, but repeated setup is rarely necessary in permadeath play when Buzzwole already has enough power to secure safe knockouts.

pokemon.name: Buzzwole
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Buzzwole is a mosquito-like Ultra Beast native to Ultra Jungle whose exaggerated muscles are fluid-filled structures rather than ordinary mammalian musculature. It can absorb energy through its exceptionally hard proboscis and trigger a chemical reaction between that energy and its own body fluids, causing the muscular sacs to swell dramatically and increasing both offensive and defensive power. Those structures become dense enough to be described as stronger than steel, and Buzzwole itself is powerful enough to destroy a dump truck with a single punch. The proboscis is likewise described as harder than diamond, making both feeding and combat adaptations unusually extreme even by Ultra Beast standards. Buzzwole habitually flexes and strikes conspicuous poses after many actions; Aether Foundation researchers suspect that these poses may function as communication, although their exact meaning remains unknown. Like the other Ultra Beasts studied by the Foundation, it stores a form of Z-Power within its body, linking its unusual physiology to the same energy associated with Alola's Totem Pokémon.

playthrough: Pheromosa is a single-stage Bug/Fighting Ultra Beast built almost entirely around attacking before the opponent: base 151 Speed and equal base 137 Attack and Special Attack make physical, special, and mixed approaches all genuinely viable. It is obtained only in late or optional Ultra Beast content rather than as a normal early-story encounter, and in the original Alola pair it is specifically associated with Moon while Ultra Moon provides repeat encounters through Ultra Desert. Bug/Fighting gives useful resistances to Bug, Dark, Fighting, Grass, and Ground, but base 37 Defense and Special Defense are extraordinarily low and its typing includes a 4× Flying weakness alongside Fire, Psychic, and Fairy weaknesses. Close Combat provides powerful, accurate physical Fighting STAB, U-turn lets Pheromosa strike and escape while preserving momentum, and Ice Beam is especially useful on mixed sets because base 137 Special Attack requires no special investment to punish Flying-, Ground-, and Dragon-type targets. High Jump Kick is even stronger in generations where available but creates substantial crash risk on a miss or immunity, while Beast Boost can raise Speed or an attacking stat depending on the chosen Nature and investment. Naive or Hasty are legitimate for mixed sets that want to preserve the extraordinary Speed while using both offenses, while Jolly or Timid suit fully physical or special approaches; because Pheromosa is so frail, sacrificing a defensive stat often matters less than it would for a bulkier Pokémon.
competitive: Pheromosa is one of the clearest examples of a Pokémon proving too strong for standard OU despite also having obvious weaknesses. Early in Generation VII it was an exceptionally difficult OU attacker because base 151 Speed, equal base 137 offenses, U-turn, Fighting STAB, Ice Beam, Poison coverage, and Beast Boost made defensive counterplay dependent on correctly predicting its set and move choice. The resulting suspect test ended with Pheromosa being banned from OU, placing it in Ubers for the remainder of the generation; there it remained useful as an ultra-fast revenge killer and pivot but faced much stronger competition from Pokémon such as Marshadow and Deoxys-A. Its mixed offenses were crucial to the original ban-level pressure because conventional physically defensive answers could be punished by Ice Beam or other special coverage, while nominal checks such as Tapu Fini, Toxapex, and Mega Scizor could be overwhelmed by the correct Z-Move or coverage choice. Sword and Shield again placed Pheromosa in Ubers, where Triple Axel, Close Combat, U-turn, and other coverage preserved its anti-offense role, although the presence of Regieleki and the greater raw power of the Ubers environment prevented it from dominating that tier. It also maintained smaller doubles niches as an extremely fast attacker and speed-control user, but its base 37 defenses make almost any strong neutral hit dangerous and keep its success dependent on positioning. Pheromosa is unavailable in standard Scarlet and Violet, so it has no ordinary Generation IX usage-tier history.
nuzlocke: Pheromosa is extraordinarily powerful but unusually unforgiving in a Nuzlocke because its entire safety model depends on moving first and preventing the opponent from attacking. Base 151 Speed accomplishes that against nearly every unboosted opponent, and its physical, special, or mixed offense can often secure one-hit knockouts without needing setup. The problem is base 37 Defense and Special Defense: even resisted attacks can cause meaningful damage, strong neutral attacks can knock it out outright, and priority moves ignore the Speed advantage that normally protects it. Its 4× Flying weakness makes unexpected Flying coverage especially catastrophic, while Fire, Psychic, and Fairy moves are also dangerous enough that Pheromosa should almost never remain in merely because it expects to survive one hit. U-turn is one of its safest tools because it can exploit its Speed to deal damage and leave before the opponent attacks, while Close Combat is accurate but its defensive drops make any failed knockout even more dangerous. High Jump Kick is particularly poor risk management in permadeath play because a miss or immunity causes severe crash damage, so a slightly weaker accurate Fighting option is often preferable whenever it still secures the knockout.

pokemon.name: Pheromosa
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Pheromosa is a slender insect-like Ultra Beast native to Ultra Desert and possesses extraordinary acceleration, with Aether Foundation research describing it as reaching speeds above 120 miles per hour almost instantly. Other accounts suggest it can move quickly enough to evade lightning, making extreme speed one of the species' defining natural adaptations rather than only a battle statistic. Pheromosa displays an intense reluctance to touch objects or living things in the Pokémon world, apparently regarding the unfamiliar environment as unclean. Its other major adaptation is a powerful pheromonal effect: creatures facing Pheromosa can become confused, captivated by its appearance, and lose the will to fight. Researchers suspect that an unknown organ produces this pheromone-like substance, but its exact biological mechanism remains unresolved. Like the other Ultra Beasts investigated by the Aether Foundation, Pheromosa stores Z-Power within its body, reinforcing that its unusual physiology is fundamentally tied to the energy systems of Ultra Space and Alola.

playthrough: Xurkitree is a single-stage Electric Ultra Beast defined by one extraordinary number: base 173 Special Attack, one of the highest unboosted Special Attack stats in the series, lets even ordinary Thunderbolt deal enormous damage. Its Alola availability is again late or optional rather than part of a normal early-game team, but unlike Buzzwole and Pheromosa it is obtainable in both versions once the relevant Ultra Beast content becomes available. Pure Electric typing is straightforward defensively, providing resistances to Electric, Flying, and Steel and only one weakness to Ground, though base 71 Defense and Special Defense mean neutral hits are not especially comfortable. Thunderbolt is the safest general STAB, Volt Switch provides momentum, and Energy Ball is extremely important because it threatens Ground-types that would otherwise be immune to Electric attacks; Dazzling Gleam can add neutral coverage against several Dragon- and Dark-types. Tail Glow raises Special Attack by three stages and can turn Xurkitree into an absurd wallbreaker, while Calm Mind offers a slower but more defensive setup route; Beast Boost usually raises Special Attack again after every knockout. The limiting statistic is base 83 Speed, which leaves Xurkitree slower than many offensive Pokémon despite its extraordinary power, so Timid is valuable for maximizing the number of natural outspeeds while Modest is appropriate when the team supplies external speed control.
competitive: Xurkitree debuted as an intimidating but imperfect offensive Pokémon: its base 173 Special Attack and Tail Glow suggested overwhelming wallbreaking power, yet mediocre base 83 Speed and only average bulk prevented it from consistently dominating the highest tier. In Generation VII it was UUBL, with OU sets using Tail Glow, Thunderbolt, Energy Ball, Hidden Power Ice, or occasionally Z-Hypnosis to create setup opportunities and patch the Speed problem. The Z-Hypnosis strategy could grant a Speed boost while attempting to put the opponent to sleep, but its dependence on Hypnosis accuracy made it inconsistent; straightforward Tail Glow and coverage generally provided more dependable pressure. Sword and Shield moved Xurkitree down to RU, where it became one of the tier's most restrictive Electric-type wallbreakers because Heavy-Duty Boots and Volt Switch let it repeatedly pressure conventional Electric checks while Energy Ball punished Ground-types such as Gastrodon and weakened Steelix or Flygon. Choice Scarf remained a useful alternative when speed control mattered more than immediate wallbreaking, while Beast Boost could make either cleaner or breaker sets increasingly dangerous after a knockout. Its career illustrates the difference between raw offensive stats and complete competitive performance: 173 Special Attack is spectacular, but limited Speed, middling defenses, predictable Electric-centered offense, and dependence on coverage prevent that number alone from producing OU dominance. Xurkitree is unavailable in standard Scarlet and Violet, so its established ordinary singles history currently ends with its important Generation VIII RU role.
nuzlocke: Xurkitree is excellent at ending favorable Nuzlocke matchups quickly because base 173 Special Attack often removes opponents before repeated damage or status can accumulate. Pure Electric typing is easy to plan around and has only one weakness, but that weakness is Ground and therefore often appears on extremely powerful moves such as Earthquake, making an incorrect immunity prediction potentially fatal. Its base 83 Speed is the main safety problem: Xurkitree does not reliably move first against faster offensive Pokémon, and its 71/71 defenses do not provide enough margin to absorb strong neutral attacks casually. Volt Switch is valuable for escaping slower unfavorable opponents while preserving momentum, while Energy Ball provides a direct answer to several Ground-types that would otherwise switch in freely. Tail Glow can make virtually any subsequent neutral hit devastating, but spending a turn on setup is safest only against an opponent that cannot meaningfully damage Xurkitree; in many Nuzlocke situations its unboosted Special Attack is already high enough that setup is unnecessary. Thunderbolt and Energy Ball are generally preferable to inaccurate options such as Thunder or Zap Cannon unless weather or a specific strategy removes the accuracy risk.

pokemon.name: Xurkitree
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Xurkitree is an electrical Ultra Beast native to Ultra Plant whose entire body resembles a network of bundled power cables, with exposed copper structures at its extremities and a plug-like tail. Its world contains individuals standing with their limbs embedded in the ground like enormous trees, and Xurkitree enters this same posture when its reserves run low so that it can absorb electricity through the soil. Individuals vary enormously in size, ranging from somewhat larger than a human to specimens described as mountain-sized in Ultra Plant. Aether Foundation research identifies a specialized power-generating organ as its most distinctive feature, while its cable-like body conducts electricity with exceptional efficiency. Xurkitree can discharge as much as one million volts at once and has reportedly raided a power plant, supporting the idea that electricity serves not merely as a weapon but as a resource the species actively seeks and replenishes. Animated material also depicts Xurkitree competing with Blacephalon over which can produce the brighter display, adding a documented behavioral rivalry beyond its feeding and power-storage biology.

playthrough: Celesteela is a single-stage Steel/Flying Ultra Beast with one of the most defensively efficient type combinations in the series and unusually balanced offensive statistics, allowing it to function as a wall, mixed attacker, or setup sweeper depending on the game. Its original Alola availability is late or postgame and version-dependent—Celesteela is associated with Moon and Ultra Moon—so it generally does not replace ordinary story Pokémon until the player is already near or beyond the main ending. Steel/Flying provides immunities to Ground and Poison, a 4× resistance to Bug and Grass, numerous additional resistances, and only two weaknesses in Fire and Electric, while base 97 HP with 103 Defense and 101 Special Defense gives those resistances substantial weight. Heavy Slam is particularly effective because Celesteela weighs 999.9 kilograms, Flamethrower punishes Steel-types that resist Heavy Slam, and Leech Seed plus Protect creates steady recovery even though Celesteela lacks a conventional instant-healing move. Its base 101 Attack and 107 Special Attack are close enough that physical, special, and mixed sets are all workable, while Autotomize can compensate for base 61 Speed by raising Speed two stages and later-generation Meteor Beam sets can exploit its special side. Relaxed or Sassy are natural defensive Natures, while more offensive sets can justify Modest or Adamant depending on which attacking side they emphasize.
competitive: Celesteela was one of Generation VII's premier defensive Pokémon, holding an OU placement thanks to exceptional Steel/Flying typing, balanced bulk, Leech Seed, Protect, Heavy Slam, Flamethrower, and enough offensive presence to avoid becoming purely passive. Its typing let it check important threats such as Tapu Lele, Tapu Bulu, Landorus-T, Garchomp, Mega Alakazam, and numerous Fairy- and Psychic-types, while Leech Seed and Leftovers compensated for the absence of reliable recovery. Celesteela was also highly relevant in VGC 2017, where its bulk, Ground immunity, Wide Guard, and ability to match up well into prominent Pokémon such as Tapu Lele and Tapu Bulu gave it a role that few other Steel-types reproduced exactly. Sword and Shield shifted Celesteela down to UU, but it remained one of that tier's strongest bulky Steel-types, checking threats such as Salamence, Scizor, Hippowdon, Excadrill, and Nihilego while still threatening progress through Leech Seed and mixed coverage. Generation VIII also opened a more offensive path through Power Herb Meteor Beam and Autotomize: after a Special Attack increase and Speed boost, Celesteela could use Beast Boost to snowball through weakened teams rather than relying only on defensive attrition. Its weaknesses are concentrated but exploitable—Fire- and Electric-types force it out, Knock Off and status make its imperfect recovery easier to exploit, and Grass-types ignore Leech Seed—yet its combination of typing, weight-based Heavy Slam, and flexible stats has given it one of the most substantial competitive histories among the Ultra Beasts. Celesteela is unavailable in standard Scarlet and Violet, so its ordinary usage-tier record currently ends with Generation VIII UU.
nuzlocke: Celesteela is one of the safest Ultra Beasts for Nuzlocke-style play because Steel/Flying gives it two immunities, a huge resistance profile, and balanced bulk on both defensive sides rather than forcing the player to guess whether an incoming attack will target one weak defense. Ground immunity is especially valuable because Earthquake and similar moves are common high-power threats, while immunity to poison eliminates another source of long-term attrition. Leech Seed plus Protect can restore substantial health and scout an opponent's move, although Leech Seed's imperfect accuracy means the strategy should not be treated as guaranteed recovery when Celesteela is already in danger. Heavy Slam is accurate and extremely strong against lighter targets because of Celesteela's enormous weight, while Flamethrower provides safe coverage against many opposing Steel-types without recoil or defensive drops. Fire and Electric are its only normal type weaknesses, but both are common offensive types, so the impressive resistance list should not encourage blind switching into unknown coverage. Explosion is generally inappropriate in permadeath play despite being available in older movepools, while Autotomize or other setup is best used only when Celesteela's natural bulk and typing make the setup turn genuinely safe.

pokemon.name: Celesteela
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Celesteela is a gigantic Steel/Flying Ultra Beast native to Ultra Crater whose body combines characteristics of bamboo, a rooted plant, and a spacecraft. In its homeworld it can grow from the ground while absorbing nutrients through the soil, then tear free explosively and launch itself skyward for reasons that remain unclear. Its enormous arm structures and lower body contain flammable gas that can be expelled as rocket-like thrust for both flight and combat, with enough lift that researchers believe Celesteela can reach outer space. Those exhaust blasts are powerful enough to destroy an entire bamboo forest, making takeoff itself potentially devastating to the surrounding environment. Despite its machine-like appearance, its nutrient absorption and growth patterns are explicitly plant-like, and at 999.9 kilograms it is tied among the heaviest Pokémon recorded in the standard Pokédex. Animated canon depicts a Celesteela remaining buried and growing for more than two centuries before finally launching, providing evidence that the species can have an extraordinarily long developmental lifespan.

playthrough: Kartana is a single-stage Grass/Steel Ultra Beast whose ordinary story usefulness is limited by late availability: in Sun and Moon it is part of the postgame Ultra Beast missions and is exclusive to Sun, while Ultra Sun allows repeat encounters through Ultra Forest after Ultra Warp Ride becomes available. When it can actually be used, its base 181 Attack is extraordinary, base 109 Speed is excellent, and base 131 Defense lets it survive many physical hits despite only 59 HP. Grass/Steel supplies a Poison immunity, a 4× Grass resistance, and useful resistances to Dragon, Electric, Fairy, Normal, Psychic, Rock, Steel, and Water, but it also leaves a 4× Fire weakness and a Fighting weakness. Leaf Blade, Smart Strike, Sacred Sword, and later Knock Off give it accurate physical coverage, while Swords Dance can turn an already extreme Attack stat into sweeping power and Choice Scarf sets can exploit its Speed without setup. Beast Boost normally raises Attack after each knockout, allowing Kartana to snowball rapidly, although specialized EV spreads can instead make Speed the boosted stat. Jolly is usually the safest Nature because preserving Kartana's strong Speed tier helps it avoid taking hits at all, while Adamant is a legitimate wallbreaking choice when maximum damage matters more.
competitive: Kartana was an OU Pokémon in both Generation VII and Sword and Shield and is one of the clearest examples of an Ultra Beast whose extreme stat distribution translated directly into long-term top-tier singles relevance. In Sun and Moon, base 181 Attack, base 109 Speed, Swords Dance, Leaf Blade, Sacred Sword, Smart Strike, and Z-Moves made it a terrifying wallbreaker, while Choice Scarf sets used Beast Boost to become excellent revenge killers and late-game cleaners. Its physical Defense is also surprisingly high, allowing it to survive some neutral physical attacks despite the low HP, but base 31 Special Defense means virtually any strong special hit is dangerous and Fire attacks are especially devastating because of the 4× weakness. Generation VIII strengthened its utility further through access to Knock Off, and Sword/Shield OU prominently used Swords Dance, Choice Band, and Choice Scarf variants to overwhelm or cripple common checks such as Corviknight and Zapdos. Kartana also had meaningful doubles and VGC relevance, where Tailwind, its huge Attack, and Beast Boost gave it offensive value, although its fragility and Fire weakness made positioning crucial. Its historical limitation has never been lack of damage but rather finding safe entry opportunities and avoiding status or contact-punishing effects such as Flame Body, Static, and Iron Barbs. Kartana is unavailable in standard Scarlet and Violet, so its established main-series singles history currently ends with its Generation VIII OU career.
nuzlocke: Kartana is exceptionally effective in a Nuzlocke when it can move first and secure the knockout, but its defensive profile is one of the most polarized in the series. Its high physical Defense and huge list of resistances create many safe entries against known physical attacks, while Poison immunity removes one common source of long-term attrition. Base 31 Special Defense is the major danger: even resisted or neutral special attacks can deal far more damage than Kartana's physical bulk suggests, and a special Fire move is especially likely to be fatal because of the 4× weakness. Leaf Blade, Smart Strike, Sacred Sword, and Knock Off are accurate and do not impose recoil or defensive penalties, making them excellent permadeath tools compared with riskier alternatives. Swords Dance is often unnecessary because base 181 Attack already secures many knockouts, and spending a setup turn can expose Kartana to an unexpected special coverage move or critical hit. Beast Boost can safely turn one favorable knockout into a sweep, but it is better to earn that momentum through known matchups than to leave Kartana in against an uncertain special attacker merely to chase another boost.

pokemon.name: Kartana
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Kartana is an origami-like Ultra Beast native to Ultra Forest whose body is extraordinarily thin and light, resembling a folded sheet of paper with blade-like arms. Aether Foundation research describes essentially every edge of its body as razor sharp, with the arm blades being particularly dangerous and capable of cutting down an attacking opponent in a single stroke. Its extremely thin construction also lets it evade attacks with light, dance-like movements despite the rigid appearance of its body. That same paper-thin physiology creates pronounced environmental vulnerabilities: Kartana is particularly susceptible to both fire and moisture. Animated canon shows one Kartana cutting objects with extraordinary precision, including slicing through large structures, and also depicts the species opening an Ultra Wormhole by cutting through space. It can even imitate human speech in a reversed form, giving the otherwise faceless Ultra Beast one of the stranger documented communication abilities among its group.

playthrough: Guzzlord is a single-stage Dark/Dragon Ultra Beast whose main-story availability is again late or postgame, but when permitted it functions as a slow mixed tank and wallbreaker rather than a fast Legendary-style sweeper. Its defining statistic is base 223 HP, one of the highest in the series, while both defenses are only base 53; the enormous HP still produces substantial effective bulk but is much less impressive against repeated super-effective hits than the raw HP number suggests. Dark/Dragon gives a Psychic immunity and resistances to Dark, Electric, Fire, Ghost, Grass, and Water, but weaknesses to Bug, Dragon, Fighting, and Ice and a severe 4× Fairy weakness sharply constrain defensive matchups. Base 101 Attack and 97 Special Attack support physical, special, or mixed approaches with moves such as Knock Off, Dragon Claw or Draco Meteor, Heavy Slam, Earthquake, Flamethrower, and later Heat Crash depending on the game. Beast Boost normally raises whichever attacking stat has been emphasized, but base 43 Speed means Guzzlord usually has to absorb a hit before benefiting from a knockout. Brave or Quiet can suit intentionally slow physical or special builds, especially under Trick Room, while Adamant or Modest are reasonable when the team simply wants maximum damage without reducing Speed further.
competitive: Guzzlord has never been a high-tier singles staple, but it developed a legitimate lower-tier niche because its massive HP and Dark/Dragon typing let it switch into several offensive and defensive Pokémon that ordinary wallbreakers could not exploit as easily. In Generation VII it was PUBL with meaningful NU use, where Knock Off, Draco Meteor, Dark Pulse, Heavy Slam, and other coverage let it pressure bulky cores built around Pokémon such as Slowking, Steelix, and Golbat. Its huge HP allowed it to survive many neutral attacks despite poor defenses, and the Psychic immunity plus Fire, Water, Grass, Electric, Ghost, and Dark resistances created real defensive utility rather than purely offensive value. Sword and Shield placed Guzzlord in PU, but it received serious RU analysis because Heavy-Duty Boots, Knock Off, Draco Meteor, and broad coverage allowed it to check Pokémon such as Celebi, Chandelure, Heliolisk, and Raikou while still threatening progress. The species' competitive ceiling is limited by base 43 Speed, the 4× Fairy weakness, mediocre defensive stats relative to its HP, and the ease with which Fighting-, Ice-, Bug-, or Fairy-type coverage can punish it. Guzzlord is therefore best described as a specialized bulky wallbreaker and sponge rather than a conventional tank; its enormous HP gives it time to function, but does not fix poor typing matchups or the lack of dependable recovery. It is unavailable in standard Scarlet and Violet, so its ordinary main-series singles record currently ends with Generation VIII.
nuzlocke: Guzzlord's enormous HP creates a large visible health buffer in Nuzlocke play, but that buffer can be deceptive because base 53 Defense and Special Defense allow strong attacks to remove surprisingly large percentages of its health. Its Psychic immunity and six useful resistances can nevertheless create excellent switch opportunities when the opponent's moveset is known, especially against Fire-, Water-, Grass-, Electric-, Ghost-, and Dark-type attacks. The 4× Fairy weakness is the most important danger and should be treated as a hard stop in uncertain matchups, while Fighting, Ice, Bug, and Dragon coverage can also overwhelm its HP quickly. Knock Off is especially safe and useful because it is accurate and removes held items without recoil or stat drops, while Heavy Slam can punish Fairy-types if Guzzlord is already safely on the field rather than switching directly into their attacks. Draco Meteor provides strong emergency damage but sharply lowers Special Attack, so physical or accurate repeatable Dragon moves may be safer over multiple opponents. Because Guzzlord has no reliable instant recovery in its conventional movepool and is extremely slow, preserving HP through resistances and careful switching is more important than assuming its enormous maximum HP can simply absorb every mistake.

pokemon.name: Guzzlord
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Guzzlord is an enormous Dark/Dragon Ultra Beast defined by an apparently limitless appetite and a body dominated by a gigantic mouth lined with teeth and long tongue-like appendages. It consumes almost anything in its path, including plants, soil, buildings, vehicles, and other organic or inorganic material, and Aether Foundation reports describe it as feeding continuously whenever awake. Despite the vast amount it consumes, no Guzzlord excrement has been documented, leading researchers to suspect that it converts nearly everything it eats directly into energy. The Ultra Ruin encountered in Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon is a devastated alternate version of Hau'oli City populated by Guzzlord; animation clarifies that Guzzlord was not originally native to that ruined world but arrived through an Ultra Wormhole and helped reduce the already damaged environment to a barren wasteland. Its two large tongues can seize material and pull it into the main mouth while smaller mouths on those appendages assist feeding, allowing it to consume enormous quantities with very little pause. Guzzlord's ecology is therefore dominated by resource consumption at a scale capable of reshaping entire environments rather than by ordinary predator-prey relationships.

playthrough: Necrozma does not evolve, but it has four mechanically distinct states: base Necrozma, Dusk Mane after fusion with Solgaleo, Dawn Wings after fusion with Lunala, and Ultra Necrozma, which can be reached only in Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon by using Ultra Burst from one of the fused forms while holding Ultranecrozium Z. Base Necrozma is a bulky Psychic-type with 127 Special Attack, solid 97/101/89 bulk, base 79 Speed, and Prism Armor, which reduces damage from super-effective attacks and makes its apparent weaknesses less punishing than they would be on most Psychic-types. Dusk Mane becomes Psychic/Steel with 157 Attack and 127 Defense, gaining a huge resistance profile and Sunsteel Strike; Dawn Wings becomes Psychic/Ghost with 157 Special Attack and 127 Special Defense but suffers 4× weaknesses to Dark and Ghost, making it much less forgiving defensively. Ultra Necrozma radically changes the role again, becoming Psychic/Dragon with equal base 167 Attack and Special Attack, base 129 Speed, and Neuroforce, which strengthens super-effective moves; Photon Geyser also uses whichever attacking stat is higher. Dusk Mane and Dawn Wings remain available in later generations through the N-Solarizer and N-Lunarizer, but Ultra Necrozma is a Generation VII-specific transformation because later games do not support Ultranecrozium Z and Ultra Burst. Jolly or Adamant are natural for physical Dusk Mane builds, Timid or Modest support Dawn Wings and special base Necrozma, and Ultra Necrozma can legitimately use Jolly, Timid, Naive, or Hasty depending on whether the set is physical, special, or mixed.
competitive: Necrozma's competitive history varies dramatically by form and is one of the most form-dependent records in the series. Base Necrozma was RU in Generation VII and is again RU in Scarlet/Violet, where Prism Armor, Calm Mind or Dragon Dance, Stealth Rock, Moonlight, Photon Geyser, and wide coverage give it a flexible bulky-offense niche without making it a top-tier Psychic-type. Dusk Mane Necrozma, by contrast, has been one of the defining Ubers Pokémon since Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon: Psychic/Steel typing, Prism Armor, 157 Attack, strong mixed bulk, Stealth Rock, recovery, Swords Dance or Dragon Dance, and Sunsteel Strike let it check Xerneas historically and later Zacian-C, Calyrex-I, and other elite threats while also threatening sweeps. Dawn Wings has always been much less successful despite enormous Special Attack because its Psychic/Ghost typing carries 4× Dark and Ghost weaknesses and it lacks Lunala's Shadow Shield; both Generation VII and VIII analyses describe it as heavily outclassed, although Trick Room or Ultra Burst access created small niches. Ultra Necrozma was a top Generation VII Ubers threat: base 129 Speed, equal 167 offenses, Neuroforce, broad coverage, and the ability to enter battle disguised as Dusk Mane or Dawn Wings made it extremely difficult to scout, while Light That Burns the Sky supplied a devastating one-time Z-Move. Generation VIII removed Ultra Necrozma but left Dusk Mane as one of Ubers' premier defensive and setup Pokémon, and Scarlet/Violet again places Dusk Mane in Ubers while base Necrozma sits far lower in RU. The family therefore ranges from a good lower-tier bulky attacker to one of the strongest Ubers role-compression Pokémon ever, depending entirely on form.
nuzlocke: Base Necrozma is already unusually safe for a Psychic-type because Prism Armor reduces damage from super-effective attacks, giving more margin against Bug-, Dark-, and Ghost-type coverage than the type chart alone implies. Dusk Mane is generally the safest form for blind play because Psychic/Steel provides many resistances and a Poison immunity while Prism Armor softens its Fire, Ground, Ghost, and Dark weaknesses; reliable Sunsteel Strike also ignores opposing Abilities without recoil or accuracy risk. Dawn Wings is far riskier despite its excellent special bulk because its 4× Dark and Ghost weaknesses can still be catastrophic even after Prism Armor's reduction, and base 77 Speed means those attacks often land first. Ultra Necrozma is exceptionally powerful and fast, but Ultra Burst replaces Prism Armor with Neuroforce and leaves only 97/97/97 defenses, so transforming trades defensive insurance for sweeping power and should not be treated as an automatic safety upgrade. Photon Geyser is especially useful because it is accurate and automatically uses the stronger attacking stat, while setup moves such as Swords Dance, Dragon Dance, or Calm Mind should be limited to genuinely controlled matchups rather than stacked greedily. In Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon, the decision to remain Dusk Mane for bulk or Ultra Burst for Speed and offense is a real survival choice rather than a simple question of which form has the higher base-stat total.

pokemon.name: Necrozma
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Base Necrozma is not its healthy natural condition but a damaged, light-starved state formed after the ancestors of the Ultra Recon Squad injured it while attempting to control and exploit its power. Its black crystalline body contains accumulated impurities, while the prism-like structure in its head functions as a brain prism that glows while absorbing light. The injury left Necrozma in constant severe pain and drove its violent search for light, leading it to drain entire places or living beings in an attempt to remain active and recover its original form. Professor Kukui and Lillie theorize that fragments broken from Necrozma during that ancient injury became Alola's Sparkling Stones and Z-Crystals, tying the Pokémon directly to the origin of Z-Power. Necrozma can convert absorbed light into powerful laser attacks and can travel through Ultra Wormholes, while worlds from which it steals too much light can be left in near-total darkness. Ancient Alolan accounts consequently remembered it as a 'pillager of light,' although its destructive behavior is inseparable from the injury and deprivation that reduced it to this form.

pokemon.name: Necrozma
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Dusk Mane Necrozma forms when Necrozma fuses with Solgaleo and absorbs its light, covering the lion-like body with black crystalline armor while using the Legendary Pokémon as an energy source. In forced fusion, Necrozma can dominate Solgaleo's body and suppress its will, becoming extremely violent and difficult to control as it attempts to feed continuously on the captured light. The fused form inherits Solgaleo's Sunsteel Strike and greatly exceeds base Necrozma's physical strength, attacking with claws formed from both the host body and Necrozma's crystalline structures. Necrozma can also coexist willingly with its host under some circumstances, so fusion is not canonically limited to involuntary parasitism even though the Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon story emphasizes the violent version. Dusk Mane can open multiple Ultra Wormholes across a wide area, showing how much of Necrozma's lost spatial and energetic power returns once it obtains a major source of light.

pokemon.name: Necrozma
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Dawn Wings Necrozma is created when Necrozma fuses with Lunala and absorbs its light, coating the bat-like body in black crystalline structures while drawing energy from the host. In the forced state depicted in Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon, Lunala loses its own will and continuously expels energy for Necrozma, which uses that supply to sustain a relentless rampage. The fused form inherits Moongeist Beam and can fire dark energy from crystalline spines before rushing opponents with its enormous claws. As with Dusk Mane, later canon establishes that Necrozma and its host can also coexist willingly, although the original story portrays the transformation as a predatory takeover. Its body can open multiple Ultra Wormholes and channels enough absorbed light to approach the threshold needed for Necrozma's true Ultra form.

pokemon.name: Necrozma
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Ultra Necrozma is Necrozma's original, fully restored form rather than a separate species, appearing after it absorbs overwhelming quantities of light energy and Z-Power. Its enormous dragon-like body is composed mostly of pure light supported by the glowing remnants of the black crystalline skeleton seen in its damaged state. At full power it radiates energy that affects both living organisms and the surrounding natural environment, explaining the ancient title 'the Blinding One' and the association between its light, Totem auras, and Z-Power. Its body temperature exceeds 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit, enough to melt anything it touches, and it can fire laser beams from throughout its body across distances measured in tens of miles. Ultra Necrozma can maintain this state only while sufficient light remains available; exhausting that energy causes it to revert to its dark, damaged form and may send it into a deep sleep until more light is absorbed. The contrast between this radiant state and base Necrozma shows that its destructive hunger for light is fundamentally tied to the loss of the energy needed to sustain its natural body.
