playthrough: Magearna is a single-stage Steel/Fairy Mythical Pokémon and is normally a special-distribution or optional acquisition rather than part of a standard first playthrough, but its 600 base-stat total and excellent typing make it immediately powerful whenever a ruleset allows it. Base 130 Special Attack, 115 Defense, and 115 Special Defense combine with Steel/Fairy's Dragon and Poison immunities, numerous resistances, and only Fire and Ground weaknesses, giving Magearna unusually safe opportunities to attack or set up. Soul-Heart raises Special Attack whenever another Pokémon faints, including opposing Pokémon and in doubles potentially other combatants, so Magearna can snowball naturally without spending a separate setup turn. Fleur Cannon provides enormous Fairy damage at the cost of a two-stage Special Attack drop, while Flash Cannon, Thunderbolt, Ice Beam, Aura Sphere or Focus Blast, Volt Switch, Shift Gear, Calm Mind, and Trick Room support very different roles across generations. Original Color Magearna is mechanically identical to the standard silver form; its red-and-gold appearance represents the paint scheme it had when first presented to royalty roughly 500 years ago. Mega Magearna, introduced in Pokémon Legends: Z-A – Mega Dimension, remains Steel/Fairy but rises to a 700 base-stat total with 170 Special Attack, 125 Attack, and 95 Speed while retaining the same defensive stats, turning the already powerful artificial Pokémon into a dramatically faster and stronger attacker. Modest is excellent for ordinary special wallbreaking, Timid supports Shift Gear or faster offensive sets, and Quiet can be useful on dedicated Trick Room teams.
competitive: Magearna has one of the strongest competitive histories of any Mythical Pokémon introduced in Generation VII. It was a defining Sun and Moon OU Pokémon rather than immediately being confined to Ubers, with Steel/Fairy typing, 80/115/115 bulk, base 130 Special Attack, Soul-Heart, Shift Gear, Calm Mind, Trick Room, Assault Vest, Volt Switch, and huge coverage making it exceptionally difficult to identify from team preview. Shift Gear sets could sweep offense, Assault Vest sets functioned as bulky pivots, Trick Room variants reversed the Speed problem, and Z-Moves let Magearna convert inaccurate or stat-dropping coverage into devastating one-time attacks; it also retained a niche in Ubers as a Xerneas and Yveltal check despite technically being OU. Sword and Shield pushed Magearna beyond standard OU tolerance and it was ultimately an Uber, where Steel/Fairy typing and Soul-Heart still gave it strong defensive and offensive utility. Scarlet and Violet likewise currently place Magearna in Ubers, with the combination of Stored Power, Calm Mind, Shift Gear or Trick Room-style speed manipulation, Terastallization, and Soul-Heart proving far too strong for ordinary OU play. Mega Magearna is a brand-new 2026-era development rather than an established historical competitive archetype; its 170 Special Attack and 95 Speed clearly raise the offensive ceiling, but it is too new to assign a long-term tier or tournament reputation with the same confidence as base Magearna. Historically, the defining feature of Magearna is versatility: opponents often knew it was dangerous but could not know whether the immediate problem was sweeping, pivoting, Trick Room, defensive support, or coverage until the set was revealed.
nuzlocke: Magearna is exceptionally safe by ordinary Nuzlocke standards because Steel/Fairy provides two immunities, a large resistance profile, excellent mixed defenses, and enough offensive power to end many fights before repeated damage accumulates. Soul-Heart rewards knockouts without requiring a setup turn, allowing Magearna to grow stronger during multi-Pokémon boss battles while remaining free to attack or use support moves each turn. The main type-chart dangers are Fire and Ground, both of which are common high-power offensive types, so the enormous resistance list should not encourage blind switching into unknown Earthquake or strong Fire coverage. Fleur Cannon is powerful but lowers Special Attack by two stages, so accurate repeatable options such as Flash Cannon, Aura Sphere, or other coverage can be safer over several opponents when maximum Fairy damage is unnecessary. Shift Gear or Calm Mind can make Magearna nearly unstoppable from a controlled position, but repeated setup still exposes it to critical hits and is often unnecessary given its excellent natural stats. Mega Magearna's increased Speed and offensive power reduce the number of opponents that can attack before it, but the form does not change the underlying Fire and Ground weaknesses, so Mega Evolution should enhance safe matchups rather than justify taking poor ones.

pokemon.name: Magearna
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Magearna is an artificial Pokémon created by a scientist roughly 500 years ago, but the metal body is only a vessel: its true life-form is the Soul-Heart housed in its chest. The Soul-Heart is an artificial soul made using the life energy of other Pokémon and remains conscious even if removed from the mechanical body, although the body itself becomes unable to move without it. Magearna can synchronize its consciousness with humans and Pokémon to understand their feelings, which makes it an unusually capable caretaker despite being unable to speak. Its arms conceal multiple mechanisms, including a cannon and flower arrangements, and animated canon depicts it watering plants and singing a calming lullaby. When dormant, sad, or inactive, Magearna can retract its limbs and upper body into its spherical lower shell until it resembles a Poké Ball. Its Original Color appearance is the red-and-gold decoration it wore when first presented as a gift to a king's daughter; the modern silver appearance results from those colors fading over the centuries.

pokemon.name: Magearna
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Mega Evolution activates a secret mechanism that had remained hidden inside Magearna since its creation roughly 500 years ago, explicitly removing limitations built into the artificial Pokémon. The transformation restores colors associated with Magearna's original appearance and reorganizes its body, including floating half-gears that orbit independently and can combine with its flower-shaped cannon into a much larger firing mechanism. The increased performance comes at a disturbing behavioral cost: Magearna's developed emotions are locked away while the hidden mode is active, leaving it as a relentless, heartless fighting machine focused on defeating one opponent after another. Its Soul-Heart remains visually central to the transformed body, but the personality normally associated with that artificial soul is effectively suppressed by the mechanism that unlocks Mega Magearna's full combat potential.

playthrough: Marshadow is a single-stage Fighting/Ghost Mythical Pokémon obtained through special distributions rather than ordinary wild encounters in its debut era, so it is generally unavailable during a standard first playthrough unless event or transfer rules specifically permit it. When usable, base 125 Attack and 125 Speed make it an exceptional physical attacker, while Fighting/Ghost STAB is extraordinarily difficult to resist and provides Normal and Fighting immunities defensively. Spectral Thief is its defining move: it steals the target's positive stat boosts before dealing damage, allowing Marshadow to punish opposing setup rather than merely surviving it, while Close Combat supplies powerful Fighting STAB. Technician boosts moves with 60 base power or less, making Shadow Sneak particularly dangerous priority and strengthening coverage such as Rock Tomb in generations where it is available. The main drawback is only moderate 90/80/90 bulk, so Marshadow is much safer when attacking first than when repeatedly switching into neutral damage; weaknesses to Fairy, Flying, Ghost, and Psychic remain important despite its Mythical status. Jolly is normally the safest Nature because preserving base 125 Speed is essential for outrunning other offensive Pokémon, while Adamant can be justified when external speed control already guarantees the first move.
competitive: Marshadow has been an Ubers Pokémon throughout its conventional competitive life and immediately established itself as one of that tier's most threatening offensive tools. In Generation VII, Fighting/Ghost STAB was effectively unresisted by ordinary type combinations, while base 125 Speed let Marshadow outrun maximum-Speed Arceus forms and Spectral Thief allowed it to reverse the advantage of setup sweepers by stealing their boosts before attacking. Technician-boosted Shadow Sneak gave it exceptional revenge-killing utility against faster or boosted threats, and Marshadium Z converted Spectral Thief into Soul-Stealing 7-Star Strike for a one-time 195-power Ghost attack capable of breaking defensive answers. Sword and Shield kept Marshadow in Ubers, where it remained one of the format's best revenge killers and wallbreakers because Spectral Thief could punish setup from threats such as Zygarde or Kyogre while Shadow Sneak threatened Calyrex-Shadow and other fast sweepers. Its limitations are primarily defensive: base 80 Defense and 90 Special Defense make switching in difficult, and strong Fairy-, Flying-, Ghost-, or Psychic-type attacks can force it out or remove it before its offensive utility matters. Marshadow is unavailable in standard Scarlet and Violet, so its established main-series tier history currently ends with Generation VIII, though National Dex formats preserve its characteristic anti-setup role. Few Pokémon combine wallbreaking and emergency anti-sweep insurance as directly as Marshadow, which is why its competitive value has remained far greater than a simple 600-BST comparison would imply.
nuzlocke: Marshadow is an exceptionally useful emergency Pokémon in a Nuzlocke because Spectral Thief can neutralize an enemy that has accumulated dangerous positive stat boosts while simultaneously dealing damage. Base 125 Speed and Technician-boosted Shadow Sneak give two separate forms of speed control: Marshadow naturally outruns most opponents, and priority can finish weakened threats that are faster or have boosted their own Speed. Its Normal and Fighting immunities create genuinely free switches when enemy moves are known, while resistances to Bug, Poison, and Rock provide additional entry opportunities. The danger is that Marshadow is not especially bulky, and Close Combat lowers both defenses after use, making a failed knockout or multi-Pokémon sequence much riskier than the initial damage number suggests. Spectral Thief is particularly safe against setup compared with attempting to race the opponent with one's own boosts, because Marshadow removes the opponent's positive stat stages before damage resolves. Jolly sets using accurate STAB and Shadow Sneak minimize variance, while recoil-free priority and the ability to steal boosts make Marshadow one of the most dependable offensive Mythicals for preventing a single unexpected setup sweeper from ending a run.

pokemon.name: Marshadow
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Marshadow is an exceptionally elusive shadow-like Pokémon that remained unknown to most people for so long that its existence survived mainly in myths and legends. It can sink completely into another being's shadow, using that hidden position to understand the target's emotions and copy its movements and abilities without being noticed. The imitation is not merely superficial: by repeatedly copying skilled fighters, Marshadow can eventually surpass the original and is said to learn even the ultimate techniques of martial arts masters it observes. Its shadow body can stretch and change shape, and animated canon shows it capable of causing nightmares and, under extraordinary corruption by the Rainbow Feather, controlling large numbers of Pokémon through their shadows. Recent Lumiose accounts describe a hidden Marshadow being mistaken for a 'ghostly child' near Prism Tower, showing that even in populated areas it can remain almost completely undetected. Its signature Spectral Thief reflects the same biological theme mechanically by taking an opponent's accumulated battle boosts before striking.

pokemon.name: Marshadow
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Zenith Marshadow is a temporary full-power state that appears when Marshadow becomes angry or actively commits itself to battle rather than a separate species or permanent alternate body. Its fighting spirit visibly ignites, causing the smoky structures around its head, collar, wrists, and eyes to flare into bright green and yellow flame-like energy. The transformation therefore provides a direct visible indicator of an otherwise secretive Pokémon abandoning concealment and bringing its copied martial skill fully into combat. Zenith Marshadow does not have separate base stats or typing in the core games, so the distinction is primarily behavioral and visual rather than a mechanically independent battle form.

playthrough: Poipole is an unusual Ultra Beast because it genuinely evolves: it becomes Naganadel when it levels up while knowing Dragon Pulse, with no fixed minimum evolution level beyond satisfying that move requirement. In Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon, Poipole is received late in the story, so the evolution can occur quickly if Dragon Pulse is taught or relearned; Sword and Shield's Crown Tundra likewise provides Poipole only through late optional content, keeping the family out of ordinary early-game team building. Naganadel gains Dragon typing and jumps to base 127 Special Attack and 121 Speed, turning a relatively modest first stage into a very fast special sweeper with excellent Poison/Dragon STAB. Sludge Wave or Sludge Bomb handles Fairy-types that would normally block Dragon attacks, Draco Meteor supplies enormous burst damage, and Flamethrower or Fire Blast covers most Steel-types that resist both STAB types. Beast Boost is especially dangerous on Naganadel because a Timid build can be arranged so that Speed becomes the boosted stat after a knockout, making revenge killing increasingly difficult, while Special Attack-boosting variants instead snowball raw damage. Nasty Plot can make Naganadel overwhelming after one safe turn but its 73/73/73 defenses leave little margin for setup mistakes, so Timid is the most broadly useful Nature while Modest is reasonable when external speed control is already available.
competitive: Naganadel made one of the most explosive competitive debuts of Generation VII: shortly after Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon released, it proved so difficult to answer in OU that the council quickbanned it to Ubers after roughly a week. The defining set combined Nasty Plot, Draco Meteor, Sludge Wave, Fire Blast, Dragonium Z, and Beast Boost, with Poison/Dragon STAB plus Fire coverage leaving only a small number of reliable defensive answers and a Speed-boosting Beast Boost making ordinary revenge killing extremely difficult. Its short OU stay is historically important because the ban was not based on overwhelming bulk or an enormous base-stat total; instead, base 127 Special Attack, 121 Speed, nearly complete offensive coverage, and post-knockout snowballing compressed too much offensive pressure into one slot. In Generation VII Ubers it remained usable as an anti-stall and hyper-offense sweeper, but its mediocre bulk and competition from much stronger restricted Pokémon made successful setup considerably harder than it had been in OU. Sword and Shield kept Naganadel in Ubers, where Nasty Plot and Life Orb still created a dangerous cleaner and Beast Boost could again raise Speed after a knockout, but threats such as Calyrex-Shadow, Choice Scarf users, priority, and Eternatus limited its consistency. Naganadel therefore has the unusual historical distinction of being unequivocally too strong for standard OU while never becoming a dominant Ubers staple, illustrating how a Pokémon can sit awkwardly between metagames. It is unavailable in standard Scarlet and Violet, so its established main-series tier history currently ends with Generation VIII Ubers.
nuzlocke: Poipole's late acquisition means a Nuzlocke rarely has to protect the weaker first stage for very long, but the player must know the Dragon Pulse evolution requirement or risk carrying Poipole substantially longer than necessary. Once evolved, Naganadel is safest when its base 121 Speed and powerful special attacks prevent opponents from moving at all, because 73/73/73 defenses provide little room for an incorrect damage estimate. Poison/Dragon gives useful resistances to Bug, Electric, Fighting, Fire, Poison, Water, and a 4× resistance to Grass, but Ground, Psychic, Ice, and Dragon coverage can be lethal when Naganadel fails to secure the first knockout. Sludge Wave and Flamethrower are accurate and dependable, while Draco Meteor's 90% accuracy and two-stage Special Attack drop make it better as an emergency burst option than as the only plan for multiple consecutive opponents. Nasty Plot is extremely powerful but should be used only against an enemy that cannot meaningfully punish the setup turn; in many Nuzlocke situations Naganadel already has enough natural Special Attack to avoid taking that risk. A successful Beast Boost can turn one safe knockout into a sweep, but priority attacks remain especially dangerous because they bypass the Speed advantage that normally keeps this very frail Ultra Beast alive.

pokemon.name: Poipole
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Poipole originates from Ultra Megalopolis in the core games and is notable for being popular there as a first partner Pokémon, making it one of the clearest examples of an Ultra Beast filling an ordinary companion role in its home culture. Its oversized head is filled with a luminous, highly adhesive poison that it can spray from several needles projecting from the head. Poipole can learn to understand human speech after spending enough time around people, indicating a level of social adaptability unusual among the more alien Ultra Beasts. Animated portrayals show Poipole living socially, expressing strong curiosity, and using its colorful venom to make drawings or markings rather than employing the substance only as a weapon. Like other Ultra Beasts, it stores the same kind of Z-Power associated with Alola's Totem Pokémon within its body.

pokemon.name: Naganadel
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Naganadel is a flying Poison/Dragon Ultra Beast whose greatly enlarged abdomen contains both its brain and a large reservoir of poisonous liquid, making the lower half of its body neurologically as well as offensively important. Three hollow stingers connect directly to that brain, and Naganadel reacts violently if the stingers are touched because interference with them affects a highly sensitive part of its nervous system. Its primary stinger can launch a glowing, adhesive poison over distances greater than six miles, giving the species an extraordinary long-range chemical weapon. Animated canon depicts Naganadel living in nests with and leading large groups of Poipole, establishing a social relationship between the two evolutionary stages rather than portraying adult Naganadel as purely solitary. The same portrayal gives Naganadel telepathic communication capable of conveying images and memories of past events to humans. Like Poipole and the other Ultra Beasts, Naganadel stores Z-Power within its body.

playthrough: Stakataka is a single-stage Rock/Steel Ultra Beast introduced in Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon and obtained only very late, so it is generally a postgame or optional-content powerhouse rather than a normal island-challenge team member. Its base 211 Defense is among the highest in the series, while 131 Attack and 101 Special Defense give it real offensive and mixed defensive value; the price is base 13 Speed, which is so low that Stakataka virtually always moves last outside Trick Room. That extreme slowness is actually an offensive advantage for Gyro Ball, which can reach maximum power against fast opponents, and Trick Room can reverse turn order so that Stakataka becomes one of the fastest practical attackers for several turns. Rock/Steel grants a Poison immunity, 4× resistances to Normal and Flying, and several other resistances, but it also creates catastrophic 4× weaknesses to Fighting and Ground plus a Water weakness. Stone Edge or Rock Slide provides secondary STAB, Earthquake and Superpower or Body Press offer coverage in appropriate generations, and Beast Boost will normally increase Defense unless the stat spread is deliberately manipulated to make Attack highest. Brave is the natural ordinary Nature because it increases Attack while reducing a Speed stat Stakataka actively wants as low as possible for both Trick Room and Gyro Ball.
competitive: Stakataka carved out one of the most distinctive Trick Room niches of Generation VII thanks to a combination of base 13 Speed, base 131 Attack, and a monstrous base 211 Defense. It was classified RUBL while receiving serious UU use, where its extraordinarily slow Gyro Ball reached enormous power against ordinary targets and Trick Room allowed it to reverse the Speed disadvantage and begin sweeping. A famous optimization used a Lonely Nature and carefully reduced Defense IVs so that Attack became Stakataka's highest actual stat, causing Beast Boost to raise Attack after a knockout rather than making its already excessive Defense even higher. It also had meaningful doubles and VGC use because Trick Room is naturally stronger in doubles, Rock Slide can pressure both opponents, and its low Speed allows it to move extremely early once the room is established. Sword and Shield lowered Stakataka to NU, where it remained an excellent defensive Steel-type and Trick Room breaker; Body Press additionally gave later sets a way to convert the enormous Defense stat directly into Fighting-type damage. Its competitive flaws are impossible to ignore, however: 4× Fighting and Ground weaknesses mean common attacks such as Close Combat and Earthquake can bypass its impressive raw bulk, while bulky Water-types exploit its only ordinary weakness and poor Speed outside Trick Room. Stakataka is unavailable in standard Scarlet and Violet, so Generation VIII NU is its latest conventional usage-tier placement.
nuzlocke: Stakataka can make physical neutral attacks look trivial in a Nuzlocke because base 211 Defense is extraordinary, but its typing creates two matchup failures so severe that raw Defense cannot be treated as universal safety. Ground and Fighting attacks deal 4× damage, meaning moves such as Earthquake, High Horsepower, Close Combat, and even weaker coverage can be fatal despite Stakataka's enormous defensive stat. Against Normal-, Flying-, Rock-, Psychic-, Ice-, Dragon-, Fairy-, or Bug-type physical moves it can be exceptionally reliable, and the Poison immunity prevents one common form of attrition. Gyro Ball is accurate and becomes extremely powerful precisely because Stakataka is so slow, while Trick Room can let it attack first without requiring a risky Speed-boosting setup strategy. Stone Edge's imperfect accuracy is less attractive in survival-critical situations than Rock Slide or another accurate option when the lower power still secures the knockout. Body Press in later games is an unusually safe offensive tool because it exploits the same massive Defense that keeps Stakataka alive, but the player should still switch immediately rather than attempting to tank a known 4×-effective Ground or Fighting attack.

pokemon.name: Stakataka
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Stakataka is not one indivisible organism but a colony of many brick-like stone life-forms assembled into the shape of a four-sided tower. Phyco describes one Stakataka as containing almost 150 individual components, while the visible model can be counted as 137 separate stones, each with its own glowing eye on the underside. The eyes normally glow blue but turn red when the colony is angry or engaged in battle. Stakataka can rearrange its component organisms, forming legs, opening sections of the tower to allow attacks to pass through, or enclosing an opponent inside the structure. When sleeping it plants itself against the ground and disguises the entire colony as an ordinary stone building. It strongly dislikes having objects placed on top of it and may thrash violently to remove them, but animated canon shows that an individual capable of enduring the shaking and successfully riding Stakataka can earn the colony's respect.

playthrough: Blacephalon is a single-stage Fire/Ghost Ultra Beast introduced in Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon, with its ordinary Alola availability restricted to Ultra Sun near the very end of the game, so it is better understood as a late-story or postgame attacker than a normal long-term team member. Its base 151 Special Attack and 107 Speed make it an excellent special wallbreaker or cleaner, while Fire/Ghost STAB provides powerful neutral coverage and immunities to Normal and Fighting. Shadow Ball and Flamethrower are the safest repeatable STAB choices, whereas Fire Blast trades accuracy for power and the signature Mind Blown reaches 150 base power at the enormous cost of half of Blacephalon's maximum HP each time it is used. Beast Boost normally raises Special Attack after a knockout, but specialized spreads can make Speed the highest stat and turn a Choice Scarf or cleaning set into an increasingly difficult target to revenge kill. Its 53 HP and 53 Defense are extremely poor and it is weak to Dark, Ghost, Ground, Rock, and Water, so Blacephalon should generally enter through a free switch or pivot rather than absorb an attack directly. Timid is normally preferable because base 107 Speed is good but still vulnerable to several faster offensive Pokémon, while Modest is reasonable for Choice Scarf or maximum wallbreaking sets.
competitive: Blacephalon was an OU Pokémon in both Generation VII and Sword and Shield, giving it one of the strongest sustained singles records among the Ultra Beasts introduced in Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon. In Generation VII, Fire/Ghost STAB, base 151 Special Attack, base 107 Speed, Beast Boost, Choice Specs, Choice Scarf, and access to Trick made it both a devastating wallbreaker and a dangerous late-game cleaner. Choice Scarf sets could revenge kill faster offensive Pokémon and then snowball through Beast Boost, while Choice Specs could break would-be defensive answers after modest chip damage; Tyranitar was historically one of its most important checks because it resisted Fire, threatened it with Dark attacks, and could exploit Pursuit in that generation. Sword and Shield preserved Blacephalon's OU status and arguably made the basic formula cleaner: Choice Specs pressured even bulky targets such as Toxapex and Gastrodon after chip, while Choice Scarf sets threatened Dragapult, Weavile, and weakened offensive teams. Heavy-Duty Boots could reduce the cost of Stealth Rock for non-Choice sets, but Blacephalon's miserable physical bulk and weaknesses to common priority remained fundamental constraints. Mind Blown was competitively powerful in the formats where it was used, but losing half of maximum HP is an enormous price and ordinary Flamethrower or Fire Blast often provided better longevity. Blacephalon is unavailable in standard Scarlet and Violet, so its conventional main-series tier history currently ends with a second consecutive OU generation.
nuzlocke: Blacephalon is the kind of Pokémon that can erase dangerous opponents before they move but offers almost no forgiveness if the knockout calculation is wrong. Base 107 Speed and 151 Special Attack make accurate Shadow Ball and Flamethrower excellent Nuzlocke tools, while Normal and Fighting immunities can create genuinely free entries when enemy movesets are known. Its base 53 HP and Defense make strong physical attacks especially dangerous, and weaknesses to Dark, Ghost, Ground, Rock, and Water mean it should almost never be used as a blind defensive switch. Mind Blown is usually a poor permadeath choice because every use costs half of Blacephalon's maximum HP regardless of the enormous damage it inflicts, potentially placing the user in priority or hazard range even after a successful knockout. Fire Blast introduces additional accuracy risk, so Flamethrower is normally preferable whenever its lower power still secures the required result. Beast Boost can produce a safe sweep after the first controlled knockout, but the player's goal should be to deny opponents turns rather than expecting this extremely frail Ultra Beast to survive mistakes.

pokemon.name: Blacephalon
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Blacephalon is a humanoid Ultra Beast whose detachable spherical head is composed of countless tiny sparks and is used as an expendable explosive weapon. It deliberately approaches targets with exaggerated, foolish-looking movements that lower their guard, then abruptly throws or detonates its own head to shock them. While the victim is startled, Blacephalon drains its vitality and converts that stolen life energy into power for itself. The head regenerates after exploding, allowing the behavior to be repeated rather than functioning as a one-time self-destructive attack. The colors and shapes of the sparks and star-like structures around its head change with its mood, giving the unusual head an expressive role as well as an offensive one. Animated canon also establishes a rivalry with Xurkitree in which the two Ultra Beasts compete to produce increasingly spectacular displays of light.

playthrough: Zeraora is a single-stage Electric Mythical Pokémon and historically was event-only in Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon and Sword/Shield, making it unavailable to a normal first playthrough without a distribution or transfer; Pokémon Legends: Z-A – Mega Dimension finally gives the species a current in-game encounter and its own Mega Evolution. Base Zeraora is built around exceptional base 143 Speed and solid mixed offenses of 112 Attack and 102 Special Attack, with Volt Absorb providing an Electric immunity and healing one quarter of maximum HP when struck by an Electric move in games that use conventional Abilities. Plasma Fists is its signature physical Electric attack at 100 power and perfect accuracy, while Close Combat, Knock Off, Play Rough, Grass Knot, and Volt Switch give it unusually broad ways to punish Ground-types or other conventional Electric checks. Its only normal type weakness is Ground, but 88/75/80 bulk is merely average, so Zeraora is safest when it uses Speed and pivoting rather than repeatedly absorbing neutral hits. Mega Zeraora remains pure Electric but rises to 157 Attack, 147 Special Attack, and 153 Speed for a 700 base-stat total, massively strengthening both physical and mixed offense without adding defensive bulk. Because Legends: Z-A uses a different real-time battle system and does not reproduce conventional competitive Ability mechanics exactly, the Mega form is best treated as a current offensive transformation rather than simply assuming that every older turn-based Zeraora strategy transfers unchanged. Jolly is the clearest Nature for conventional physical Zeraora, while Naive or Hasty can legitimately support established mixed sets that use Grass Knot or other special coverage.
competitive: Zeraora's competitive history improved dramatically between its first two generations. In Generation VII it was a UU Pokémon: base 143 Speed let it outrun threats such as Mega Manectric, Latias, Gengar, and Starmie, while Plasma Fists, Close Combat, Knock Off, Grass Knot, and Volt Switch made it a flexible offensive pivot, but its modest bulk and only good rather than overwhelming Attack kept it from establishing itself as a top OU staple. Sword and Shield transformed that reputation, and Zeraora became a genuine OU Pokémon and one of the metagame's premier offensive pivots because it naturally outran Dragapult, Weavile, Tornadus-T, and most other unboosted threats. Heavy-Duty Boots made repeated pivoting easier, Volt Absorb punished opposing Volt Switch, Knock Off generated long-term progress, and Close Combat or Grass Knot prevented many Ground-types and Steel-types from serving as completely safe answers. Bulk Up sets offered a second identity beyond pure pivoting and could overwhelm some defensive checks that were comfortable against immediate attacks. Mega Zeraora is a newly introduced 2025–2026 form rather than an established historical competitive archetype; its 157 Attack, 147 Special Attack, and 153 Speed clearly produce a much higher offensive ceiling, but its long-term tier stability and tournament reputation are still developing and should not be projected backward onto base Zeraora's record. The important historical distinction is therefore base Zeraora's rise from a strong Generation VII UU attacker into an elite Generation VIII OU speed-control and momentum Pokémon.
nuzlocke: Zeraora is exceptionally safe offensively when legitimately obtainable because base 143 Speed lets it move first against almost every ordinary unboosted opponent, reducing the number of turns in which its merely average defenses matter. Volt Absorb creates a complete Electric immunity and heals Zeraora in conventional Ability-based games, making correctly predicted Electric moves some of the safest possible switch opportunities. Plasma Fists is ideal for permadeath play because it combines high power and perfect accuracy without recoil, while Knock Off and Volt Switch provide utility without requiring a risky setup turn. Close Combat is powerful but lowers both defenses, so after using it Zeraora becomes far more vulnerable if another opponent enters or the expected knockout fails; Grass Knot can sometimes answer heavy Ground-types without taking that penalty. Ground attacks remain the central danger and can be especially punishing because moves such as Earthquake are both common and powerful, while Zeraora's Speed offers no protection when switching directly into one. Mega Zeraora's even greater Speed and offenses reduce the chance that an opponent gets to attack, but its defensive stats do not improve, so Mega Evolution amplifies the same fast-hit-first strategy rather than turning Zeraora into a safe tank.

pokemon.name: Zeraora
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Zeraora is an Electric-type Mythical Pokémon that lacks a conventional electricity-generating organ and instead gathers and stores electrical energy from outside sources. Strong currents released from the pads on its limbs create powerful magnetic fields that help it levitate and propel itself at extraordinary speeds, with lightning flashing and thunder sounding as it runs. Its claws can be electrified for close combat, and even an opponent that avoids the physical slash may still be struck by sparks thrown from the attack. Accounts portray Zeraora as capable of moving with lightning-like speed, and more recent ecological material places it among the fastest known Pokémon. Although often elusive, Zeraora has occasionally appeared around towns either seeking battles or serving as a bodyguard for humans, showing that the species is not uniformly hostile or isolated. Its origin remains mysterious in the core games, although one manga adaptation relates a story in which a lightning strike on an erupting volcano created the first Zeraora.

pokemon.name: Zeraora
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Mega Evolution removes an internal limiter that normally restrains the enormous quantity of electricity stored inside Zeraora's body. Mega Zeraora can accumulate energy equivalent to roughly ten lightning strikes, with the most highly charged areas of its body glowing light blue and its fur darkening and becoming more dramatically shaped around the head and upper body. When it stops holding that energy back, official material describes it as belonging to the strongest class of Electric-type Pokémon and capable of defeating multiple nearby opponents in a single attack. The form does not simply obey commands like a machine: Mega Zeraora releases its full energy according to its own judgment, meaning a Trainer must either trust its timing or achieve an exceptionally close synchronization with it. This behavioral requirement makes Mega Evolution an amplification of Zeraora's independent fighting instincts as well as a removal of its physical electrical limiter.

playthrough: Meltan and Melmetal have one of the most unusual evolution systems in the series: Meltan cannot evolve in any core-series game and must instead be evolved in Pokémon GO by spending 400 Meltan Candy, after which Melmetal can be transferred into compatible games. That restriction means a player using Meltan directly in Let's Go, Sword/Shield, or later compatible titles cannot simply level it into Melmetal, making external game connectivity a practical requirement rather than an optional shortcut. Meltan itself has very low overall stats and is poorly suited to normal battling, while Melmetal becomes a massive physical tank with base 135 HP, 143 Attack, and 143 Defense but only base 34 Speed and 65 Special Defense. Double Iron Bash is Melmetal's defining move: it strikes twice, each hit benefits from Iron Fist, and each hit can flinch, giving the move exceptional damage and utility despite Melmetal's low Speed; Earthquake, Thunder Punch, Ice Punch, and Superpower or similar coverage handle many Steel resists. Pure Steel supplies a Poison immunity and ten resistances while leaving only Fighting, Fire, and Ground weaknesses, but the low Special Defense means strong special attacks of those types remain dangerous even through Melmetal's huge HP. Gigantamax Melmetal was available in Sword and Shield to specimens with the Gigantamax Factor and replaced its Steel-type Max Move with G-Max Meltdown, which damages the target and inflicts Torment-like move restriction; the transformation lasts only three turns like other Dynamax states. Brave is excellent for Trick Room-oriented Melmetal, while Adamant maximizes ordinary damage without further sacrificing an already minimal Speed stat.
competitive: Melmetal immediately became a major competitive force rather than following the low-tier trajectory of many newly introduced Mythical Pokémon. In Let's Go Pikachu/Eevee OU it was one of the central Pokémon in the entire metagame because its huge HP, Attack, Defense, rare Steel typing, Double Iron Bash, Earthquake, and elemental punch coverage let it check major offensive threats while threatening almost every switch-in. Sword and Shield gave Melmetal a turbulent but ultimately important OU history: it was initially quickbanned shortly after release, later retested, eventually reintroduced as the metagame developed, and spent a long period as one of OU's strongest physical tanks and wallbreakers. Double Iron Bash is the core reason the stat line is so oppressive, combining enormous Iron Fist-boosted Steel damage with two separate contact hits and flinch chances, while Thunder Punch, Ice Punch, Earthquake, and Superpower make conventional Steel resistances unreliable answers. Its huge physical bulk can survive attacks from offensive Pokémon that would destroy most wallbreakers, but base 65 Special Defense, base 34 Speed, lack of reliable recovery, and susceptibility to repeated hazards or special Fire-, Ground-, and Fighting-type damage keep it from being universally safe. Gigantamax Melmetal was not part of standard Smogon OU play and is listed separately in unrestricted formats; in official Dynamax-enabled environments, G-Max Meltdown added a unique disruptive effect but did not replace the importance of ordinary Melmetal's Double Iron Bash identity. Melmetal is unavailable in standard Scarlet and Violet, although it is again obtainable in the current Legends: Z-A environment, so its longest established traditional singles history remains centered on Let's Go and Sword/Shield.
nuzlocke: Melmetal is an exceptional physical Nuzlocke tank once the player has solved the external evolution requirement, but Meltan itself is weak enough that attempting to use it as though normal leveling will eventually produce Melmetal is a serious mistake. Pure Steel typing gives Melmetal a Poison immunity and a vast resistance profile, while 135 HP and 143 Defense provide enormous margin against physical neutral attacks and many resisted hits. Double Iron Bash is accurate and powerful, and because it hits twice it can break substitutes, Sturdy, Focus Sash, and similar one-hit protections before the second strike, making it unusually reliable at finishing certain opponents. The main danger is special damage: base 65 Special Defense is much weaker than the physical side, and strong Fire-, Fighting-, or Ground-type special coverage can remove large portions of Melmetal's HP before its low base 34 Speed allows it to respond. Superpower and similar defense-lowering coverage should be used cautiously in multi-Pokémon battles, while recoil-free punch coverage and Earthquake generally preserve Melmetal's excellent staying power better. Gigantamax can provide three turns of doubled HP in Sword/Shield challenge formats and G-Max Meltdown adds disruption, but the player should remember that the temporary HP increase disappears afterward and does not solve Melmetal's long-term lack of reliable recovery.

pokemon.name: Meltan
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Meltan has a body of liquid metal—official concept material identifies the substance with gallium—and a hard golden hexagonal nut surrounding a floating eye-like sphere. Its liquid body can corrode and absorb other metals, which Meltan circulates internally to generate the electricity used as both metabolic energy and an offensive discharge from its eye. Meltan commonly live and forage in groups, can call one another by spinning their hexagonal heads to create sound, and have also used the same motion as an expression of affection. Their group behavior is directly connected to evolution: when the proper time comes, one especially strong Meltan absorbs the others and becomes Melmetal. The life cycle also runs in reverse on a much longer timescale, because an aging Melmetal eventually rusts and falls apart and the resulting metal shards can later be reborn as new Meltan. Ancient followers of Melmetal preserved Meltan associated with that cycle inside Mystery Boxes, connecting the species' modern reappearance with human religious or cultural practices from thousands of years earlier.

pokemon.name: Melmetal
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Melmetal is a massive being of liquid metal and individually mobile hexagonal nuts, with a body strong enough to form enormous arms while remaining flexible enough to stretch and reshape during attacks. Ancient people revered it for an apparently unique ability to create iron from nothing and used metal shed by Melmetal to manufacture special tools. Professor Willow's research places the ancient species in secluded wooded land rich in magnetite-bearing sedimentary rock, providing an environmental source closely associated with its metal-based physiology. Melmetal's signature punches use centrifugal force from its heavy rotating arms, and Pokédex accounts describe those blows as among the strongest punches produced by any Pokémon. The species disappeared for roughly 3,000 years before returning, and its life cycle is unusual: at the end of its lifespan the body rusts and collapses into fragments that can eventually produce new Meltan. This makes Melmetal both the product of a group of Meltan and, after death, a source from which future Meltan can arise.

pokemon.name: Melmetal
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Gigantamax energy transforms Melmetal into the cyclopean giant described in old legends, greatly enlarging the central body and rearranging its hexagonal nuts into massive hands, feet, shoulders, and armored structures. Its normally flexible liquid-metal arms can extend over great distances, allowing Gigantamax Melmetal to strike without bringing its entire body close to the opponent. By bringing the giant nuts in its hands together, it can form even larger fists for exceptionally powerful punches. The rapid flow of liquid metal through its enormous body also generates electrical energy that can be fired from the opening in its abdomen as beams powerful enough to vaporize an opponent or even an entire hill. Its signature G-Max Meltdown therefore reflects a form whose exaggerated liquid-metal circulation produces both enormous mechanical striking force and destructive electrical output.

playthrough: Grookey evolves into Thwackey at level 16 and Rillaboom at level 35, giving the line a normal starter progression and allowing its final stage to contribute through a large portion of both Sword/Shield and any later game in which the family is obtained early enough. Rillaboom is a bulky physical Grass-type with base 125 Attack, 100 HP, and 90 Defense; Drum Beating provides accurate Grass STAB while lowering the target's Speed, and stronger options such as Wood Hammer trade substantially more damage for recoil. Its Hidden Ability Grassy Surge is transformative: entering battle automatically creates Grassy Terrain, boosting grounded Grass attacks, restoring grounded Pokémon each turn, and weakening Earthquake, Bulldoze, and Magnitude, while Grassy Glide gains priority under the terrain. That combination makes Rillaboom much more useful than a typical slowish Grass attacker, although the Hidden Ability is not guaranteed on an ordinary starter and therefore should not be assumed in every playthrough. Pure Grass leaves weaknesses to Bug, Fire, Flying, Ice, and Poison, but useful Water, Ground, Electric, and Grass resistances plus terrain recovery give Rillaboom good staying power against favorable opponents. In Sword/Shield, a compatible Rillaboom can gain the Gigantamax Factor through Max Soup in the Isle of Armor; Gigantamax Rillaboom's G-Max Drum Solo provides exceptionally powerful Grass damage during Dynamax but is available only within Generation VIII's Dynamax rules. Adamant is excellent for maximizing Rillaboom's physical damage, while Jolly is genuinely useful when preserving base 85 Speed against nearby offensive benchmarks matters.
competitive: Rillaboom became one of the defining offensive Grass-types of Generation VIII after Grassy Surge and Grassy Glide were released, and Smogon classifies it as OU in both Sword/Shield and Scarlet/Violet. In Sword/Shield OU, terrain-boosted Grassy Glide had 70 base power and priority, letting Rillaboom revenge kill faster attackers while Choice Band or Swords Dance sets also threatened defensive teams with Wood Hammer, Knock Off, Superpower or Drain Punch, and U-turn. Grassy Terrain made the Pokémon valuable beyond its own damage by healing grounded teammates and weakening Earthquake, which created strong defensive synergy with partners such as Heatran, Melmetal, and Galarian Slowking. It also became a major doubles and VGC support Pokémon because Fake Out, Grassy Surge, Grassy Glide, Wood Hammer, and U-turn combine terrain control, priority, disruption, damage, and pivoting in one slot. Scarlet and Violet reduced Grassy Glide to 55 base power, but Rillaboom remains OU and a premier wallbreaker, revenge killer, and terrain setter; Knock Off and U-turn continue to make conventional Grass-resistant switch-ins pay a long-term cost. Its recurring limitations are the many common Grass resistances, vulnerability to Fire-, Flying-, Ice-, Poison-, and Bug-type attacks, and dependence on contact or recoil-heavy moves for maximum damage. Rillaboom's history is therefore not simply that of a strong starter: Grassy Surge fundamentally changed its role into one of the most important terrain-based offensive and support Pokémon of Generations VIII and IX.
nuzlocke: The Grookey line is a dependable Nuzlocke starter because it evolves at ordinary levels, has good physical bulk, and gains strong reliable Grass damage without requiring unusual items or trade mechanics. Rillaboom's base 100 HP and 90 Defense give it more margin for an incorrect physical damage estimate than many offensive starters, while Water and Ground resistance creates especially useful switch opportunities in ordinary play. If Grassy Surge is legitimately available, passive terrain recovery improves long-term survival and the reduction to Earthquake, Bulldoze, and Magnitude damage can protect both Rillaboom and grounded teammates from some of the most dangerous physical attacks in the series. Grassy Glide is an excellent permadeath tool under terrain because priority can remove a weakened faster threat before it attacks, while Drum Beating is accurate and can lower an opponent's Speed without requiring a separate support turn. Wood Hammer is considerably riskier because recoil can erase the health advantage gained from Grassy Terrain, and Superpower or similar self-debuffing coverage can leave Rillaboom vulnerable after a knockout. Its five weaknesses are common enough that blind switching remains dangerous, especially against Fire, Flying, and Ice coverage, so the safest use is as a bulky attacker that exploits known resistances rather than as a universal tank.

pokemon.name: Grookey
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Grookey carries a wooden stick taken from a branch in the forest where its troop lived; exposure to the energy inside Grookey makes the stick harder and more flexible than an ordinary twig. When Grookey rhythmically beats the stick against surrounding objects, the released energy can stimulate plants, causing grass to grow and wilted leaves or flowers to regain their color; animation has even shown the effect revitalizing weakened plantlike Pokémon. Its green fur can create energy from sunlight in a photosynthesis-like process, connecting the line's musical behavior directly to plant energy rather than making the Grass typing purely decorative. Grookey is extremely curious, enjoys music and dancing, and likes climbing to high places. The species has also been established in Blueberry Academy's Terarium outside its native Galar.

pokemon.name: Thwackey
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: When Grookey evolves, its single stick splits into two, and Thwackey develops an intense lifelong focus on rhythm. The faster and more skillfully an individual can beat its sticks, the more respect it receives from other Thwackey, turning percussion ability into a direct social-status signal. Thwackey constantly rehearses rhythms during everyday movement, swaying as it walks and drumming almost compulsively to sharpen its sense of timing. In battle it can become so absorbed in a fast rhythm that it fails to notice an opponent has already been knocked out and may even ignore its Trainer's commands while continuing the performance. Animation also depicts Thwackey grooming companions to cheer them up, using physical care as an expression of friendship and trust.

pokemon.name: Rillaboom
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Rillaboom carries a drum made from a special tree stump and can direct the stump's roots through the rhythm it plays, turning percussion into a form of plant manipulation during battle. Troops settle leadership challenges through drumming contests, and the Rillaboom with the greatest technique becomes the group's leader rather than simply the physically strongest individual. Despite its imposing build, Rillaboom is normally calm and values social harmony; it watches carefully for discord within the troop and disciplines members that threaten group unity. That restraint disappears when its companions are endangered, because Rillaboom is described as fighting ferociously to defend its allies. Its social structure therefore combines artistic skill, hierarchy, discipline, and group defense in a way that makes drumming central to both ecology and combat.

pokemon.name: Rillaboom
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Gigantamax energy causes Rillaboom and its stump to become integrated into an enormous drum kit resembling a forest of percussion instruments. Its leafy growth expands into four additional arm-like structures that wield drumsticks as naturally as its own limbs, while accumulated energy drives it to perform techniques beyond what ordinary Rillaboom can produce. The resulting sound can carry across oceans and into distant regions, and official accounts claim that listeners can be compelled to dance uncontrollably to the rhythm. Gigantamax Rillaboom thus amplifies the species' normal relationship with rhythm and vegetation into a temporary form capable of influencing enormous areas through sound.

playthrough: Scorbunny evolves into Raboot at level 16 and Cinderace at level 35, producing a fast physical Fire-type starter with one of the strongest offensive stat profiles among Galar's normal story options. Cinderace's base 119 Speed and 116 Attack let it move first against most ordinary opponents, while Pyro Ball provides exceptionally strong physical Fire STAB and U-turn, Sucker Punch, Fighting coverage, and other physical moves broaden its matchups. Pyro Ball is powerful but only 90% accurate, so Flame Charge or other accurate Fire attacks may be preferable when the extra power is unnecessary; High Jump Kick is even riskier because a miss or immunity causes severe crash damage. Court Change is uniquely useful in battles involving entry hazards, screens, Tailwind, or similar field effects because it swaps those effects between sides rather than merely removing them. Libero is the line's outstanding Hidden Ability: in Generation VIII it changed Cinderace's type before every move it used, effectively granting same-type attack bonus on nearly its entire movepool, while Generation IX nerfed the Ability so it activates only once each time Cinderace enters battle. In Sword/Shield, Max Soup can give Cinderace the Gigantamax Factor; G-Max Fireball provides enormous Fire damage during Dynamax and ignores many defensive Ability interactions, but that transformation is restricted to Generation VIII's Dynamax system. Jolly is normally the safest Nature because preserving base 119 Speed is one of Cinderace's greatest advantages, while Adamant is a legitimate choice when the team already controls Speed and wants maximum physical damage.
competitive: Cinderace has had an unusually dramatic competitive history for a starter Pokémon. Before Libero was released in Sword/Shield, Blaze Cinderace already had utility through its high Speed, U-turn, Heavy-Duty Boots, and exclusive Court Change, but Libero transformed it into one of the strongest offensive pivots in the metagame by granting STAB to every move and repeatedly changing its defensive typing. The resulting combination of Pyro Ball, High Jump Kick, Gunk Shot, Sucker Punch, U-turn, and flexible typing was strong enough for the SS OU council to quickban Cinderace in August 2020, and after later metagame changes and a retest it was banned from OU again in February 2021 and classified as Uber. Even in Ubers, Cinderace retained a niche because Court Change could reverse hazards and screens while its Speed and Libero coverage pressured Pokémon that slower utility Fire-types could not. Generation IX nerfed Libero to trigger only once per switch-in, substantially reducing the constant type manipulation that made the original form oppressive; Cinderace is currently OU in Scarlet/Violet rather than Uber. Modern sets use Pyro Ball, U-turn, Court Change, Sucker Punch, Will-O-Wisp, and varied coverage to function as a fast offensive pivot and unusually effective answer to hazard-stacking teams. Its competitive identity therefore changed from useful utility starter, to ban-worthy Gen VIII Libero attacker, to a strong but more manageable Gen IX OU pivot after the Ability nerf.
nuzlocke: Cinderace is an excellent Nuzlocke attacker because base 119 Speed allows it to avoid damage by simply moving first and securing knockouts, but some of its strongest signature options introduce significant variance. Pyro Ball's 90% accuracy is usually acceptable when its extra power is necessary, but a perfectly accurate Fire move can be safer when the weaker attack still guarantees the knockout. High Jump Kick is especially dangerous because missing or striking an immune target causes heavy crash damage, making more reliable Fighting coverage preferable in permadeath play whenever available. U-turn is one of the line's best safety tools because Cinderace can exploit its Speed to deal damage and leave before the opponent acts, while Sucker Punch provides emergency priority against faster or boosted enemies but can fail if the target uses a non-attacking move. Court Change can rescue a team from accumulated hazards or opposing screens without spending several separate removal turns, though it must be used carefully because it swaps beneficial field effects as well as harmful ones. Libero can improve offensive coverage and alter defensive weaknesses, but in Generation IX it triggers only once per switch-in, so the player must track Cinderace's current type rather than assuming every subsequent move will change it again.

pokemon.name: Scorbunny
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Scorbunny stores fire energy in a sac inside its chest and activates that energy through movement, so running as a warm-up literally prepares its body for stronger Fire attacks. Special pads on the soles of its feet and on its nose heat up as the internal fire energy circulates, and the footpads can become hot enough to ignite small fires or burn an opponent with a kick. Its powerful legs are also used to leap and run rapidly around opponents, disorienting them before it attacks. Animation has shown the heat from its feet thawing other beings trapped in ice, giving the same adaptation a practical noncombat use. Scorbunny is normally considered uncommon in the wild and is strongly associated with Trainers, although populations have since been established in Blueberry Academy's Terarium.

pokemon.name: Raboot
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Raboot's dense fur insulates it from cold and helps retain body heat, allowing the fire generated through its forehead and feet to become hotter than it was as Scorbunny. It develops its kicking skill through constant practice, knocking Berries from branches and then juggling them with its feet to improve coordination. Raboot deliberately keeps its arms tucked inside its thick chest fur while training, both to conserve heat and to force itself to rely on its footwork rather than its hands. Once sufficiently heated, the forehead can also deliver powerful headbutts rather than serving only as a passive source of warmth. The species takes obvious pride in its kicking ability, making disciplined physical training a defining behavior of this developmental stage.

pokemon.name: Cinderace
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Cinderace turns ordinary pebbles into burning projectiles by juggling them with its feet until they ignite, then launches the resulting fireballs with highly controlled spins that make the shots difficult to evade. Its anatomy is specialized for athletic movement: a strong core, excellent balance, explosive jumping ability, and exceptionally powerful legs allow it to deliver effective kicks from almost any posture. It uses feints and elaborate footwork to mislead opponents before attacking, combining showmanship with genuine tactical movement. Cinderace becomes energized when spectators cheer for it and may begin showboating when excitement becomes excessive, although it remains capable of following a trusted Trainer's instructions accurately. When Libero changes its type in animated canon, the flame-like hair on its head can visibly change color, providing a physical indicator of the otherwise battle-mechanical transformation.

pokemon.name: Cinderace
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Gigantamax Cinderace stands atop an enormous fireball produced by Gigantamax energy, with the projectile sometimes exceeding 300 feet in diameter. Its control over the ball becomes so refined that official descriptions liken the projectile to having a mind of its own, allowing it to pursue an opponent rather than travel along a simple straight trajectory. Gigantamax Cinderace is also credited with the strongest leg strength of any Pokémon, and can overpower Dynamax opponents with kicks even without relying on the gigantic fireball. The form therefore magnifies both halves of ordinary Cinderace's fighting style: precision projectile control and extreme kicking power.

playthrough: Sobble evolves into Drizzile at level 16 and Inteleon at level 35, ultimately producing a very fast special Water attacker rather than a bulky or physically oriented starter. Inteleon's base 125 Special Attack and 120 Speed let it outrun and heavily damage most ordinary opponents, while Surf provides accurate repeatable Water STAB and Hydro Pump trades reliability for significantly more power. Snipe Shot is a useful signature alternative because it has good accuracy, a heightened critical-hit rate, and ignores effects that would redirect the attack in doubles, while U-turn lets Inteleon escape Water-resistant opponents without surrendering momentum. Its Hidden Ability Sniper increases critical-hit damage and can support specialized Focus Energy or high-critical-hit strategies, but this requires more setup and item support than a normal playthrough usually needs. Pure Water leaves only Electric and Grass weaknesses and grants four useful resistances, but 70/65/65 bulk is fragile enough that Inteleon should rely on Speed rather than repeatedly absorbing neutral attacks. In Sword/Shield, Max Soup can unlock Gigantamax Inteleon; G-Max Hydrosnipe offers enormous Water damage during Dynamax, but the form exists only under Generation VIII's Gigantamax mechanics. Timid is normally the safest Nature because maintaining base 120 Speed is central to Inteleon's survival, while Modest is a reasonable alternative when the team already provides speed control.
competitive: Inteleon has never approached the competitive dominance of Rillaboom or Cinderace, but it has maintained a legitimate lower-tier niche as a very fast special Water wallbreaker and pivot. In Sword/Shield it was classified PUBL and received substantial NU use, where base 120 Speed let it outrun offensive threats such as Salazzle, Tauros, and Starmie while Choice Specs Hydro Pump could heavily punish teams lacking a sturdy Water check. U-turn was important because common Water-resistant or Water-immune Pokémon could otherwise halt its progress, allowing Inteleon to preserve momentum rather than repeatedly guess with coverage. Sniper enabled specialized critical-hit strategies with Focus Energy and appropriate items, but those sets generally required more setup than straightforward Choice Specs offense and never made Inteleon a top-tier staple. Scarlet/Violet again lists Inteleon as PUBL with NU analysis, where its high Speed and Special Attack remain its defining strengths but competition from other offensive Water-types and reliance on Hydro Pump for maximum damage limit consistency. Its poor physical bulk and weakness to priority also constrain sweeping potential even when it wins the natural Speed race. Historically, Inteleon is best described as a credible lower-tier fast Water breaker whose excellent offensive numbers are held back by shallow defensive utility and competition rather than a weak Pokémon with no competitive niche.
nuzlocke: Inteleon is a strong but low-margin Nuzlocke starter because its best defense is usually moving first rather than surviving an unexpected attack. Base 120 Speed allows it to remove many opponents before they act, while accurate Surf or Snipe Shot can avoid the miss chance attached to Hydro Pump in situations where maximum power is unnecessary. Pure Water typing is simple and useful, with only Grass and Electric weaknesses, but base 70 HP and 65 defenses mean even strong neutral attacks can be dangerous if Inteleon fails to secure a knockout. U-turn is especially valuable for escaping poor matchups after dealing chip damage, and the line's high Speed frequently lets that pivot happen before the opponent gets a turn. Critical-hit strategies built around Sniper can produce impressive damage, but they normally require setup or item dependence and should not be treated as more reliable than straightforward attacking unless the critical rate has actually been made deterministic. Hydro Pump's 80% accuracy is a substantial permadeath risk, so Surf or Snipe Shot is usually preferable whenever the lower power still produces a guaranteed knockout.

pokemon.name: Sobble
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Sobble is a cautious, timid lizard Pokémon whose skin changes color when it becomes wet, allowing it to blend into the surrounding environment with chameleon-like camouflage. Nervousness causes it to secrete large quantities of water from its body like sweat, which helps the camouflage effect become strong enough that Sobble can appear nearly invisible. When seriously frightened it cries, releasing tears containing chemicals said to affect nearby creatures as strongly as the fumes from chopping one hundred onions; everyone around it may begin crying uncontrollably, giving Sobble an opportunity to escape. Despite its timid temperament, it has excellent innate aim and can shoot Berries down with precise bullets of water from its mouth. The species can move both on two legs and on all fours and uses its chameleon-like limbs to cling to walls and climb.

pokemon.name: Drizzile
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Drizzile secretes moisture from specialized pores in its palms and shapes the liquid into water balloons that it throws as weapons. It is highly intelligent and capable of using its surroundings for hit-and-run tactics, but it is also notably lazy and avoids unnecessary effort whenever possible. Rather than relying on constant direct confrontation, Drizzile establishes homes in tree hollows or rocky spaces and surrounds its territory with traps intended to keep enemies away. Its long mucus-coated tongue can strike prey with extreme speed before Drizzile finishes the target with more deliberate attacks. Like Sobble and Inteleon, it can camouflage itself when wet, giving the entire evolutionary family a continuing stealth adaptation.

pokemon.name: Inteleon
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Inteleon has numerous concealed biological tools distributed across its body, giving it a deliberate spy-like hunting and combat style. Special nictitating membranes over its eyes function as analytical lenses capable of detecting body heat and identifying weak points, after which Inteleon can fire pressurized water from its fingertips at roughly Mach 3. The membrane along its back can extend into a gliding surface, while the dark strip along its tail conceals retractable blade-like frills that function as close-range weapons. It is highly intelligent and plans encounters carefully in order to achieve a fast, decisive result rather than relying only on reflexes. Despite its refined and chivalrous demeanor, Inteleon retains some of Drizzile's laziness and may slack off whenever it believes its Trainer is not watching.

pokemon.name: Inteleon
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Gigantamaxing amplifies Inteleon's hidden sensory and ballistic adaptations rather than simply enlarging its body. Its long tail coils into a towering platform from which it operates like a sniper, and it can form a water-based harpoon that attaches to a fingertip before firing. Enhanced membranes and crest structures can measure temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind, and humidity, allowing Inteleon to calculate gravity and environmental conditions before taking a shot. Those calculations permit water projectiles traveling around Mach 7 to strike even a moving Berry from roughly nine miles away, giving Gigantamax Inteleon one of the most precisely quantified long-range attacks in the Pokédex.

playthrough: Skwovet is available almost immediately in Sword/Shield and evolves into Greedent at level 24, so the family offers an early Normal-type option whose final stage arrives before the middle of the story. Greedent's base 120 HP and 95 Defense make it far tougher than its appearance suggests, while base 95 Attack is adequate for Body Slam, Facade, Crunch, Earthquake, and other physical coverage; the major limitation is an extremely low base 20 Speed. Cheek Pouch is the line's most distinctive Ability because eating a Berry restores one third of maximum HP in addition to the Berry's normal effect, allowing Sitrus Berry to provide unusually large bursts of healing. Belly Drum can combine with Sitrus Berry and Cheek Pouch to restore much of the HP sacrificed while immediately maximizing Attack, but spending half of maximum HP on setup is inherently dangerous during a normal playthrough and is rarely necessary against ordinary trainers. Stuff Cheeks consumes the held Berry and sharply raises Defense, offering a safer defensive use of the same food-storage mechanics when the player wants Greedent to tank physical attacks. Pure Normal provides a Ghost immunity and only one weakness in Fighting, but no standard resistances, so Greedent's survival depends more on raw bulk and healing than on advantageous typing. Adamant is useful for straightforward physical sets, while Brave is appropriate under Trick Room because Greedent is already among the slowest fully evolved Pokémon in the game.
competitive: Greedent has remained a low-tier competitive Pokémon in both generations in which it has appeared, but its combination of high HP, respectable physical bulk, Belly Drum or Swords Dance, and Cheek Pouch gives it a recognizable setup niche. In Sword/Shield it is classified ZU, where the most famous strategy combines Belly Drum with Sitrus Berry and Cheek Pouch: dropping to half HP activates the Berry, and Cheek Pouch adds another large heal while Greedent jumps immediately to maximum Attack. That interaction looks stronger on paper than it often performs in practice, because base 20 Speed leaves Greedent easy to revenge kill and Knock Off, status, Fighting-types, and the need to find a safe setup turn all interfere with the strategy. Smogon consequently describes it as outclassed in SS ZU by more immediately useful Normal-type setup attackers rather than exaggerating the Belly Drum gimmick into a major competitive role. Scarlet/Violet also places Greedent in ZU, where its 120/95/75 bulk and Swords Dance can support a more straightforward bulky wallbreaker approach using Normal STAB, Earthquake, and Crunch, while Cheek Pouch still provides unusually strong one-time recovery. Terastallization can improve specific matchups, but it does not solve Greedent's extreme slowness or dependence on its item for the most distinctive sets. Its historical niche is therefore legitimate but narrow: Greedent can absorb surprising amounts of damage and trade heavily after setup, but it has never been a broadly successful high-tier Pokémon.
nuzlocke: Greedent can be a surprisingly safe Nuzlocke encounter because it evolves early, has enormous HP for this stage of the game, and can obtain large bursts of healing from Berries through Cheek Pouch. Its Ghost immunity provides one completely safe switch category, while having only a single Fighting weakness keeps the type chart easy to manage even though Normal supplies no conventional resistances. Sitrus Berry plus Cheek Pouch can restore a very large fraction of maximum HP automatically, creating emergency survival insurance without requiring Greedent to spend a turn using a healing move. Belly Drum is far less attractive in permadeath play because voluntarily losing half of maximum HP creates an immediate critical-hit and priority window even if the Berry subsequently restores much of that health. Stuff Cheeks is a safer way to exploit a Berry when physical defense is the priority, while accurate Body Slam, Crunch, and Earthquake-type coverage avoid the recoil or crash risk associated with more extreme options. Base 20 Speed means Greedent almost always absorbs an attack before responding, so strong special Fighting coverage and repeated neutral special attacks remain meaningful dangers despite the large HP total.

pokemon.name: Skwovet
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Skwovet has cheeks capable of stretching to many times their normal volume and uses them to carry large quantities of Berries, with additional food temporarily packed into its thick tail fur when the cheeks are full. Its constant feeding makes it more resilient than its small body suggests, but it becomes visibly anxious whenever its cheeks are empty and may stuff them with pebbles if no Berries are available. Skwovet frequently enters farms in search of food and continuously hides extra supplies because it remains worried about future hunger even after eating. When it finishes eating, it spits Berry seeds into rich soil, effectively helping establish future Berry plants while replenishing the same resource it depends upon. Gumshoos is a documented natural predator of Skwovet.

pokemon.name: Greedent
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Greedent's enormous tail functions as a food store, and individuals pack it with so many Berries that the fruit frequently spills out while they move, battle, or are struck. Despite its obsession with gathering food, Greedent is inattentive enough that it often fails to notice when stored Berries fall from the tail. Its powerful front teeth can gnaw through even extremely hard Berry shells, allowing it to consume resources that would be inaccessible to weaker rodents. Greedent is attracted strongly enough to Bounsweet's sweet aroma that it may even stash a Bounsweet inside its tail along with ordinary food. The species' biology therefore exaggerates Skwovet's food-hoarding behavior into a combination of extreme storage capacity, gluttony, and unusually strong gnawing anatomy.

playthrough: Rookidee appears on the earliest routes of Sword/Shield and also very early in Scarlet/Violet, evolves into Corvisquire at level 18, and reaches Corviknight at level 38, making the family one of the most practical long-term regional bird choices in either game. Rookidee and Corvisquire are pure Flying, but Corviknight adds Steel typing and immediately gains one of the best defensive type combinations available: immunity to Ground and Poison, numerous resistances, and only Fire and Electric weaknesses. Base 98 HP, 105 Defense, and 85 Special Defense make Corviknight naturally durable, while Brave Bird, Drill Peck, Body Press, U-turn, Iron Defense, Roost, and Defog in appropriate generations let it attack, pivot, heal, remove hazards, or become a physical wall. Pressure is useful for exhausting low-PP attacks, Unnerve can deny opposing Berries, and the Hidden Ability Mirror Armor reflects stat-stage reductions back to their source, making Intimidate and moves such as Screech or Mystical Fire much less comfortable for the opponent. Brave Bird's recoil can be unnecessary in a normal story battle, so Drill Peck or another accurate non-recoil Flying move may be safer when the damage is sufficient; Body Press becomes especially potent after Iron Defense because it uses Corviknight's Defense for damage calculation. Corviknight can also Gigantamax in Sword/Shield if it has the proper factor, gaining G-Max Wind Rage and a heavily reinforced temporary body, but ordinary Corviknight is already one of the most dependable defensive Pokémon obtainable during the main Galar story. Impish is excellent for emphasizing physical defense and Body Press, while Careful is useful when the team needs Corviknight to handle more special attacks.
competitive: Corviknight has been an OU defensive staple in both Sword/Shield and Scarlet/Violet, giving it one of the most consistently successful singles careers among Generation VIII's ordinary non-legendary Pokémon. In Sword/Shield OU, Steel/Flying typing, 98/105/85 bulk, Roost, Defog, U-turn, Pressure, and Body Press allowed it to compress hazard removal, physical walling, and slow pivoting into one slot while checking numerous Ground-, Grass-, Fairy-, and Steel-oriented threats. Pressure was particularly valuable in prolonged games because repeated switching and Roost could exhaust Stealth Rock, Stone Edge, or other low-PP moves, while Mirror Armor offered an alternative against Intimidate and stat-lowering strategies. Iron Defense plus Body Press created a win condition that converted defensive boosts directly into Fighting damage, while Brave Bird prevented many Fighting- and Grass-types from treating Corviknight as passive. Scarlet/Violet again classifies Corviknight as OU, where it remains a premier defensive Pokémon and pivot despite stronger competition for hazard-control roles; Defog, U-turn, Roost, Brave Bird, Body Press, Rocky Helmet, and Terastallization all support different defensive structures. The species also had official-format value in Dynamax-era play, with Gigantamax Corviknight's G-Max Wind Rage providing a unique field-clearing effect, though standard singles typically valued ordinary Corviknight's defensive consistency more than Gigantamax itself. Its long-term weaknesses are straightforward—Fire and Electric attacks, powerful special wallbreakers, and passive wear from Knock Off or status—but the rarity of those flaws relative to its enormous resistance profile explains its sustained OU status.
nuzlocke: Corviknight is one of the safest regional birds for Nuzlocke play because the family is available early, evolves without special requirements, and eventually gains exceptional defensive typing and reliable recovery. Ground and Poison immunities create completely safe switch opportunities when movesets are known, while its large collection of resistances and strong physical Defense allow it to absorb many other attacks with significant margin for error. Mirror Armor is particularly useful because it reflects opposing stat reductions, preventing effects such as Intimidate from quietly reducing Corviknight's damage and punishing several enemy debuff strategies automatically. Roost greatly improves long-term survival, and Iron Defense plus Body Press can defeat physical opponents without exposing Corviknight to recoil; by contrast, Brave Bird should be used cautiously because repeated recoil can unnecessarily shorten the life of an otherwise exceptional defensive Pokémon. U-turn can safely bring frailer teammates into battle after Corviknight absorbs the opposing attack first, turning its moderate base 67 Speed into an advantage for defensive pivoting. Fire and Electric coverage are the principal type-chart dangers, and strong special attacks deserve more respect than physical ones, but few ordinary early-route families provide as much late-game Nuzlocke security as Corviknight.

pokemon.name: Rookidee
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Rookidee is an unusually bold and territorial small bird that willingly challenges opponents much larger and stronger than itself. Even losing contributes to its development, because it stores some of the energy gained from each battle and becomes progressively stronger through repeated confrontations. It uses nimble legwork and rapid jumps to confuse larger enemies rather than relying only on flight. Female Rookidee are described as especially fastidious and may relentlessly attack anything that dirties their wings. The species preys on Grubbin, giving it a documented predator relationship with an earlier Alolan family.

pokemon.name: Corvisquire
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Corvisquire has a proportionally large brain compared with many other bird Pokémon, and this anatomy is directly associated with exceptionally high intelligence.
