Scarlet/Violet currently places male Indeedee in PUBL and female Indeedee in ZU by singles usage, but those tier labels again fail to capture female Indeedee's much greater doubles value; Smogon's modern VGC analyses continue to describe it as exceptional redirection and Trick Room support. Male Indeedee remains the stronger independent special attacker, while female Indeedee compresses terrain setting, Follow Me, Helping Hand, Trick Room, and defensive support in a way few Pokémon can reproduce. The family's defining competitive lesson is therefore that gender is functionally important: identical typing and Ability access do not produce identical roles because the stat spreads and movepools differ meaningfully.
nuzlocke: Indeedee can be a very safe Nuzlocke Pokémon because Psychic/Normal grants a complete Ghost immunity, only two weaknesses, and good special attacking or defensive stats depending on sex. Psychic Surge improves safety for the whole grounded team by preventing opposing priority attacks and strengthening Psychic moves, removing many surprise revenge-kill scenarios while the terrain remains active. Male Indeedee's greater Speed and Special Attack make it better at ending singles matchups before taking damage, while female Indeedee's extra HP and defenses provide more margin when it must absorb attacks. Female Follow Me can be extremely valuable in double battles by redirecting attacks away from a vulnerable partner, but that role deliberately concentrates danger on Indeedee and therefore requires accurate damage planning in a permadeath run. Helping Hand and Trick Room can support allies without relying on inaccurate moves, while Healing Wish is usually inappropriate in a strict Nuzlocke because it causes Indeedee to faint by design. Dark and Bug attacks are the main direct type-chart threats, and the player should remember that Psychic Terrain protects grounded Pokémon from priority rather than making the entire team immune regardless of position. Because the two sexes have different stats and learnsets, identifying which Indeedee was caught is genuinely relevant to safe planning rather than merely cosmetic.

pokemon.name: Indeedee
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Male Indeedee are highly intelligent, service-oriented Pokémon whose upward-curving horns allow them to sense the emotions of nearby people and Pokémon. They willingly work as valets and derive energy from positive feelings, especially gratitude generated when their service makes someone happy. Indeedee can touch horns with one another to communicate and exchange information, turning the sensory structures into a social communication system as well as emotional receptors. Male individuals are particularly skilled at anticipating practical needs and are commonly associated with attentive household or personal service. Despite their preference for helping others and avoiding conflict, Indeedee can use psychic power to throw objects at anyone that disturbs their territory.

pokemon.name: Indeedee
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Female Indeedee have downward-curving horns and the same ability to sense emotions, communicate through horn contact, and gain energy from gratitude and other positive feelings. They are especially skilled at babysitting and caregiving, using their psychic perception to anticipate needs before the person or Pokémon they are watching has to ask. Female Indeedee are constantly busy seeking opportunities to serve individuals experiencing happy emotions and are strongly attached to Trainers they trust. Their behavior is normally peaceful and nurturing, but like males they will defend their territory psychically if disturbed. The sex differences therefore reflect a real division in typical service behavior alongside the species' documented differences in statistics and learnsets, rather than being merely different coloration.

playthrough: Morpeko does not evolve and is immediately usable as a fast physical Electric/Dark attacker with base 95 Attack and 97 Speed, but Hunger Switch makes its battle rhythm unlike that of almost any other Pokémon. In Sword/Shield and Scarlet/Violet, Morpeko alternates between Full Belly Mode and Hangry Mode at the end of every turn; its typing and stats do not change, but the signature Aura Wheel changes from Electric-type in Full Belly Mode to Dark-type in Hangry Mode. Aura Wheel has 110 base power, perfect accuracy, and raises Morpeko's Speed by one stage after a successful hit, making it both strong STAB and built-in speed control regardless of which form is active. Crunch or Knock Off provides dependable Dark damage when Aura Wheel happens to be Electric, while Seed Bomb, Psychic Fangs, Brick Break, Rapid Spin, and Parting Shot can add coverage, hazard removal, or pivoting depending on the game. Electric/Dark provides a Psychic immunity and resistances to Dark, Electric, Flying, Ghost, and Steel while leaving Bug, Fairy, Fighting, and Ground weaknesses, but 58/58/58 bulk gives little margin for taking strong neutral attacks. Pokémon Legends: Z-A handles the cycle differently because conventional Abilities are absent: Aura Wheel itself switches Morpeko's form each time it is used, preserving the alternating Electric/Dark concept through the move rather than an end-of-turn Hunger Switch trigger. Jolly is normally the safest Nature because Morpeko depends heavily on moving first, while Adamant can be useful when Aura Wheel's Speed boost or external support already provides sufficient speed control.
competitive: Morpeko has remained a ZU Pokémon in both Sword/Shield and Scarlet/Violet, but it has a legitimate offensive-utility niche built around Aura Wheel rather than being competitively irrelevant. In SS ZU, Choice Band sets used 110-power Aura Wheel as alternating Electric or Dark STAB while gaining Speed after every successful use, allowing Morpeko to become progressively harder to revenge kill once Ground-types and physical walls were weakened. Heavy-Duty Boots utility sets combined Aura Wheel with Rapid Spin and Parting Shot, letting Morpeko remove hazards, increase its own Speed, and pivot out after lowering the opponent's offenses. Hunger Switch makes move sequencing unusually important because an opponent can sometimes exploit the predictable form cycle, particularly with Ground-types that are immune to the Electric version of Aura Wheel. Scarlet/Violet again places Morpeko in ZU, where Knock Off improves its ability to make progress and the same Aura Wheel, Rapid Spin, and Parting Shot package supports offensive teams. Its primary limitations are 58/58/58 bulk, weaknesses to Ground, Fighting, Fairy, and Bug, and only base 95 Attack, which means bulky physical walls can survive its attacks even after its Speed becomes impressive. Current Pokémon Champions presently lists Morpeko in UU, but that environment is still new enough that this should be treated as an emerging 2026 competitive chapter rather than evidence that Morpeko historically performed at UU level in the core-series singles metagames.
nuzlocke: Morpeko can be useful in a Nuzlocke because base 97 Speed, an accurate 110-power signature move, and a Psychic immunity let it remove selected threats efficiently without lengthy setup. Aura Wheel is especially valuable because every successful use raises Speed, allowing Morpeko to become safer against subsequent opponents while alternating between Electric and Dark coverage. The form cycle must be tracked carefully: in Sword/Shield and Scarlet/Violet Hunger Switch changes mode at the end of each turn, so an opponent that is immune or resistant to the next Aura Wheel type can turn an apparently safe sequence into a lost turn. Parting Shot is an excellent safety tool because it lowers both opposing attacking stats before switching, and Rapid Spin can remove hazards while also raising Speed. Morpeko's poor 58/58/58 bulk is the major problem, meaning a failed knockout, unexpected priority attack, or strong neutral hit can be fatal despite its good Speed. Ground attacks are particularly dangerous because they are super effective and completely immune to Electric Aura Wheel, while Fighting, Fairy, and Bug coverage also deserves immediate respect. In Legends: Z-A the form instead changes when Aura Wheel itself is used, so the player should not apply the conventional end-of-turn Hunger Switch rhythm to that game's battle system.

pokemon.name: Morpeko
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Morpeko has a very small stomach and must eat almost constantly to prevent hunger from returning immediately. It carries Berry seeds inside pocket-like pouches, electrically roasts the seeds, and treats the stored food as precious treasure until it needs another snack. Eating those seeds both satisfies hunger temporarily and provides the energy used by the electrical organs in its cheeks. Generating electricity consumes energy so quickly that even a well-fed Morpeko inevitably becomes hungry again after a short time. When completely full, it can become unwilling to eat anything else and may even attack someone who continues trying to feed it, showing that its food-seeking behavior has a genuine saturation point despite the species' constant hunger cycle.

pokemon.name: Morpeko
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Prolonged hunger changes Morpeko's hormonal balance strongly enough to alter its fur color, facial expression, temperament, and even the elemental nature of the energy stored in its cheek sacs. The normally Electric energy converts into Dark-type energy as the hungry Pokémon becomes increasingly aggressive. In this state Morpeko is described as wild and brutish and may commit acts of extreme violence or other destructive behavior until its hunger is finally satisfied. Even after the accumulated Dark energy has been used up, the aggression can continue because the underlying hormonal and metabolic problem remains unresolved until Morpeko eats. Hangry Mode is therefore a genuine physiological hunger state rather than a voluntary battle stance, directly linking metabolism, hormone balance, behavior, coloration, and energy type.

playthrough: Cufant evolves into Copperajah at level 34, giving the family a straightforward midgame evolution with no item, friendship, trade, or location requirement. Copperajah is a slow but extremely strong Steel-type built around 122 HP and 130 Attack, with only base 30 Speed, so it usually succeeds by surviving a hit and answering with a very powerful physical attack rather than trying to move first. Steel is excellent for normal play because it provides a Poison immunity and numerous resistances, while the main weaknesses to Fire, Fighting, and Ground are common enough that the player still needs reliable switch partners. Heavy Slam is particularly effective because Copperajah is extremely heavy, while Iron Head offers fixed, accurate Steel damage; Earthquake, Play Rough, Power Whip, Rock Slide, Heat Crash, and Superpower or comparable coverage give it answers to many Pokémon that resist Steel. Sheer Force can boost attacks with secondary effects, whereas Heavy Metal doubles Copperajah's already enormous weight and strengthens weight-based options such as Heavy Slam and Heat Crash in favorable matchups. It can also contribute Stealth Rock rather than functioning only as an attacker, although its lack of reliable recovery means repeated chip damage accumulates quickly over a long route or boss sequence. In Sword and Shield, a Copperajah with the Gigantamax Factor gains G-Max Steelsurge, which damages the target and leaves sharp steel on the opposing field; incoming Pokémon then take hazard damage according to their weakness or resistance to Steel, making the Gigantamax form unusually good at generating value beyond three turns of enlarged attacks.
competitive: Copperajah became one of the defining Steel-types of Sword/Shield NU and is much more historically important than its modest overall tier placement might suggest. Smogon ranked it fifth among the Top Ten Titans of Generation 8 NU, noting that when it arrived in the tier its combination of Heavy Slam, Power Whip, Heat Crash, Stone Edge, and other coverage attacks could dismantle defensive cores while still fitting Stealth Rock onto the same set. Its 122 HP and Steel typing also let it check several special attackers and Fairy-types despite only base 69 defenses, and Heavy Metal made Heavy Slam extraordinarily powerful against lighter targets. As SS NU became faster and alternative Steel-types such as Bronzong and later Stakataka competed for teamslots, Copperajah lost some of its earlier dominance, but it remained an effective wallbreaker and hazard setter; the final SS Smogon Dex lists it in NU. Scarlet/Violet also currently lists Copperajah in NU, where its role has shifted somewhat toward a bulky tank that combines Knock Off, Earthquake, Whirlwind or Protect, Stealth Rock, and strong coverage while checking selected special attackers. Its recurring competitive flaw is longevity: Copperajah has no reliable recovery, is very slow, and can be worn down by hazards, pivoting moves, and repeated neutral hits even when its typing initially gives it a favorable matchup. Gigantamax Copperajah's G-Max Steelsurge creates a powerful Steel-type entry hazard, but standard Smogon Sword/Shield singles banned Dynamax and Gigantamax, so that form's most distinctive mechanic belongs to formats where Dynamax is actually legal rather than Copperajah's ordinary NU history.
nuzlocke: Cufant and Copperajah are generally dependable Nuzlocke Pokémon because Steel typing provides a large number of safe switch opportunities and Copperajah's enormous HP gives it meaningful room for error against neutral attacks. The greatest advantage is consistency: strong accurate options such as Heavy Slam in favorable weight matchups, Iron Head, Earthquake, and Play Rough allow Copperajah to deal substantial damage without relying entirely on setup. Its base 30 Speed is the main risk because Copperajah normally takes a hit before moving, so repeated battles can wear it down even when no individual attack looks threatening. Fire, Fighting, and Ground coverage should be scouted carefully, especially from strong physical attackers or special attackers that can exploit Copperajah's merely average base 69 defenses. Sheer Force is often a safer general-purpose Ability than building around weight calculations, while Heavy Metal can make Heavy Slam and Heat Crash extremely strong when the target's weight is known. Stealth Rock is useful in major trainer battles with repeated switching, but in ordinary story play an immediate attack may be safer than giving the opponent a free damage turn. If Gigantamax is available, G-Max Steelsurge can provide lasting field control, but Dynamax's temporary HP increase should not encourage careless play once Copperajah returns to normal size and retains any damage it accumulated.

pokemon.name: Cufant
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Cufant is an elephantine Steel-type whose body contains copper, with rain gradually producing the green tarnish visible across parts of its skin. Its trunk ends in a shovel-like shape that it uses to dig through earth and carve out rocks and ore, which form part of its diet. Despite its small size, a Cufant can carry loads weighing more than five tons with little difficulty. Cufant is naturally docile and travels in herds; in the morning, groups head into caves to search for the ore they eat. The species was brought to regions such as Galar and Paldea to assist humans with heavy labor, establishing a long practical relationship with people rather than a purely wild existence.

pokemon.name: Copperajah
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Copperajah is a massive copper-bodied elephant Pokémon whose green, tarnished skin is resistant to water. Its trunk has tremendous grip and crushing power, enough to pulverize giant boulders into powder, and the species is strong enough to pull extremely heavy machinery such as an airplane. Copperajah lives socially in herds and has a notably proud disposition; individuals with brighter and more vibrant skin are described as being especially boastful. Humans have worked with Copperajah for generations, and the species can cooperate with Pokémon such as Gigalith at mines and construction sites. Pokédex records state that Copperajah arrived from another region long ago, reinforcing that its modern presence in Galar is connected to historical human movement and labor rather than necessarily representing its original native range.

pokemon.name: Copperajah
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Gigantamax Copperajah becomes much more block-like and stands upright on enlarged hind legs while its trunk expands into an enormous rectangular structure with serrated ridges. The trunk contains enough force to level mountains and can destroy very large structures with a single blow. This form's signature G-Max Steelsurge scatters sharp steel across the opposing field, matching the transformed trunk's emphasis on smashing and reshaping the surrounding terrain.

playthrough: Dracozolt is a standalone Galarian Fossil Pokémon restored in Sword and Shield by combining a Fossilized Bird with a Fossilized Drake, so it has no evolution stage to train through once the fossils are obtained. Its Electric/Dragon typing is excellent offensively and offers useful resistances to Fire, Flying, Grass, Steel, Water, and especially Electric, while Dragon, Fairy, Ground, and Ice attacks are its primary weaknesses. The defining move is Bolt Beak, an 85-power physical Electric attack in Sword/Shield that doubles to 170 power if Dracozolt moves before its target, making speed control dramatically more important than the species' ordinary base 100 Attack would imply. Base 75 Speed is only moderate, so Thunder Wave support, Choice Scarf, or the Hidden Ability Sand Rush can help Dracozolt activate Bolt Beak's doubled power more consistently; under sand, Sand Rush doubles its Speed and also prevents sandstorm damage. Hustle instead raises physical Attack by 50% but reduces the accuracy of physical moves to 80% of their normal value, creating spectacular damage at the cost of exactly the sort of misses that can make a story battle unreliable. Dragon Claw or Breaking Swipe gives dependable secondary STAB, while Earthquake, Fire Fang, Rock Slide, Low Kick, and special options such as Draco Meteor or Fire Blast can fill coverage gaps depending on the set. For a normal playthrough, Volt Absorb is often the most forgiving Ability because it creates an Electric immunity and healing opportunity without requiring weather or accepting Hustle's accuracy penalty.
competitive: Dracozolt finished Sword/Shield in UUBL and developed a genuine OU niche because Sand Rush fixes its middling base 75 Speed and turns Bolt Beak into an extraordinarily threatening wallbreaking tool whenever Dracozolt moves first. Smogon's SS OU analysis describes it as one of sand's most dangerous breakers, capable of threatening staples such as Toxapex and Corviknight while using mixed coverage to pressure the Ground- and Grass-types normally expected to absorb Electric attacks. Bolt Beak is the centerpiece: its power doubles from 85 to 170 when Dracozolt attacks before its target, and Sand Rush can make that condition routine rather than exceptional. Mixed sets used Draco Meteor for Ground- and Dragon-types and Fire Blast or Fire Spin for targets such as Ferrothorn, while Earthquake supplied physical coverage; this flexibility made simply switching a Ground-type into Bolt Beak less automatic than the type chart suggested. Hustle was another offensive route earlier in the generation, multiplying Attack at the cost of physical accuracy, but competitive sand teams preferred Sand Rush's ability to guarantee favorable Speed interactions without introducing an accuracy tax. Its limitations were equally clear: Dracozolt was strongly dependent on sand support, could be pressured easily outside weather, and often had to predict correctly during a limited number of sand turns. It is unavailable in Scarlet/Violet and Legends: Z-A, so it has no normal Generation IX usage tier; its established singles history remains primarily a Generation VIII sand offense story rather than a current SV metagame role.
nuzlocke: Dracozolt is powerful enough to trivialize many favorable Nuzlocke matchups, but its safest configuration is not always the one that produces the highest theoretical damage. Volt Absorb is particularly valuable in permadeath play because an Electric attack becomes a healing opportunity, while Electric/Dragon typing supplies several useful resistances for controlled switches. Bolt Beak is excellent when Dracozolt is definitely faster because its doubled power can prevent the opponent from attacking at all, but base 75 Speed is not sufficient to assume that condition against every evolved opponent. Hustle should be treated cautiously: increasing Attack by 50% is attractive, but multiplying physical accuracy by 0.8 turns otherwise reliable moves into potential run-ending misses, and Bolt Beak is already strong without accepting that risk. Sand Rush can make Bolt Beak safer by doubling Speed in sand, but a Nuzlocke team should not depend on temporary weather unless the setter and turn count are under control. Dragon Claw, Earthquake, and other 100%-accurate attacks are preferable when Bolt Beak's doubled power is unnecessary, while Draco Meteor and Fire Blast bring accuracy or stat-drop concerns better suited to specific planned matchups than routine travel. Fairy, Ground, Ice, and Dragon moves remain the major matchup hazards, and Dracozolt's merely average special bulk means a wrong prediction can still be costly despite its strong offensive pressure.

pokemon.name: Dracozolt
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Dracozolt is a restored hybrid Fossil Pokémon assembled from a small bird-like upper fossil and a much larger draconic lower fossil, producing an intentionally mismatched body rather than a conventional prehistoric anatomy. Its enormous tail and lower-body muscles generate electricity, making the oversized lower half directly responsible for its Electric-type power. Galar's Pokédex claims that Dracozolt was once unbeatable because of its powerful lower body and eventually went extinct after consuming all of its plant-based food supply. Because the restored Pokémon is formed by combining fossils from two different creatures, that extinction narrative is best treated as an in-universe reconstruction claim rather than certain evidence about a naturally occurring ancient Dracozolt species.

playthrough: Arctozolt is another standalone Galarian Fossil Pokémon, restored in Sword and Shield by combining a Fossilized Bird with a Fossilized Dino. Electric/Ice is an outstanding attacking combination because Electric pressures Water and Flying types while Ice punishes Ground, Grass, Dragon, and Flying types, but defensively it leaves Arctozolt weak to Fire, Fighting, Ground, and Rock and resistant only to Electric, Flying, and Ice. Like Dracozolt, it learns Bolt Beak, whose 85 base power in Sword/Shield doubles when Arctozolt moves first; unlike Dracozolt, Arctozolt starts from only base 55 Speed and therefore needs much more help to exploit that condition consistently. Its Hidden Ability Slush Rush doubles Speed in hail, converting that poor Speed into an advantage and creating the classic hail sweeper role, while Volt Absorb supplies an Electric immunity and healing and Static can punish contact with paralysis. Arctozolt's balanced 100 Attack and 90 Special Attack also make mixed offense practical: Icicle Crash provides physical Ice STAB, while Freeze-Dry and Blizzard use Special Attack and can punish Water-types that otherwise resist Ice or Electric coverage differently. Low Kick, Stomping Tantrum, Rock Slide, and other coverage moves help with Steel-, Rock-, or Ground-oriented answers, although Ice's Stealth Rock weakness means repeated switching can become expensive. In a story run without deliberate hail support, Volt Absorb is normally the simpler and safer Ability; on a dedicated weather team, Slush Rush dramatically improves Bolt Beak and turns an otherwise slow Pokémon into a fast mixed attacker.
competitive: Arctozolt became one of Generation VIII's most dangerous hail abusers and the final SS Smogon Dex lists it in UUBL, far above what its base 55 Speed would suggest in isolation. Slush Rush doubles that Speed under hail, allowing Bolt Beak to reach its doubled 170 base power condition while Arctozolt simultaneously threatens Ground-types with Ice STAB, a combination with unusually limited defensive counterplay. Smogon's SS OU analysis used mixed hail sets with Bolt Beak plus Blizzard or Freeze-Dry, exploiting the fact that the Pokémon resisting Electric attacks are often precisely the targets hit hardest by Ice. Its base 100 Attack and 90 Special Attack support that mixed role better than most weather sweepers, while Low Kick or other coverage can punish Steel-types that withstand both STABs. The strength of hail offense caused problems across lower tiers during the generation; Arctozolt was specifically banned from NU during an earlier stage of the metagame, illustrating that its weather interaction was not merely theoretical. Outside hail, however, the entire profile changes: base 55 Speed becomes a severe liability, Electric/Ice has poor defensive longevity, and the Pokémon is vulnerable to Stealth Rock and common Fire-, Fighting-, Ground-, and Rock-type pressure. Arctozolt is not available in Scarlet/Violet or Legends: Z-A, so its principal competitive legacy remains the Sword/Shield hail archetype rather than an ordinary Generation IX ladder role.
nuzlocke: Arctozolt has excellent offensive coverage for a Nuzlocke but requires more careful speed planning than Dracozolt because base 55 Speed is genuinely slow outside hail. Volt Absorb is a strong safety Ability, providing both an Electric immunity and healing, whereas Static can occasionally rescue a bad contact matchup through paralysis but should never be treated as guaranteed. Slush Rush is extremely powerful if the player controls hail, since doubling Speed both reduces incoming attacks and activates Bolt Beak's doubled power against many opponents. Without weather, the player should avoid assuming Bolt Beak will receive its power boost and can instead use it as a normal accurate Electric attack when the matchup is still favorable. Freeze-Dry is especially useful because it is accurate and hits Water-types super effectively despite being Ice-type, while Icicle Crash and Blizzard introduce 90% or 70% accuracy unless hail makes Blizzard perfectly accurate in Generation VIII. The combination of Fire, Fighting, Ground, and Rock weaknesses plus vulnerability to Stealth Rock makes blind switching dangerous, and Arctozolt's bulk is solid rather than overwhelming. A weather-supported Arctozolt can sweep very safely once the field is prepared, but using it as an unsupported generalist exposes exactly the low Speed and awkward defensive typing that competitive hail teams were designed to hide.

pokemon.name: Arctozolt
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Arctozolt is a restored hybrid Fossil Pokémon with a small bird-like upper body attached to a large cold-adapted marine lower body, and the mismatch makes ordinary movement difficult. Its upper half is constantly freezing and produces nasal mucus; by shaking that cold upper body, Arctozolt generates electricity. Pokédex records describe it as living around prehistoric shores and preserving food with the ice on its body. The same records claim it went extinct because it moved too slowly, but, as with the other Galarian fossil combinations, the body was reconstructed from two different fossil components and that explanation should not be treated as certain paleobiology.

playthrough: Dracovish is restored from a Fossilized Fish and a Fossilized Drake and has no evolution, making its full 505 base-stat total available as soon as the player completes the fossil restoration on Route 6. Its Water/Dragon typing is exceptionally efficient defensively, leaving only Dragon and Fairy weaknesses while resisting Steel and taking only one-quarter damage from both Fire and Water. The defining combination is Strong Jaw plus Fishious Rend: Fishious Rend has 85 base power in Sword/Shield, doubles to 170 if Dracovish moves before its target, and then receives the 1.5× Strong Jaw boost because it is a biting move, before even accounting for STAB, rain, or held items. Base 75 Speed is only moderate, so a Choice Scarf or speed support greatly increases the number of targets against which Fishious Rend receives its doubled power, while Choice Band maximizes damage when Dracovish already outspeeds the opponent. Crunch and Psychic Fangs are also boosted by Strong Jaw and supply useful coverage, while Dragon STAB such as Outrage or Dragon Rush can punish Water-immune Pokémon and opposing Dragons. Water Absorb offers a much more defensive playthrough option by turning Water attacks into healing, and the Hidden Ability Sand Rush can double Speed in sand, although Strong Jaw is usually the simplest way to exploit what makes Dracovish exceptional. For ordinary story battles, Dracovish combines favorable typing, good physical bulk, and a perfectly accurate signature move with extraordinary damage, making it one of the most immediately powerful fossil restorations in the series.
competitive: Dracovish was one of the most metagame-warping Pokémon introduced in Sword and Shield and ultimately became an Uber despite an otherwise ordinary-looking 505 base-stat total. Its central interaction was Choice Band or Choice Scarf Strong Jaw Fishious Rend: the move doubles from 85 to 170 base power whenever Dracovish attacks before the target, receives Strong Jaw's 1.5× boost, gains Water STAB, and can be amplified still further by rain. From the beginning of SS OU, this allowed Dracovish to overwhelm nominal Water resists such as Toxapex and Ferrothorn and forced teams to rely heavily on Water immunities such as Seismitoad, Gastrodon, or Jellicent if they wanted a truly safe initial answer. That teambuilding pressure led to an official OU suspect test beginning in May 2020, and on June 1, 2020, Dracovish was banned from SS OU. It remained viable even after entering Ubers: Smogon's Ubers analysis describes Fishious Rend as strong enough to break defensive staples such as Necrozma-Dusk-Mane, Blissey, and Ho-Oh, with Choice Band maximizing wallbreaking and Choice Scarf improving the chance of moving first. The counters became more realistic at that power level—Eternatus could resist Water and threaten Dragon damage, faster offensive teams reduced the Fishious Rend bonus, and lack of recovery made Dracovish susceptible to status and chip—but the basic wallbreaking mechanism remained dangerous. Dracovish is unavailable in Scarlet/Violet and Legends: Z-A and was not part of Pokémon Champions' initial 2026 roster, so its defining competitive résumé remains the extraordinary Generation VIII rise from new fossil Pokémon to OU ban and Ubers wallbreaker.
nuzlocke: Dracovish is outstanding in a Nuzlocke because Water/Dragon typing gives it only two weaknesses and strong Fire and Water resistances, while 90 HP and 100 Defense provide respectable physical durability. Strong Jaw Fishious Rend is also unusually safe for such a powerful attack because it has perfect accuracy, and moving first can turn many planned battles into one-hit knockouts rather than damage trades. The important caveat is Speed: base 75 is not fast enough to assume the doubled Fishious Rend power against every opponent, so damage calculations based on 170 power are unsafe unless the speed order is known. Water Absorb can be preferable when the team needs a defensive Water immunity and healing pivot, while Sand Rush can provide speed control in a planned sand composition; both sacrifice Strong Jaw's enormous damage boost. Psychic Fangs and Crunch are accurate Strong Jaw coverage moves and usually safer than Dragon Rush, whose 75% accuracy is difficult to justify in permadeath play. Outrage is powerful but locks Dracovish into multiple turns and causes confusion afterward, making it risky when the opponent has Fairy-types, revenge killers, or multiple remaining Pokémon. Fairy and Dragon attacks should be scouted carefully, but outside those matchups Dracovish's typing, bulk, and accurate high-power STAB give it one of the largest safety margins among the Galar fossils.

pokemon.name: Dracovish
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Dracovish is a reconstructed hybrid Fossil Pokémon in which a fish-like head is attached to the tail end of a powerful draconic lower body, creating a radically mismatched anatomy. Its legs and jaws are tremendously strong, and Galar's Pokédex describes it as capable of running faster than 40 miles per hour while functioning as an apex predator. Paradoxically, it can breathe only while underwater, making the powerful terrestrial legs difficult to reconcile with the fish head's respiratory needs. Pokédex records claim that it drove its prey toward depletion and thereby caused its own extinction, but the creature is assembled from two separate fossil species, so that narrative is better understood as an in-universe reconstruction theory rather than certain natural history. In Pokémon Journeys, Ash's Dracovish also displayed a dormant power that surrounded its chest spikes with a red aura and allowed those spikes to extend or bind targets, adding an animated-series behavior not explained by the game Pokédex.

playthrough: Arctovish is restored from a Fossilized Fish and a Fossilized Dino and has no evolution, giving it a complete defensive stat profile immediately after restoration. Its Water/Ice typing provides strong offensive STAB coverage but is much less comfortable defensively than Dracovish's Water/Dragon combination, leaving weaknesses to Electric, Grass, Fighting, and Rock and only Water and Ice resistances. Fishious Rend again defines the species: the 85-power Water move doubles if Arctovish moves first, but base 55 Speed makes that condition difficult without dedicated support. The Hidden Ability Slush Rush solves that problem by doubling Speed in hail, while Ice Body instead restores HP each turn in hail and Water Absorb turns Water attacks into healing, giving Arctovish three genuinely different weather or defensive identities. Freeze-Dry is especially useful alongside Water STAB because it hits Water-types super effectively and uses Arctovish's workable base 80 Special Attack, while Icicle Crash, Crunch, Psychic Fangs, Rock Slide, and other moves provide mixed or physical coverage. Base 90 HP, 100 Defense, and 90 Special Defense give Arctovish the best all-around raw bulk of the four fossils, but the awkward typing and low Speed mean those numbers do not automatically make it the safest of them. For a story run, Water Absorb is the simplest defensive Ability, whereas a deliberately built hail team can transform Slush Rush Arctovish into a much faster attacker capable of exploiting Fishious Rend properly.
competitive: Arctovish never approached Dracovish's OU-level dominance, but it became a serious lower-tier threat and ultimately finished Sword/Shield in ZUBL rather than ordinary ZU. The underlying idea was the same as Dracovish's: Fishious Rend doubles from 85 to 170 base power when Arctovish attacks first, but Arctovish lacks Strong Jaw and has only base 55 Speed, so it needed Slush Rush and hail to recreate the terrifying speed-plus-power interaction. Under hail, Slush Rush doubled its Speed and enabled Choice Band or other offensive sets to overwhelm many conventional Water checks, while Freeze-Dry punished opposing Water-types that could otherwise absorb or resist Fishious Rend. Arctovish had already caused tiering problems earlier in the generation, including a PU quickban, and a later SS ZU suspect process concluded with Arctovish residing in ZUBL. Its lower-tier success illustrates why raw tier labels need context: outside hail, Arctovish is a slow Water/Ice Pokémon with common weaknesses, but automatic weather transformed it into a breaker whose strongest move was specifically rewarded for winning the Speed interaction. Water Absorb and Ice Body offered defensive alternatives, but neither reproduced the offensive pressure that made Slush Rush the competitively defining Ability. Like the other Galar fossils, Arctovish is unavailable in Scarlet/Violet and Legends: Z-A, so there is no ordinary Generation IX usage-tier continuation of its SS history.
nuzlocke: Arctovish has excellent raw bulk for a Nuzlocke, with 90 HP, 100 Defense, and 90 Special Defense, but Water/Ice has enough common weaknesses that it should still be used as a matchup specialist rather than a universal tank. Water Absorb is extremely safe when the opponent is known to use Water attacks, creating both immunity and healing, while Ice Body can provide gradual recovery in hail and Slush Rush offers the strongest offensive snowball potential. Fishious Rend is perfectly accurate and very strong even before its doubling condition, but base 55 Speed means the player should not plan around 170 power unless Slush Rush or another form of speed control is active. Freeze-Dry is one of Arctovish's most valuable reliable moves because it threatens Water-types without depending on Fishious Rend speed order and has perfect accuracy. Icicle Crash is stronger physical Ice STAB but carries a 10% miss chance, and Blizzard should normally be reserved for hail because 70% accuracy is unnecessarily dangerous outside guaranteed-weather accuracy. Electric, Grass, Fighting, and Rock attacks are the key threats, and Stealth Rock can also punish repeated switching because Arctovish is Ice-type. When weather is controlled, Slush Rush can convert Arctovish from a slow bulky Pokémon into a fast cleaner; without weather, Water Absorb and careful defensive switching are usually the safer permadeath strategy.

pokemon.name: Arctovish
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Arctovish is a reconstructed hybrid Fossil Pokémon whose fish-like head has been attached upside down to a cold-adapted marine lower body, placing its mouth on the top of its head. It captures prey by freezing the surrounding area, but the misplaced mouth makes actually eating that prey difficult afterward. The skin covering its face is described as impervious to attack, giving the head extraordinary physical protection despite the body's other anatomical problems. Galar's Pokédex claims that breathing difficulties eventually caused its extinction, but because Arctovish is assembled from two separate fossil creatures, that explanation is best treated as an uncertain reconstruction story rather than definitive evidence of how a natural ancient species died out.

playthrough: Duraludon and Archaludon form an unusual cross-generational family: Duraludon was fully evolved in Sword and Shield, while Scarlet and Violet's Indigo Disk added Archaludon, which evolves from Duraludon when exposed to a Metal Alloy. Both are Steel/Dragon, an excellent defensive typing with a Poison immunity, many resistances, and only Fighting and Ground weaknesses. Duraludon already has strong base 120 Special Attack, 115 Defense, and 85 Speed, but its base 50 Special Defense is a major flaw. Archaludon raises the family to a 600 base-stat total with 90 HP, 130 Defense, 125 Special Attack, 65 Special Defense, and the same 85 Speed, making it substantially harder to remove physically while still vulnerable to strong special attacks. Archaludon's Stamina raises Defense every time it is damaged by a move, which pairs naturally with Body Press, while Sturdy guarantees survival from full HP and Stalwart prevents its attacks from being redirected in doubles. Its signature Electro Shot raises Special Attack and attacks on the following turn, but rain removes the charge turn entirely, turning Archaludon into an especially effective rain attacker alongside Draco Meteor or Dragon Pulse, Flash Cannon, and Body Press. Duraludon cannot evolve in Sword and Shield because Metal Alloy and Archaludon did not yet exist there; in those games, a Gigantamax-capable Duraludon can instead use G-Max Depletion, which damages the target and reduces the PP of the last move used by each opposing Pokémon. For ordinary Scarlet/Violet play, evolving Duraludon is usually a direct upgrade unless the player specifically values Duraludon's lower weight or different Ability options.
competitive: Duraludon and Archaludon have had radically different competitive ceilings. In Sword/Shield singles, Duraludon finished in PUBL and functioned mainly as a lower-tier special wallbreaker or Stealth Rock setter, using Draco Meteor, Flash Cannon, Body Press, Thunderbolt, and occasionally Eject Pack to generate momentum. Its Steel/Dragon typing and physical Defense were useful, but base 50 Special Defense left it vulnerable even to some resisted special attacks, and stronger Steel- and Dragon-type competition kept it from becoming a major upper-tier threat. Scarlet/Violet currently lists unevolved Duraludon in NU, where it retains a useful mixture of offense, physical bulk, and utility. Archaludon was dramatically stronger from the moment it arrived in The Indigo Disk: Stamina, 130 Defense, 125 Special Attack, Body Press, and rain-accelerated Electro Shot made it an exceptional tank and snowballing wallbreaker. Rain sets commonly paired Stamina with Assault Vest, letting Archaludon patch its weaker special side while repeatedly gaining Defense and using one-turn Electro Shot to raise Special Attack before dealing damage. That combination proved too constraining for standard SV OU; after a formal suspect test, 94 of 124 counted votes favored a ban, a 75.81% majority, and Archaludon was removed from OU in February 2024. It is therefore currently classified as Uber in standard SV tiering, although it also sees play in formats such as Ubers UU, draft, doubles, and VGC where its defensive profile and rain synergy remain valuable. Gigantamax Duraludon's competitive history should be separated from ordinary singles tiering because Smogon's standard Sword/Shield singles formats banned Dynamax; its G-Max Depletion niche belongs to Dynamax-legal formats rather than Duraludon's normal PUBL résumé.
nuzlocke: The Duraludon family is generally excellent for permadeath play because Steel/Dragon supplies many safe switch-in opportunities and only two weaknesses, while both stages possess strong physical Defense. Duraludon's greatest danger is special damage: base 50 Special Defense can make seemingly harmless neutral or even resisted special attacks much more threatening than the typing suggests. Archaludon improves that side only to base 65, so evolving does not remove the need to scout special Fighting-, Ground-, or strong neutral coverage, but 90 HP and 130 Defense give it excellent physical margin. Stamina is particularly Nuzlocke-friendly because every damaging hit raises Defense, allowing Archaludon to become progressively safer against physical opponents and strengthen Body Press without spending a setup turn. Sturdy offers a different form of insurance by preventing a one-hit knockout from full HP, although hazards, weather, or prior chip can disable that protection. Electro Shot is risky outside rain because the charging turn leaves Archaludon exposed, whereas rain makes it both immediate and self-boosting; Dragon Pulse and Flash Cannon are safer routine attacks than Draco Meteor when accuracy and stat consistency matter more than peak power. In Sword and Shield, Gigantamax Duraludon can gain temporary HP and field pressure, but it should still be treated as a Pokémon with weak special durability once the Dynamax turns end.

pokemon.name: Duraludon
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Duraludon's body is made from a special metal that is both strong and surprisingly light, allowing an 88-pound Pokémon with substantial armor to move with considerable agility. Its polished body resists scratches but rusts easily, so Duraludon favors caves and cold mountain environments and actively avoids rain. The metal body also retains heat, which Duraludon vents through slits in its tail to prevent overheating. It grinds down rock surfaces with its differently shaped arms to obtain food. In Galar's mountains it shares habitat with Tyranitar, and the two species are known to battle one another as rivals.

pokemon.name: Duraludon
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Gigantamax Duraludon grows into a skyscraper-like structure with luminous window-like sections across its enormous body. The transformation fills it with so much energy that portions of the body visibly glow. Its cells become exceptionally hard even by Steel-type standards, and its altered body structure is specifically resistant to earthquakes. This form uniquely produces G-Max Depletion, extending the species' building-like transformation into an attack that also drains opponents' move PP.

pokemon.name: Archaludon
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Archaludon is a massive metallic Pokémon adapted to boreal mountains, where it digs holes while searching for food and possesses enough structural durability to remain unfazed even by cave-ins. Unlike an Electric-type that generates its own electricity, Archaludon gathers static electricity from the environment through terminal-like structures on its limbs, head, and tail and stores that charge for later use. When threatened, it drops onto all fours, straightens and braces its body into a bridge-like configuration that sacrifices mobility for a much sturdier center of gravity. From that position it connects its electrical terminals like suspension cables and fires a tremendously powerful beam through the tube inside its mouth. Storms and other inclement weather allow the terminals to collect static charge more quickly, directly explaining why its signature Electro Shot can be fired without a charging turn in rain.

playthrough: Dreepy evolves very late compared with most three-stage families, becoming Drakloak at level 50 and Dragapult at level 60, so the line asks the player to carry an extremely weak first stage for a long time unless Dreepy is caught at a high level. The payoff is substantial: Dragapult has base 142 Speed, 120 Attack, 100 Special Attack, and useful Dragon/Ghost typing, giving it two immunities and several resistances while allowing it to attack effectively from either side. Dragon Darts is its signature physical Dragon move and hits twice for 50 power each, while Draco Meteor and Dragon Pulse give special Dragon options; Shadow Ball is the most reliable special Ghost STAB, whereas physical Ghost options are generally less convenient. U-turn allows Dragapult to exploit its exceptional Speed without remaining in unfavorable matchups, and Will-O-Wisp or Thunder Wave can cripple dangerous opponents when immediate damage is unnecessary. Clear Body prevents opposing stat drops, Infiltrator ignores Substitute and protective screens, and Cursed Body can occasionally disable an attack after Dragapult is hit; Infiltrator is usually the most broadly useful offensive Ability. The main weaknesses are Dark, Dragon, Fairy, Ghost, and Ice, and Dragapult's 88/75/75 bulk is good enough to survive selected neutral hits but not strong enough to encourage repeated trading. The family is therefore mediocre for much of its development but becomes one of Galar's strongest fast attackers once level 60 is reached.
competitive: Dragapult has been an elite singles Pokémon for its entire competitive life, remaining OU in both Sword/Shield and Scarlet/Violet rather than experiencing the usual generational falloff of many fast attackers. In SS OU, its base 142 Speed outpaced nearly the entire unboosted metagame and its near-unresisted Dragon/Ghost coverage, U-turn, and broad special movepool made Choice Specs one of its defining sets. Heavy-Duty Boots pivot sets used Hex with Will-O-Wisp or Thunder Wave, while rarer Dragon Dance physical sets punished teams built only to absorb special attacks; Infiltrator made screens and Substitute unreliable counterplay. Scarlet/Violet preserved all of those core strengths, and modern OU still treats Dragapult as one of the tier's premier wallbreakers and fast utility pivots. Choice Specs Draco Meteor and Shadow Ball pressure defensive teams, while Boots sets use status, Hex, and U-turn to control tempo; Terastallization can strengthen Ghost attacks or alter defensive matchups, although Dragapult's natural typing is already excellent. Its long-term limitations are relatively modest offensive base stats compared with modern dedicated breakers, imperfect physical Ghost STAB, vulnerability to chip damage, and competition with new extremely fast threats, but its Speed, mixed offenses, utility, and unpredictability consistently compensate. Dragapult has also been valuable in doubles and VGC at different points, particularly because Clear Body protects it from Intimidate and its Speed enables support or fast offensive roles, though its clearest historical identity remains as a perennial OU threat.
nuzlocke: The Dreepy line has one of the sharpest risk-reward curves in a Nuzlocke because Dreepy is exceptionally weak and does not evolve until level 50, then requires another ten levels before reaching Dragapult. If the encounter occurs late enough that those levels are immediately practical, the weakness of the first stage matters much less; otherwise, switch-training or experience items are safer than exposing Dreepy to ordinary combat. Drakloak is usable but still only an intermediate stage, while Dragapult's base 142 Speed is outstanding for permadeath play because it can reliably move first against most unboosted story opponents and avoid damage by scoring clean knockouts. Dragon Darts is perfectly accurate and does not lock Dragapult in, making it much safer than Outrage, while Shadow Ball and Dragon Pulse are similarly reliable special options. U-turn is excellent for scouting and escaping predicted bad matchups, but the switch occurs only after Dragapult attacks, so it cannot rescue a mistaken Speed assumption against a faster foe. Will-O-Wisp can greatly reduce physical danger but carries an accuracy risk, whereas Thunder Wave provides speed control with its own chance to miss. Once fully evolved, Dragapult is one of the safest offensive Pokémon in the region, but its merely moderate bulk means the player should exploit Speed and immunities rather than use it as a general-purpose damage sponge.

pokemon.name: Dreepy
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Dreepy are the reborn ghosts of a prehistoric species that once lived in ancient seas, and they continue many of the behaviors they apparently followed while alive. They wander the locations where their former species once lived and may bite at Clauncher as though trying to eat them. A lone Dreepy is extraordinarily weak—weak enough that even a child could defeat one—but it has enormous evolutionary potential when supported by companions. In the evening, groups of Dreepy fly rapidly over the sea and poke at Pokémon beneath the water for amusement. Dreepy also willingly associate with Drakloak and Dragapult, eventually becoming the young Pokémon carried and even launched by their evolved relatives.

pokemon.name: Drakloak
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Drakloak can fly at speeds exceeding 120 miles per hour and normally carries a Dreepy on its head. It takes care of that Dreepy and fights alongside it until the younger Pokémon eventually evolves. This caregiving drive is so strong that a Drakloak without a Dreepy becomes uneasy and desperately searches for another Pokémon to serve as a substitute dependent. Drakloak attacks by firing energy blasts from its lungs. If Drakloak loses a battle, the Dreepy it was caring for may wander away, tying its social behavior directly to the outcome of conflicts.

pokemon.name: Dragapult
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Dragapult carries two Dreepy inside the hollow structures on its head and launches them at opponents like supersonic missiles by building pressure with air in its cheeks. The Dreepy are not unwilling ammunition: they eagerly anticipate being fired at Mach speed, and Dreepy reportedly gather around the fastest Dragapult in a group specifically for the opportunity to experience that flight. Dragapult can make both itself and the Dreepy it carries invisible by emptying its mind and concentrating, matching the species' classification as the Stealth Pokémon. Its signature Dragon Darts reflects this social attack behavior directly, using the carried Dreepy as coordinated projectiles rather than treating the young as passive passengers. The family therefore develops from an extremely vulnerable ghost juvenile into a fast caretaker and finally into an adult whose combat strategy depends on cooperation with younger members of its own species.

playthrough: Zacian is obtained only near the end of Pokémon Sword's postgame story, so it cannot contribute to most of the main campaign, but once available it is one of the strongest physical attackers a player can use. Hero of Many Battles is pure Fairy, while holding the Rusted Sword changes Zacian in battle into Crowned Sword, a Fairy/Steel form with higher Attack and Speed and access to Behemoth Blade in place of Iron Head. In Generation VIII, Hero Zacian had base 130 Attack and Crowned Sword had an enormous base 170 Attack, while Intrepid Sword raised Attack every time Zacian entered battle; Generation IX reduced those Attack stats to 120 and 150 and made Intrepid Sword activate only once per battle. Crowned Sword still retains base 148 Speed and exceptional defensive typing, with only Fire and Ground weaknesses, while Hero form's pure Fairy typing leaves Poison and Steel as its only weaknesses. Play Rough supplies Fairy STAB, while Behemoth Blade, Close Combat or Sacred Sword, Crunch, Wild Charge, Swords Dance, and other coverage give Zacian answers to most opponents; in Sword/Shield, Behemoth Blade also doubles in power against Dynamaxed targets. Zacian itself cannot Dynamax, so its strength comes entirely from its native statistics, Ability, typing, and moves rather than the generation's central transformation mechanic. For postgame battles where legendary use is permitted, Crowned Sword is normally the stronger default form, while Hero of Many Battles preserves the held-item slot and can use items such as Choice Band or Choice Scarf.
competitive: Zacian produced one of the most extreme tiering histories of Generation VIII. Crowned Sword entered SS Ubers with base 170 Attack, base 148 Speed, Fairy/Steel typing, Swords Dance, broad coverage, and an Intrepid Sword boost every time it switched in, making defensive counterplay exceptionally narrow. Smogon banned Zacian-Crowned from SS Ubers in January 2021, sending it to Anything Goes; Hero of Many Battles then inherited many of the same offensive qualities while gaining freedom to hold Choice items and other equipment. Hero Zacian was itself suspect-tested and banned from Ubers on June 14, 2021 with 66 ban votes, 16 do-not-ban votes, and one abstention—a 79.52% ban result—leaving both forms in AG by the end of the generation. Crowned Sword was also arguably the best Restricted Pokémon in VGC 2022, where Intrepid Sword, enormous Speed, Fairy/Steel typing, and Behemoth Blade's anti-Dynamax damage gave it extraordinary role compression. Generation IX deliberately reduced Zacian's power: Hero Attack fell from 130 to 120, Crowned Attack from 170 to 150, and Intrepid Sword now activates only once per battle rather than on every entry. Those nerfs were enough for both forms to remain in the ordinary SV Uber ecosystem rather than being automatically exiled from it; Zacian-Crowned is still considered one of the tier's premier physical threats thanks to Swords Dance, base 148 Speed, excellent typing, and broad coverage. Its competitive history therefore spans two distinct eras: a Generation VIII form so oppressive that even Ubers banned it, and a nerfed but still elite Generation IX restricted Pokémon.
nuzlocke: Zacian is normally a postgame-only encounter in Sword, so its value in a conventional Nuzlocke depends on whether the ruleset continues beyond the Champion and whether legendary Pokémon are permitted. If allowed, Zacian offers an enormous safety margin because its Speed, Attack, Fairy typing, and strong accurate coverage let it remove many opponents before they can act. Crowned Sword's Fairy/Steel typing is particularly safe, supplying two immunities and many resistances while leaving only Fire and Ground weaknesses, although the Rusted Sword occupies the held-item slot. Behemoth Blade is perfectly accurate and extremely strong, especially against Dynamax targets in Generation VIII, while Sacred Sword offers a safer Fighting option than Close Combat because it does not lower Zacian's defenses. Play Rough's 90% accuracy is the main reliability concern among its standard STAB attacks, and Wild Charge's recoil should be avoided when the extra coverage is unnecessary. Swords Dance is rarely required against ordinary story opponents because Zacian's raw damage is already enormous, and spending a turn setting up can introduce avoidable crit or status exposure. Its only meaningful Nuzlocke drawback is therefore availability and ruleset legality rather than battle performance.

pokemon.name: Zacian
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Zacian is a scarred lupine Legendary whose damaged ear and numerous battle scars visually reflect an exceptionally long history of conflict. It is believed either to be Zamazenta's elder sister or its rival, and 3,000 years ago the pair fought beside two human youths to defeat Eternatus and end the original Darkest Day. Afterward Zacian returned to the Slumbering Weald, where it can transform into a statue-like dormant state and sleep for immense spans of time. Even while dormant, Zacian can cast illusions or projections of itself, and it is also capable of flight. The people of Galar eventually forgot that Zacian and Zamazenta had truly existed until Sonia reconstructed their history in the modern era.

pokemon.name: Zacian
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Zacian assumes Crowned Sword by wielding the Rusted Sword and absorbing metal particles from the air, transforming the ancient weapon into a longer golden blade while golden armor appears across its body. One of its braids can wrap around the sword when the weapon is not being used, effectively functioning as a sheath. This is described as Zacian's true full-power form, and legends claim that its sword can cut through virtually anything, including the scales of Dragon Pokémon and the bodies of Dynamax or Gigantamax Pokémon, as though they were paper. Its movements are so fast and graceful that its attacks are compared to a dance, with some slashes occurring too quickly for the unaided eye to perceive. Together with Crowned Shield Zamazenta, Crowned Sword Zacian can negate the mysterious power that otherwise prevents attacks against Eternamax Eternatus; ancient legend remembered this form as the Fairy King's Sword.

playthrough: Zamazenta is obtained during Pokémon Shield's postgame story and therefore, like Zacian, arrives too late to influence most of the normal campaign. Hero of Many Battles is pure Fighting, while holding the Rusted Shield changes it in battle into Crowned Shield, a Fighting/Steel form with substantially greater Defense and Special Defense and access to Behemoth Bash in place of Iron Head. In Generation VIII, Hero Zamazenta had 130 Attack and Crowned Shield had 145 Defense and Special Defense; Generation IX reduced Attack to 120 and Crowned defenses to 140, while Dauntless Shield changed from activating on every switch-in to activating only once per battle. Hero form is faster at base 138 Speed and can hold any item, while Crowned Shield drops to 128 Speed but gains Steel's Poison immunity and extensive resistances in exchange for Fighting, Fire, and Ground weaknesses. Close Combat is its strongest straightforward Fighting STAB, Crunch and Wild Charge provide coverage, and in Generation IX Body Press finally gives Zamazenta a way to convert its enormous Defense and Dauntless Shield boost directly into offense. Iron Defense plus Body Press is especially effective in Scarlet/Violet, while Crowned Shield's Behemoth Bash is a perfectly accurate Steel attack and doubled in power against Dynamaxed targets in Sword/Shield. For postgame play, both forms are powerful, but Hero's item freedom and greater Speed can be preferable when Steel typing is unnecessary, whereas Crowned Shield provides the greatest raw defensive margin.
competitive: Zamazenta's competitive history is almost the reverse of Zacian's. In Sword/Shield, both Hero and Crowned Shield were classified as Uber, but neither approached Zacian's dominance because Zamazenta lacked reliable recovery, lacked Body Press in that generation, and had a much weaker offensive movepool. Hero Zamazenta's Choice Band sets could use Close Combat, Crunch, Psychic Fangs, and Wild Charge, but common Ubers walls could exploit its limited STAB and repeated defense drops; Crowned Shield possessed immense bulk but was forced to hold Rusted Shield and was often compared unfavorably with Necrozma-Dusk-Mane. Crowned Shield was even formally suspect-tested for possible release into SS OU, illustrating how unusual it was for a box-art legendary to be considered potentially manageable below Ubers, but it remained outside standard OU. Generation IX nerfed its raw stats and limited Dauntless Shield to one activation per battle, yet the addition of Body Press transformed the practical value of its Defense. Hero Zamazenta is now an actual SV OU Pokémon and Smogon describes it as one of the tier's most consistent glue pieces and win conditions, with Iron Defense + Body Press sets using its natural bulk and base 138 Speed to check major physical threats and sweep weakened teams. Crowned Shield remains Uber, where its 140 Defense and Special Defense, Fighting/Steel typing, Dauntless Shield, Iron Defense, Body Press, and Rest can produce formidable defensive setup sets; it has also had a much stronger modern VGC role than its Generation VIII singles reputation suggests. The line therefore demonstrates that movepool changes can matter more than a nominal stat nerf: Generation IX Zamazenta lost raw numbers but gained the move that finally converted its signature defensive mechanic into reliable offensive pressure.
nuzlocke: Zamazenta is normally relevant only to postgame Nuzlocke extensions and rulesets that permit legendary encounters, but if allowed it is one of the safest physical tanks available. Hero form combines excellent 92/115/115 bulk with base 138 Speed, while Crowned Shield greatly increases both defenses and adds Steel's extensive resistances, though it introduces Fighting, Fire, and Ground weaknesses. Dauntless Shield provides an immediate Defense boost on entry—every entry in Generation VIII but only once per battle in Generation IX—which can turn already favorable physical matchups into extremely safe ones. In Scarlet/Violet, Body Press is ideal for permadeath play because it is perfectly accurate, uses Zamazenta's massive Defense for damage, and avoids Close Combat's self-inflicted Defense and Special Defense drops. Iron Defense can compound that strategy but is often unnecessary against ordinary opponents and still leaves Zamazenta exposed to critical hits or strong special attacks during setup. Wild Charge introduces recoil and Close Combat lowers both defensive stats, so those moves should be reserved for targets that require their coverage or power. Crowned Shield is the safer general defensive form, while Hero's item flexibility and higher Speed can reduce risk by letting Zamazenta act first more often.

pokemon.name: Zamazenta
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Zamazenta is a lupine Legendary closely linked to Zacian and to Galar's ancient history. Three thousand years ago it joined Zacian and two human youths in defeating Eternatus during the original Darkest Day, after which it returned to the Slumbering Weald and slept for ages in a statue-like dormant form. It can absorb metal for use in battle, cast illusions or projections even while dormant, and is capable of flight. The species' existence faded so completely from public memory that the ancient hero story eventually centered on human kings rather than the two Pokémon themselves. Modern historical research by Sonia restored Zamazenta's role as one of the actual legendary protectors of Galar.

pokemon.name: Zamazenta
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Zamazenta assumes Crowned Shield while wielding the Rusted Shield, absorbing metal particles to form elaborate golden armor and expanding the shield-like mane around the front of its body. The armor can shift forward over its forelimbs when Zamazenta braces against frontal attacks or uses Behemoth Bash, while its enlarged mane and ponytail protect much of the rest of the body. This is described as Zamazenta's true full-power form, and its shield can withstand attacks from Dragon claws as well as assaults by Dynamax and Gigantamax Pokémon. Legends claim that a full-force shield bash can crack the earth, send shockwaves through hundreds of opponents, and even bore through mountains. Together with Crowned Sword Zacian, it can break Eternamax Eternatus's mysterious attack-blocking power; ancient Galar remembered this form as the Fighting Master's Shield.

playthrough: Eternatus is encountered during Sword and Shield's climax before the Champion battle, making it extraordinarily late but still technically available for the final major story fight once it is caught. Its Poison/Dragon typing, base 140 HP, 145 Special Attack, and 130 Speed give it immediate legendary-level performance, while 95 Defense and Special Defense are strong enough that its huge HP pool makes both sides genuinely durable. Dynamax Cannon is a perfectly accurate 100-power Dragon move and in Generation VIII doubles in power against Dynamaxed targets, while Sludge Bomb or Sludge Wave provides Poison STAB and Flamethrower or Fire Blast punishes Steel-types. Recover gives Eternatus reliable healing, and options such as Toxic Spikes, Cosmic Power, or other utility let it function as much more than a fast attacker. Pressure increases the opponent's PP consumption when targeting Eternatus, which can matter in long defensive battles even though most normal story encounters end before PP pressure becomes decisive. Eternatus cannot Dynamax despite being the source of Galar's Dynamax phenomenon; instead, the story-only Eternamax transformation represents its overloaded state and is not a form the player can freely use. If legendary Pokémon are allowed, Eternatus is one of the strongest late-game additions possible because it combines speed, bulk, recovery, and special damage without requiring an item or setup turn to become effective.
competitive: Eternatus has been a defining Ubers Pokémon in both Sword/Shield and Scarlet/Violet. In SS Ubers it was considered one of the tier's 'big three' threats and appeared on an enormous share of serious teams because Poison/Dragon typing, base 140 HP, Recover, Pressure, and base 130 Speed let it check major threats while remaining dangerous offensively. Defensive sets absorbed Toxic Spikes, checked Pokémon such as Kyogre and Yveltal depending on the build, and used Toxic, Recover, and Pressure to exhaust opposing resources; offensive sets exploited 145 Special Attack with Dynamax Cannon, Sludge Bomb, Flamethrower, and Meteor Beam or similar coverage. Unlike nearly every other Sword/Shield Pokémon, Eternatus could not Dynamax, but it did not need that mechanic to remain central because its natural statistics and recovery were already exceptional. Scarlet/Violet still classifies Eternatus as Uber, and current Smogon analysis treats it as a premier special attacker that can also serve as one of the tier's most important Kyogre and Ho-Oh checks while absorbing Toxic Spikes. Life Orb or other offensive sets use Dynamax Cannon, Sludge Bomb, Fire Blast, and Recover, while bulkier structures exploit Pressure and status; Terastallization can patch weaknesses or increase offensive pressure even though the native Poison/Dragon typing is already valuable. Its principal modern problems are powerful Ground- and Dragon-type attackers such as Arceus-Ground, Koraidon, or Miraidon, and Steel-types that can exploit sets lacking Fire coverage. Eternamax Eternatus has no ordinary competitive tiering history because it is not a player-selectable battle form; its enormous boss statistics should not be conflated with standard Eternatus's legitimate Ubers record.
nuzlocke: Eternatus is an extraordinarily safe Nuzlocke encounter if the ruleset allows legendaries, although it arrives so late that it affects only the end of Sword and Shield's main story and any postgame continuation. Its 140 HP and balanced 95 defenses provide enormous raw survivability, while base 130 Speed means it usually attacks before ordinary opponents and base 145 Special Attack makes clean knockouts common. Dynamax Cannon and Sludge Bomb are both perfectly accurate, and Flamethrower offers safer Fire coverage than Fire Blast when the extra power is unnecessary. Recover is one of its greatest permadeath advantages because it allows Eternatus to restore health without relying exclusively on consumable items, while Pressure can help in unusually long fights. Ground, Psychic, Ice, and Dragon attacks are the main super-effective threats, and powerful physical Ground attackers deserve particular caution because Eternatus's Defense, while good, is not remotely comparable with its huge HP and offensive stats. Cosmic Power can make Eternatus even harder to remove, but setting up is often unnecessary and still exposes it to critical hits or status. Eternamax is encountered only as a scripted boss state rather than a usable team member, so Nuzlocke evaluation should be based on the normal form the player actually catches.

pokemon.name: Eternatus
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Eternatus is an extraterrestrial Legendary that crash-landed in Galar inside a giant asteroid roughly 20,000 years before the events of Sword and Shield. Its chest contains an energy core that absorbs enormous quantities of power, especially Galar particles, and this relationship makes Eternatus the underlying source of the region's Dynamax phenomenon. Around 3,000 years ago it awakened and triggered the original Darkest Day, forcing Pokémon across Galar to Dynamax and rampage until Zacian and Zamazenta defeated it and sent it back into dormancy. Eternatus can both force other Pokémon to Dynamax by supplying Galar particles and prevent Dynamaxing by absorbing those particles away from them. Later animated and manga portrayals complicate its reputation as a purely malicious monster: its catastrophic effects can result from an inability to control its immense power, and after gaining greater control it has even acted as a protector of Galar.

pokemon.name: Eternatus
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Eternamax is Eternatus's original, massively overloaded form, reached when it reabsorbs the region's Galar particles and also briefly reflected when normal Eternatus uses Eternabeam. Its body expands into an immense coiled serpentine structure whose upper portion resembles a gigantic five-fingered hand; Pokémon Adventures identifies those finger-like projections as separate heads. Eternamax Eternatus releases such extreme Dynamax energy that it creates a vast storm, tears holes in spacetime, and is described as producing an effectively limitless flow of energy responsible for the Darkest Day. While gathering that power it can mysteriously prevent opposing Pokémon from attacking at all, an effect that Crowned Sword Zacian and Crowned Shield Zamazenta can overcome together. This form is larger than ordinary Dynamax and Gigantamax Pokémon and functions as a story boss rather than a form Trainers can normally select for their own Eternatus.

playthrough: Kubfu is received during The Isle of Armor story after completing Mustard's trials, and its evolution is unusual because the player chooses which permanent Urshifu style it becomes. In Sword and Shield, Kubfu evolves after completing either the Tower of Darkness or Tower of Waters and examining that tower's scroll; in Generation IX, exposing Kubfu directly to the Scroll of Darkness or Scroll of Waters produces Single Strike Style or Rapid Strike Style respectively. Both Urshifu forms share 100 HP, 130 Attack, 100 Defense, and 97 Speed, making either one an immediately powerful physical attacker, but their typings change the matchups substantially: Single Strike is Fighting/Dark and has a severe 4× Fairy weakness, while Rapid Strike is Fighting/Water and trades that vulnerability for weaknesses to Electric, Fairy, Flying, Grass, and Psychic. Single Strike's Wicked Blow is a perfectly accurate Dark attack that always lands a critical hit; it had 80 base power in Generation VIII and was reduced to 75 in Generation IX. Rapid Strike's Surging Strikes hits three times, each hit is a guaranteed critical hit, and each strike has 25 base power in Generation IX, giving the style a reliable way to bypass opposing Defense boosts and Attack drops. Unseen Fist lets Urshifu's contact moves hit through Protect and similar protection, making defensive stalling less reliable against either style, while Close Combat supplies extremely strong Fighting STAB at the cost of lowering both defenses. Rapid Strike also has Aqua Jet for priority, whereas Single Strike has Sucker Punch, and U-turn gives both styles a strong pivoting option. In Sword and Shield, Max Soup combined with Max Honey can unlock each style's unique Gigantamax form: G-Max One Blow for Single Strike and G-Max Rapid Flow for Rapid Strike both bypass even Max Guard, making Urshifu unusually difficult to stop with protective moves.
competitive: Urshifu has one of the clearest examples of two forms developing different but equally important competitive histories. Single Strike entered Sword/Shield OU as a devastating Choice Band and Bulk Up wallbreaker because 130 Attack, Wicked Blow's guaranteed critical hit, Close Combat, U-turn, Sucker Punch, and Unseen Fist made defensive scouting exceptionally difficult. Smogon formally suspect-tested Urshifu-Single-Strike in late 2020 and banned it from SS OU on January 10, 2021; it finished the generation in Ubers, where it remained a usable wallbreaker despite competition from stronger restricted and mythical threats. Rapid Strike, by contrast, remained legal and finished Sword/Shield in OU, where Choice Band Surging Strikes could break physically defensive targets through guaranteed critical hits while Aqua Jet and U-turn gave it excellent offensive utility. Generation IX eventually pushed both styles above OU: Single Strike began the Pokémon HOME metagame as Uber, while Rapid Strike initially remained legal but was quickbanned from SV OU on June 11, 2023 after proving too difficult to contain with Surging Strikes, Swords Dance, Terastallization, and its broad coverage. Rapid Strike also became one of the defining Pokémon of Scarlet/Violet VGC, where Surging Strikes ignores Intimidate's damage reduction through its critical hits and Unseen Fist punishes Protect, two properties that are particularly valuable in doubles. Single Strike has remained similarly dangerous in restricted and Battle Stadium environments, with Wicked Blow, Sucker Punch, Close Combat, and Tera Dark giving it enormous one-turn pressure despite its 4× Fairy weakness. Gigantamax Urshifu belongs mainly to Dynamax-legal formats rather than standard SS singles, where Dynamax was banned; its G-Max moves are notable because they can bypass Max Guard as well as ordinary protection.
nuzlocke: Kubfu can be a valuable Nuzlocke encounter because it is guaranteed through The Isle of Armor story rather than dependent on random encounter luck, but the permanent choice between Urshifu styles should be made around the team's existing weaknesses rather than raw power alone. Single Strike is excellent against Psychic- and Ghost-oriented opponents but its 4× Fairy weakness is dangerous enough that even modest Fairy coverage can threaten a knockout, while Rapid Strike has more individual weaknesses but no 4× weakness and gains a useful Fire resistance. Wicked Blow is unusually safe for a high-impact attack because it is perfectly accurate and always critical, while Surging Strikes is also perfectly accurate and breaks Focus Sash, Substitute, and Sturdy-like one-hit protections through multiple hits. The drawback to Surging Strikes is contact being made three times, which can multiply damage from Rocky Helmet, Iron Barbs, Rough Skin, or similar effects and should be checked before committing to the attack. Close Combat is powerful and accurate but lowers both defenses, so repeatedly using it can turn an initially safe matchup into a dangerous one; Aqua Jet is a particularly useful emergency tool for Rapid Strike, whereas Sucker Punch can save Single Strike against faster attackers but fails if the opponent does not use an attacking move. Guaranteed critical hits also ignore defensive stat boosts that might otherwise make damage estimates unreliable, but they do not protect Urshifu from recoil, contact punishment, or faster special attackers exploiting its base 60 Special Defense. Gigantamax can provide a large temporary HP buffer in Sword and Shield, but its three-turn duration should be planned around the battle rather than treated as permanent durability.

pokemon.name: Kubfu
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Kubfu is a small bear-like Fighting-type that trains its body and mind intensely and treats defeat as motivation to become stronger rather than as a reason to retreat from training. It possesses a specialized organ in its lower abdomen that generates fighting energy through controlled breathing and intense concentration. Kubfu also pulls on the two long ribbons of fur behind its head to raise its fighting spirit and build power before or during training. Wild Kubfu live in remote mountainous regions outside Galar, although historical records indicate that the species once lived in Galar and traveled with humans who were exploring or trading in distant lands.

pokemon.name: Urshifu
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Single Strike Style Urshifu trains in remote mountains, racing across sheer cliffs to strengthen its legs and refine its martial techniques. This style favors direct, decisive combat and strongly believes in ending a confrontation with a single overwhelming blow rather than gradually wearing an opponent down. Its movements are straight and aggressive: from a measured distance it suddenly rushes or leaps directly into range and strikes with a hardened fist. When enraged, Single Strike Urshifu is described as merciless, continuing its assault until the opponent is completely crushed. Its unique Wicked Blow reflects that philosophy mechanically by producing a guaranteed critical hit rather than relying on repeated attacks.

pokemon.name: Urshifu
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Rapid Strike Style Urshifu trains in the same distant mountainous environments as Single Strike individuals but develops a fundamentally different fighting philosophy. It calmly observes opponents, studies their strengths, and uses evasive flowing movements to deflect or avoid attacks before countering. Its style is traditionally compared with a river, alternating between calm movement and sudden relentless force rather than advancing in a straight line.
