Once it commits to offense, Rapid Strike Urshifu overwhelms the target with an uninterrupted succession of blows. Its signature Surging Strikes embodies this behavior by delivering three consecutive guaranteed critical hits.

pokemon.name: Urshifu
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Gigantamax Single Strike Style Urshifu becomes more angular and imposing, with elongated headband-like fur, sharper leg fur, glowing eyes and mouth, and red coloration replacing portions of its ordinary black markings. It has been described in Galarian tradition both as the embodiment of rage and as a divine emissary capable of driving away evil spirits through its fury. The shockwaves created by its fists are said to be powerful enough to blow away a Dynamax Pokémon with a single strike. Its G-Max One Blow translates that overwhelming-force motif directly into battle by striking through Max Guard rather than allowing an opponent to shelter behind Dynamax protection.

pokemon.name: Urshifu
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Gigantamax Rapid Strike Style Urshifu develops blue-and-white markings, flowing headband-like fur, and smoother, rounder leg fur than its Single Strike counterpart. It maintains an exceptionally calm one-legged stance without wavering, even while enormous, emphasizing control rather than rage. Those facing it are said to experience either intense agitation or an unusual feeling of relief, as though evil influence has been removed from them. Tradition even claims that a sufficiently malevolent opponent can be destroyed merely by meeting its glare. Its G-Max Rapid Flow carries the same unstoppable martial theme into battle by breaking through Max Guard despite the opponent's attempted protection.

playthrough: Zarude is a Mythical Pokémon rather than a normal story encounter, so in both Sword and Shield and Scarlet/Violet it is relevant to ordinary play only if the player already has access to a legitimate event or transferred individual. If available, its 105 HP, 120 Attack, 105 Defense, 95 Special Defense, and 105 Speed make it a fast and naturally bulky physical attacker with far more durability than many offensive Pokémon. Dark/Grass gives useful resistances to Dark, Electric, Ghost, Grass, Ground, and Water plus a Psychic immunity, but it also creates weaknesses to Fairy, Fighting, Fire, Flying, Ice, and Poison and a severe 4× Bug weakness. Power Whip is its strongest Grass STAB but has imperfect accuracy, while Knock Off or Darkest Lariat supplies dependable Dark offense and U-turn gives Zarude an easy way to exploit its good Speed. Bulk Up or Swords Dance can turn the already high Attack into a sweeping threat, and Synthesis provides direct recovery in Generation IX. Its signature Jungle Healing restores 25% of maximum HP to Zarude and its active allies while also curing non-volatile status conditions, making it especially valuable in double battles or item-restricted challenge runs. Leaf Guard prevents new status conditions while harsh sunlight is active, but because sun also weakens Synthesis outside favorable weather interactions and strengthens enemy Fire attacks, it is a situational protection rather than a universally safe Ability.
competitive: Zarude finished Sword/Shield in UU, where its excellent overall physical stats, base 105 Speed, Dark/Grass typing, and access to recovery gave it a substantial role as a pivot, setup attacker, and answer to selected Water-, Ground-, and Psychic-types. Bulk Up and Jungle Healing sets could exploit passive opponents while curing status, whereas Choice Scarf or offensive sets used Power Whip, Darkest Lariat, and U-turn to maintain momentum. Its major weakness was defensive type overload: six ordinary weaknesses plus a 4× Bug weakness made common U-turn users and faster offensive Pokémon difficult to handle, while Fairy- and Fighting-types punished its Dark typing. Scarlet/Violet currently classifies Zarude as UUBL, reflecting a stronger-than-UU power level even though it does not occupy a regular OU usage slot. Modern Swords Dance sets use Knock Off, Power Whip, and Synthesis to pressure defensive teams, while Terastallization can remove the disastrous Bug weakness or improve matchups against Fairy, Fighting, and Fire attacks. Dada Zarude is functionally identical in battle to ordinary Zarude, so it does not possess a separate tier, stats, Ability, or competitive role despite being recognized as a distinct official form. Zarude's competitive record is therefore respectable rather than dominant: it has consistently had excellent raw tools, but its crowded weakness profile and only moderately fast Speed tier keep it from functioning as effortlessly as the strongest Mythical Pokémon.
nuzlocke: Zarude is normally excluded from a conventional Nuzlocke because it is an event Mythical rather than a naturally obtainable encounter, but rulesets that permit transferred or event Pokémon gain a very strong all-purpose physical attacker. Its 105/105/95 bulk and base 105 Speed provide far more room for error than most offensive Pokémon, and a Psychic immunity plus several useful resistances create legitimate switch-in opportunities. The danger is the enormous weakness list, especially the 4× Bug weakness: U-turn can become unexpectedly lethal because opponents frequently carry it as coverage even when they are not Bug-type. Jungle Healing is exceptionally useful in permadeath play because it is perfectly accurate, restores one-quarter of maximum HP, and cures status for Zarude and any active ally without consuming an item. Synthesis provides stronger direct healing in appropriate weather, while Knock Off and other perfectly accurate physical moves are preferable when Power Whip's 85% accuracy is not required for a knockout. Leaf Guard can block status in sun, but deliberately creating sun also strengthens incoming Fire attacks against a Fire-weak Pokémon, so that interaction should be planned carefully. Dada Zarude has identical battle properties to ordinary Zarude and therefore requires no separate Nuzlocke strategy.

pokemon.name: Zarude
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Zarude is a social, highly territorial simian Pokémon that lives in troops within dense forests and normally reacts aggressively to anything outside its own pack. It can extend strong prehensile vines from its wrists, neck, and the soles of its feet, using them to swing through trees, attack, gather food at a distance, and wrap injured areas. Those vines can absorb energy from trees and accelerate healing, while shed vines eventually decompose into nutrients that enrich the forest soil and support plant growth. The number of visible vines can vary among individuals and, as shown in Secrets of the Jungle, may correspond with age or social rank, with older or more dominant Zarude carrying more. Its combination of sharp claws, quick judgment, group living, and regenerative vines makes Zarude both an effective forest combatant and an active contributor to the ecosystem it defends.

pokemon.name: Zarude
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Dada Zarude is not a separate biological subspecies but a specific unusual Zarude whose documented behavior differs sharply from the species' normally territorial social pattern. It left its troop after finding an orphaned human infant and chose to raise the child itself, eventually developing a deep parental bond instead of rejecting an outsider. Dada wears a torn pink cape bearing Celebi's National Pokédex number, and the cloth was used to wrap the infant; its scent was comforting enough to calm the child when he cried. Pokédex records attribute Dada's unusual strength to the love and care it developed while raising the child. The form is functionally identical to ordinary Zarude in battle, so its significance lies in individual life history, nurturing behavior, and appearance rather than different anatomy, statistics, typing, or Ability.

playthrough: Regieleki is a late Crown Tundra Legendary encountered in the Split-Decision Ruins after the player has captured Regirock, Regice, and Registeel, and the save file must choose between encountering Regieleki or Regidrago there. Its defining statistic is base 200 Speed, the highest base Speed of any Pokémon, allowing it to move first against virtually every unboosted opponent without needing a Choice Scarf. Both Attack and Special Attack are base 100, but the defensive profile is extremely fragile at 80 HP, 50 Defense, and 50 Special Defense, so Regieleki is built to create pressure before the opponent can retaliate rather than absorb hits. Transistor strengthens Electric attacks; in Generation VIII it multiplied the relevant attacking stat by 1.5, while Generation IX reduced the multiplier to roughly 1.3. Thunderbolt and Volt Switch provide reliable special offense and momentum, Rapid Spin removes entry hazards while raising Speed, and Thunder Cage traps the target while dealing residual damage for several turns. The severe limitation is coverage: pure Electric typing has only one weakness, Ground, but Ground-types are completely immune to Electric attacks and Regieleki has historically had very few strong ways to punish them without generation-specific mechanics such as Terastallization. For normal play, its extreme Speed makes it excellent at finishing weakened opponents and avoiding damage, but the player should switch rather than leave it exposed when a Ground move or strong neutral attack is expected.
competitive: Regieleki's competitive history is defined by the tension between the highest base Speed in the series and one of the narrowest offensive movepools. In Sword/Shield it finished in UU, where Transistor's original 1.5× Electric boost made Thunderbolt and Volt Switch threatening while base 200 Speed let it serve as a nearly guaranteed Rapid Spin user, screen setter, or revenge killer. Its ceiling in higher tiers was capped by Ground-types, because opponents such as Landorus-T, Garchomp, or specially bulky Ground-types could invalidate most Electric-only sets and force Regieleki out. Scarlet/Violet temporarily removed that structural weakness: Terastallization gave Regieleki access to coverage through Tera Blast, allowing it to turn into types such as Ice and directly eliminate many Ground-type answers. The result was immediate tiering action—Regieleki was quickbanned from SV OU on May 31, 2023, only one day after Pokémon HOME compatibility expanded the metagame. Generation IX had already nerfed Transistor from a 1.5× to roughly a 1.3× attacking-stat multiplier, but that reduction was not enough to make Tera Blast coverage manageable. In 2026, after Tera Blast itself was banned from SV OU, the council unbanned Regieleki because its ordinary movepool once again left Ground-types as robust counterplay; its usage subsequently fell and its current Smogon tier is RU. That unusual trajectory makes Regieleki a good example of a Pokémon whose tier changed less because its own stats were altered than because a universal generation mechanic temporarily erased the single weakness that had kept it balanced.
nuzlocke: Regieleki offers enormous Nuzlocke safety when Speed is the deciding factor because base 200 Speed means it almost never has to take a normal unboosted attack before moving. Thunderbolt is perfectly accurate and strong enough for routine Electric damage, while Volt Switch lets Regieleki attack and immediately pivot into a safer teammate after confirming the matchup. The problem is survivability if anything goes wrong: 80 HP with base 50 in both defenses gives little margin against strong neutral hits, priority attacks, or unexpected coverage. Ground-type opponents are especially dangerous because they are immune to Electric STAB and can threaten super-effective damage in return, so blindly clicking Volt Switch against an unknown team is unsafe if a Ground switch-in is possible. Thunder Cage can trap targets and add residual damage, but its imperfect accuracy makes Thunderbolt preferable when trapping is unnecessary. Rapid Spin is useful for removing hazards and even raises Speed, although Regieleki is already so fast that the hazard removal is usually more important than the boost. Explosion should generally be excluded from a permadeath moveset because it deliberately causes Regieleki to faint; the species is safest when treated as a fragile high-speed attacker and pivot rather than a sacrificial utility Pokémon.

pokemon.name: Regieleki
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Regieleki is a golem-like Legendary composed largely of electrical energy generated by a single organ that effectively makes up its entire body. According to legend, Regigigas created it from pure electrical energy, and ancient people once worshipped it before becoming frightened by its power and sealing it inside the Split-Decision Ruins. The five blue rings around its body are made from insulating material and are theorized to have been installed by those ancient people specifically to restrain its output; removing them is said to release Regieleki's latent power. Regieleki survives by absorbing electrons and is described as capable of generating enough electricity to supply all of Galar. Its signature Thunder Cage reflects that physiology by surrounding opponents with a sustained cage of electrical energy that traps and damages them over time.

playthrough: Regidrago is encountered through the same late Crown Tundra Split-Decision Ruins sequence as Regieleki, meaning the player normally chooses one of the two new giants rather than catching both on a single save without trading or transferring. Its stat spread is extremely unusual: base 200 HP is paired with only 50 Defense and 50 Special Defense, while both attacking stats are 100 and Speed is a moderate 80. Dragon's Maw multiplies the relevant attacking stat by 1.5 whenever Regidrago uses a Dragon-type move, making even its merely average raw offenses hit much harder than the numbers initially suggest. Its signature Dragon Energy reaches 150 base power at full HP and decreases in direct proportion to Regidrago's remaining HP, so keeping the enormous HP pool healthy is directly tied to offensive output. Dragon Pulse offers a reliable special alternative, while Dragon Claw provides dependable physical STAB; Draco Meteor and Outrage supply greater power but introduce accuracy, stat-drop, locking, or confusion risks. Pure Dragon grants Fire, Water, Electric, and Grass resistances with weaknesses only to Dragon, Fairy, and Ice, but Fairy-types are completely immune to Regidrago's defining STAB and therefore require teammates or non-Dragon coverage. Its huge HP total makes individual hits look less dangerous than base 50 defenses imply, but percentage-based healing and Dragon Energy both reward entering important battles at or near full health.
competitive: Regidrago has spent both Sword/Shield and Scarlet/Violet in NUBL, but the identical tier label hides a distinctive niche centered on one of the strongest full-health spread attacks available. Dragon's Maw gives all Dragon attacks a 1.5× offensive-stat multiplier, and Dragon Energy begins at 150 base power when Regidrago is at full HP, allowing Choice Specs or Dragon Fang sets to deal enormous neutral damage when Fairy-types have been removed. Choice Scarf is another natural option because base 80 Speed is only middling, while preserving full HP lets Regidrago threaten offense with a fast maximum-power Dragon Energy before taking chip. In Sword/Shield, its most severe flaw was a famously shallow coverage pool: Fairy-types could switch into Dragon attacks for complete immunity, and many Steel-types could exploit sets lacking the appropriate physical or special coverage. Scarlet/Violet gave Regidrago a more flexible environment because Terastallization can remove the Fairy immunity problem or strengthen Dragon attacks further, but the same dependence on health, middling Speed, and exploitable base 50 defenses has kept it from becoming a sustained upper-tier singles staple. It has also found situational doubles and VGC use because Dragon Energy hits both opposing Pokémon, meaning a healthy Regidrago under speed control can exert enormous immediate spread pressure. Its competitive identity is therefore less about broad versatility than about forcing opponents to respect a highly amplified Dragon attack whose power is strongest at the beginning of each healthy engagement.
nuzlocke: Regidrago's base 200 HP can make it look nearly impossible to knock out, but a Nuzlocke should account for its base 50 Defense and Special Defense rather than treating the raw HP number as universal bulk. Pure Dragon gives four useful elemental resistances and only three weaknesses, which creates good defensive opportunities against known Fire, Water, Grass, and Electric attackers. Dragon Energy is exceptionally strong when Regidrago is healthy, but because its power falls with remaining HP, taking damage can simultaneously reduce both survivability and offensive reliability during a long boss battle. Dragon Pulse and Dragon Claw are perfectly accurate alternatives when maximum power is unnecessary, whereas Draco Meteor's 90% accuracy and Special Attack drop or Outrage's multi-turn lock and eventual confusion are meaningful permadeath risks. Fairy-types are the most important matchup warning because they are completely immune to Dragon attacks and can often threaten Regidrago super effectively in return. A Choice Scarf can turn base 80 Speed into a much safer revenge-killing profile, but being Choice-locked into a Dragon move is dangerous if an opposing Fairy remains in reserve. Regidrago is safest when kept healthy, brought into known resisted attacks, and used to secure clean knockouts rather than asked to absorb repeated neutral hits simply because its HP bar is unusually large.

pokemon.name: Regidrago
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Regidrago is a golem-like Legendary whose body is formed from crystallized dragon energy, with the densest concentration of that energy located in its central core. Legend says Regigigas created it from crystallized Dragon-type power but ran out of material after completing only the head, leaving the creature in an unfinished state. Ancient people are said to have feared the destruction a completed Regidrago might cause and sealed the incomplete Pokémon inside the Split-Decision Ruins after a period in which it had been worshipped. Its two arm structures resemble the upper and lower jaws of a dragon; Regidrago brings them together into a mouth-like shape when firing Dragon Energy. An unproven academic theory proposes that those arms may derive from the head of an ancient Dragon Pokémon, but canon presents that specifically as speculation rather than established anatomy.

playthrough: Glastrier is obtained through The Crown Tundra's Calyrex storyline if the player plants Carrot Seeds in the Snowslide Slope field and grows an Iceroot Carrot, making it mutually exclusive with Spectrier during the initial story choice. After Calyrex tames it and the player eventually catches Ice Rider Calyrex, the Reins of Unity can separate the pair so Glastrier can be used independently. Standalone Glastrier is a pure Ice physical tank with 100 HP, 145 Attack, 130 Defense, 110 Special Defense, and only 30 Speed, so it is exceptionally powerful and bulky but almost always moves last outside Trick Room. Icicle Crash is its main high-power physical Ice STAB in Sword/Shield, while Generation IX also provides safer options such as Ice Spinner; Close Combat, High Horsepower, Crunch, Heavy Slam, and similar coverage let it punish common Ice resists. Chilling Neigh raises Attack by one stage whenever Glastrier directly knocks out a Pokémon with a damaging move, allowing it to snowball through teams once it secures the first KO. Its pure Ice typing is much worse defensively than its raw stats, giving only an Ice resistance and weaknesses to Fire, Fighting, Rock, and Steel, while Stealth Rock also punishes repeated switching. Trick Room support is the clearest way to turn base 30 Speed into an advantage, but even without it Glastrier can often survive a neutral hit and retaliate extremely hard.
competitive: Glastrier finished Sword/Shield in ZUBL and currently remains ZUBL in Scarlet/Violet, but its most important competitive success came in doubles rather than standard singles. In lower-tier SS singles, 145 Attack and excellent 100/130/110 bulk made it a frightening wallbreaker with Icicle Crash, Close Combat, High Horsepower, and Crunch, while Chilling Neigh threatened to turn one knockout into an escalating sweep. Its base 30 Speed and poor pure-Ice defensive typing nevertheless made ordinary singles positioning difficult, and common hazards plus weaknesses to Fighting, Fire, Rock, and Steel repeatedly limited how often it could enter safely. Early Crown Tundra VGC was a much better environment: Glastrier became one of the premier Trick Room Dynamax attackers, where its low Speed became an advantage, Dynamax patched its HP, Weakness Policy could exploit its natural bulk, and Chilling Neigh rewarded every knockout. Scarlet/Violet removed Dynamax and introduced much faster offensive pressure, leaving standalone Glastrier primarily a lower-tier breaker even though snow now grants Ice-types a 50% physical Defense boost. Terastallization can improve its defensive typing or amplify coverage, but it does not solve the need for careful speed control and hazard management. Its historical reputation should therefore distinguish standalone Glastrier from Ice Rider Calyrex: the fused Calyrex form is an entirely separate Uber-level entity, whereas Glastrier itself has been a dangerous lower-tier singles breaker and a notably stronger Generation VIII Trick Room Pokémon.
nuzlocke: Glastrier is naturally suited to Nuzlocke play because 100 HP, 130 Defense, and 110 Special Defense give it enormous raw bulk, while base 145 Attack means it rarely needs multiple setup turns to threaten a knockout. The major safety issue is base 30 Speed: Glastrier almost always takes an attack before moving, so every matchup should be evaluated around the incoming hit rather than assuming its offense will prevent damage. Chilling Neigh is extremely valuable in multi-Pokémon trainer battles because the first knockout raises Attack automatically and can make subsequent knockouts easier without spending a turn on setup. In Generation IX, snow further raises its physical Defense by 50%, giving an already massive base 130 Defense even more margin against physical attackers. Ice Spinner is perfectly accurate and therefore safer for routine use than Icicle Crash, whose 90% accuracy introduces unnecessary risk when the additional power is not required; Close Combat should also be used selectively because it lowers both defenses after attacking. Fire, Fighting, Rock, and Steel attacks remain dangerous despite Glastrier's bulk, and Stealth Rock chip matters because a slow Pokémon often needs as much HP as possible before entering combat. Trick Room support can turn its greatest weakness into an advantage, but even without Trick Room Glastrier is safest when switched into attacks it is known to survive rather than used as a blind lead.

pokemon.name: Glastrier
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Glastrier is an immensely strong equine Legendary that generates extremely cold air inside its body and releases that cold through its nose and hooves. An ice mask covers part of its face and is described as roughly one hundred times harder than diamond, while additional ice forms its mane, tail, and armor-like coverings around the legs. Although Glastrier runs slowly, it can freeze the ground beneath itself and slide across the resulting ice at high speed, allowing it to cross deep snow and difficult roads. It is aggressive, proud, and territorial, once ruling the Crown Tundra like a lord and terrorizing people who entered its domain until Calyrex defeated and tamed it with the Reins of Unity. Glastrier respects strength, seeks worthy opponents, and is willing to serve only someone it considers powerful enough; it also has a strong fondness for carrots, particularly Iceroot Carrots.

playthrough: Spectrier is a late legendary encounter rather than a normal team-building option. In The Crown Tundra, the player chooses it indirectly by growing a Shaderoot Carrot for Calyrex's steed; after the story culminates in catching Shadow Rider Calyrex, the Reins of Unity can separate Spectrier so it can be used independently. Scarlet and Violet make Spectrier obtainable only in the postgame DLC environment after receiving the appropriate treat from Snacksworth, so it again arrives far too late to influence a normal first playthrough. Its battle profile is extremely specialized: base 145 Special Attack and 130 Speed make it a devastating fast special attacker, but base 60 Defense gives it little margin against strong physical hits. Pure Ghost is nevertheless a useful defensive typing, granting complete immunity to Normal and Fighting attacks and weaknesses only to Ghost and Dark. Shadow Ball is the most reliable primary STAB, while Nasty Plot can double Special Attack and Hex can become very powerful when status support is available; Generation IX also gives Spectrier tools such as Draining Kiss to punish some Dark-type answers while restoring HP. Grim Neigh raises Special Attack every time Spectrier directly knocks out an opponent, allowing one safe KO to begin a sweep without spending a separate setup turn. For ordinary in-game battles where legendary use is allowed, Spectrier is safest when exploiting its Speed and immunities rather than trying to use its respectable 100 HP as justification for taking repeated physical attacks.
competitive: Spectrier immediately proved much stronger competitively than its narrow movepool initially suggested. In early Crown Tundra SS OU, base 145 Special Attack, base 130 Speed, strong Ghost STAB, Nasty Plot or Calm Mind, Substitute, Will-O-Wisp, and Grim Neigh made it extremely difficult to contain once conventional Dark- and Normal-type counterplay had been weakened. Its SS OU suspect concluded with an overwhelming pro-ban result, moving Spectrier to Ubers, where its own niche was greatly diminished because Shadow Rider Calyrex largely performed the same fast Ghost-special-attacker role at an even higher power level. The final SS Smogon Dex therefore lists Spectrier as Uber but describes it as almost completely outclassed by Calyrex-Shadow, with pure Ghost typing being one of its few distinct advantages. Scarlet/Violet still classifies Spectrier as Uber, but Terastallization and access to Draining Kiss give it more ways to challenge Dark-type checks in formats where it is legal. Nasty Plot, Substitute, Shadow Ball or Hex, status support, and Grim Neigh remain the defining interactions: once Spectrier secures a knockout, its Special Attack snowballs without using another setup turn. Its major structural weakness has never changed—coverage is limited, physical Defense is poor, and sufficiently bulky Dark-types or priority users can stop it if they survive the initial attack. Spectrier's historical importance therefore lies mainly in demonstrating that extraordinary Speed, a nearly spammable Ghost STAB, and snowballing can be banworthy even when a Pokémon lacks the broad coverage normally associated with elite offensive threats.
nuzlocke: Spectrier is normally relevant only to a Crown Tundra or Scarlet/Violet postgame Nuzlocke extension, and many rulesets exclude legendaries entirely, but if permitted it is an exceptionally safe offensive cleaner when matchups are known. Base 130 Speed lets it move first against most unboosted opponents, and a perfectly accurate Shadow Ball often removes targets before they can retaliate. Grim Neigh improves safety in multi-Pokémon trainer battles because every direct knockout raises Special Attack automatically, reducing the need to spend turns setting up with Nasty Plot. Its two immunities are valuable switch tools, especially against clearly telegraphed Normal- or Fighting-type moves, but physical attacks must still be respected because base 60 Defense is the weakest part of its stat spread. Will-O-Wisp can patch that physical vulnerability by halving a physical attacker's damage, but its imperfect accuracy introduces a meaningful permadeath risk; using an immediate knockout is safer whenever the damage is already sufficient. Draining Kiss can provide limited recovery against suitable targets in Generation IX, while Substitute deliberately consumes one-quarter of maximum HP and should be used more cautiously than in competitive play. Dark- and Ghost-type priority or coverage are the principal threats, and Spectrier should generally be switched away from a bad matchup rather than asked to survive an unknown physical hit.

pokemon.name: Spectrier
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Spectrier is a nocturnal equine Pokémon that strongly prefers silence and isolation, becoming more energetic at night while avoiding unnecessary contact with other creatures. Its eyesight is poor from those nocturnal habits, but its other senses are exceptionally sharp, allowing it to map terrain and locate living beings without depending on sight. Spectrier feeds by stealing ambient life-force, including from sleeping creatures, and legends claim that its powerful kicks can separate a soul from its body. It is proud and territorial and once ruled over the Crown Tundra's Pokémon while terrorizing humans who entered its domain, until Calyrex defeated and tamed it with the Reins of Unity. Like Glastrier, Spectrier respects strength and prefers to serve an individual it considers sufficiently powerful; it is also notably fond of carrots, especially Shaderoot Carrots.

playthrough: Calyrex is obtained only at the end of The Crown Tundra's major storyline, so neither it nor its rider forms are normal main-campaign choices. The Reins of Unity can fuse Calyrex with Glastrier to create Ice Rider Calyrex or with Spectrier to create Shadow Rider Calyrex, and the same item can separate the partners again. Base Calyrex is Psychic/Grass with 100 HP and exactly 80 in every other base stat, making it balanced but dramatically weaker than either mounted form; it also suffers a 4× Bug weakness alongside six other weaknesses. Ice Rider becomes Psychic/Ice with 165 Attack, 150 Defense, 130 Special Defense, and only 50 Speed, turning it into an extremely slow physical juggernaut suited to Trick Room and its powerful Glacial Lance. Shadow Rider instead becomes Psychic/Ghost with 165 Special Attack and 150 Speed, making Astral Barrage one of the fastest and most immediately dangerous spread-capable Ghost attacks available. Both rider forms use As One, combining Calyrex's Unnerve with the steed's Chilling Neigh or Grim Neigh so opponents cannot consume Berries and every direct knockout can raise the relevant attacking stat. Ice Rider's Glacial Lance was 130 power in Generation VIII and was reduced to 120 in Generation IX, while Shadow Rider's Astral Barrage remains a perfectly accurate 120-power Ghost attack; both hit adjacent opponents in doubles. For postgame use, the rider forms are enormous upgrades over base Calyrex, with Ice Rider favoring bulk and Trick Room and Shadow Rider favoring immediate Speed and special offense.
competitive: Calyrex has one of the widest competitive gaps between forms in the series. Base Calyrex finished Sword/Shield in ZU and is currently ZU in Scarlet/Violet, where its mediocre 80 offenses and Speed, poor Psychic/Grass defensive profile, and shallow immediate pressure leave it largely unviable compared with stronger Psychic- or Grass-types. Ice Rider Calyrex is the opposite: it is Uber in both SS and SV, combining 165 Attack with 100/150/130 bulk, Trick Room, Swords Dance, and Glacial Lance to function as one of the strongest physical wallbreakers and sweepers in restricted formats. Its poor Psychic/Ice defensive typing and base 50 Speed create real weaknesses outside Trick Room, but Terastallization in Generation IX can dramatically improve those matchups while preserving its huge Attack and Chilling Neigh snowballing through As One. Shadow Rider Calyrex was even more influential in SS Ubers: base 165 Special Attack, base 150 Speed, Astral Barrage, As One, Trick, Nasty Plot, Substitute, and broad utility made it the single most centralizing offensive force of the tier, and it remained legal after an SS Ubers suspect test in 2022. Generation IX pushed Shadow Rider over even that exceptionally high threshold. After Pokémon HOME restored it to Scarlet/Violet, the Ubers council quickbanned it and then formally suspect-tested it; on June 12, 2023, the result had reached 42 ban votes to 3 do-not-ban votes, a 93.3% pro-ban majority, permanently sending it to Anything Goes. Shadow Rider is therefore currently AG, while Ice Rider remains Uber and base Calyrex remains ZU, an extraordinary three-tier spread for forms sharing one National Pokédex number. Both riders have also been major VGC restricted Pokémon, with Ice Rider thriving under Trick Room and Shadow Rider exploiting Astral Barrage's spread damage and exceptional Speed.
nuzlocke: Calyrex normally appears only in a Crown Tundra postgame extension, and legendary clauses may exclude it, but if allowed the rider choice has major implications for permadeath safety. Base Calyrex is substantially less secure than its legendary status suggests because Psychic/Grass carries seven weaknesses including a 4× Bug weakness, while its non-HP stats are only base 80. Ice Rider offers extraordinary raw durability and Attack, making it excellent when the player can confidently survive the first hit, but base 50 Speed means it usually accepts damage before moving unless Trick Room is active. Shadow Rider takes the opposite approach: base 150 Speed often prevents damage entirely by moving first, but its Psychic/Ghost typing creates 4× weaknesses to both Dark and Ghost, so Sucker Punch and other priority deserve immediate respect. Glacial Lance and Astral Barrage are both perfectly accurate and hit extremely hard, making them safer than many legendary signature moves whose power comes with an accuracy penalty. As One can snowball a major trainer battle after the first knockout, but the player should remember that critical hits can still bypass favorable defensive calculations and that Chilling Neigh or Grim Neigh only trigger from a knockout caused directly by the rider. For strict Nuzlocke safety, Ice Rider is generally preferable when the incoming attacks are known and survivable, while Shadow Rider excels when Speed and immediate knockouts are the best defense.

pokemon.name: Calyrex
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Calyrex is an ancient Psychic/Grass Legendary remembered as the merciful king who once ruled Galar and brought abundant harvests to its people. It is extraordinarily intelligent and, at full power, can communicate fluently with humans through telepathy; while weakened, it can temporarily take control of a person's body in order to speak through them. Calyrex can perceive events across the past, present, and future, and one legend credits that foresight with saving the inhabitants of a forest from a meteor strike. Its right hand can cause grass and flowers to cover the land, while its left can ripen fields of fruit; it can also create Radiant Petals, mend wounds or hearts, and even relocate an entire forest together with the Pokémon living inside it. Its strength is connected to the faith and remembrance of people, explaining why Calyrex became physically diminished after the Crown Tundra's inhabitants gradually forgot the old king and its deeds.

pokemon.name: Calyrex
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Ice Rider Calyrex is Calyrex restored toward its former full power while mounted on Glastrier through the Reins of Unity. Calyrex amplifies its steed with psychic energy, while Glastrier's cold allows the combined Pokémon to emit temperatures as low as about −500 °F (−300 °C). Glastrier's endurance is also heightened enough to run for seven consecutive days and nights, smashing and freezing obstacles instead of slowing for difficult terrain. Calyrex can shape the steed's intense cold into enormous icicles, firing them like arrows or wielding them as lances while charging; the resulting projectiles are said to punch completely through rocky mountains. Ancient accounts portray the rider as both severe and merciful: it would show no mercy during a conflict, yet afterward heal the wounds of those it had defeated.

pokemon.name: Calyrex
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Shadow Rider Calyrex forms when Calyrex mounts Spectrier with the Reins of Unity, restoring its full power while greatly intensifying Spectrier's spectral abilities. The combined Pokémon is swift enough to cover roughly one thousand miles in a single day, while Calyrex's psychic influence can manifest across an area said to extend about 30 miles. It creates countless small will-o'-the-wisps and rains them down like meteors, using their burning spectral energy to steal an opponent's life-force. Shadow Rider can also compress Spectrier's spectral aura into a black mass described as absorbing life-force and souls like a black hole. Legends remember Calyrex and its bonded steed racing throughout Galar to return vegetation to wastelands, linking this frightening offensive power to the same agricultural kingship associated with base Calyrex.

playthrough: Enamorus is a very late legendary rather than a normal Legends: Arceus team member. It becomes available through the postgame Forces of Nature quest after the player has dealt with Tornadus, Thundurus, and Landorus, so it contributes mainly to completion and optional late battles rather than the core story. It is unobtainable natively in Scarlet and Violet and must be transferred through Pokémon HOME there; the Reveal Glass changes it freely between Incarnate and Therian Forme. Both forms are Fairy/Flying, granting complete immunity to Dragon and Ground plus strong Fighting and Bug resistances, but they are weak to Electric, Ice, Poison, Rock, and Steel. Incarnate Forme has 135 Special Attack and 106 Speed with only 70 Defense, making it a fast special wallbreaker, while Therian Forme keeps the same 135 Special Attack but redistributes Speed down to 46 in exchange for 110 Defense and 100 Special Defense. Abilities do not function in Legends: Arceus, but when Enamorus is used in Scarlet/Violet, Incarnate Forme can use Contrary to reverse stat changes while Therian Forme has Overcoat, protecting it from powder moves and weather chip. Moonblast is the most reliable Fairy STAB, while Earth Power, Mystical Fire, Psychic, and physical Superpower can cover Steel- and Poison-oriented answers; Contrary can even turn Superpower's usual Attack and Defense drops into boosts in main-series battles. Incarnate is normally the better choice for immediate offense, whereas Therian's much greater bulk suits slower teams or situations where surviving a hit matters more than moving first.
competitive: Enamorus entered standard competitive play only after Pokémon HOME made the Legends: Arceus species usable in Scarlet and Violet, but Incarnate Forme immediately established itself as a genuine OU Pokémon. Its combination of 135 Special Attack, 106 Speed, Fairy/Flying STAB, Earth Power, Mystical Fire, and Contrary gives it excellent wallbreaking coverage and makes otherwise defensive stat-lowering moves such as Spirit Break or Parting Shot potentially dangerous for the opponent to use. Choice Specs and Heavy-Duty Boots sets focus on Moonblast and coverage, while Calm Mind, Agility, or mixed Contrary Superpower variants exploit its unusual 115 Attack in addition to the much higher Special Attack. Current Smogon data still classifies Incarnate Enamorus as OU, and it remains a valuable offensive piece because Fairy STAB pressures Dragons, Fighting-types, and many neutral targets while Ground immunity gives it useful entry opportunities. Therian Forme has a much more defensive 74/110/100 bulk profile but only base 46 Speed; it is currently RUBL and uses Calm Mind, Moonblast, Earth Power, Mystical Fire, and Overcoat to function as a slow bulky breaker or setup sweeper. The forms therefore are not interchangeable: Incarnate's Speed is the key to its sustained OU relevance, while Therian sacrifices that speed for substantial physical and special durability. Enamorus has no Generation VIII Smogon usage-tier history despite debuting in a Generation VIII title because Legends: Arceus uses a different battle structure and the species was not transferable into Sword and Shield.
nuzlocke: Enamorus is only available very late in Legends: Arceus, so its practical Nuzlocke value depends heavily on whether the run includes postgame content and allows legendary encounters. Fairy/Flying is excellent for controlled switching because Dragon and Ground attacks do nothing and Fighting and Bug deal only one-quarter damage, but five separate weaknesses mean blind switching is still dangerous. Incarnate Forme's base 106 Speed is much safer for cleaning weakened opponents, whereas Therian Forme's base 46 Speed often forces it to absorb a hit before attacking despite its improved defenses. In Scarlet/Violet challenge formats, Contrary can produce unusual safe opportunities by reversing enemy stat drops, but the player should not assume that benefit in Legends: Arceus because conventional Abilities are absent there. Moonblast and Earth Power are reliable, perfectly accurate core attacks, while Springtide Storm's imperfect accuracy makes it less attractive when a miss could cost the run. Healing Wish should normally be avoided in strict permadeath play because it causes the user to faint in exchange for healing a teammate. Incarnate is the safer offensive form when moving first prevents damage, while Therian is better when a specific known hit must be survived.

pokemon.name: Enamorus
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Incarnate Enamorus is a female-only member of the forces of nature known in Hisui as both the Herald of Spring and the God of Spring. It arrives in Hisui from across the sea as winter ends, and legend claims that the love it brings causes new life to bud throughout the region. Despite that association with love and renewal, Enamorus is highly vengeful toward anyone who disrespects living things and descends from the clouds to administer ruthless punishment. It controls winds filled symbolically with both love and hate and can surround itself with a wind barrier for protection. Its seasonal behavior is partly migratory: it dislikes cold weather, appears when spring returns, and remains in Incarnate Forme while residing within a region.

pokemon.name: Enamorus
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Therian Enamorus has a radically different turtle-like, cloud-borne body while retaining the long snake-like tail and heart imagery of its Incarnate Forme. This form is suspected to be Enamorus's true guise and can be revealed through the Reveal Glass. Rather than remaining settled within one region, Therian Enamorus is known to travel across oceans while searching for a place to reside. The Legends: Arceus Pokédex emphasizes the severe side of its nature in this form, describing it descending from clouds to punish those who treat any form of life with disrespect. It is also associated with the mysterious Interdream Zone, giving the form a broader roaming existence than the seasonal regional presence normally described for Incarnate Enamorus.

playthrough: Sprigatito is one of Scarlet and Violet's three first partner Pokémon, evolves into Floragato at level 16, and becomes Meowscarada at level 36, so the line is available for the entire Paldea adventure with standard starter evolution timing. Meowscarada becomes Grass/Dark and reaches base 123 Speed and 110 Attack, making it one of the fastest naturally obtainable physical attackers in the game, although 76/70/70 bulk means it performs much better by acting first than by trading hits. Its signature Flower Trick is exceptionally reliable: it has 70 base power, bypasses the normal accuracy check, and always scores a critical hit, allowing it to ignore unfavorable Defense boosts when calculating damage. Knock Off gives strong Dark STAB and removes held items, U-turn lets Meowscarada pivot out after attacking, and Play Rough, Acrobatics, Low Kick, Thunder Punch, or later access to Triple Axel provide coverage depending on the available TMs and DLC. Protean changes Meowscarada's type to match the first move it uses after entering battle, but Generation IX limits this to once per switch-in, so the Ability rewards planned sequencing rather than constant type changes every turn. Grass/Dark provides a Psychic immunity and several useful resistances but also seven weaknesses, including a dangerous 4× weakness to Bug, so Meowscarada should not be treated as a defensive pivot simply because it has many resistances. For a normal playthrough, the line's combination of early availability, excellent Speed, accurate Flower Trick, item removal, and pivoting makes it one of Paldea's strongest offensive starter choices.
competitive: Meowscarada has remained competitively relevant throughout Scarlet/Violet because base 123 Speed, Knock Off, Flower Trick, U-turn, Protean, and broad physical coverage give it much more utility than a straightforward starter sweeper. It spent substantial periods functioning directly in SV OU as a fast offensive pivot and remains commonly analyzed for OU play even though its current usage classification is UUBL. Heavy-Duty Boots sets repeatedly use Knock Off to remove opposing items, U-turn to preserve momentum, and Flower Trick to punish bulky targets whose Defense boosts would normally slow physical attackers. Choice Band increases its immediate wallbreaking power, while Choice Scarf lets it revenge kill even faster threats; Triple Axel is especially important in modern sets because it pressures Dragon-, Flying-, and Ground-types that can otherwise exploit its Grass STAB. Protean still expands its offensive typing but is less oppressive than the pre-Generation IX version because it activates only on the first move used after each switch-in, forcing Meowscarada to commit to that type until it leaves the field. Its limitations are equally persistent: 76/70/70 bulk is fragile, Grass/Dark has numerous weaknesses and a 4× Bug weakness, and faster Choice Scarf users or priority can punish it after its role is revealed. Meowscarada is also currently listed as OU in the emerging Pokémon Champions environment, where the same Flower Trick, Knock Off, U-turn, and Speed profile continues to define its role rather than a fundamentally new strategy.
nuzlocke: The Sprigatito line is valuable in a Nuzlocke because it is guaranteed from the beginning, evolves at the normal starter levels of 16 and 36, and ultimately becomes fast enough to avoid many dangerous damage trades. Flower Trick is one of the safest high-value signature moves for permadeath play because it does not perform a normal accuracy check and always critically hits, eliminating both miss risk and many defensive-boost surprises. Knock Off is also perfectly accurate and provides useful Dark coverage, while U-turn lets Meowscarada damage an opponent before escaping a matchup that is becoming unfavorable. The problem is defensive fragility: Meowscarada's seven weaknesses include a 4× Bug weakness, so common coverage such as U-turn can deal far more damage than a player expecting only ordinary super-effective damage may anticipate. Protean can defensively alter the matchup by changing Meowscarada's type, but because it activates only once per switch-in the player must account for the resulting type before predicting the opponent's response. Play Rough and Triple Axel provide valuable coverage but introduce miss chances, so they are less attractive than Flower Trick or Knock Off when the safer move already secures the knockout. Meowscarada should generally be used to move first, score a clean knockout, or pivot away—not to absorb uncertain neutral attacks with its mediocre defenses.

pokemon.name: Sprigatito
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Sprigatito's pale green fur is similar in composition to plant material and can absorb sunlight as an energy source. It regularly grooms itself to pull moisture into that fur, helping it perform photosynthesis, and frequently washes its face because allowing the fur to dry out interferes with this process. By rubbing its paws together, Sprigatito releases a sweet therapeutic aroma that can mesmerize nearby creatures and even make opponents lose the desire to continue fighting; sunlight strengthens the scent. Sprigatito is capricious and strongly attention-seeking, often sulking when people ignore it. Pokémon Sleep adds that it may spread its relaxing scent while moving in its sleep, apparently helping both itself and nearby Pokémon rest.

pokemon.name: Floragato
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Floragato is a dexterous bipedal feline whose long fur changes hardness with its mood, becoming pointed and needle-sharp when it prepares for battle. A vine is concealed beneath that fur and ends in a hard flower bud, which Floragato swings like a yo-yo or flail to strike opponents; official card Pokédex text repeats this distinctive use of the hidden vine and hardened bud. The vine is flexible enough to pull other creatures closer or knock objects from their grasp, and Floragato also uses the bud simply for play and entertainment. It is intelligent, mischievous, and highly showy, retaining Sprigatito's desire for attention while becoming more willing to perform pranks. If a trusted Trainer ignores it, Floragato may even tie that person up with its vine while they sleep, turning its need for companionship into deliberate misbehavior.

pokemon.name: Meowscarada
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Meowscarada develops the Sprigatito line's attention-seeking behavior into the persona of a skilled stage magician, using misdirection and visual tricks during combat. Reflective fur lining its cape camouflages the stem of the flower it carries, creating the illusion that the flower is floating independently; this same detail appears in official TCG Pokédex text. The flower can develop into a pollen-filled explosive, and Meowscarada secretly plants these flower bombs on nearby surfaces before detonating them when opponents are distracted. Its hidden flower stem can also bind opponents, showing that the apparent floating prop remains physically connected and useful outside the explosion itself. Meowscarada is proud, theatrical, and sensitive to attention, becoming jealous or upset when a Trainer it is attached to focuses on another Pokémon.

playthrough: Fuecoco is available from the beginning of Scarlet and Violet, evolves into Crocalor at level 16, and reaches Skeledirge at level 36, giving the family the same straightforward starter progression as the other Paldean first partners. Skeledirge becomes Fire/Ghost with 104 HP, 100 Defense, 110 Special Attack, and only 66 Speed, shifting the line from a simple Fire starter into a slow bulky special attacker with useful Normal and Fighting immunities. Its signature Torch Song is a perfectly accurate 80-power Fire attack that always raises Special Attack by one stage, allowing Skeledirge to increase damage while attacking instead of sacrificing momentum for a conventional setup move. Shadow Ball provides reliable secondary STAB, while Slack Off restores half of maximum HP and Will-O-Wisp can cripple physical attackers; Hex becomes significantly stronger against statused targets. The Hidden Ability Unaware is one of the line's greatest assets because it ignores the opponent's relevant stat stages when calculating damage, preventing many Attack-, Special Attack-, Defense-, or Special Defense-boosting sweepers from exploiting setup in the usual way. Fire/Ghost supplies strong resistances and two immunities but leaves weaknesses to Water, Ground, Rock, Ghost, and Dark, while the low Speed means Skeledirge frequently has to take a hit before retaliating. For normal play, the combination of early availability, reliable recovery, excellent physical bulk, Unaware, and Torch Song makes Skeledirge one of the most forgiving and self-sufficient Paldean starter evolutions.
competitive: Skeledirge established itself immediately as one of Scarlet/Violet's notable defensive starter Pokémon, spending major portions of the generation as a viable OU wall because its bulk, Fire/Ghost typing, Slack Off, Will-O-Wisp, and Unaware let it answer numerous setup sweepers. Torch Song is crucial to that success: unlike many defensive walls, Skeledirge can raise its own Special Attack simply by using its normal Fire STAB, gradually converting defensive turns into a genuine late-game win condition. Heavy-Duty Boots are common because Stealth Rock otherwise chips a Fire-type every time it enters, while Hex synergizes with Will-O-Wisp and Slack Off gives it the longevity needed to repeatedly check offensive threats. Terastallization has also been unusually useful for Skeledirge, especially defensive Tera types such as Fairy or Water that can reverse normally dangerous Dark-, Ground-, or Water-type matchups without sacrificing Unaware. Its current standard SV usage tier is UU, but Smogon continues to maintain an OU defensive analysis because Skeledirge remains capable of checking important OU attackers such as Zamazenta, Dragonite, Iron Valiant, and Iron Moth depending on its defensive investment. Its weaknesses are low base 66 Speed, susceptibility to Knock Off and hazard chip without Boots, imperfect Will-O-Wisp accuracy, and strong special attackers that can overwhelm sets invested mainly in physical Defense. Skeledirge is also currently UU in Pokémon Champions data, where Unaware, Torch Song, Slack Off, and burn support continue to define it as an anti-setup physical wall rather than a fundamentally different competitive Pokémon.
nuzlocke: The Fuecoco family is particularly strong in a Nuzlocke because it is guaranteed from the start and reaches Skeledirge at level 36 with enough bulk and recovery to survive many mistakes that would cost frailer attackers. Torch Song is ideal for permadeath play: it is perfectly accurate, deals solid Fire damage, and raises Special Attack every time it is used, so Skeledirge can become progressively stronger without spending a vulnerable turn on setup. Slack Off restores half of maximum HP and provides sustainable recovery during long trainer battles, greatly reducing dependence on items when the ruleset limits healing. Unaware is another major safety feature because enemy offensive boosts do not inflate damage calculations in the normal way, although it does not make Skeledirge immune to critical hits, status, Speed changes, or raw super-effective attacks. Will-O-Wisp can make physical opponents dramatically safer but has only 85% accuracy, so relying on a burn to survive the next hit is inherently riskier than using a guaranteed knockout when available. Water, Ground, Rock, Ghost, and Dark attacks should still be scouted carefully, and base 66 Speed means the player should usually calculate the incoming hit before selecting an attack. Among Paldea's starter families, Skeledirge is unusually well suited to conservative play because its strongest strategy simultaneously attacks, boosts, heals, and denies opposing setup rather than depending on fragile sweeping conditions.

pokemon.name: Fuecoco
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Fuecoco has a small internal flame sac that cannot completely contain the fire energy it produces, so excess energy constantly leaks from the dent on top of its head as flickering yellow flames. Square scales across its body absorb external warmth—especially from the warm rocks it likes to lie on—and convert that heat into additional fire energy. When Fuecoco becomes excited, more flame tufts can appear, and animated portrayals show those flames providing enough illumination to function as a light source. It has a laid-back temperament and generally acts at its own pace, but its behavior changes immediately around food: Fuecoco enthusiastically rushes toward anything edible that catches its attention. Pokémon Sleep depicts it sometimes sleeping with one eye open and moving its mouth as though chewing even while asleep.

pokemon.name: Crocalor
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Crocalor's overflowing vitality and fire energy create a nest-like mass of flame on its head containing a distinct egg-shaped fireball. It can control that fireball independently enough to send it away from its head and use it directly in attacks, yet the orb remains stable even while Crocalor sways during sleep. Its internal flame sac connects to its vocal cords through a valve, so releasing fire also produces deep guttural vocalizations. The stronger the flames Crocalor exhales, the more destructive and forceful its voice becomes, establishing the musical component that later defines Skeledirge. Like Fuecoco, Crocalor may sleep with one eye open, and its development combines the line's fire physiology with increasingly prominent rhythmic and vocal behavior.

pokemon.name: Skeledirge
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Skeledirge's most unusual feature is the fiery bird resting on its head, which is an independent living entity rather than simply a flame shaped like an animal. The bird originates when Crocalor's egg-shaped fireball gains a soul during evolution, and this event is directly associated with Skeledirge acquiring the Ghost type. Skeledirge's singing is gentle but extremely powerful and full of vitality, soothing the souls of listeners and making opponents feel warm and fulfilled enough to lose the desire to fight. When battle demands greater force, it can produce flames hotter than 5,400 °F (3,000 °C); the bird can transform into a microphone-like shape during singing, become empowered by the performance, and fly toward the target. Despite its intimidating appearance and destructive fire, Skeledirge is meddlesome but deeply caring and is described as an excellent caretaker; even when the fiery bird plays pranks on it while it sleeps, Skeledirge does not become angry.

playthrough: Quaxly is one of Scarlet and Violet's three starters, so a player who chooses it receives the line immediately and can rely on it for the entire story; it evolves into Quaxwell at level 16 and Quaquaval at level 36 with no special evolution requirement. Quaquaval is a strongly physical attacker with base 120 Attack, and its Water/Fighting typing gives it useful STAB against Fire-, Rock-, Ground-, Normal-, Ice-, Dark-, and Steel-type targets while leaving it weak to Electric, Grass, Flying, Psychic, and Fairy attacks. Its signature Aqua Step is one of the line's defining advantages: it is a reliable physical Water attack that raises Quaquaval's Speed every time it lands, letting an initially middling base 85 Speed turn into sweeping momentum without spending a turn on a pure setup move. Close Combat supplies extremely strong Fighting STAB, while options such as Aqua Jet, Knock Off, Ice Spinner or the later-added Triple Axel, Rapid Spin, U-turn, Roost, Swords Dance, and Bulk Up let Quaquaval shift between straightforward offense and utility. Moxie compounds Aqua Step especially well because a knockout can raise Attack at the same time Aqua Step raises Speed, but Moxie is the line's Hidden Ability, so an ordinary story starter normally uses Torrent unless the player deliberately obtains the Hidden Ability later. Adamant and Jolly are the most broadly useful Natures for its physical role, with Adamant maximizing damage and Jolly improving the number of opponents it can outrun before or after an Aqua Step boost.
competitive: Quaquaval has established itself as a legitimate Generation IX singles threat rather than merely a starter with good story utility, and Smogon's current Scarlet/Violet Pokédex places it in UUBL while still providing OU sets. Its defining competitive interaction is Aqua Step plus Moxie: Aqua Step raises Speed with every successful use, and a knockout under Moxie simultaneously raises Attack, allowing Quaquaval to snowball without relying entirely on a conventional one-turn setup move. Swords Dance and Bulk Up can accelerate that process, while Close Combat gives it immediate wallbreaking power and current Generation IX options such as Triple Axel and Knock Off improve its ability to punish traditional Water/Fighting checks. Quaquaval is also unusually flexible for an offensive starter because Rapid Spin, Roost, Knock Off, Flip Turn or U-turn, Encore, and Taunt can support utility or bulky sets instead of forcing it into a single sweeper role. Assault Vest sets exploit its respectable natural bulk and strong two-STAB coverage, while offensive sets usually prefer Adamant or Jolly depending on whether power or pre-boost Speed is more important; defensive Terastallization, particularly into a type that removes its many common weaknesses, can create an extra setup opportunity. Its limitations are equally important: base 85 Speed is mediocre before boosting, its Water/Fighting typing carries five common weaknesses, and bulky foes able to stomach its STAB combination can interrupt the Moxie chain, so it is dangerous but not an effortless top-tier sweeper. Quaquaval also had a clearer niche in early Battle Stadium Singles formats such as Regulation C, but that relevance declined as the legal pool expanded, illustrating the difference between its enduring singles utility and its more format-dependent official-ladder presence.
nuzlocke: For a Nuzlocke, the Quaxly line's greatest structural advantage is encounter certainty: if Quaxly is chosen as the starter, there is no capture roll, encounter-table competition, or unusual evolution requirement between the player and a fully evolved Quaquaval. The level-16 and level-36 evolutions arrive at sensible story points, and Quaquaval's combination of 120 Attack, workable bulk, and Aqua Step's guaranteed Speed boost can turn many favorable matchups into controlled sweeps in which it becomes less likely to take a second hit. Aqua Jet is valuable emergency priority, while the line's Water typing before final evolution and Water/Fighting typing afterward give numerous safe resistances but demand caution around Electric-, Grass-, Flying-, Psychic-, and Fairy-type coverage. Aqua Step is often preferable to riskier maximum-power options because it is accurate, has no recoil, and improves future safety; by contrast, Wave Crash and Brave Bird consume HP through recoil, while Close Combat's Defense and Special Defense drops can make a surviving opponent or immediate follow-up enemy unexpectedly dangerous. Triple Axel can provide excellent coverage but introduces multi-hit accuracy variance, so Ice Spinner is often the safer choice when survival matters more than maximum damage. Moxie makes Quaquaval even more capable of chaining knockouts if the Hidden Ability is available, but a standard starter usually has Torrent, which is less spectacular yet still useful without changing the line's core reliability. Overall it is a strong Nuzlocke starter: powerful, fast after one Aqua Step, and reasonably durable, but it rewards disciplined move selection rather than repeatedly clicking recoil moves or defense-lowering attacks just because they have the highest base power.

pokemon.name: Quaxly
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Quaxly is a small duck-like Pokémon whose large blue coif is held smooth by a rich, moist cream; the cream can repel grime, while glossy gel secreted by its feathers protects its body from water and dirt. It is notably tidy, earnest, and prone to overthinking, and it especially dislikes getting its head dirty or allowing its coif to dry out and become unkempt. Its strong legs let it swim even in fast currents and also deliver rapid repeated kicks in battle. Although associated with Paldea, Quaxly is not native to the region: its species is said to have migrated there from distant lands long ago. Pokémon Sleep material adds that an unusually long sleep can leave its coif dry and messy, an uncommon state for a species so attentive to grooming.

pokemon.name: Quaxwell
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Quaxwell is a long-legged duck-like Pokémon whose enlarged crest can absorb impacts and be used as a shield against incoming attacks. Damage or disorder to that crest affects it strongly: if the crest becomes messy, Quaxwell feels physically and mentally unwell and quickly restores it with gel. It is serious, hardworking, and sometimes temperamental, learning dance movements by observing people and Pokémon from many regions and incorporating what it sees into its own routines. Groups of Quaxwell repeatedly run through shallow water to strengthen their legs, then compete to see which individual can perform the most graceful kicks. Pokémon Sleep descriptions reinforce its disciplined posture while also noting that exhaustive daily training can occasionally leave it too tired to maintain its coif while asleep.

pokemon.name: Quaquaval
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Quaquaval is a humanoid waterfowl Pokémon with an elaborate tail whose organs eject decorative, teardrop-shaped water feathers. In battle those water feathers can move forward and spin around its body like cutting blades, while its exceptionally trained legs are strong enough to launch a truck with a single kick. Its combat and display movements are expressed through dance, including styles said to draw from faraway lands, and its dancing is captivating enough to mesmerize observers; Tsareena is described as viewing Quaquaval as a rival. Quaquaval is cheerful and energetic but also intensely serious about continual practice, becoming focused in critical situations rather than treating every dance as frivolous display. Even in sleep it may sway its body or strike elegant poses, and animated depictions have shown it using small fountains of water from its wing-arms as part of celebratory movement. Its signature move, Aqua Step, directly reflects this combination of dance and battle technique.

playthrough: Lechonk appears extremely early in Scarlet and Violet and evolves into Oinkologne at level 18, making this one of the easiest Paldean families to obtain and fully evolve during a normal run. Oinkologne is a mono-Normal Pokémon with only one direct type weakness, Fighting, plus a valuable Ghost immunity, but its base 65 Speed means it usually takes hits before moving and its overall offensive ceiling is modest compared with stronger late-game attackers. The two sexes are mechanically distinct: male Oinkologne has 110 HP, 100 Attack, 75 Defense, and 80 Special Defense, while female Oinkologne shifts some of that physical power into durability with 115 HP, 90 Attack, 70 Defense, and 90 Special Defense. Their regular Ability pools also differ, with male Oinkologne able to use Lingering Aroma and female Oinkologne Aroma Veil; both can have Gluttony and share Thick Fat as a Hidden Ability, the latter effectively improving matchups into Fire- and Ice-type attacks. Its move progression gives it practical story tools such as Dig, Headbutt, Yawn, Body Slam through TM access, Double-Edge later by level, and coverage including Seed Bomb, Stomping Tantrum, Iron Head, and Play Rough, although it lacks the raw stats or STAB variety to dominate difficult battles. Adamant can improve the male form's stronger physical offense, while Impish, Careful, or other bulk-oriented Natures are reasonable when the goal is to exploit Oinkologne's HP and simple defensive profile rather than race faster attackers.
competitive: Oinkologne's competitive record has been much more modest than the flashier Paldean newcomers, and Smogon's current Scarlet/Violet Pokédex places the species in ZU without a standard recommended moveset. Male Oinkologne has the more offensive stat spread and access to Lingering Aroma, an unusual contact-triggered Ability that replaces the attacker's Ability with Lingering Aroma until it leaves the field; this can interfere with contact attackers that depend heavily on abilities, but it is reactive and does not compensate for Oinkologne's low Speed or limited pressure. Female Oinkologne sacrifices 10 points of Attack and 5 Defense for higher HP and Special Defense and can use Aroma Veil instead, giving the two forms genuinely different defensive profiles even though neither has become a major singles staple. Thick Fat is often the most broadly useful ability when the goal is simple durability, while Yawn, Body Slam, Rest, and coverage moves can support bulky or disruptive sets. The fundamental problems are that mono-Normal STAB is easy to prepare for, base 65 Speed leaves Oinkologne exposed to faster offensive Pokémon, and its 489 BST is distributed toward bulk without providing reliable instant recovery or enough damage to force progress consistently. As a result, Oinkologne is best described as a low-tier bulky utility Pokémon with a few distinctive form-specific tools rather than an overlooked high-level wallbreaker; competitive analysis should not overstate Lingering Aroma simply because it is unique.
nuzlocke: Lechonk is a useful Nuzlocke encounter largely because it is common, available almost immediately, and evolves at only level 18, so the player can obtain a reasonably bulky fully evolved Pokémon with very little risk or investment. Oinkologne's pure Normal typing is easy to understand defensively: it is immune to Ghost and has only Fighting as a type weakness, which can create predictable switch-in opportunities when enemy movesets are known. Its large HP stat gives it a better margin for surviving neutral attacks than many early-route Pokémon, and female Oinkologne is especially suited to taking special hits, while male Oinkologne trades some of that special bulk for higher physical damage. Lingering Aroma can occasionally make physical contact attackers safer by stripping an important Ability after they hit the male form, and Thick Fat is excellent insurance against unexpected Fire- or Ice-type coverage when the Hidden Ability is available. Yawn is a valuable low-risk control tool, and accurate attacks such as Body Slam or Dig are generally preferable to repeatedly leaning on Take Down or Double-Edge, whose recoil can turn otherwise safe victories into accumulated death risk. Oinkologne's chief Nuzlocke weakness is tempo: because it is slow and does not possess exceptional defenses or reliable one-turn recovery, it often has to absorb damage before acting, so it is a dependable early- and midgame body rather than a Pokémon that should be left in against every neutral matchup.

pokemon.name: Lechonk
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Lechonk is a stout hog-like Pokémon with an exceptionally developed sense of smell, which it uses to locate fragrant wild grasses and rich Berries. That diet causes its body to give off a herbal odor that repels Bug-type Pokémon, and it has also been observed feeding on the sweet nectar produced on Appletun's back. Although it looks plump, much of its mass is muscle developed by constantly walking in search of food. Lechonk is timid and faint-hearted, tending to panic and charge straight ahead when startled or attacked. Humans can take advantage of its nose to search for cooking ingredients, while animated depictions show that food carried by people can also draw an aggressive response from hungry individuals.

pokemon.name: Oinkologne
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Male Oinkologne is a stout, glossy-coated hog Pokémon with a predominantly gray-black body and a tail that ends in a bulb- or flower-bud-like structure. The tip of that tail can release a concentrated sweet scent over its body, and the aroma is specifically used to attract female Pokémon. Its skin is a point of apparent pride, and the male's scent biology is reflected mechanically by Lingering Aroma, an Ability unique to male Oinkologne. Like the species generally, it has powerful leg muscles, but its most distinctive documented biological trait is the deliberate production and use of this concentrated alluring odor.

pokemon.name: Oinkologne
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Female Oinkologne has a dark brown coat with lighter facial and ear coloration and a tail that divides into three long appendages rather than ending in the male's bulb-like tip. Its body gives off a flowerlike fragrance that has a calming effect on nearby Pokémon instead of the male form's specifically alluring scent. The female form is described as meticulous and particularly concerned with keeping things tidy. Oinkologne's leg muscles are sufficiently developed to let it leap more than 16 feet, a striking athletic ability for such a heavy-bodied Pokémon. These documented scent and temperament differences support treating the female as a separate biology entry rather than reducing the distinction to appearance alone.

playthrough: Tarountula is available near the beginning of Scarlet and Violet and evolves into Spidops at level 15, so the family reaches its final stage earlier than almost any other new Paldean line. Spidops is a pure Bug type with respectable base 92 Defense and 86 Special Defense but only 60 HP, 79 Attack, and an extremely low base 35 Speed, which makes it much better at utility than at sweeping story battles. Its signature Silk Trap functions as a protective move that also lowers the Speed of an opponent that makes contact, and it can combine that with Sticky Web, Spikes, Toxic Spikes, U-turn, Memento, Circle Throw, or Taunt to shape battles rather than simply trade damage. In a normal playthrough, however, enemy trainers switch infrequently and most ordinary encounters reward direct offense, so setting multiple hazards is rarely as efficient as using a stronger attacker; First Impression and Leech Life help Spidops contribute damage without pretending its offensive stats are better than they are. Stakeout can punish opponents that switch into its attacks, but story AI does not switch consistently enough to make the Ability a dependable centerpiece, while Insomnia is situational protection from sleep. Defensive or Attack-boosting Natures such as Impish, Careful, or Adamant can each be justified depending on whether the player wants a dedicated support lead or simply the most damage possible from a low-powered early Bug type.
competitive: Spidops has one of the clearest examples in Generation IX of a good utility movepool failing to overcome poor base stats, and Smogon's current Scarlet/Violet Pokédex places it in ZU. Its theoretical selling point is exceptional hazard compression: Sticky Web, Spikes, and Toxic Spikes can all fit on the same species, with Taunt, Memento, U-turn, Circle Throw, Lunge, Pounce, and Knock Off offering additional ways to support an offensive team. Silk Trap adds a species-specific Protect variant that punishes contact by lowering Speed, but the move does not solve Spidops's central problem of base 35 Speed and only modest 60/92/86 bulk, which means it often struggles to act repeatedly against competent offensive teams. In practice, its most defensible role is a dedicated entry-hazard lead that tries to establish Sticky Web and perhaps another layer before leaving the field through U-turn or Memento. Stakeout sounds threatening on paper, but Spidops lacks the raw Attack and Speed to capitalize on forced switches as consistently as stronger Stakeout users, while Insomnia offers only narrow defensive utility. Smogon's draft analysis similarly treats it as a late, very low-cost selection whose value comes from Webs and utility rather than battle-to-battle power, so describing Spidops as anything more than a specialized support Pokémon would overstate its actual competitive standing.
nuzlocke: Tarountula's early availability and level-15 evolution make the family easy to obtain and develop in a Nuzlocke, but Spidops's survival profile is mixed rather than simply good because of its respectable defensive stats. Base 60 HP and base 35 Speed mean it commonly takes a hit before moving, and weaknesses to Fire, Flying, and Rock include several attack types that appear frequently enough to punish careless use. Silk Trap is more valuable in permadeath play than in many ordinary story battles because it can scout a damaging move while lowering the Speed of a contact attacker, potentially turning an unsafe matchup into one a teammate can control. First Impression gives Spidops immediate priority damage on the first turn after entering, while U-turn can reduce exposure by getting it out after making progress; Leech Life supplies some recovery without requiring a passive turn. Entry hazards are less universally valuable in a Nuzlocke because most in-game opponents do not switch often, although Sticky Web can still matter in important battles with multiple Pokémon by reducing the Speed of later grounded opponents. Spidops is therefore usable as a tactical support Pokémon, but it should not be mistaken for a tank: slow turns, mediocre HP, and common weaknesses make repeated neutral hits dangerous, and its safest value comes from scouting, priority, pivoting, and controlled utility rather than prolonged face-to-face exchanges.

pokemon.name: Tarountula
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Tarountula is a small green arachnid Pokémon whose body is wrapped in a ball of white thread secreted from its rear, with the abdomen visible when it ejects or loosens that covering. Its silk is both elastic and extraordinarily strong, described as being as tough as wire and capable of deflecting attacks from its natural enemy, Scyther. The mechanism behind that silk's strength is still an active subject of research within the setting. Tarountula can hang upside down from trees by its thread, making its webbing both protective covering and climbing apparatus rather than a purely decorative cocoon.

pokemon.name: Spidops
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Spidops is a net-casting-spider-like Pokémon with spinnerets on all eight feet and an additional spinneret at the end of its abdomen, allowing it to produce silk from many points around its body. It can separate its eight legs for a conventional arachnid crawl or cluster them into pairs that create a more humanoid stance. Spidops is a covert ambush predator: its sticky, resilient threads let it cling to surfaces and move silently, and it can hang upside down before spreading a net between its upper legs and smothering prey before the target can react. It favors the sides of trees and marks its territory with silk hazards and tripwires designed to trap intruders. The spool-like bands of silk wrapped around its abdomen and its many spinnerets are therefore functional parts of a hunting system, not merely visual resemblance to a yarn spool.

playthrough: Nymble is obtainable during the early portion of Scarlet and Violet and evolves into Lokix at level 24, giving the player a fully evolved attacker well before the late game. Lokix's Bug/Dark typing, base 102 Attack, and base 92 Speed make it dramatically more offensively useful than many traditional early-route Bug Pokémon, and it also gains a complete immunity to Psychic attacks together with useful resistances to Ground, Grass, Ghost, and Dark. First Impression is its signature play pattern even outside competitive battling: the move has very high priority and strong base power but only works on the first turn after Lokix enters, encouraging repeated switching rather than staying in indefinitely.
