Ghost-type Curse is normally a poor Nuzlocke choice because it sacrifices half of Brambleghast's maximum HP, directly conflicting with survival unless there is an unusually specific tactical reason to use it.

pokemon.name: Bramblin
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Bramblin resembles a tumbleweed composed of dry, thorny plant stalks, with floating leaf-like eyes that rotate rather than blink to express emotion. It is formed when a wandering soul that cannot move on becomes tangled with dried grass. Wind is its primary means of locomotion, carrying it unpredictably across dry, rocky wilderness, and even Bramblin itself does not know where it will end up. It strongly dislikes getting wet and is associated with arid habitats such as deserts.

pokemon.name: Brambleghast
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Brambleghast is a larger and thornier tumbleweed-like Pokémon whose loose branches can open outward and completely envelop prey. It holds captured prey until it has absorbed the life energy it needs, then expels and discards it. Like Bramblin, it wanders through arid regions by rolling with the wind. Rare mass outbreaks can become so extensive that entire towns are said to be buried beneath groups of Brambleghast.

playthrough: Toedscool is widely obtainable in Paldea's wooded and humid areas and evolves normally into Toedscruel at level 30, so this line does not require an item or elaborate late-game condition. The final evolution has an unusual 515 base-stat total distribution: base 120 Special Defense and 100 Speed make it both specially durable and naturally fast, while its offensive stats are only moderate. Ground/Grass gives Toedscruel an Electric immunity plus Ground and Rock resistances, but the combination is extremely vulnerable to Ice and is also weak to Fire, Flying, and Bug. Its signature Ability, Mycelium Might, forces its status moves to act last within their priority bracket but lets those status moves ignore the target's Ability; in story battles this makes moves such as Spore more reliable against Ability-based protection, at the cost of giving opponents a chance to move first. Earth Power and Grass STAB provide solid special coverage, while Giga Drain offers sustain and Rapid Spin, Knock Off, Spikes, Toxic Spikes, or other support moves can make Toedscruel useful even when raw damage is insufficient. Timid is a natural offensive or utility nature because it preserves the excellent Speed for damaging moves and Rapid Spin, whereas Calm or Bold can emphasize bulk if the player is using Toedscruel primarily as a status and support Pokémon.
competitive: Toedscruel is currently listed in ZU on Smogon's Scarlet/Violet Pokédex, but its competitive history is more interesting than that final usage tier implies. Early in Generation IX, Mycelium Might made Spore especially notable because its status moves could ignore defensive Abilities such as Good as Gold, giving Toedscruel a rare way to threaten Pokémon such as Gholdengo while also serving as a Rapid Spin user. As Scarlet/Violet's standard Smogon singles rules evolved, sleep-inducing moves were eventually banned from OU and the standard usage-tier structure, removing one of Toedscruel's most distinctive early selling points there. Its current lower-tier identity instead leans on offensive utility: Timid Rapid Spin sets use Leaf Storm or Giga Drain with Earth Power, then choose among Knock Off, Sludge Bomb, Spikes, or Toxic depending on the format and team. The 120 Special Defense and 100 Speed are excellent individual traits, but 80 Special Attack is only moderate, 65 Defense leaves it vulnerable to physical pressure, and the 4× Ice weakness is extremely exploitable. As a result, Toedscruel has remained a useful specialist for hazard control and role compression rather than a consistently high-tier threat, with Mycelium Might simultaneously granting unique Ability-bypassing utility and imposing a major tempo cost on status moves.
nuzlocke: Toedscool is more usable before evolution than many early forms because it already has excellent Special Defense for an unevolved Pokémon, but its low HP and physical Defense mean that physical attackers can still remove it quickly. Evolving at level 30 gives Toedscruel a major survivability upgrade, and the combination of an Electric immunity, strong Special Defense, and base 100 Speed provides several useful defensive and tempo advantages. The largest warning is the 4× Ice weakness: even relatively modest Ice coverage can be fatal, so switching Toedscruel into an unknown movepool is dangerous despite its impressive special bulk. Spore is exceptionally attractive in a Nuzlocke because perfectly accurate sleep can create safe healing or switching turns, but Mycelium Might makes Toedscruel move last when using it, so the Pokémon must first survive the opponent's action; this makes Spore much safer against slower or weak opponents than against powerful attackers. Giga Drain can provide repeatable recovery while Earth Power offers reliable 100%-accurate Ground STAB, and Rapid Spin can remove hazard chip without forcing a dedicated support teammate. Conservative play should therefore exploit known Electric attacks and favorable special matchups while avoiding blind stays against anything likely to carry Ice, Flying, Fire, or strong physical coverage.

pokemon.name: Toedscool
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Toedscool is a mushroom-like Pokémon that resembles Tentacool despite being a biologically unrelated species. It lives in humid forests and clings to tree roots, moving on two long, thin leg-like structures that can carry it at about 30 mph. Flaps hanging from its body sometimes fall off naturally; these shed pieces are chewy, considered delicious, and are used as food. Its resemblance to Tentacool is therefore superficial rather than evidence of an evolutionary relationship.

pokemon.name: Toedscruel
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Toedscruel is a large mushroom-like Pokémon supported by ten tentacle-like structures resembling mycelium. Groups gather in colonies deep within forests and strongly dislike strangers approaching their territory. It captures prey by coiling its tentacles around the victim and sucking out nutrients, a process described as painful for the prey. The folded rim of its mushroom cap is itself considered a popular delicacy, creating an unusual contrast between Toedscruel's predatory feeding and its own use as food.

playthrough: Klawf is a standalone Pokémon available unusually early in Scarlet and Violet around South Province (Area Three), the same region where the Stony Cliff Titan is fought, so it can contribute for much of the main story without waiting for an evolution. Its base 100 Attack and 115 Defense are strong for that stage of the game, while base 75 Speed is respectable for a physically bulky Rock-type; the main statistical weakness is only 55 Special Defense. Pure Rock provides useful resistance to Normal, Fire, Flying, and Poison attacks but leaves Klawf weak to Water, Grass, Fighting, Ground, and Steel, all of which are common enough to require careful matchup selection. Anger Shell can turn surviving a hit that drops Klawf to half HP or lower into an offensive swing by raising Attack, Special Attack, and Speed while lowering both defenses, whereas Shell Armor is much simpler and prevents critical hits entirely; the Hidden Ability Regenerator restores one-third of maximum HP when Klawf switches out and is the best long-term defensive option when available. Its practical movepool includes strong Rock attacks plus coverage and utility such as Knock Off, High Horsepower, Crabhammer, Stealth Rock, and Swords Dance, letting it function as either a bulky attacker or support Pokémon. Adamant is appropriate for straightforward physical offense, while Impish, Careful, or even Speed-boosting natures can be justified for defensive or utility roles depending on what the player wants Klawf to outrun and survive.
competitive: Klawf is currently listed in ZU in Scarlet/Violet, but it has had a documented lower-tier defensive niche built much more around Regenerator than around its signature Anger Shell. During SV PU play, Smogon analyses used Regenerator with Stealth Rock, Knock Off, a Rock STAB move, and either coverage or Swords Dance, taking advantage of the fact that automatic one-third healing on switches makes Klawf unusually difficult to wear down for a Pokémon without a conventional recovery move. Heavy-Duty Boots has commonly supported that pivoting style, while Rock Slide trades power for reliability and Stone Edge or Rock Blast provide higher offensive ceilings; Loaded Dice Rock Blast also appeared in experimental higher-tier builds. Klawf even received some early OU experimentation because the combination of Regenerator, Stealth Rock, and Knock Off compressed several useful jobs into one slot, but this remained a niche choice rather than evidence that Klawf was broadly OU-caliber. Anger Shell offensive sets can create a surprise sweep after crossing half health, yet the accompanying Defense and Special Defense drops make them fragile and the setup is difficult to engineer safely against stronger teams. Its present ZU status reflects the larger problem: mono-Rock typing gives it too many common weaknesses, 55 Special Defense is exploitable, and stronger or more reliable Rock setters compete for the same team slot even though Regenerator keeps Klawf from being competitively worthless.
nuzlocke: Klawf is valuable in a Nuzlocke because it can be encountered early with fully evolved-level physical stats, immediately providing a strong answer to many Normal, Fire, Flying, and Poison attacks. Shell Armor is especially desirable under permadeath rules because removing critical hits eliminates one of the most dangerous sources of unexpected damage; Regenerator is also excellent if the Hidden Ability is available, since repeated switching can restore health without consuming healing moves or items. Anger Shell is more volatile: the Attack and Speed boosts can rescue a battle, but the simultaneous defensive drops mean that a Klawf already at half health may be much easier to finish off on the following turn. Its five weaknesses and poor Special Defense make blind switches into special attackers dangerous, especially against Water-, Grass-, Ground-, Fighting-, or Steel-type coverage. Reliable Rock Slide can be preferable to Stone Edge when the extra power is not needed, because a miss in a key matchup can be catastrophic, while Stealth Rock and Knock Off add low-risk value without forcing Klawf to remain in prolonged combat. The former Titan Klawf can also be captured after its story encounter, giving players a distinctive marked specimen, but standard wild Klawf already offer the line's main practical advantages.

pokemon.name: Klawf
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Klawf is a crustacean Pokémon protected by a rugged, stony carapace, with freely rotating eyes on stalks that let it survey its surroundings in many directions. It lives on sheer cliffs, where it can hang sideways or upside down while waiting to ambush prey, although remaining inverted too long causes blood to rush to its head and makes it dizzy. Its powerful claws can immobilize prey, exploit an opponent's weak points, and grow back if lost; shed or harvested claws and shell material are also used in Paldean foods such as Klawf-based dishes and Klawf Sticks. The Stony Cliff Titan is an abnormally large Klawf that grew after consuming Herba Mystica in South Province.

playthrough: Capsakid can be obtained relatively early in Paldea and evolves into Scovillain simply by using a Fire Stone, allowing the player to choose the timing rather than waiting for a specific level. Scovillain is the line's major jump in power, gaining the unusual Grass/Fire typing and equal base 108 Attack and Special Attack, though its base 65 defenses and 75 Speed keep it from being naturally durable or especially fast outside of support. Chlorophyll is normally the most immediately useful story Ability because sunlight doubles Scovillain's Speed, and Growth becomes particularly dangerous in sun because it can raise both offenses sharply; Insomnia provides a simpler immunity to sleep, while Moody is the Hidden Ability and is inherently unpredictable. Its special movepool makes a sun-oriented attacker the most straightforward approach, using Fire STAB with Grass attacks such as Giga Drain or Solar Beam, although its equal offenses allow mixed coverage when desired; Modest or Timid fits special sets, while Naive or Hasty can support mixed attacking if there is a real reason to preserve both offenses. Spicy Extract is its signature status move, raising the target's Attack by two stages while lowering its Defense by two, which can create strong physical-support combinations but can also make an enemy more dangerous if used carelessly. Current 2026 canon adds Mega Scovillain through Pokémon Legends: Z-A's Mega Dimension content: Scovillainite allows the Mega Evolution, raising both attacking stats to 138 and both defenses to 85 while leaving Speed at 75; Pokémon Champions implements Mega Scovillain with the new Spicy Spray Ability, so those Champions Ability mechanics should be distinguished from Scarlet/Violet and from Z-A's different battle system.
competitive: Base Scovillain is currently ZU in Smogon's Scarlet/Violet singles tiers, and its original competitive identity was that of a specialized sun sweeper rather than a generally splashable attacker. Chlorophyll doubles its otherwise middling Speed in sun, Growth can boost both offenses more aggressively under the same weather, and Fire plus Grass STAB lets it pressure many Water-, Ground-, and Steel-type targets; common sets have used Flamethrower or Fire Blast alongside Giga Drain, Solar Beam, Leaf Storm, or limited coverage such as Stomping Tantrum. Its drawbacks are equally clear: 65/65/65 bulk is poor, base 75 Speed is unimpressive without sun, and the movepool offers limited coverage outside its STAB combination, so stronger weather sweepers and more self-sufficient attackers frequently outclass it. Moody gave Scovillain a very different luck-driven identity in Battle Stadium Singles, but Moody is banned from standard SV OU play and therefore is not part of its ordinary Smogon usage-tier niche. The family's competitive profile changed dramatically in 2026 with Mega Scovillain in Pokémon Champions, where Smogon currently lists both Scovillain and its Mega form in UU and documents a Regulation M-A support set built around Rage Powder, Overheat, Giga Drain or Leech Seed, and Spicy Spray. Official Pokémon coverage of Regulation M-B goes further: Mega Scovillain became an early tournament success because Spicy Spray burns any Pokémon that damages it, even with a special attack, while Rage Powder can deliberately redirect attacks into that punishment; an especially successful composition featuring Lycanroc and Mega Froslass converted well at both the Turin Special Event and the North American International Championship. That is genuine contemporary tournament history, but it belongs specifically to the newly established Champions environment rather than being retroactively applied to Scovillain's much weaker Scarlet/Violet singles résumé.
nuzlocke: Capsakid is frail enough that evolving it with a Fire Stone as soon as the player is ready to use Scovillain is generally safer than carrying the unevolved form for long. Scovillain's Grass/Fire typing is useful because the Fire half removes Grass's normal weakness to Fire and Ice while the Grass half removes Fire's weaknesses to Water and Ground, leaving only Flying, Poison, and Rock weaknesses; nevertheless, 65/65/65 bulk means neutral damage can still become dangerous quickly. Chlorophyll is the most reliable offensive Nuzlocke Ability because a sun setter can turn Scovillain into a much faster attacker, while Insomnia can create completely safe lines against known sleep moves; Moody is powerful when it rolls favorable boosts but introduces exactly the sort of randomness that conservative permadeath play normally tries to avoid. Giga Drain is especially valuable because it combines damage with recovery, whereas Solar Beam is excellent only when sun is dependable and becomes a dangerous two-turn commitment if weather changes. Spicy Extract should be used cautiously because lowering an enemy's Defense does not compensate for granting it +2 Attack if the target survives and can strike back. In formats where Mega Scovillain is available, its improved 65/85/85 bulk and enormous dual 138 offenses are meaningful upgrades, and Champions' Spicy Spray can greatly reduce physical danger after an attacker is burned, but its unchanged base 75 Speed means Mega Evolution does not by itself solve every revenge-killing problem.

pokemon.name: Capsakid
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Capsakid is a small green plant Pokémon with a white cap-like growth and a single prominent front tooth. It uses sunlight to produce spicy chemicals inside its body, and greater exposure to sunlight increases the intensity of those chemicals. Its front tooth falls out naturally and is traditionally used as an ingredient in extremely spicy Paldean dishes. Legends: Z-A adds that Capsakid is prone to intense mood swings, possibly because of those internal chemicals, and will bite things it takes a dislike to.

pokemon.name: Scovillain
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Scovillain has two pepper-like heads with distinct temperaments and fighting styles, usually a red head on one side and a green head on the other; Pokémon Horizons has shown that rare individuals can have the colors reversed or even share the same head color, but these are not established as separate gameplay forms. Spicy chemicals stimulate the green head's brain and make it vicious, while the red head converts those chemicals into fiery energy that it blasts outward. The species is described as ferocious once it begins rampaging, yet Legends: Z-A establishes that the two differing personalities can act in perfect harmony during battle. This division of behavior between the heads closely parallels Scovillain's dual Grass/Fire identity and its signature use of spicy chemicals.

pokemon.name: Scovillain
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Mega Evolution makes Scovillain bulkier and more aggressively spiked, with enlarged fangs and tongues and a darkened upper body that resembles a suit. A glowing, jagged pepper-like structure hangs from its collar like a necktie, while its heads, tail, and limbs gain additional spikes. Its spiciness is explicitly intensified by Mega Evolution, and it attacks by swinging the necktie-like growth to wallop opponents. Mega Scovillain was introduced in the Mega Dimension DLC for Pokémon Legends: Z-A and is the only known Pokémon associated with the Spicy Spray Ability in formats that implement it.

playthrough: Rellor is found in the Asado Desert and begins as a very weak Bug-type with only a 270 base-stat total, so the line's real value appears after evolution. Like Bramblin and Pawmo, Rellor evolves through Scarlet and Violet's Let's Go! walking mechanic: after walking 1,000 steps with Rellor outside its Poké Ball, it must level up while still outside to become Rabsca. Rabsca changes to Bug/Psychic and becomes a slow special attacker and support Pokémon, with base 115 Special Attack, 100 Special Defense, 85 Defense, and only 45 Speed. Psychic and Bug STAB can be backed by coverage such as Earth Power or Dazzling Gleam, while Recover, Trick Room, screens, Memento, and other support options let Rabsca contribute without relying only on damage. Its most famous move is Revival Blessing, which can restore a fainted party member to half HP in ordinary play; that effect is mechanically extraordinary but depends heavily on the rules of the challenge or format being played. Quiet is especially appropriate for Trick Room builds because Rabsca naturally benefits from being slow, while Modest can maximize normal special attacking and Bold or Calm can suit support-focused sets.
competitive: Rabsca is currently listed in ZU in Scarlet/Violet, but it attracted immediate competitive attention at Generation IX's launch because it combines Trick Room with the then-new Revival Blessing. Revival Blessing's ability to return a fainted teammate at half health created early controversy, and players quickly explored Leppa Berry and Sleep Talk interactions to obtain additional revivals, making the move itself a central topic of early SV tiering discussion even though Rabsca was never a dominant general-purpose Pokémon. In more conventional use, Rabsca can set Trick Room, use Recover to remain functional, attack from base 115 Special Attack, and employ Revival Blessing to restore an important teammate; Telepathy additionally has doubles value because it avoids damage from allied spread attacks such as Earthquake. The line has also appeared on successful ranked-ladder VGC teams, including Regulation C constructions that used Rabsca specifically for Trick Room and Revival Blessing support, showing that its niche was real even if narrow. Its weaknesses explain why that niche never translated into a high usage tier: base 45 Speed is helpful only under Trick Room, Bug/Psychic leaves six weaknesses, it can become passive when its support moves are not immediately valuable, and stronger dedicated setters or attackers often fit teams more easily. Consequently, its current ZU placement is consistent with its history as a specialized support Pokémon whose unique move can swing individual games without making Rabsca broadly efficient in standard singles.
nuzlocke: Rellor is one of the more dangerous Pokémon in this batch to carry unevolved because its stats are extremely low, so the 1,000-step evolution requirement is worth completing before exposing it to serious trainer battles. Rabsca's much better defenses and Special Attack make it a legitimate team member, but its base 45 Speed means it will often take a hit before acting outside Trick Room, increasing the importance of known matchups and careful switching. Recover substantially improves long-term survival, and its 4× resistance to Fighting plus resistances to Grass, Ground, and Psychic can create useful defensive entries, but six weaknesses to Bug, Flying, Rock, Ghost, Fire, and Dark make blind switching hazardous. Trick Room can reverse the Speed disadvantage for Rabsca and slower teammates, though spending a turn setting it carries its own risk if the opponent can deal heavy damage immediately. Revival Blessing is normally incompatible with conventional Nuzlocke rules because a fainted Pokémon is considered permanently dead even if the game engine permits revival; if a custom ruleset explicitly allows the move, it becomes one of the strongest emergency resources available. Synchronize can punish certain opposing status users by reflecting burn, poison, or paralysis, but it does not prevent Rabsca from suffering the status itself, so it should not be treated as a substitute for status immunity.

pokemon.name: Rellor
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Rellor creates the ball it pushes by mixing sand and dirt together with psychic energy. It values this mud ball more than its own life and continually rolls it as the energy needed for evolution develops within it. The species' entire daily behavior is therefore tied to protecting and moving the ball rather than treating it as disposable material. Its design and behavior closely parallel dung-rolling scarab beetles, but the Pokédex explicitly gives the ball a psychic function in addition to its physical composition.

pokemon.name: Rabsca
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Rabsca carries a large ball above its body while the body supporting it moves very little, leading the Scarlet Pokédex to suggest that the Pokémon's true body may actually be inside the sphere. Violet clarifies that an infant sleeps within the ball and that Rabsca gently rotates it with its legs to keep the infant comfortable. The infant is visibly represented inside the translucent ball in Rabsca's game model, reinforcing that the sphere is not merely an external tool. Its biology therefore centers on protecting and soothing developing young rather than the mud-ball construction behavior of Rellor.

playthrough: Flittle evolves into Espathra at level 35, so the line spends a noticeable portion of a Scarlet/Violet playthrough as a small, relatively frail Psychic-type before receiving a major statistical jump. Espathra's base 101 Special Attack and 105 Speed immediately make it a capable special attacker, and its signature Lumina Crash is especially valuable in ordinary play because it combines 80 base power and perfect accuracy with a guaranteed two-stage Special Defense drop, allowing repeated uses to break bulky targets without requiring setup. Its Hidden Ability Speed Boost is the most explosive option, raising Speed at the end of each full turn and pairing naturally with Calm Mind and Stored Power, while Opportunist can occasionally punish opposing stat boosts without requiring Hidden Ability access. Psychic typing is offensively useful but leaves Espathra weak to Bug, Ghost, and Dark attacks, and its 60 Defense and 60 Special Defense mean that careless setup attempts can end quickly. Terastallization can patch those defensive problems or give it coverage against Dark-types, but a straightforward Lumina Crash set is usually more practical for the story than building entirely around a long Stored Power sweep. Beneficial Natures include Modest for immediate special damage and Timid when maximizing natural Speed matters; bulkier Calm Mind approaches can also justify Bold.
competitive: Espathra became one of Generation IX's most notorious early setup sweepers because Speed Boost, Calm Mind, and Stored Power all increase its sweeping threat at the same time: Speed Boost raises Speed while also increasing Stored Power's base power, and Calm Mind adds both power and special bulk. Terastallization made conventional counterplay less reliable by allowing Espathra to change away from its Psychic weaknesses or gain coverage for Dark- and Steel-types, while Substitute, Protect, and Roost could buy additional turns for automatic Speed boosts. Smogon's SV OU council ultimately banned Espathra in February 2023, and it remains classified as Uber in the current SV Strategy Pokédex; its ban was driven by the combination of rapid snowballing, Stored Power, Speed Boost, and Tera rather than by exceptional raw base stats alone. It has alternatives to the classic setup set, most notably Lumina Crash, whose guaranteed two-stage Special Defense reduction can pressure special walls, but that role never defined its competitive reputation as strongly as Stored Power sweeping. Espathra is not automatically dominant in Ubers because priority, phazing, strong immediate attackers, Dark-types, and the opportunity cost of spending turns setting up can all contain it. In the current Pokémon Champions environment, Smogon lists Espathra as UUBL and still documents Calm Mind, Stored Power, Speed Boost, and defensive support moves as its central strategy, showing that the basic engine remains competitively relevant even under the newer ruleset.
nuzlocke: Espathra can become an excellent Nuzlocke sweeper once Flittle reaches level 35, but the line's greatest danger is how little room its mediocre defenses leave for mistakes. Lumina Crash is particularly attractive under permadeath rules because it is perfectly accurate, deals respectable immediate damage, and guarantees a two-stage Special Defense drop, giving Espathra a predictable way to snowball without first sacrificing a turn to setup. Speed Boost can become outstanding safety insurance if the Hidden Ability is available, since surviving one turn can let Espathra outrun threats that would otherwise force risky damage trades; Opportunist is less consistent but can punish bosses that rely on stat boosts. Calm Mind and Stored Power can produce devastating sweeps, yet attempting to accumulate several boosts against an unknown moveset exposes Espathra to critical hits, physical attacks, status, and Dark-type interruptions. Hypnosis is usually a poor safety tool in a Nuzlocke because its accuracy creates unnecessary variance, while Roost, Substitute, Reflect, or other controlled support options can improve survival when available. Overall, the line has a high ceiling but should be treated as a fast offensive Pokémon rather than a durable switch-in; known matchups and careful positioning make it substantially safer than blind play.

pokemon.name: Flittle
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Flittle is a tiny Psychic-type whose toes hover about half an inch above the ground because psychic power is emitted from the frills on its belly. It spends much of its time running through wastelands and is notably attached to berries; if another creature steals its berries, Flittle will pursue the thief to retaliate. Its hovering gait and frilled body foreshadow the much larger psychic plumage of its evolution.

pokemon.name: Espathra
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Espathra is a tall, flightless, ostrich-like Pokémon whose elaborate frills conceal openings from which it emits psychic power. It can project psychic energy from its eyes strongly enough to immobilize opponents, while its long legs allow it to run at more than 120 mph (200 km/h). The species inhabits deserts and mountainous regions and is regarded as aggressive; when it notices people nearby, it may spread its feathers, cry out, and charge. Despite its tremendous straight-line speed, observed Espathra do not turn well and must slow or stop before changing direction.

playthrough: Tinkatink evolves into Tinkatuff at level 24 and Tinkaton at level 38, giving the family convenient level-based progression with no special item or multiplayer requirement. Fairy/Steel is one of the strongest defensive type combinations available in Scarlet/Violet: the line has only Fire and Ground weaknesses, two immunities in Dragon and Poison, and a large collection of resistances, making it unusually easy to bring into favorable matchups. Tinkaton's base 75 Attack is modest, but Gigaton Hammer compensates dramatically with 160 base power and perfect accuracy; its restriction is that the move cannot be selected on consecutive turns, so Play Rough, Knock Off, coverage, or utility moves are needed between swings. Mold Breaker is generally the most useful conventional Ability because it lets Tinkaton's moves ignore opposing Abilities, while Own Tempo blocks confusion and, in modern mechanics, prevents Intimidate from lowering its Attack; Pickpocket is more situational. Its 105 Special Defense and base 94 Speed support a flexible role that can mix direct attacks with Thunder Wave, Encore, Stealth Rock, Knock Off, or Swords Dance rather than behaving like a simple slow bruiser. Tinkaton and Tinkatuff also became obtainable in Legends: Z-A through later 2026 content, but their conventional Scarlet/Violet Ability mechanics should not be assumed to function identically in Z-A's different battle system. Adamant can maximize physical damage, Jolly can exploit the useful Speed tier, and Careful or Impish can suit more defensive utility-focused builds.
competitive: Tinkaton has been a genuine Generation IX utility Pokémon despite a mediocre offensive stat line, because Fairy/Steel typing, base 94 Speed, excellent Special Defense, Gigaton Hammer, and a deep support movepool let it compress several roles at once. Smogon currently lists it in SV UU, where it can set Stealth Rock, remove items with Knock Off, disrupt slower or setup-oriented opponents with Encore and Thunder Wave, and still threaten substantial damage with a 160-base-power Steel STAB attack. Mold Breaker is particularly valuable on support sets because it allows moves to ignore defensive Abilities that would otherwise block or alter their effects, while Gigaton Hammer prevents passive foes from treating Tinkaton as harmless even though its base Attack is only 75. It has also appeared as an OU utility option, often relying on its defensive typing and speed rather than attempting to compete directly with stronger Steel-type wallbreakers. Its main constraints are weak sustained damage between Hammer turns, vulnerability to strong Ground- and Fire-type attacks, only moderate physical bulk, and competition from Pokémon with greater raw power or recovery. Smogon's current Pokémon Champions Pokédex likewise places Tinkaton in UU, with its signature Hammer and broad utility movepool intact, so its competitive identity remains that of a disruptive enabler rather than a conventional powerhouse.
nuzlocke: The Tinkatink line is unusually attractive in a Nuzlocke because its Fairy/Steel typing offers a large number of safe switch-in opportunities and only two ordinary weaknesses. Evolution at levels 24 and 38 is simple and predictable, so there is no rare item, friendship threshold, walking counter, or multiplayer requirement that can delay reaching Tinkaton. Gigaton Hammer is excellent for controlled boss fights because it is perfectly accurate and extraordinarily strong, but the inability to select it on consecutive turns means the player must plan the following turn instead of assuming repeated Steel damage will finish every target. Own Tempo can be a very safe Ability because it prevents confusion and modern Intimidate Attack drops, while Mold Breaker is often better offensively but provides less direct survival value. Tinkaton's good Special Defense and resistances make it dependable, but its physical bulk is less impressive and Ground or Fire coverage from an unexpected opponent can be fatal. Play Rough's 90% accuracy is also worth respecting in permadeath battles; when Gigaton Hammer or another perfectly accurate move can achieve the same knockout, the lower-variance option is preferable.

pokemon.name: Tinkatink
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Tinkatink is a small, female-only Fairy/Steel Pokémon that carries a crude hammer resembling a metal rattle. It forges the hammer itself from iron scraps and repeatedly remakes it until satisfied, scavenging tools and fragments from places such as mines and steel factories. The species' reliance on self-made tools begins immediately at this stage and becomes increasingly specialized as it evolves.

pokemon.name: Tinkatuff
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Tinkatuff constructs a larger, sturdier hammer from collected metal and commonly lives around ruins or piles of scrap. It attacks groups of Pawniard and Bisharp to gather metal for the weapon; the animated series has additionally depicted a Tinkatuff attacking Corviknight to obtain feathers for its hammer. Tinkatuff test their craftsmanship by smashing their hammers against those of other Tinkatuff, and they may visit factories and warehouses in human settlements while gathering material needed for their eventual evolution. Pokémon Sleep material shows that the hammer is not only a tool and weapon but also functions as a pillow when Tinkatuff sleeps.

pokemon.name: Tinkaton
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Tinkaton wields a gigantic metal hammer weighing more than 220 pounds (100 kg) and can swing it with remarkable ease despite being much smaller than the weapon. It is described as intelligent and daring, stealing objects that interest it and carrying the plunder back home. Tinkaton also launches rocks into the sky with its hammer to target flying Corviknight. Legends: Z-A adds social detail to the species by identifying Tinkaton as leaders of Tinkatink groups that teach younger members the skills needed to pound and shape metal. Its signature Gigaton Hammer reflects this extreme specialization in weapon use.

pokemon.name: Tinkaton
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: The Supervisor form is represented by Tinkmaster, a distinctive Tinkaton introduced in Pokémon Pokopia with an unusual multi-purpose version of the species' giant hammer incorporating additional tools such as a wrench and saw. Tinkmaster is exceptionally skilled at handcrafting and engineering, showing a strong interest in human-made buildings and machines and helping reconstruct large structures from salvaged material. Its Engineer specialty allows it to lead major building projects more efficiently, and it can process iron ingots into specialized Tinkagears. Because these documented tool-use and construction behaviors go well beyond the ordinary form's appearance, the Supervisor form represents a meaningful official behavioral specialization rather than a simple color or costume variation.

playthrough: Wiglett evolves into Wugtrio at level 26, making the line easy to complete early enough for a normal Scarlet/Violet playthrough if a coastal encounter is obtained. Wugtrio is an extreme fast attacker rather than a bulky Water-type: base 120 Speed and 100 Attack are strong for the story, but base 35 HP and 50 Defense make physical hits especially dangerous. Its signature Triple Dive is a 30-base-power physical Water attack that hits three times for 90 total base power when all hits connect, while Aqua Jet gives useful priority for finishing weakened opponents. Gooey can punish contact by lowering the attacker's Speed, Rattled can turn certain Bug-, Dark-, Ghost-type hits or Intimidate into a Speed boost, and Sand Veil is mainly relevant on dedicated sand teams. The line's narrow pure-Water typing leaves only Electric and Grass weaknesses, but its low bulk means even neutral attacks can be threatening despite that favorable chart. Adamant improves its damage without giving up an already excellent Speed tier in many story battles, while Jolly is useful when absolute Speed is the priority.
competitive: Wugtrio's competitive profile has been defined by the contrast between excellent base 120 Speed and very poor durability. Smogon currently places it in SV ZU, reflecting how difficult it is for base 100 Attack and a limited offensive toolkit to compensate for 35/50/70 bulk in a metagame where switching opportunities are scarce. Triple Dive gives it a distinctive 90-base-power multi-hit Water STAB and can break Focus Sash or Substitute-like protections through repeated hits, while Aqua Jet supplies priority despite Wugtrio already being fast. Gooey can create occasional speed-control value if an opponent makes contact, but relying on being struck is dangerous for a Pokémon with such low HP and Defense. It can still function as a fast attacker or emergency revenge killer in low-power environments, but stronger Water-types generally provide more damage, bulk, coverage, or utility with far less risk. Its low tier therefore reflects real limitations rather than a hidden top-level niche being overlooked.
nuzlocke: Wiglett is easy to evolve at level 26, but this is one of the riskier Water lines to keep alive because Wugtrio has only base 35 HP and 50 Defense. The 120 Speed stat is its strongest survival tool: when it can secure a clean knockout before being hit, it avoids damage entirely, and Aqua Jet adds insurance against weakened faster or priority-sensitive targets. Triple Dive is strong and can bypass effects such as Focus Sash through multiple hits, but its 95% accuracy introduces more failure risk than a perfectly accurate Water attack, which matters greatly when a miss could expose Wugtrio to retaliation. Gooey may salvage a bad contact matchup by reducing the opponent's Speed, but Wugtrio is too frail to treat taking that contact hit as a normal strategy. Pure Water typing is defensively clean, yet neutral physical attacks can still cause severe damage and unexpected Electric or Grass coverage is particularly dangerous. It is best used as a carefully positioned finisher rather than a general-purpose switch-in.

pokemon.name: Wiglett
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Wiglett is a long, white coastal Pokémon that remains mostly buried in sand, leaving only its head and part of its body visible; the full extent of its underground body remains unknown. It feeds while protruding from beach sand and has an exceptional sense of smell capable of detecting scents from more than 60 feet (20 meters) away. Wiglett is timid and cautious, retreating beneath the sand when it detects nearby Pokémon such as Veluza. Although it resembles Diglett, researchers determined that the two are separate species whose similar body plans are associated with adaptation to different environments.

pokemon.name: Wugtrio
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Wugtrio consists of three long red bodies emerging from a dark, spiky coastal rock, with much of its anatomy hidden inside the den. Unlike the timid Wiglett, Wugtrio is described as vicious and aggressive. It wraps its long bodies around prey and drags the captured animal into its lair, making its hunting behavior one of the clearest ecological details known for the species. Its resemblance to Dugtrio initially caused confusion, but Wugtrio and Dugtrio are separate species rather than regional forms of one another.

playthrough: Bombirdier is a standalone Flying/Dark Pokémon with a useful combination of immediate physical power, immunities to Ground and Psychic, and no evolution delay. Its base 103 Attack and 82 Speed are sufficient for story battles, while STAB Flying and Dark attacks cover a broad range of opponents and Sucker Punch can provide valuable priority. The standout Ability is Rocky Payload, which multiplies the offensive stat used for Rock-type attacks by 1.5, effectively giving Bombirdier a third heavily boosted attacking type without changing its defensive typing. Its movepool also supports utility through options such as Knock Off, Taunt, Stealth Rock, and Roost, so it does not have to rely entirely on Brave Bird or other high-damage attacks. The main drawbacks are weaknesses to Electric, Fairy, Ice, and Rock, plus the recoil of Brave Bird if used as its principal Flying STAB. Adamant emphasizes wallbreaking and Sucker Punch damage, while Jolly can be preferable when the extra Speed changes important matchups.
competitive: Bombirdier has settled into a legitimate lower-tier role rather than disappearing as a novelty Pokémon. Smogon currently lists it in SV PU and describes it as one of the tier's better offensive pivots and Knock Off users, supported by its Dark/Flying typing, useful defensive profile, and broad utility movepool. Knock Off and Brave Bird provide strong STAB pressure, Sucker Punch gives priority, and Taunt, Stealth Rock, or Roost let Bombirdier adapt between offensive and support responsibilities. Rocky Payload is unusual because it grants a 1.5× offensive modifier to Rock attacks, allowing Stone Edge or other Rock coverage to function almost like an additional STAB type, although competitive sets may choose Big Pecks depending on the role. Heavy-Duty Boots are valuable because Bombirdier's Flying typing leaves it vulnerable to Stealth Rock and because repeated pivoting is central to many of its sets. Its moderate Speed and only decent bulk keep it out of stronger tiers, but within PU it has real role compression and should not be dismissed merely because its overall stat total is modest.
nuzlocke: Bombirdier can be a strong Nuzlocke encounter because it arrives fully evolved and immediately offers two immunities, several resistances, respectable 70/85/85 bulk, and useful offensive stats. Ground immunity in particular creates safe switch opportunities against predictable moves, while Sucker Punch can finish dangerous weakened opponents before they attack. Rocky Payload improves damage without recoil, making Rock coverage appealing when it secures a knockout, whereas Brave Bird's one-third recoil can turn an otherwise safe victory into dangerous accumulated damage and should be used selectively. Roost substantially improves long-term reliability when available, and Knock Off or Taunt can reduce threats without demanding a risky all-out attack. Its four common weaknesses—Electric, Fairy, Ice, and Rock—mean blind switching is still dangerous, especially against coverage moves. Compared with frailer offensive birds, Bombirdier offers a useful margin for error, but conservative move choice is important if Brave Bird is part of the set.

pokemon.name: Bombirdier
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Bombirdier is a stork-like Pokémon with a long apron formed from shed feathers hanging from its chest. While flying, it grips the end of this apron in its beak and uses it to carry food—including Basculin—back to its nest. It also collects rocks and other objects in the apron and deliberately drops them from high places for amusement, especially favoring objects that make loud noises when they land. This object-dropping behavior is reflected directly in its signature ecological identity and in its unique Rocky Payload Ability.

playthrough: Finizen evolves into Palafin starting at level 38 only when it levels up while the player is connected with another player through a Union Circle, making this family's evolution unusually dependent on multiplayer access. Once evolved, Palafin initially appears underwhelming because Zero Form has only base 70 Attack, but its signature Zero to Hero Ability transforms it into Hero Form after it switches out without fainting; Hero Form jumps to base 160 Attack with much stronger defenses while retaining base 100 Speed. Flip Turn is especially convenient because it can deal damage while activating the required switch, allowing Palafin to return later in Hero Form without wasting as much momentum. Hero Palafin's signature Jet Punch is a perfectly accurate 60-base-power priority Water attack, while Wave Crash provides enormous direct damage and Bulk Up can turn it into a powerful setup sweeper. Pure Water typing gives only Grass and Electric weaknesses, and Hero Form's 100/97/87 defenses make it far sturdier than its Zero Form presentation suggests. Terastallization can amplify Water damage or alter defensive matchups, though the line is already extremely powerful without depending on Tera. Adamant is excellent for maximizing Jet Punch and wallbreaking damage, while Jolly can matter when Palafin must outspeed other base-100 or nearby Speed threats before priority is relevant.
competitive: Palafin produced one of the fastest major tiering reactions of early Scarlet/Violet because Zero to Hero effectively turns an ordinary-looking base form into a Pokémon with base 160 Attack, base 100 Speed, strong bulk, and exceptional Water attacks after a single switch. Smogon's SV OU council quickbanned Palafin on November 25, 2022, only a week after the generation began, and the current SV Strategy Pokédex still classifies it as Uber. Choice Band sets use Wave Crash for overwhelming wallbreaking and Jet Punch for unusually strong priority, while Bulk Up variants can exploit Hero Form's improved defenses and use coverage such as Close Combat or Ice Punch. Flip Turn naturally satisfies Zero to Hero's switching requirement while maintaining momentum, so the Ability's activation cost is much smaller in practice than it first appears. Palafin is less dominant in Ubers than it was in OU because Pokémon such as Koraidon and Miraidon reshape Water matchups and the overall power level is much higher, but it still has a clear niche as a physical breaker and revenge killer. As of 2026, Smogon's Pokémon Champions Pokédex also lists Palafin as Uber, showing that its defining stat transformation and priority remain powerful under the newer competitive ruleset.
nuzlocke: Palafin has exceptional Nuzlocke potential, but obtaining it is conditional: Finizen must reach at least level 38 and level up while connected through Union Circle, so runs without multiplayer access may be unable to evolve it at all. After evolution, the player must still activate Zero to Hero by switching Palafin out without fainting, making safe positioning on its first appearance important; Flip Turn is ideal because it combines the switch with damage. Once Hero Form is active, base 160 Attack, improved 100/97/87 bulk, and priority Jet Punch create an excellent survival profile because many opponents can be removed before they are allowed to attack. Wave Crash is immensely powerful but its recoil is a significant permadeath hazard, and Close Combat's Defense and Special Defense drops can make the following turn unsafe, so Liquidation, Jet Punch, Drain Punch, or other lower-risk options may be preferable when their damage is sufficient. Pure Water typing keeps the weakness list short, but strong Electric and Grass attacks remain serious threats and Zero Form should not be left exposed simply because Hero Form is durable. If the multiplayer evolution requirement is satisfied and recoil is managed conservatively, Palafin is one of the strongest ordinary non-legendary Nuzlocke assets available in Paldea.

pokemon.name: Finizen
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Finizen produces the water ring around its tail from seawater mixed with a sticky fluid secreted through its blowhole. It is notably social, playing with others of its own species by using the tail ring. Finizen also emits ultrasonic waves that allow it to sense the emotions of other living creatures, giving the species a well-defined sensory ability beyond ordinary echolocation-like behavior.

pokemon.name: Palafin
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Zero Form Palafin closely resembles Finizen and serves as the species' ordinary outward appearance; Palafin remains in this form outside battle and begins battles in it. Its physical capabilities are described as essentially no different from Finizen's until its allies are in danger and it transforms. Palafin deliberately conceals the moment of transformation and is said never to let anyone witness the change itself, reinforcing the secret-identity behavior associated with this form.

pokemon.name: Palafin
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Hero Form Palafin is a dramatically enlarged and more powerful state that appears after Palafin withdraws from battle and activates Zero to Hero. Its ancient genes are said to awaken during this transformation, granting enough strength to lift a cruise ship with a single fin. It can swim at roughly 50 knots and is known for rescuing drowning people and Pokémon, giving the form an explicitly protective behavioral role rather than merely a battle transformation. Although Hero Form has much greater offensive and defensive capabilities than Zero Form, the two forms retain the same HP and Speed base stats, and Palafin returns to Zero Form after the battle ends.

playthrough: Varoom evolves into Revavroom at level 40, so the line requires a fairly long investment before reaching its much stronger final form, but the payoff is a physically oriented Steel/Poison Pokémon with base 119 Attack and useful defensive typing. Revavroom resists or strongly resists many common attacking types and is immune to Poison, but its 4× Ground weakness is the defining defensive liability; even its Hidden Ability Filter only reduces super-effective damage by 25%, so a Ground attack remains extremely dangerous. Shift Gear is its most important setup tool, raising Attack by one stage and Speed by two and turning base 90 Speed into a sweeping asset, while Gunk Shot, Iron Head, High Horsepower, Temper Flare, and other coverage can support physical sets. Its signature Spin Out is a perfectly accurate 100-base-power Steel attack, but the two-stage Speed drop directly works against Shift Gear's speed-building game plan and makes Iron Head more comfortable when repeated attacks are expected. Overcoat provides immunity to powder moves and sandstorm damage, while Filter is often more broadly useful when available because it softens Fire and especially Ground hits without removing their danger. Terastallization can eliminate the 4× Ground weakness or improve coverage, and Adamant is excellent for maximizing damage while Jolly is useful when Revavroom must act before opponents prior to setting up. The five Team Star Starmobiles are special opponent-only Revavroom constructs with completely different types, Abilities, and Torque moves; they are not obtainable player forms and therefore do not expand the usable Revavroom moveset during a normal playthrough.
competitive: Revavroom has developed into a solid SV UU setup sweeper whose value comes from combining Steel/Poison defensive utility with Shift Gear and a genuinely strong base 119 Attack. After one Shift Gear it outspeeds the entire unboosted UU metagame, and sets commonly combine Gunk Shot with Iron Head or Temper Flare and High Horsepower to pressure Steel-types and other conventional checks. Air Balloon is particularly synergistic because it temporarily erases Revavroom's crippling 4× Ground weakness and can create the free turn needed to use Shift Gear, while Filter provides insurance once the Balloon is gone. Parting Shot and Toxic Spikes also let it serve as an offensive pivot or utility Pokémon rather than committing every set to sweeping. Its limitations are substantial: base 67 Special Defense is mediocre, common Ground coverage is dangerous even through Filter, and its coverage is not broad enough to guarantee that one Shift Gear will break every defensive core. Spin Out is rarely the centerpiece of competitive sets despite being the family's signature move because its harsh Speed reduction conflicts with the exact stat Revavroom usually spends a turn boosting. The Starmobiles have no standard competitive history because they are scripted, unobtainable boss constructs with special battle rules rather than legal player forms.
nuzlocke: Revavroom can be a strong Nuzlocke Pokémon once Varoom reaches level 40, but the evolution comes late enough that Varoom's much weaker 300 BST can require careful protection beforehand. Steel/Poison provides a large number of resistances and a Poison immunity, making many predicted switches comfortable, but the 4× Ground weakness is severe enough that unknown Earthquake, Stomping Tantrum, or High Horsepower coverage can cause an immediate death. Filter is therefore the safest Hidden Ability when available, though reducing a 4× weakness to effectively 3× damage is mitigation rather than immunity; Overcoat is more situational but removes powder and sandstorm variance. Shift Gear can enable decisive sweeps in known matchups, yet spending a setup turn against an opponent with Ground or strong special coverage is dangerous because Revavroom's Special Defense is only moderate. Spin Out's perfect accuracy is attractive, but dropping Speed by two stages after attacking can expose Revavroom on the following turn, so Iron Head or another reliable move is often safer when its lower power still secures the knockout. Parting Shot offers valuable controlled repositioning, while self-destructive or highly inaccurate options should be avoided when a safer route exists. The Starmobiles are enemy boss units rather than obtainable forms, so their unusual types and status immunities matter when planning Team Star battles but cannot be used as Nuzlocke assets.

pokemon.name: Varoom
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Varoom is an inorganic Pokémon said to have originated when an unknown Poison-type Pokémon entered and possessed an unused engine at a scrap-processing factory. The steel engine section is its actual body, and it attaches itself to wheel-like rocks whose minerals it consumes and converts into energy. Despite its mechanical appearance, Varoom normally levitates rather than rolling across the ground. Team Star incorporates Varoom into its Starmobiles as the pair of rear wheels.

pokemon.name: Revavroom
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Revavroom is an aggressive engine-like Pokémon that normally attaches itself to rocks resembling a wagon body and wheels, although it is also capable of levitating and flying without them. It combines minerals from those rocks with its own poison to create gas, then detonates that gas inside its cylinders to generate energy. Its true mouth is the large serrated opening on top of the engine body, and it uses a long tongue to discharge toxic fluids. Revavroom threatens opponents with the sound of its exhaust and is capable of operating machinery when installed as an engine. Ortega exploited that capability when constructing Team Star's Starmobiles, whose central Revavroom are larger than ordinary members of the species and operate alongside two Varoom used as rear wheels.

pokemon.name: Revavroom
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: The Segin Starmobile is Giacomo's Dark-type Team Star vehicle, powered by a large Revavroom in the hood with two Varoom acting as rear wheels. It has Intimidate and the exclusive Wicked Torque rather than ordinary Revavroom's Steel/Poison typing and normal Ability selection. Like the other Starmobiles, it is an engineered, unobtainable boss construct with special battle properties including immunity to negative status conditions and resistance to having its type altered; Scarlet/Violet does not implement it as an ordinary interchangeable player form.

pokemon.name: Revavroom
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: The Schedar Starmobile is Mela's Fire-type Starmobile and uses a Revavroom as its central living engine with Varoom incorporated into the rear of the machine. Its battle identity is distinguished by Speed Boost and the exclusive Blazing Torque. It shares the Starmobiles' engineered boss-only properties, including immunity to negative status and special rules not possessed by an obtainable Revavroom.

pokemon.name: Revavroom
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: The Navi Starmobile is Atticus's Poison-type version of Ortega's Team Star vehicle, again combining a central Revavroom with two rear-wheel Varoom. Its unique battle configuration gives it Toxic Debris and the exclusive Noxious Torque. Although officially grouped among Revavroom's Starmobile forms, it is an unobtainable constructed boss unit whose stats and battle rules are imposed specially by Scarlet/Violet rather than those of a normal trainable Revavroom.

pokemon.name: Revavroom
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: The Ruchbah Starmobile is Ortega's own Fairy-type Starmobile, built around the same living-machine arrangement of one large Revavroom and two Varoom. It establishes Misty Terrain through Misty Surge and uses the exclusive Magical Torque. Its Fairy typing, Ability, signature attack, and special boss immunities belong specifically to the engineered Starmobile configuration and are not traits of ordinary wild or player-owned Revavroom.

pokemon.name: Revavroom
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: The Caph Starmobile is Eri's Fighting-type Team Star vehicle, powered by a large Revavroom and supported by two Varoom as rear wheels. Its specialized battle configuration uses Stamina and the exclusive Combat Torque. As with the other Starmobiles, it is an unobtainable engineered boss construct rather than a form that a player's Revavroom can freely assume.

playthrough: Cyclizar is a standalone Dragon/Normal Pokémon that can be encountered relatively early in Scarlet/Violet and immediately offers exceptional base 121 Speed, making it faster than most ordinary story opponents without setup. Its offenses are only moderate at base 95 Attack and 85 Special Attack, so its greatest value comes from flexible utility rather than raw sweeping power: U-turn maintains momentum, Rapid Spin removes hazards, Knock Off disrupts held items, and Dragon or Normal STAB provides workable damage. Regenerator is the standout Hidden Ability because every switch restores one-third of maximum HP, synergizing perfectly with a fast pivoting role, while Shed Skin can occasionally clear status at the end of a turn. Cyclizar learns Shed Tail in Scarlet/Violet, sacrificing half of its maximum HP to create a substitute and pass it to a teammate while switching, which can safely enable a slower or more fragile attacker but demands careful HP management. Its Normal typing grants a Ghost immunity alongside Dragon's Fire, Water, Grass, and Electric resistances, but it is weak to Fighting, Ice, Dragon, and Fairy and has only 70/65/65 natural bulk. Terastallization can erase those weaknesses or strengthen an offensive option, though Cyclizar's support role often makes spending the team's Tera elsewhere more valuable. Jolly suits physical utility sets, Timid supports special or Draco Meteor-focused approaches, and mixed sets can function because neither attacking stat is unusable.
competitive: Cyclizar has one of Generation IX's more unusual tiering histories because its original competitive notoriety came from Shed Tail rather than from its own damage output. Early SV OU banned Cyclizar while Shed Tail strategies were still legal, but on April 18, 2023 Smogon instead banned Shed Tail itself and unbanned Cyclizar after the move was recognized as the underlying problem. Without Shed Tail, Cyclizar settled into a high-value utility role and is currently RU, where Smogon describes it as one of the defining Pokémon of the tier and its premier Rapid Spin user. Base 121 Speed lets it remove hazards or pivot before most opponents, Regenerator repeatedly restores HP as it switches, and Knock Off, U-turn, Dragon Tail, Taunt, and Rapid Spin allow it to compress hazard removal, item disruption, phazing, and momentum into one slot. Assault Vest variants can compensate for its mediocre natural special bulk, while Heavy-Duty Boots sets maximize repeated pivoting and access to status moves. Its main limitation is passivity: base 95 Attack and 85 Special Attack are modest by higher-tier standards, and strong Fighting attackers or faster Choice Scarf users can force it out. Its competitive history therefore shifted from being the delivery system for a banned support move to being valued on its own merits as an exceptionally fast Regenerator utility pivot.
nuzlocke: Cyclizar's base 121 Speed and immediate availability make it a useful Nuzlocke pivot because acting first often lets it attack, remove hazards, or escape before taking damage. Regenerator is exceptional for permadeath play when available: U-turn or ordinary switching restores one-third of its maximum HP and reduces dependence on limited healing resources between encounters. Shed Tail can create a powerful safety advantage by transferring a substitute to an incoming teammate, but it costs half of Cyclizar's maximum HP rounded up, so using it from the wrong health threshold can convert a safe Pokémon into a vulnerable one. Rapid Spin removes entry hazards without sacrificing Cyclizar, while U-turn gives predictable positioning and is generally safer than leaving its only moderate 70/65/65 bulk exposed. Its Ghost immunity and four Dragon-derived elemental resistances generate useful switch opportunities, but Fighting, Ice, Dragon, and Fairy weaknesses are common enough that blind switching is dangerous. Shed Skin is less consistent than Regenerator but can occasionally remove poison, paralysis, burn, or sleep without consuming an item. Cyclizar is therefore safest as a fast support Pokémon that repeatedly enters favorable positions rather than as a wall expected to absorb heavy neutral attacks.

pokemon.name: Cyclizar
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Cyclizar is a mild-tempered reptilian Pokémon that has lived closely with humans as transportation since ancient times; Paldean murals show people riding it as far back as 10,000 years ago. The relationship is mutually beneficial because a rider's body heat warms Cyclizar's back and lifts its spirits, while Cyclizar can carry both people and luggage at speeds exceeding 70 mph (120 km/h). It stores energy in folds around its throat, allowing it to run continuously over long distances, and uses its hard head and thick but flexible tail to maintain balance, absorb shock, and attack. Jacq describes basic, battle, and ride postures: it ordinarily moves on four legs, rises onto its hind legs to battle, and in ride posture inflates its throat sac and curls its tail into wheel-like shapes. Koraidon and Miraidon visibly resemble Cyclizar; Scarlet/Violet initially describes them as ancient and future relatives, while later Crystal Pool dialogue characterizes them more specifically as Cyclizar counterparts from parallel timelines.

playthrough: Orthworm is a standalone pure Steel-type whose defining playthrough trait is Earth Eater, an Ability that converts the normally super-effective Ground type into an immunity and heals Orthworm for one-quarter of its maximum HP when a Ground move hits it. That dramatically improves an already excellent physical defensive profile built around base 145 Defense and Steel's many resistances, allowing Orthworm to switch into physical Ground attacks that would destroy most Steel-types. Its weaknesses are therefore primarily Fire and Fighting when Earth Eater is active, while base 55 Special Defense remains a much broader vulnerability even against neutral special attacks. Body Press takes advantage of its enormous Defense, and Iron Defense or Coil can make it increasingly difficult for physical opponents to break; Stealth Rock and Spikes add useful team support. Orthworm also learns Shed Tail at level 52 in Scarlet/Violet, but unlike Regenerator Cyclizar it has no automatic switching recovery, so sacrificing half of its maximum HP is a significant cost despite the value of passing a substitute. Terastallization can change its defensive matchups, though losing Steel's excellent resistance profile or Earth Eater's Ground interaction should be weighed carefully. Impish maximizes physical durability and Body Press potential, while Careful can help patch the much weaker Special Defense.
competitive: Orthworm has had two distinct competitive identities in Generation IX: early in the generation it was one of the few Shed Tail users, but standard SV OU later banned Shed Tail itself, removing that strategy from ordinary OU play. Its current SV placement is ZU, where it instead succeeds as a physically defensive Steel-type built around base 145 Defense, Earth Eater, entry hazards, and Body Press. Earth Eater is especially valuable because it turns Steel's Ground weakness into both an immunity and 25% healing, creating opportunities against Pokémon that would normally pressure Steel-types with Earthquake. Stealth Rock and Spikes allow Orthworm to function as a hazard setter, while Iron Defense or Coil can convert its physical bulk into a Body Press win condition. The weaknesses that prevent it from climbing higher are clear: base 55 Special Defense makes strong special attackers threatening, it lacks reliable ordinary recovery, and losing Leftovers or being repeatedly forced into Fire and Fighting attacks wears it down quickly. The newer Pokémon Champions environment is materially different: Smogon's current Champions Pokédex places Orthworm in UU, and Shed Tail is once again available to it there, so that format restores part of the support identity that standard SV tiering removed. This distinction is important because its ZU status in SV and its UU status in Champions refer to different rulesets rather than a single uninterrupted metagame.
nuzlocke: Earth Eater makes Orthworm one of the safer specialist switch-ins available in Paldea because a correctly predicted Ground attack not only deals no damage but restores one-quarter of its maximum HP. Base 145 Defense and Steel's extensive resistance list let it absorb many physical attacks with a large margin for error, and Body Press turns that defensive investment into meaningful offensive pressure. The danger is special damage: base 55 Special Defense is low enough that even neutral special attacks can remove large portions of its HP, while Fire and Fighting moves remain super effective. Iron Defense and Coil can dominate known physical matchups, but setup should not be attempted blindly against opponents that may carry special coverage or critical-hit opportunities. Shed Tail is powerful support but costs half of Orthworm's maximum HP and, unlike Cyclizar, Orthworm lacks Regenerator to restore that sacrifice automatically; in a Nuzlocke it should therefore be reserved for situations where the substitute meaningfully reduces greater danger. Stealth Rock and Spikes are safe long-term utility options when the opponent cannot threaten Orthworm directly. Impish is excellent for maximizing its defining physical role, while Careful improves overall balance and may be preferable when surviving mixed boss movesets matters more than maximizing Body Press.

pokemon.name: Orthworm
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Orthworm is a long, six-segmented metallic worm whose second body segment can extend multiple blue parapodia-like appendages resembling simple fists. It lives in arid deserts and maintains its metal body by consuming iron from the soil, sometimes remaining buried with only its head exposed. When threatened, Orthworm extends its fist-like tendrils and pelts attackers with a rapid series of blows. A particularly enormous individual in East Province (Area Three) became the Lurking Steel Titan after feeding on Salty Herba Mystica, demonstrating that exceptional diet can produce a dramatically oversized specimen.

playthrough: Glimmet evolves into Glimmora at level 35, transforming a relatively small Rock/Poison Pokémon into a fast-enough special attacker with base 130 Special Attack and unusually strong hazard utility. Toxic Debris automatically scatters Toxic Spikes on the opposing side when Glimmora is struck by a physical attack, while its Hidden Ability Corrosion allows it to poison Steel- and Poison-type opponents that would normally be immune. Power Gem and Sludge Wave or Sludge Bomb provide reliable special STAB, Earth Power covers many Steel-types, and Mortal Spin simultaneously damages opponents, poisons them, and removes hazards or binding effects from Glimmora's side. Stealth Rock and Spikes let it serve as a lead or general support Pokémon even during the story, but Rock/Poison carries a dangerous 4× Ground weakness in addition to Water, Psychic, and Steel weaknesses. Its 83/90/81 bulk is respectable enough to survive some neutral hits but should not be confused with true defensive durability, especially when a physical Ground attack can exploit both the typing and Toxic Debris bait. Timid improves the useful but imperfect base 86 Speed, Modest maximizes immediate special damage, and defensive Natures are possible when emphasizing hazard support. Mega Glimmora was added later in the Mega Dimension DLC for Legends: Z-A and is therefore not part of an ordinary Scarlet/Violet playthrough; in Pokémon Champions its Mega form reaches 150 Special Attack, 101 Speed, 105 Defense, and 96 Special Defense and gains Adaptability, while Z-A itself uses its own battle-system rules rather than the conventional Ability framework.
competitive: Glimmora has remained one of SV OU's defining dedicated leads because few Pokémon compress hazard setting, hazard removal, poisoning pressure, and substantial special damage as efficiently. Toxic Debris punishes physical attacks by laying Toxic Spikes automatically, while Stealth Rock can be set manually and Mortal Spin removes opposing hazards while poisoning susceptible targets, forcing opponents to think carefully about how they attack or remove Glimmora. Base 130 Special Attack prevents it from being passive: Power Gem, Earth Power, Sludge Wave, or Meteor Beam can punish removal attempts and common switch-ins rather than merely sacrificing itself after setting hazards. Focus Sash is a natural lead item and Tera Ghost can deny Rapid Spin in emergencies, although spending Terastallization on a Pokémon designed to establish early-game tempo carries a real opportunity cost. Its 4× Ground weakness, average base 86 Speed, vulnerability to strong special walls, and the ability of Poison-types or Heavy-Duty Boots teams to blunt hazard pressure are the principal limitations. Mega Glimmora adds a genuinely new 2026 competitive branch in Pokémon Champions: Smogon's current Champions Pokédex lists both Glimmora and Mega Glimmora in OU, with Mega Glimmora using Adaptability and a 625 BST distribution of 83/90/105/150/96/101. Because Mega Glimmora is new, its confirmed current role as an Adaptability special attacker or lead should be distinguished from regular Glimmora's much longer-established SV OU hazard history rather than presented as though the Mega has years of tournament development.
nuzlocke: Glimmora is powerful in a Nuzlocke because level 35 evolution, base 130 Special Attack, good coverage, and perfectly accurate options such as Power Gem and Earth Power allow many opponents to be removed before they can exploit its weaknesses. Toxic Debris can generate free long-term value when Glimmora survives a physical hit, but deliberately inviting contact just to create Toxic Spikes is poor permadeath strategy when safer hazard setup is available. The 4× Ground weakness is the central survival problem: Earthquake and other Ground coverage can overwhelm its otherwise respectable 83/90/81 bulk, so unknown physical attackers should be treated cautiously. Mortal Spin is useful because it clears entry hazards without self-sacrifice and is perfectly accurate, though its low physical damage means it should be used for utility rather than expected knockouts. Corrosion enables Toxic against Steel and Poison foes, but Toxic Debris generally provides more passive value unless a specific matchup rewards Corrosion. Self-Destruct, Explosion, and Memento directly conflict with keeping the Pokémon alive and should normally be excluded from a conventional Nuzlocke moveset. Mega Glimmora's later Z-A appearance substantially improves its combat stats, but that form belongs to a different game and battle system and should not be projected backward onto Scarlet/Violet Nuzlocke planning.

pokemon.name: Glimmet
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Glimmet is a small flower-bud-like mineral Pokémon whose six petal-like structures are clusters of crystallized poison. It attaches itself to cave walls and ceilings to absorb nutrients and can defend itself by scattering poisonous powder like pollen or striking with its poison-packed bud. Groups of Glimmet have been observed cooperating with Glimmora to repel enemies, and Pokémon Horizons depicts Glimmet rotating their petals like propellers to move through the air. A connection between the species and the Terastal phenomenon is suspected rather than fully explained, based on its distribution around Area Zero and other crystal-rich locations, the resemblance between Glimmora's petals and Tera Jewels, and the use of Glimmet Crystals to create the Tera Blast TM.

pokemon.name: Glimmora
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Glimmora is a flower-like mineral Pokémon composed of layered petals made from crystallized poison, normally keeping its body partly closed around a translucent central cone. It attaches itself to walls, disguises itself as a plant, and draws energy and nutrients from the surface; when threatened it opens its petals and fires beams from its body. Glimmora can cooperate with groups of Glimmet when defending against enemies. Its distribution in Area Zero, the underdepths, and Kitakami's Crystal Pool, together with the resemblance of its petals to Tera Jewels, has prompted an in-universe suspected connection to Terastallization, although the precise relationship remains unresolved.

pokemon.name: Glimmora
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Mega Glimmora was introduced in the Mega Dimension DLC for Pokémon Legends: Z-A and is produced with Glimmoranite. Mega Evolution enlarges and separates its outer petals so that they orbit continuously around the body, while its central cone elongates, its eyes turn red, and the flower remains open to expose additional layers of crystalline petals. The orbiting petals improve its defenses and allow it to scatter poisonous debris over a wider area. In Pokémon Champions, Mega Glimmora retains Rock/Poison typing and has Adaptability, strengthening its same-type attacks; this conventional Ability should be treated as Champions mechanics rather than assumed to operate identically in Legends: Z-A's different battle system.

playthrough: Greavard evolves into Houndstone starting at level 30 when it levels up at night, making the family straightforward to complete once the time-of-day requirement is understood. Houndstone is a physically oriented Ghost-type with base 101 Attack and solid 72/100/97 defenses, granting useful Normal and Fighting immunities and far more staying power than many offensive Ghost-types. Its signature Last Respects begins at 50 base power and becomes 50 points stronger each time a Pokémon on the user's side has fainted during the battle, but ordinary story teams should not intentionally lose teammates merely to maximize it. Sand Rush doubles Houndstone's Speed during sandstorm and can support an offensive role, while the Hidden Ability Fluffy halves damage from contact moves at the cost of doubling the damage of Fire-type attacks, creating a very different defensive profile. Poltergeist, Shadow Sneak, Body Press, Play Rough, Will-O-Wisp, and coverage or utility moves let it function as either an attacker or a bulky Ghost, although some of its strongest options are less accurate than ideal. Terastallization can remove the Ghost weaknesses to Dark and Ghost or amplify a finishing attack, but changing type also removes the valuable Normal and Fighting immunities. Adamant supports Sand Rush or offensive sets, while Impish or Careful can fit bulkier Fluffy approaches.
competitive: Houndstone's competitive history is inseparable from Last Respects: it was quickbanned from early SV OU in November 2022 because the move could become overwhelmingly strong late in battles, especially on Sand Rush sets. After Pokémon HOME introduced additional Last Respects users, Smogon shifted the tiering action to the move itself; Last Respects was unanimously banned from SV OU in May 2023 and Houndstone was allowed back into standard play. Without that move, Houndstone settled much lower and is currently NU, where it functions as a bulky Ghost-type and spinblocker rather than an automatic late-game sweeper. Fluffy lets defensive sets absorb contact attacks exceptionally well, while Will-O-Wisp, Night Shade, Roar, Body Press, and item choices such as Rocky Helmet or Heavy-Duty Boots help it punish physical attackers and support hazard-stacking teams. Sand Rush remains available for offensive builds, and Poltergeist plus Shadow Sneak can give those sets meaningful damage and priority, but they no longer possess the extreme scaling that made the original Last Respects set oppressive. Poor reliable recovery, vulnerability to strong special attackers, and reliance on imperfect options such as Pain Split or Rest limit its defensive ceiling. Its path from OU quickban to legal NU defensive Pokémon is therefore a clear case where a single move, rather than the species' ordinary stat line, created the original tiering problem.
nuzlocke: Houndstone is a good Nuzlocke evolution once Greavard reaches level 30 at night because its two immunities, solid mixed bulk, and useful base 101 Attack give it more margin for error than many Ghost-types. Fluffy can be exceptional survival insurance against contact moves by halving their damage, but it also doubles Fire damage, so an unexpected contact-free Fire attack or coverage move can turn the Ability into a liability. Sand Rush is more straightforward on teams that can reliably create sand, allowing Houndstone to outspeed threats rather than absorbing their attacks. Last Respects is perfectly accurate and can become stronger after teammates faint, but conventional Nuzlocke goals make those deaths a cost rather than a resource; it is best viewed as compensation after losses, not a strategy that should encourage sacrificing party members.
