Its singles strengths are straightforward but substantial—base 154 HP, 140 Attack, and 108 Defense make it exceptionally difficult to remove physically, while Swords Dance, Drain Punch, Electric STAB, Ice Punch, Heavy Slam, Earthquake, and Volt Switch provide both wallbreaking and pivoting options. Drain Punch is particularly important because it converts Iron Hands's enormous offensive pressure into recovery, and Assault Vest variants can invest heavily in Special Defense to patch the one major weakness in its natural bulk. Its low base 50 Speed and vulnerabilities to Ground, Fairy, and Psychic attacks prevent it from sweeping freely in faster environments, while more specialized OU Pokémon often offer greater speed, recovery, or defensive utility. Iron Hands had an even more distinguished VGC career, where Fake Out, Assault Vest, Volt Switch, Drain Punch, Wild Charge, and immense mixed bulk allowed it to provide immediate disruption and board presence on a wide variety of teams. A particularly well-documented example is Marco Silva's 2024 Latin America International Championships-winning team; The Pokémon Company later distributed his Adamant, Water-Tera, Assault Vest Iron Hands with Drain Punch, Volt Switch, Wild Charge, and Fake Out. Its doubles success reflects qualities that singles tiering does not fully capture: low Speed can function well under Trick Room, Fake Out has enormous tactical value, and its bulk makes it difficult to remove before it has influenced several turns.
nuzlocke: Iron Hands is an exceptionally durable late-game Violet Nuzlocke Pokémon because 154 HP and 108 Defense allow it to survive physical attacks that would overwhelm most offensive Pokémon. Drain Punch is one of its best permadeath moves because it combines perfect accuracy, Fighting STAB, and direct healing, allowing Iron Hands to restore health while maintaining offensive pressure rather than spending separate turns on recovery. Its low Speed means it will often be hit before moving, however, and base 68 Special Defense is the major vulnerability; powerful special Psychic, Fairy, or Ground attacks can inflict unexpectedly high damage despite the huge HP stat. Thunder Punch is normally safer than Wild Charge because it has no recoil, and vastly safer than Supercell Slam because a failed Supercell Slam can remove half of Iron Hands's maximum HP—an especially severe penalty on a Pokémon whose maximum HP is enormous. Fake Out can provide one guaranteed flinch on the first turn after entering against susceptible targets, letting the player collect chip damage or information without immediate retaliation. Belly Drum can create overwhelming Attack at the cost of half of maximum HP and is generally unnecessary risk in a conventional Nuzlocke, while Swords Dance offers slower but substantially safer setup when a known opponent cannot threaten Iron Hands. Careful positioning around special attackers turns Iron Hands from merely powerful into one of the most forgiving physical tanks available in the late game.

pokemon.name: Iron Hands
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Iron Hands is a massive cyborg-like Pokémon resembling Hariyama, with two enormous three-fingered hands that are physically detached from its arms and capable of moving independently from the body. Reports claim those fists are powerful enough to throw large, fast-moving vehicles, and Iron Hands can press its palms together before releasing energy from the panels embedded within them. Despite its great mass, it can hover a short distance above the ground to make rapid movements and turns. When it sleeps, Iron Hands powers down, reconnecting its hands to its body as the yellow energy in its palms and armor goes dark; the popular story that it was once a mortally injured athlete rebuilt as a cyborg remains explicitly unproven. AI Turo calls Iron Hands a future descendant of Hariyama, while the Crystal Pool Professor instead describes it as a Hariyama counterpart from another timeline, so its actual origin remains unknown.

playthrough: Iron Jugulis is a standalone Dark/Flying Paradox Pokémon naturally available only in Violet's Area Zero late in the story, while Scarlet players normally need trade, event, or Union Circle access. Its 122 Special Attack and 108 Speed make it a capable fast special attacker, and Dark/Flying grants complete Ground and Psychic immunities plus useful resistances to Dark, Ghost, and Grass. Dark Pulse is its most dependable offensive STAB because it is perfectly accurate, while Flying STAB creates a reliability choice between Air Slash's moderate power and 95% accuracy and Hurricane's 110 base power but only 70% accuracy outside rain. Earth Power and Flamethrower provide excellent perfectly accurate special coverage against many Steel-, Electric-, and Rock-type answers, while Taunt and Tailwind can give Iron Jugulis a genuine support role beyond damage. Quark Drive can strengthen Special Attack or Speed under Electric Terrain or through Booster Energy depending on the actual stat spread, and a Speed boost can make an already quick Pokémon difficult for ordinary opponents to catch. Its 94/86/80 bulk is decent but not exceptional, it lacks the conventional reliable recovery that would make repeated defensive switching easy, and weaknesses to Electric, Fairy, Ice, and Rock include a Stealth Rock vulnerability. Timid is usually the strongest general-purpose Nature for fast special offense and support, while Modest can be useful when maximizing immediate damage matters more than the extra Speed.
competitive: Iron Jugulis currently sits in SV UU, where it has carved out a niche as a fast special attacker and disruptive pivot with an unusually flexible movepool. Base 108 Speed, 122 Special Attack, and Booster Energy allow offensive sets to function as cleaners, with Dark Pulse providing reliable STAB and Hurricane delivering much greater Flying damage when its accuracy is acceptable or rain support is present. Earth Power covers many Electric-, Rock-, and Steel-type answers, while Taunt can shut down recovery or setup and U-turn or other utility options help maintain momentum rather than forcing Iron Jugulis to stay in every matchup. Its doubles identity emphasizes support more strongly: Smogon's Regulation F analysis specifically highlights Tailwind and Snarl, giving it both teamwide speed control and a means to reduce opposing special damage while retaining offensive threat. That niche appeared in early official tournaments as well; an Iron Jugulis reached the semifinals of the 2023 Charlotte Regional Senior Division with Hurricane, Snarl, Earth Power, and Protect, while another Iron Jugulis on a quarterfinal team used Tailwind. Its limitations explain why it has not become a dominant OU staple: Hurricane is unreliable without rain, Dark Pulse is comparatively modest in power, Stealth Rock punishes repeated switching, and faster or stronger special attackers often compete for the same offensive slot. Its UU status therefore reflects genuine versatility and speed rather than top-tier raw efficiency.
nuzlocke: Iron Jugulis is a useful late-game Nuzlocke attacker because Ground and Psychic immunities create completely safe switch opportunities against known moves and base 108 Speed lets it avoid many neutral hits by acting first. Dark Pulse is the safest routine STAB because it is perfectly accurate, while Flamethrower and Earth Power also offer reliable coverage; Hurricane's 70% accuracy is a major liability when a miss could expose Iron Jugulis to lethal retaliation. Air Slash improves reliability to 95% but still carries miss risk and much less power, so the choice between Flying attacks should depend on whether the matchup genuinely requires Flying STAB. Tailwind can double the Speed of the player's side for four turns, creating teamwide safety in difficult fights even if Iron Jugulis itself does not need the help, while Taunt can prevent dangerous setup, status, or recovery from known opponents. Its 94/86/80 bulk gives more margin for error than Iron Bundle, but Electric, Fairy, Ice, and Rock weaknesses are common and Stealth Rock removes one-quarter of its maximum HP whenever it enters while hazards are active. Quark Drive can further improve Speed or Special Attack, yet a Nuzlocke should still account for enemy priority and avoid assuming that boosted Speed alone guarantees safety. Timid is particularly useful for minimizing exposure, while Modest is viable when the team already provides speed control and the additional damage improves knockout consistency.

pokemon.name: Iron Jugulis
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Iron Jugulis is a three-headed mechanical draconic Pokémon whose faces are LED-like displays capable of showing emotion, with six jointed wings and armor plating around its necks and shoulders. Its two secondary heads are unusually independent: they can wander away from the main body, appear to make separate decisions and express their own emotions, and can even be launched like missiles at enemies. Occulture reports describe an Iron Jugulis destroying an entire building with a high-energy blast before flying away, while the magazine's claim that it is a machine-Hydreigon hybrid remains speculative rather than established fact. When sleeping, Iron Jugulis powers down and the colored energy across its faces and body turns black. Its true relationship to Hydreigon is unresolved because AI Turo describes it as a future descendant, whereas the Crystal Pool Professor calls it a Hydreigon counterpart from another timeline; Heath also recorded the creature around 200 years before Turo's time machine was created.

playthrough: Iron Moth is a standalone Fire/Poison Paradox Pokémon found naturally only in Pokémon Violet's Area Zero, so it normally joins the team during the final portion of the main story; Scarlet players need trade, event, or Union Circle access. Its base 140 Special Attack and 110 Speed make it an immediately dangerous special attacker, while base 110 Special Defense lets it survive many special hits far better than its frail-looking design suggests. Fiery Dance is an especially efficient story move because it is perfectly accurate, receives STAB, and has a 50% chance to raise Special Attack, while Sludge Wave supplies a stronger perfectly accurate Poison STAB and Energy Ball or Psychic can cover common answers. Morning Sun is learned at a very high level but provides genuine recovery once available, and Toxic Spikes gives Iron Moth a useful support option if direct attacking is not always needed. Quark Drive raises its highest stat in Electric Terrain or after Booster Energy activates, with Speed receiving a 50% increase rather than the 30% increase used for other stats, so different stat spreads can emphasize either sweeping speed or immediate special power. Its major defensive problem is typing and physical frailty: Fire/Poison takes 4× damage from Ground and is also weak to Water, Psychic, and Rock, while base 60 Defense means even strong neutral physical attacks can be dangerous. Timid is generally the safest offensive Nature because it maximizes the line's excellent Speed, while Modest is useful when additional Special Attack changes important knockout ranges.
competitive: Iron Moth currently sits in SV OU and has remained a prominent special attacker because few Pokémon combine base 140 Special Attack, base 110 Speed, Booster Energy, and such broad special coverage. Booster Energy sets can use Quark Drive to increase Speed for cleaning or Special Attack for wallbreaking, while Fiery Dance threatens to snowball further through its 50% Special Attack boost after each successful hit. Sludge Wave provides strong secondary STAB and is particularly valuable against Fairy-types, while Energy Ball, Psychic, Dazzling Gleam, Tera Blast, Substitute, Toxic Spikes, and Whirlwind allow Iron Moth to tailor itself to different defensive cores. Its high base 110 Special Defense can let it survive attacks from special threats that would overwhelm many offensive Pokémon, but 80 HP and only 60 Defense make physical priority and strong physical attackers much more difficult to handle. The 4× Ground weakness and vulnerability to Stealth Rock also make safe entry and hazard control important, and many common Ground-types can force Iron Moth to rely on coverage or defensive Terastallization. Iron Moth has often competed with Volcarona for a Fire-type special-sweeper slot, but instant Booster Energy activation, higher natural Speed, Poison STAB, and immediate coverage give it a distinct role even without Quiver Dance. Its current OU placement reflects a Pokémon that can function as a cleaner, wallbreaker, or offensive utility piece rather than one dependent on a single gimmick.
nuzlocke: Iron Moth is an extremely strong late-game Violet Nuzlocke attacker because base 110 Speed and 140 Special Attack let it end many battles before taking damage, especially with reliable moves such as Fiery Dance and Sludge Wave. Fiery Dance is particularly attractive under permadeath rules because it is perfectly accurate and can increase Special Attack without spending a separate setup turn, letting Iron Moth gain momentum while continuing to deal damage. Morning Sun can provide renewable recovery once available, although its healing varies with weather, and Quark Drive can create safer knockouts when Electric Terrain or Booster Energy is available. The central survival issue is the 4× Ground weakness: Earthquake, Earth Power, Stomping Tantrum, or unexpected Ground coverage can erase Iron Moth despite its good Special Defense, and base 60 Defense makes physical attacks generally dangerous. Fire Blast, Hurricane, and Overheat offer higher ceilings but introduce accuracy or stat-drop costs, so Flamethrower, Fiery Dance, Sludge Wave, Energy Ball, and Psychic are usually preferable when they already secure the required knockout. Toxic Spikes can help in long boss fights, but spending a turn on hazards is only worthwhile when the opposing Pokémon cannot threaten Iron Moth directly. It is safest when treated as a fast special attacker with selective recovery rather than as a general defensive switch-in.

pokemon.name: Iron Moth
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Iron Moth is a robotic moth-like Paradox Pokémon resembling Volcarona, with six large diamond-shaped wing panels that levitate separately from its central body rather than attaching conventionally. Reports describe it descending from the sky, following people, and sometimes attacking them. Occulture speculates that it may be a UFO controlled by extraterrestrial life and used to observe humanity before an invasion, but that explanation is explicitly sensational speculation rather than established canon. Its true relationship to Volcarona is likewise unresolved: AI Turo presents future Paradox Pokémon as distant descendants, while the Professor encountered at the Crystal Pool describes them as counterparts from other timelines, leaving Iron Moth's actual origin uncertain.

playthrough: Iron Thorns is a standalone Rock/Electric Paradox Pokémon naturally available only in Pokémon Violet's Area Zero near the end of the story, while Scarlet players normally require trade, event, or Union Circle access. Its base 134 Attack, 110 Defense, and 100 HP make it a powerful physical bruiser, although base 72 Speed means it usually needs Dragon Dance or other speed support before it can sweep faster opponents. Dragon Dance raises both Attack and Speed and is the line's most important setup option, while Rock and Electric STAB can be supplied by attacks such as Rock Slide, Stone Edge, Thunder Punch, Wild Charge, or Supercell Slam depending on how much power and risk the player accepts. Earthquake and Ice Punch provide valuable coverage, while Stealth Rock and Spikes let Iron Thorns contribute even when a matchup does not favor direct setup. Quark Drive can strengthen its highest stat in Electric Terrain or through Booster Energy, usually Attack on straightforward builds, though specialized spreads can manipulate which stat receives the boost. Rock/Electric gives useful resistances and a strong resistance to Flying, but it has a crippling 4× Ground weakness plus ordinary weaknesses to Fighting, Grass, and Water, so its excellent physical bulk cannot be treated as universal safety. Adamant maximizes its already enormous physical power, while Jolly is useful when a Dragon Dance set needs to reach important Speed thresholds.
competitive: Iron Thorns is currently NUBL in SV, meaning it is banned from NU despite not having the usage required for a standard higher usage tier. Its defining lower-tier strategy is Dragon Dance: base 134 Attack becomes extremely threatening after one boost, and Terastallization can remove the otherwise debilitating 4× Ground weakness while creating additional setup opportunities. The species has also used Booster Energy, Earthquake, Ice Punch, Supercell Slam, Rock STAB, and occasionally Loaded Dice combinations involving Rock Blast and Pin Missile, giving defensive teams several different coverage patterns to account for. Its history in NU was turbulent rather than merely theoretical: Iron Thorns was banned from SV NU multiple times during tier restructuring, and an October 2024 council vote again removed it from the tier; 2026 NU discussion still treated it as an NUBL-level threat whose Dragon Dance sets remained too dangerous for a routine unban. The weaknesses that keep it out of stronger metagames are equally clear: base 72 Speed requires setup, the native defensive typing is exploitable, special bulk is only moderate, and it often consumes Terastallization to become the threatening sweeper its raw stats suggest. It can also set Stealth Rock or Spikes, but using such utility generally means giving up part of the coverage or setup package that makes Iron Thorns threatening in the first place. Its NUBL status therefore reflects genuine power in lower tiers without implying that it is broadly dominant in OU-level play.
nuzlocke: Iron Thorns offers excellent physical bulk and damage for a late-game Violet Nuzlocke, but its 4× Ground weakness creates one of the clearest single-move survival hazards among the future Paradox Pokémon. A known physical attacker lacking Ground coverage can struggle to break through 100 HP and 110 Defense, while Dragon Dance can turn a favorable matchup into a sweep by simultaneously fixing Speed and increasing Attack. That setup should not be attempted blindly, however, because an unexpected Earthquake or special Water, Grass, or Fighting attack can bypass the margin for error its physical bulk normally provides. Thunder Punch is a much safer Electric STAB than Wild Charge because it has no recoil, and it is dramatically safer than Supercell Slam, whose 95% accuracy and crash penalty can cost half of Iron Thorns's maximum HP if the move fails. Rock Slide and Stone Edge bring their own accuracy risks, so a Nuzlocke player should prefer the most reliable attack that still secures the needed knockout rather than automatically choosing maximum base power. Stealth Rock and Spikes can support the entire party when Iron Thorns has a safe turn, but its late availability means immediate battle performance will usually matter more than long-term route utility. With Ground coverage identified in advance, Iron Thorns can be a durable and devastating physical attacker; without that information, its defensive typing makes blind play much more dangerous.

pokemon.name: Iron Thorns
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Iron Thorns is a large robotic dinosaur-like Pokémon resembling Tyranitar, with metallic green armor, transparent sections exposing glowing green energy, and retractable spikes made from the same luminous material. Unlike Tyranitar's famously destructive temperament, reports characterize Iron Thorns as highly intelligent, coolheaded, and inclined to avoid unnecessary fights. When it sleeps, it effectively shuts itself down, causing the green energy in its torso, legs, tail, and spikes to turn black. Occulture's claim that it represents Tyranitar one billion years in the future remains speculative, while the games themselves leave its origin unresolved between AI Turo's future-descendant explanation and the Crystal Pool Professor's description of a Tyranitar counterpart from another timeline.

playthrough: Frigibax evolves into Arctibax at level 35 and Baxcalibur at level 54, giving the family the long developmental curve expected of Paldea's 600-BST pseudo-legendary line and making the final evolution a relatively late payoff. Baxcalibur rewards that investment with 115 HP, 145 Attack, respectable mixed bulk, and Dragon/Ice STAB, while Thermal Exchange makes it impossible to burn and raises Attack by one stage whenever it is damaged by a Fire-type move; the Fire move still deals damage, so the Ability should not be mistaken for a Fire immunity. Glaive Rush is its signature 120-base-power, perfectly accurate Dragon attack, but until Baxcalibur's next action opposing attacks cannot miss it and deal double damage, making Dragon Claw or another safer Dragon move preferable when the extra power is unnecessary. Ice Spinner and Icicle Spear provide physical Ice STAB, Ice Shard supplies priority, Earthquake covers many Steel-types, and Dragon Dance can correct Baxcalibur's middling base 87 Speed while increasing its already enormous Attack. Its Hidden Ability Ice Body restores HP each turn in snow, and Generation IX snow also raises an Ice-type's Defense by 50%, creating a much bulkier physical profile than Dragon/Ice typing alone would suggest. The weaknesses to Fighting, Rock, Dragon, Steel, and Fairy remain significant, and Stealth Rock removes one-quarter of Baxcalibur's HP on entry unless mitigated. Mega Baxcalibur is now official through Pokémon Legends: Z-A – Mega Dimension, where Baxcalibur can use Baxcalibrite to Mega Evolve into a 700-BST form with 175 Attack, but that form is separate from Scarlet/Violet's playthrough and Z-A's battle mechanics should not be projected backward onto SV. Adamant maximizes physical damage, while Jolly is often preferable for Dragon Dance sets that need specific post-boost Speed thresholds.
competitive: Baxcalibur is currently Uber in SV, and its path there is one of the clearest examples of DLC changing a Pokémon's tiering fate. Before The Teal Mask it was already a formidable Dragon Dance wallbreaker, but the DLC restored Scale Shot and added optimized snow and Aurora Veil support from Alolan Ninetales; Loaded Dice could then make both Scale Shot and Icicle Spear hit four or five times consistently while Scale Shot simultaneously increased Speed. Combined with base 145 Attack, Thermal Exchange's burn immunity, Earthquake coverage, Dragon Dance or Swords Dance, and Terastallization that could erase normal revenge-killing weaknesses, the package became overwhelming enough that the SV OU council unanimously banned Baxcalibur on September 16, 2023. In Ubers it is much less dominant but still retains a niche as a wallbreaker or setup sweeper using Loaded Dice Icicle Spear, Scale Shot or Glaive Rush, Earthquake, and offensive boosting, with Ice Shard offering useful priority against faster weakened targets. Its VGC history is also meaningful: Loaded Dice Scale Shot and Icicle Spear sets appeared in official 2026 competition, including a Baxcalibur on a Senior Division quarterfinal team at the 2026 Latin America International Championships. Mega Baxcalibur adds a new competitive branch rather than rewriting that history: the Mega Dimension form reaches 700 BST with 175 Attack, 117 Defense, 105 Special Attack, 101 Special Defense, and unchanged 87 Speed. Because Mega Baxcalibur was introduced only in late 2025, its confirmed new mechanics and extraordinary stats should be discussed separately from regular Baxcalibur's established multi-year SV tiering résumé rather than treated as though the Mega has the same historical record.
nuzlocke: The Frigibax family has an excellent Nuzlocke ceiling but demands patience because the final evolution does not arrive until level 54, leaving the player with Frigibax or Arctibax through much of the period in which the line is first obtainable. Once evolved, Baxcalibur's 115 HP and respectable defenses give it good natural survivability, while Thermal Exchange removes burn as a way for opponents to cripple its physical Attack and can reward a correctly judged Fire matchup with an Attack boost. Glaive Rush is much more dangerous in permadeath play than its perfect accuracy suggests: after using it, attacks against Baxcalibur cannot miss and deal double damage until Baxcalibur acts again, so a surviving opponent or faster replacement can exploit the drawback brutally. Dragon Claw, Ice Spinner, Icicle Spear, Earthquake, and Ice Shard generally provide lower-risk alternatives, and Ice Shard's priority is particularly valuable for ending a fight before a weakened faster enemy can move. Dragon Dance can enable reliable sweeps against known teams, but spending a setup turn against an unknown Fairy, Fighting, Rock, Steel, or Dragon attack still creates unnecessary risk, and critical hits remain dangerous even under snow's Defense boost. Ice Body is a useful recovery option on dedicated snow teams, but Thermal Exchange's burn immunity is broadly valuable even without weather support. Mega Baxcalibur belongs to Legends: Z-A rather than an SV Nuzlocke; its enormous 700 BST and new battle system should therefore be evaluated separately instead of silently replacing regular Baxcalibur's Scarlet/Violet profile.

pokemon.name: Frigibax
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Frigibax is a small Dragon/Ice Pokémon whose dorsal fin absorbs heat from the surrounding environment and converts it into ice energy; the hotter its surroundings become, the more ice energy it can store. It inhabits forests and rough, craggy terrain and uses its dorsal fin to cool the interior of its nest like a refrigerator. Frigibax has a documented rivalry with Bergmite and fights them whenever the two species meet. Legends: Z-A further specifies that the dorsal fin can convert heat from fiery attacks into Ice-type energy strong enough to freeze the surrounding air.

pokemon.name: Arctibax
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Arctibax is a more agile theropod-like Pokémon that can freeze the air around its head into an ice mask, protecting its face while also coating its large dorsal fin in sharp ice to form a blade. Its powerful back and leg muscles let it launch itself into a front flip and slash an opponent with that frozen dorsal blade while airborne. Legends: Z-A emphasizes the species' mobility, describing it as springing rapidly upon foes to deliver slashing attacks. Wild Arctibax are uncommon and are most often associated with cold caverns and mountainous environments.

pokemon.name: Baxcalibur
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Baxcalibur is a large upright Dragon/Ice Pokémon whose back supports a massive axe- or glaive-like frozen sail. It exhales cryogenic air cold enough to freeze liquid-hot lava, using that breath both to immobilize opponents and as propulsion for its distinctive attack in which it flips upside down and launches itself dorsal-blade-first. Legends: Z-A adds that it can freeze a foe with its breath before pulverizing the target with a blow from its tail. Its enormous physical strength and the blade-like dorsal structure are reflected directly in Glaive Rush, the signature attack unique to Baxcalibur.

pokemon.name: Baxcalibur
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Mega Baxcalibur was introduced in the Mega Dimension DLC for Pokémon Legends: Z-A and retains Dragon/Ice typing while becoming substantially heavier and more powerfully built. Mega Evolution causes the dorsal blade to grow enormously and fuse visually with an icy structure around the solar plexus, producing a sword-like formation whose front resembles a hilt. The Mega form generates much more ice energy and channels it through an enhanced nerve at the solar plexus, stabilizing its center of gravity despite the enormous blade while also allowing it to fire beams from the hilt. Ice energy permeates its muscles, nerves, internal organs, and even its optic system, increasing reaction speed and explosive movement; its enlarged blade is described as capable of cutting through or smashing apart almost anything.

playthrough: Gimmighoul evolves into Gholdengo when it levels up while the player has at least 999 Gimmighoul Coins in the Bag, consuming 999 coins in the process, so the family's main playthrough obstacle is exploration and collection rather than combat experience. Chest Form Gimmighoul is the only form natively catchable in Scarlet/Violet and is extremely slow, while Roaming Form appears throughout Paldea only as an overworld coin source unless a catchable specimen is transferred from Pokémon GO; both forms ultimately evolve into the same Gholdengo. The reward for completing the coin requirement is substantial: Gholdengo has base 133 Special Attack, solid 87/95/91 bulk, Steel/Ghost typing with three immunities and many resistances, and the unique Ability Good as Gold, which makes it immune to status moves used by other Pokémon. Its signature Make It Rain is a 120-base-power, perfectly accurate Steel special attack that hits both opponents in doubles and lowers Gholdengo's Special Attack by one stage after use, while Shadow Ball supplies reliable Ghost STAB without that drawback. Recover gives it direct longevity, Nasty Plot can turn it into a setup sweeper, and Thunder Wave, Trick, coverage moves, or Hex can support more specialized roles. Good as Gold does not make Gholdengo immune to every possible status effect or secondary effect, so it should not be treated as blanket protection from all battle disruption. Fire, Ground, Ghost, and Dark attacks remain the primary defensive threats, and base 84 Speed is good rather than elite. Timid is excellent for offensive or Choice Scarf approaches, Modest maximizes immediate special damage, and Bold can support more defensive Nasty Plot or utility sets.
competitive: Gholdengo has been one of the defining Pokémon of Scarlet/Violet OU and remains OU in Smogon's current SV Pokédex because Good as Gold and Steel/Ghost typing interact with entry-hazard mechanics in an unusually powerful way. Its Ghost typing blocks Rapid Spin, its Steel typing prevents Mortal Spin from functioning against it, and Good as Gold stops status-move removal such as Defog, allowing hazard-stacking teams to preserve Stealth Rock and Spikes far more reliably than in previous generations. That support role is backed by real offensive pressure: base 133 Special Attack, 120-base-power Make It Rain, Shadow Ball, Nasty Plot, Recover, Thunder Wave, Hex, and Choice Scarf or Choice Specs sets prevent opponents from treating Gholdengo as a passive spinblocker. Its weaknesses to Ground, Fire, Ghost, and Dark and only base 84 Speed create real counterplay, and Make It Rain's Special Attack drop means repeated use can surrender momentum if Gholdengo cannot switch or boost afterward. Gholdengo also developed a major VGC résumé, where Make It Rain's spread damage, Good as Gold's disruptive immunity, Nasty Plot, Choice Specs, and defensive Terastallization made it effective across multiple regulations. Official 2026 Regulation H discussion described Gholdengo as the top Pokémon in the format and highlighted the Dragonite/Ursaluna/Gholdengo core, while 2026 international results continued to show Gholdengo on multiple top-cut teams. Its longevity across singles and doubles comes from the same basic package—excellent typing, unusual status immunity, powerful spread or single-target special damage, and enough bulk to contribute defensively even when it is not sweeping.
nuzlocke: The Gimmighoul line has one of the most unusual Nuzlocke progression costs in Paldea because obtaining Gholdengo requires collecting 999 Gimmighoul Coins, which can demand substantial exploration even if the player already caught a Chest Form Gimmighoul. Once that requirement is met, Gholdengo is an exceptionally safe Pokémon in many known matchups: Steel/Ghost provides immunities to Normal, Fighting, and Poison plus numerous resistances, and Good as Gold blocks many dangerous status moves that would otherwise inflict sleep, paralysis, stat disruption, or other non-damaging effects. Make It Rain is extremely strong and perfectly accurate, but its one-stage Special Attack drop means consecutive uses become less reliable for securing knockouts, so Shadow Ball or another stable attack can be preferable when maximum Steel damage is unnecessary. Recover provides true repeatable healing, a major advantage in permadeath play, while Nasty Plot can create controlled sweeps if the opposing moveset is known and unable to exploit Gholdengo's Fire, Ground, Ghost, or Dark weaknesses. Good as Gold should not create overconfidence because it does not stop damaging moves from inflicting secondary effects, nor does it erase ordinary super-effective damage. Chest Form Gimmighoul itself is much less safe than Gholdengo because its tiny HP, weak offense, and base 10 Speed leave it highly dependent on favorable matchups before evolution. If the player is willing to complete the coin hunt, the evolved form's combination of reliable offense, immunities, recovery, and status protection makes Gholdengo one of the strongest general-purpose Nuzlocke rewards in Scarlet/Violet.

pokemon.name: Gimmighoul
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Chest Form Gimmighoul lives inside a heavy red treasure chest filled with coins and is said to have been born inside such a chest about 1,500 years ago. The chest provides strong protection but makes movement difficult, so Gimmighoul commonly remains in old watchtowers, ruins, warehouses, secluded islands, or forgotten corners where people may mistake it for an antique. When someone approaches, it can use ghostly power to control the target and compel them to collect coins for its hoard; an old story describes one Gimmighoul forcing a young girl to gather all 999 coins it wanted. It can also drain the life force of thieves who attempt to take its treasure, making its apparently passive treasure-chest disguise genuinely dangerous.

pokemon.name: Gimmighoul
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Roaming Form Gimmighoul does not inhabit a chest and instead carries a single ancient coin on its back with its tail, making it one of the smallest and lightest known Pokémon. It is said to have been born from passion that seeped into a coin and constantly wanders, apparently searching for the treasure chest it once inhabited. Unlike Chest Form, it is extremely timid and does not normally control people into collecting for it; when approached in Paldea it flees and leaves behind a Gimmighoul Coin, and it can even turn invisible when it senses that a human or Pokémon is about to find it. It can nevertheless drain the life force of humans who attempt to steal its coin. No Roaming Form can be natively caught in Scarlet/Violet; catchable specimens originate from Pokémon GO and can be transferred into the core games.

pokemon.name: Gholdengo
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Gholdengo is a humanoid Pokémon whose body is formed from approximately 1,000 tightly stacked Gimmighoul Coins, including coin-like hair and a belt made from the strap of Gimmighoul's old treasure chest. Despite literally being made from treasure, it is notably sociable, quickly befriends others, and prefers lively places such as cities. The tightly packed coins give its body considerable resilience, and when struck it can loosen coins at the point of impact to help absorb the blow. Gholdengo attacks by firing coins in rapid succession and can create a surfboard from its own coins for transportation; animated canon has shown that board flying and carrying up to two humans. Its unique Good as Gold Ability and signature Make It Rain both extend the species' coin-based physiology directly into battle mechanics.

playthrough: Wo-Chien is a standalone Dark/Grass Legendary Pokémon obtainable in both Scarlet and Violet by removing the eight purple stakes sealing the Grasswither Shrine in South Province and then challenging the level-60 Pokémon inside. Its defining battle traits are base 135 Special Defense, solid 85 HP and 100 Defense, and Tablets of Ruin, which multiplies the Attack stat of every other active Pokémon by 0.75 and therefore makes physical opponents noticeably easier for Wo-Chien to endure. Dark/Grass grants a Psychic immunity and resistances to Dark, Electric, Ghost, Grass, Ground, and Water, but the typing also carries six ordinary weaknesses plus a devastating 4× Bug weakness. Ruination removes half of a target's current HP when it hits and is excellent for wearing down high-HP opponents, while Giga Drain, Dark Pulse, Foul Play, Knock Off, Leech Seed, Protect, and Rest can support defensive or attrition-focused play. Its lack of immediate, reliable full recovery outside Rest prevents it from functioning like an effortless story wall, and Leech Seed and Ruination are only 90% accurate, so prolonged battles still contain meaningful variance. In doubles, Tablets of Ruin also weakens the Attack of Wo-Chien's own ally unless that Pokémon also has Tablets of Ruin, an important cost that does not exist in ordinary singles play. Bold or Impish can emphasize physical durability behind Tablets of Ruin, while Calm or Careful can push its already excellent special bulk even further depending on whether the set uses special attacks or Foul Play and Knock Off.
competitive: Wo-Chien is currently PU in Smogon's SV usage tiers, but it has continued to demonstrate viability above that placement because Tablets of Ruin, 85/100/135 defensive stats, and a useful resistance profile give it a specialized defensive niche. Current NU analysis highlights its ability to check or annoy dangerous attackers through Knock Off, Foul Play or Ruination, Leech Seed, Protect, and RestTalk, with Tablets of Ruin helping it survive physical damage that its typing alone would not handle. Its problems are structural: Grass/Dark has seven weaknesses including a 4× Bug weakness, U-turn is therefore especially punishing, it lacks straightforward instant recovery, and common Grass-types can ignore Leech Seed while many offensive Pokémon threaten it super effectively. Ruination is useful because it cuts through high defensive stats by removing half of current HP, but 90% accuracy and its inability to KO by itself make Wo-Chien dependent on chip damage, hazards, teammates, or follow-up attacks. In VGC, Tablets of Ruin can weaken both opposing physical attackers simultaneously but also suppresses the Attack of Wo-Chien's partner, so successful teams usually pair it with special attackers or Pokémon whose job is not primarily physical damage. Its doubles support toolkit includes Pollen Puff for ally healing, Leech Seed, Snarl, Ruination, and Protect; official 2026 EUIC preview discussion noted that Wo-Chien had previously top-cut both Worlds and NAIC before largely disappearing from the contemporary field. That history makes it a good example of a low-usage singles Pokémon whose unique Ability and support tools have still produced meaningful niches in stronger formats.
nuzlocke: Wo-Chien can be an exceptionally durable Nuzlocke Pokémon if the ruleset permits Legendary encounters, but obtaining it requires deliberately finding all eight purple stakes and opening the Grasswither Shrine rather than simply encountering it on a route. Tablets of Ruin is superb survival support in singles because every opposing physical attack is calculated from an Attack stat reduced to 75% of its normal value, substantially increasing Wo-Chien's effective physical bulk before any other defensive strategy is used. Its base 135 Special Defense is already excellent, giving Wo-Chien strong mixed durability in neutral matchups, but the seven weaknesses of Grass/Dark—especially the 4× Bug weakness—mean an unexpected U-turn or other Bug attack can bypass that apparent safety very quickly. Giga Drain is a perfectly accurate source of damage and healing, while Leech Seed can provide sustained recovery but is only 90% accurate and fails against Grass-types; Rest fully restores HP and status but forces sleep turns unless supported appropriately. Ruination is strong for controlling high-HP targets because it always removes half of their current HP when successful, yet its 90% accuracy makes it less reliable when a miss would expose Wo-Chien to lethal retaliation. Foul Play is particularly attractive against physical setup users because it uses the target's Attack stat for damage while Tablets of Ruin simultaneously reduces the damage those Pokémon can deal back. Wo-Chien is therefore safest as a deliberate attrition specialist against known neutral or resisted damage rather than a universal wall that ignores its unusually severe weakness profile.

pokemon.name: Wo-Chien
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Wo-Chien is one of the four Treasures of Ruin, appearing as a large snail-like mass of dead leaves, moss, and vines surrounding a curled row of ancient wooden writing tablets that forms its shell. Those tablets are its true core: the grudge of a person punished for recording an ancient king's evil deeds accumulated within them and gave rise to the Pokémon, while the leafy body was constructed through Wo-Chien's control over plant matter. The inscriptions on the tablets have faded until they can no longer be read. Wo-Chien can drain the life force from vegetation across a wide area, causing forests to wither and cultivated fields to become barren almost instantly, making its presence an ecological threat even without direct aggression toward people or Pokémon.

playthrough: Chien-Pao is a standalone Dark/Ice Legendary Pokémon obtainable in both Scarlet and Violet by pulling the eight yellow stakes that seal the Icerend Shrine and then challenging it at level 60. Its current base 120 Attack and exceptional base 135 Speed make it one of Paldea's fastest and most immediately dangerous physical attackers, while Sword of Ruin multiplies the Defense stat of every other active Pokémon by 0.75 and therefore makes Chien-Pao's physical attacks hit much harder than its Attack stat alone suggests. Ice Spinner and Crunch provide perfectly accurate physical STAB, while Icicle Crash offers more Ice power at 90% accuracy and Sacred Sword supplies important coverage against opposing Dark-, Ice-, Rock-, and Steel-types. Ice Shard gives reliable priority and Sucker Punch offers stronger Dark priority but depends on the target choosing an attacking move, making the two options useful for different kinds of speed control. Its offensive profile is excellent, but Dark/Ice is defensively poor: Chien-Pao is weak to Bug, Fairy, Fire, Rock, and Steel and takes 4× damage from Fighting, while 80/80/65 bulk gives it little margin for error against strong neutral hits. Ruination can remove half of a target's current HP when it hits, but 90% accuracy and Chien-Pao's enormous direct attacking power make it more situational in a normal playthrough than on defensive Ruinous Pokémon. Terastallization can erase the 4× Fighting weakness or amplify Dark or Ice offense, while Jolly is generally ideal for preserving the elite Speed tier and Adamant can be used when maximum damage is more important.
competitive: Chien-Pao is currently Uber in Scarlet/Violet singles and has one of Generation IX's clearest early tiering histories: after surviving an initial January 2023 quickban vote, it was banned from SV OU by suspect test on February 11, 2023 with 69.03% support. Sword of Ruin is central to why it became overwhelming in OU, because reducing every other active Pokémon's Defense to 75% effectively magnifies the impact of base 120 Attack, strong Dark/Ice STAB, Swords Dance, and an already elite base 135 Speed tier. In Ubers, Chien-Pao commonly functions as a revenge killer or late-game cleaner using Icicle Crash or Ice Spinner, Crunch, Sucker Punch, Ice Shard, and sometimes Swords Dance; its priority is especially valuable against faster or boosted Dragons. Its limitations are much more visible at that power level: it is frail, weak to Stealth Rock, vulnerable to common Fighting-, Fairy-, Steel-, and Fire-type attacks, and often struggles to enter the field repeatedly without support. Official VGC gives Chien-Pao a separate and highly successful identity because Sword of Ruin also reduces the Defense of both opponents, dramatically increasing the damage of physically attacking partners such as Dragonite, Urshifu, and restricted Pokémon while Chien-Pao contributes Protect, Sucker Punch, Ice attacks, or Sacred Sword. That doubles role remained relevant deep into the Scarlet/Violet era; Chien-Pao appeared on multiple top-cut teams at the 2025 World Championships, including a Masters semifinal team and Senior and Junior semifinal teams. Its singles ban and long VGC career therefore come from the same defining mechanic—Sword of Ruin—but the surrounding roles differ sharply between self-contained offense in singles and teamwide physical amplification in doubles.
nuzlocke: Chien-Pao can be extraordinarily powerful in a Nuzlocke if the ruleset permits Legendary encounters, but its survival profile is much less forgiving than its offensive numbers suggest. Base 135 Speed is its strongest defensive asset because moving first can eliminate threats before they act, while Ice Shard gives perfectly accurate priority when an opposing Pokémon is already weakened. Sword of Ruin increases physical damage without requiring a setup turn, making Chien-Pao particularly good at securing immediate knockouts, but the same Ability also reduces the Defense of allied Pokémon in Double Battles and can therefore increase risk to a partner. Ice Spinner and Crunch are safer routine STAB choices than Icicle Crash because they are perfectly accurate, and Sucker Punch should not be treated as guaranteed priority because it fails if the opponent uses a status or setup move. The 4× Fighting weakness is the largest danger, but Chien-Pao also has five additional ordinary weaknesses and only base 65 Special Defense, so blind switching is hazardous even when it outspeeds most opponents. Ruination's fixed proportional damage can be useful against very bulky targets, yet its 90% accuracy introduces unnecessary variance if a direct attack already secures the knockout. Used as a carefully positioned finisher rather than a switch-in, Chien-Pao can be one of the strongest offensive Nuzlocke assets in Paldea.

pokemon.name: Chien-Pao
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Chien-Pao is a long, panther-like Pokémon whose visible body is made from snow and ice, with crystalline claws, whiskers, and body markings. Its true core is the pair of broken sword pieces that form its enormous fangs: the hatred of people killed by that sword long ago accumulated within the weapon and eventually became the Pokémon. Chien-Pao can control roughly 100 tons of fallen snow and causes avalanches, then leaps through the moving snow in what the Pokédex describes as innocent play. The contrast between its playful behavior and the violent human hatred that created its core is a defining feature of the Sword of Ruin.

playthrough: Ting-Lu is a standalone Dark/Ground Legendary Pokémon obtained in both Scarlet and Violet by removing the eight green stakes sealing the Groundblight Shrine and then catching the level-60 Pokémon inside. Its enormous base 155 HP and 125 Defense already make it exceptionally difficult to remove, and Vessel of Ruin multiplies the Special Attack of every other active Pokémon by 0.75, effectively patching Ting-Lu's otherwise ordinary base 80 Special Defense. Dark/Ground provides complete Electric and Psychic immunities plus resistances to Dark, Ghost, Poison, and Rock, but weaknesses to Bug, Fairy, Fighting, Grass, Ice, and Water keep it from switching carelessly into every matchup. Earthquake supplies powerful, perfectly accurate physical STAB from base 110 Attack, while Ruination removes half of the target's current HP when it connects and allows Ting-Lu to make progress even against very bulky opponents. Stealth Rock, Spikes, Whirlwind, Taunt, and status or disruption options can make Ting-Lu a highly effective support Pokémon rather than merely a damage sponge. Its largest practical weakness is recovery: outside Rest it lacks straightforward reliable healing, so repeated chip damage can eventually wear down even its enormous HP pool. Impish maximizes its defining physical durability, Careful strengthens the special side even further behind Vessel of Ruin, and Adamant can be justified for more offensive Earthquake-focused play.
competitive: Ting-Lu remains OU in Scarlet/Violet and has been one of the generation's premier defensive hazard setters because 155/125/80 bulk and Vessel of Ruin let it withstand attacks from both physical and special threats that would overwhelm most Ground-types. Vessel of Ruin reduces the Special Attack of every other active Pokémon to 75%, allowing Ting-Lu to check dangerous special attackers such as Gholdengo, Iron Moth, Raging Bolt, and Darkrai while its raw Defense also lets it handle many physical attackers. Stealth Rock and Spikes exploit the switches Ting-Lu forces, Whirlwind prevents setup sweepers from using its passivity freely, and Ruination ensures that even exceptionally bulky switch-ins can be worn down without relying on Ting-Lu's modest offensive coverage. Earthquake remains a dependable source of direct damage from base 110 Attack, and Rest sets can extend Ting-Lu's lifespan when a team needs it to repeatedly check high-powered threats. Its weaknesses are long-term attrition, susceptibility to Knock Off and status, six exploitable type weaknesses, and the absence of conventional instant recovery; sufficiently strong wallbreakers can eventually force progress if Ting-Lu is asked to absorb too many hits. In VGC, Vessel of Ruin affects both opposing Pokémon at once and can drastically reduce incoming special damage, while Assault Vest, Ruination, Snarl, Stomping Tantrum, Heavy Slam, Rock Tomb, and defensive Terastallization have supported multiple archetypes since 2023. Unlike Sword of Ruin or Beads of Ruin, Vessel of Ruin can also suppress an allied special attacker's damage in doubles, so teams must account for the Ability's symmetrical cost rather than treating it as free defensive support.
nuzlocke: Ting-Lu is one of the safest Legendary Pokémon for a conventional Nuzlocke if Legendary encounters are permitted, because its raw HP and Defense are extraordinary and Vessel of Ruin reduces incoming special offense without requiring a setup turn. Electric and Psychic immunities create predictable switch opportunities, while resistances to Dark, Ghost, Poison, and Rock further expand the number of moves Ting-Lu can absorb comfortably. Earthquake is a particularly good permadeath attack because it is strong and perfectly accurate, while Ruination can control exceptionally bulky opponents but carries 90% accuracy and cannot finish a target by itself. Whirlwind can remove dangerous setup sweepers without attempting to overpower their boosts, although it has negative priority and should not be used casually when Ting-Lu is already in lethal range. The major problem is cumulative damage: Ting-Lu has no ordinary instant recovery move, so Rest or external healing is required to restore a badly depleted HP pool, and six weaknesses give opponents several ways to accelerate that attrition. Vessel of Ruin also weakens a friendly special attacker in Double Battles, potentially prolonging the fight if the team does not account for the effect. Against known opponents whose super-effective coverage has been checked, Ting-Lu provides one of the widest safety margins available in Scarlet/Violet.

pokemon.name: Ting-Lu
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Ting-Lu is a gigantic ruinous Pokémon whose visible deer- or moose-like body is constructed from layers of earth and stone. Its true core is the cracked ritual vessel carried on its head: human fear accumulated within that ancient vessel and gave it life, after which Ting-Lu formed the surrounding body through its control over the earth. The vessel is therefore not an ornament but the essential object from which the Pokémon originated. Ting-Lu possesses enough geological power to create fissures more than 160 feet (50 meters) deep simply by slowly lowering its head to the ground, giving the Vessel of Ruin a direct capacity to reshape terrain on a massive scale.

playthrough: Chi-Yu is a standalone Dark/Fire Legendary Pokémon obtainable in both Scarlet and Violet after the player removes the eight light-blue stakes sealing the Firescourge Shrine and catches the level-60 Pokémon inside. Its current base 135 Special Attack, base 120 Special Defense, and base 100 Speed already form an excellent special-offense profile, and Beads of Ruin multiplies the Special Defense of every other active Pokémon by 0.75, making Chi-Yu's attacks far stronger than its base Special Attack alone indicates. Flamethrower and Dark Pulse are perfectly accurate and reliable STAB options, while Overheat and Fire Blast offer greater immediate Fire damage at the cost of a two-stage Special Attack drop or imperfect accuracy respectively. Psychic and Tera Blast can address specific coverage problems, and Nasty Plot can raise Special Attack by two stages if Chi-Yu receives a safe setup turn. Dark/Fire provides a Psychic immunity and six useful resistances, but Fighting, Ground, Rock, and Water weaknesses are common and base 55 HP leaves Chi-Yu less physically durable than its high Special Defense may imply. Ruination can halve the current HP of bulky targets but is normally less efficient in story battles than simply exploiting Beads of Ruin with direct special damage. Timid improves the useful but not unbeatable base 100 Speed, while Modest pushes Chi-Yu's already extreme wallbreaking power even higher.
competitive: Chi-Yu is currently Uber and was one of the first ordinary Pokémon removed from SV OU, receiving a unanimous 9-0 quickban vote on January 8, 2023 after becoming one of the most centralizing early threats in the metagame. Beads of Ruin reduces every other active Pokémon's Special Defense to 75%, which effectively amplifies attacks from base 135 Special Attack before Choice Specs, sun, Nasty Plot, or Terastallization are even considered. In Ubers, Choice Specs and Choice Scarf sets use Overheat, Flamethrower or Fire Blast, and Dark Pulse to function as wallbreakers or revenge killers, while sun from Koraidon can raise Fire damage to levels that threaten even dedicated special walls. Its drawbacks are much more meaningful in Ubers than they were in OU: base 55 HP makes safe entry difficult, Stealth Rock removes one-quarter of its health, several common physical attackers can revenge kill it, and Choice-locked sets can be exploited through prediction. Chi-Yu has also enjoyed a substantial official VGC career because Beads of Ruin reduces the Special Defense of both opponents, empowering partners such as Flutter Mane, Miraidon, or other spread special attackers while Chi-Yu contributes Heat Wave, Dark Pulse, Overheat, Snarl, or Protect. That role remained successful late into SV competition: Chi-Yu appeared on multiple top-cut teams at the 2025 World Championships, including Senior Division semifinal and quarterfinal teams. As with the other Ruinous Pokémon, Beads of Ruin also lowers an allied Pokémon's Special Defense in doubles, so the extraordinary offensive payoff comes with a real team-building and positioning cost.
nuzlocke: Chi-Yu can function as an exceptional Nuzlocke wallbreaker if Legendary encounters are allowed, because perfectly accurate Flamethrower and Dark Pulse become extremely strong after Beads of Ruin reduces the target's Special Defense. Its base 120 Special Defense gives it real resilience against special attacks, and Psychic immunity plus resistances to Dark, Fire, Ghost, Grass, Ice, and Steel create several safe entry points against known movesets. The much smaller base 55 HP pool and only base 80 Defense mean physical attacks remain dangerous, particularly from Fighting-, Ground-, Rock-, and Water-type opponents. Overheat's perfect accuracy is attractive for emergency power but the two-stage Special Attack reduction can make the following turns dangerous if Chi-Yu cannot switch, while Fire Blast introduces unnecessary miss variance when Flamethrower already secures the needed knockout. Nasty Plot can produce overwhelming sweeps, but spending a turn setting up is often unnecessary for a Pokémon whose Ability already multiplies effective special damage. Ruination's 90% accuracy makes it less desirable than a direct attack when a miss could expose Chi-Yu to lethal retaliation. Used as a fast special attacker and selectively switched into resisted special moves rather than asked to tank neutral physical damage, Chi-Yu can be extremely reliable.

pokemon.name: Chi-Yu
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Chi-Yu is a fish-shaped Pokémon whose true core is the pair of ancient curved jade beads that form its eyes, while the rest of its body consists of living flame. The beads were once treated as sacred objects and became the focus of repeated conflict; the envy of people who desired them accumulated until it gave rise to the Pokémon. Chi-Yu's flames exceed 5,400°F (3,000°C), hot enough to melt rock and sand into lava. It then swims casually through the molten material it creates, making the Beads of Ruin both a supernatural artifact and the center of an organism capable of radically altering its physical environment.

playthrough: Roaring Moon is a standalone Dragon/Dark Paradox Pokémon found naturally only in Pokémon Scarlet's Area Zero, with its principal wild habitat being a hidden cave in the research-station region; Violet players normally require trade, event, or Union Circle access. Its 590 BST is unusually high even among non-Legendary Paradox Pokémon, with base 139 Attack, 119 Speed, 105 HP, and 101 Special Defense creating a fast physical attacker that is much bulkier on the special side than most sweepers. Dragon Dance is its defining setup move because one use raises both Attack and Speed, while Knock Off, Crunch, Dragon Claw, Outrage, Earthquake, Acrobatics, and later move additions such as Scale Shot provide several different offensive routes. Booster Energy activates Protosynthesis and is especially synergistic with Acrobatics because the consumed item leaves Roaring Moon itemless, doubling Acrobatics to 110 base power; Tera Flying can then turn that coverage attack into powerful STAB while removing the native 4× Fairy weakness. Its natural Dragon/Dark typing provides a Psychic immunity and six useful resistances but is weak to Bug, Dragon, Fighting, and Ice and takes 4× damage from Fairy, so an unexpected Moonblast or Play Rough can end a sweep immediately. Roost gives it genuine longevity when available, while Taunt can prevent defensive opponents from recovering or inflicting status. Jolly is ideal when maximizing the already excellent Speed matters, while Adamant pushes Dragon Dance and Protosynthesis damage even higher.
competitive: Roaring Moon is currently Uber in SV after one of the generation's most complicated OU tiering histories. It was banned from OU by suspect test in October 2023, returned when The Indigo Disk reset portions of the tier in December 2023, remained a major offensive presence for more than a year, and was banned again on April 1, 2025 after a second suspect reached 66.07% support for removal. Its defining sets combine Dragon Dance with Booster Energy, Protosynthesis, Knock Off, Earthquake, and Acrobatics or another coverage move; when Booster Energy is consumed, Acrobatics doubles in power, and Tera Flying can simultaneously provide STAB and remove the 4× Fairy weakness that would normally be its clearest defensive flaw. Knock Off's return through The Teal Mask gave Roaring Moon a strong, low-drawback Dark STAB that also strips Heavy-Duty Boots and defensive items, making long-term counterplay substantially harder than during its earliest SV phase. Base 139 Attack and 119 Speed mean it threatens teams even before setup, while 105 HP and 101 Special Defense give it enough bulk to find Dragon Dance opportunities that many comparably fast sweepers cannot safely attempt. Roaring Moon also developed legitimate doubles utility rather than being restricted to singles offense; current Doubles analyses document Booster Energy sets using Tailwind, Breaking Swipe, Knock Off, and Protect to combine speed control, physical damage reduction, and disruption. Its repeated bans reflect the way Terastallization, Booster Energy consumption, Knock Off, and Dragon Dance made defensive counterplay too inconsistent in standard OU rather than a simple claim that its raw base stats alone were excessive.
nuzlocke: Roaring Moon is an extremely powerful late-game Scarlet Nuzlocke attacker, but its Area Zero availability means it normally contributes only to the final story stretch and postgame. Base 119 Speed and 139 Attack reduce exposure by allowing immediate knockouts, while its high HP and Special Defense give it a greater chance to survive neutral special attacks than many fast physical sweepers. Dragon Dance can create decisive sweeps when opposing coverage is known, but the 4× Fairy weakness means setting up blindly against anything capable of Moonblast, Play Rough, Dazzling Gleam, or Fairy Tera Blast is particularly dangerous. Knock Off is a safe, perfectly accurate routine Dark attack with valuable item removal, while Outrage is much riskier because it locks Roaring Moon into repeated attacks and can leave it confused afterward. Acrobatics becomes especially useful after Booster Energy is consumed, offering strong perfect-accuracy coverage without recoil, although the one-use nature of Booster Energy should be accounted for during an ordinary run. Roost provides reliable recovery when available and Taunt can shut down known status or setup users before they create additional risk. A Jolly build that prioritizes moving first is generally the safest approach, while Adamant is worthwhile when additional power clearly changes knockout ranges.

pokemon.name: Roaring Moon
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Roaring Moon is a large feathered, quadrupedal dragon whose crescent-shaped wings closely resemble those of Mega Salamence, although the games never confirm a direct connection between that Mega Evolution and the Paradox species. It flies at high speed while scattering feathers and actively searches for prey, and Occulture describes it as more savage than ordinary Salamence and dangerous enough that people should avoid approaching it. Its body combines draconic scales, feather-like wing structures, large claws, and a long tail suited to an active aerial predator rather than the compact body plan of modern Salamence. Its origin remains deliberately unresolved: AI Sada describes it as an ancient ancestor of Salamence, while the Professor encountered at the Crystal Pool calls it a Salamence counterpart from another timeline, and Heath recorded the creature about 200 years before Sada's time machine existed.

playthrough: Iron Valiant is a standalone Fairy/Fighting Paradox Pokémon found naturally only in Pokémon Violet's Area Zero, primarily in the same hidden cave region that contains Roaring Moon in Scarlet; Scarlet players normally require trade, event, or Union Circle access. Its unusual 590 BST supports genuine physical, special, and mixed offense: base 130 Attack, 120 Special Attack, and 116 Speed are all excellent, allowing movesets to be built around Close Combat and Spirit Break, Moonblast and Focus Blast, or combinations that exploit both attacking stats. Quark Drive boosts its highest stat in Electric Terrain or after Booster Energy activates, and Speed-focused builds receive a 50% Speed increase rather than the 30% multiplier applied to other stats, making Iron Valiant one of Paldea's most dangerous late-game cleaners. Swords Dance, Calm Mind, Encore, Knock Off, Shadow Ball, Thunderbolt, Psyshock, Vacuum Wave, and Destiny Bond give it exceptional flexibility, so the correct moves depend heavily on whether the player wants physical setup, special setup, mixed coverage, or utility. Fairy/Fighting grants a Dragon immunity and useful Bug, Dark, Fighting, and Rock resistances, but it is weak to Fairy, Flying, Poison, Psychic, and Steel and has only base 60 Special Defense, so strong special attacks can punish careless positioning. Close Combat's defensive drops and Focus Blast's 70% accuracy create real risks even when their power is attractive, while Moonblast and Spirit Break provide much safer routine Fairy damage. Jolly or Adamant suit physical builds, Timid or Modest suit special builds, and Naive or Hasty can be justified when a genuinely mixed set needs to preserve both attacking stats.
competitive: Iron Valiant remains OU and is one of the most versatile offensive Pokémon in Scarlet/Violet singles because opponents often cannot identify its counterplay from Team Preview alone. Base 130 Attack, 120 Special Attack, and 116 Speed support Swords Dance, Calm Mind, mixed Booster Energy, Choice Specs, Choice Scarf, Encore utility, and priority-oriented sets, with each archetype threatening a different collection of defensive answers. Booster Energy Speed sets function as elite revenge killers and late-game cleaners because Quark Drive pushes Iron Valiant beyond the entire unboosted metagame and many already-boosted threats, while Moonblast and Close Combat give it powerful mixed STAB that cannot be handled by a single defensive stat. Calm Mind variants can use Shadow Ball or Thunderbolt to punish Fairy resists, Swords Dance sets exploit Knock Off and physical coverage, and Encore can convert Protect, recovery, or setup moves into free opportunities rather than merely adding another attack. The drawbacks are equally important: base 74 HP and especially base 60 Special Defense make it vulnerable to strong special priority or revenge killing, repeated entry can wear it down, and many sets become much easier to check once their fourth move or attacking orientation is revealed. Iron Valiant has had a smaller official VGC footprint than Chien-Pao, Chi-Yu, or Ting-Lu because singles better rewards its unpredictable one-on-one coverage and setup variety, but its Quark Drive, mixed offenses, Encore, Wide Guard, Spirit Break, and speed still give it situational doubles applications. Its sustained OU status is therefore based less on one overpowering mechanic than on extreme set diversity: preparing for one Iron Valiant set can leave a team exposed to another.
nuzlocke: Iron Valiant is one of Violet's strongest late-game offensive Pokémon, but it should be treated as a fast attacker rather than a durable all-purpose switch-in. Base 116 Speed and either 130 Attack or 120 Special Attack allow it to remove many targets before they can respond, while Fairy typing gives complete Dragon immunity and useful resistance to Dark, Fighting, Bug, and Rock. Moonblast is a particularly safe special STAB because it is perfectly accurate, and Spirit Break offers similarly reliable physical Fairy damage while also lowering the target's Special Attack when it hits. Close Combat is powerful but lowers both defenses, Focus Blast is only 70% accurate, and Destiny Bond normally conflicts with the goal of preserving Iron Valiant, so competitive sets should not be copied blindly into a permadeath run. Calm Mind can improve Special Defense while increasing damage, making it safer than purely offensive setup against known special attackers, whereas Swords Dance provides greater immediate physical pressure but no defensive benefit. Booster Energy can make Speed-based sweeps exceptionally reliable, yet the item activates only once per battle and should not substitute for checking opposing priority or Choice Scarf users. Timid or Jolly builds generally maximize survival by moving first, while mixed Natures are worthwhile only when the additional coverage genuinely solves important matchups.

pokemon.name: Iron Valiant
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Iron Valiant is a robotic humanoid Paradox Pokémon combining major anatomical features of both Gardevoir and Gallade, including skirt-like armor, blade-equipped arms, and luminous head structures. Its arm blades can detach and join into a double-ended weapon, while it can alternatively leave them connected and rotate the entire upper half of its body independently from the lower half to attack. Iron Valiant is described as cruel and willing to cut down opponents without hesitation, contrasting sharply with the protective behavior associated with modern Gardevoir and Gallade. When sleeping it powers itself down and the normally pink energy across its blades, head structures, chest cannon, feet, and body turns black. Its true origin is unresolved: AI Turo describes it as a future descendant of both Gardevoir and Gallade, whereas the Professor encountered at the Crystal Pool calls it their counterpart from another timeline; Heath also recorded it roughly two centuries before Turo's time machine was created.

playthrough: Koraidon is a standalone Fighting/Dragon Legendary Pokémon and the mascot of Pokémon Scarlet, but the player's ride Koraidon cannot be used as an ordinary battler until the climax of The Way Home, when it regains the confidence and strength needed to assume Apex Build in battle. After the main story, the ride specimen can be shifted between ride and battle use, and the second, aggressive Koraidon encountered deep in Area Zero can also be caught, so its practical battle availability is overwhelmingly endgame and postgame rather than something that shapes most of the badge journey. Its base 135 Attack and 135 Speed are backed by 100/115/100 bulk, and Orichalcum Pulse automatically summons harsh sunlight while multiplying Koraidon's Attack by roughly four-thirds during sun, making its physical offense extraordinary before any setup. Collision Course is its signature 100-base-power, perfectly accurate Fighting attack and receives an additional roughly 33% damage increase when it is super effective, giving it a powerful no-drawback alternative to Close Combat in favorable matchups. Dragon Claw offers reliable Dragon STAB, while Flare Blitz becomes unusually strong under Koraidon's own sun but inflicts heavy recoil; U-turn, Swords Dance, Flame Charge, Drain Punch, and coverage moves can support different offensive roles. Fighting/Dragon provides useful resistances to Bug, Dark, Electric, Fire, Grass, Rock, and Water, but weaknesses to Dragon, Flying, Ice, and Psychic are joined by a dangerous 4× Fairy weakness. Koraidon's five named builds—Apex, Limited, Sprinting, Swimming, and Gliding—reflect battle, weakened/resting, and traversal states rather than separately obtainable species forms; only Apex Build is normally used in battle. Jolly preserves its elite Speed tier, while Adamant maximizes its already extreme sun-boosted physical damage.
competitive: Koraidon remains Uber in current Scarlet/Violet singles and is one of the generation's defining restricted-level physical attackers. Orichalcum Pulse simultaneously creates sun and multiplies Koraidon's Attack by roughly 1.333× while the weather is active, so Choice Band, Choice Scarf, Swords Dance, and other offensive sets begin from a power level far beyond the raw base 135 Attack statistic. Collision Course and Close Combat provide Fighting STAB, Dragon Claw or Outrage supplies Dragon pressure, and sun-boosted Flare Blitz is especially important because it punishes Steel- and Fairy-types that would otherwise exploit Koraidon's Dragon typing. Choice Scarf Koraidon is one of the format's premier revenge killers, while Choice Band can function as a devastating wallbreaker and setup variants use Swords Dance or Flame Charge to overwhelm slower teams. Its 4× Fairy weakness and vulnerability to fast revenge killers, defensive Terastallization, Ho-Oh, bulky Ground-types, and recoil from Flare Blitz provide meaningful counterplay, which is part of why Koraidon remains legal in Ubers while Miraidon was eventually removed from the tier. Koraidon was also a major restricted Pokémon in official VGC: its sun supports partners as well as itself, and Clear Amulet, Flame Charge, Collision Course or Low Kick, Flare Blitz, and Protect all appeared in high-level play. Its competitive peak is well documented by the 2025 World Championships, where Giovanni Cischke won the Masters Division with Koraidon and another Koraidon team also reached the Masters top cut, confirming that its sun offense remained elite through the final major Scarlet/Violet championship era.
nuzlocke: Koraidon is an exceptionally strong Nuzlocke asset if the ruleset permits box Legendaries, but it joins actual battles so late that it cannot carry the player through most of Scarlet's main progression. Base 135 Speed lets it remove many threats before they act, while 100/115/100 bulk is genuinely strong enough to survive neutral hits that would punish frailer sweepers. Collision Course is ideal under permadeath rules because it combines 100% accuracy, 100 base power, no defensive or recoil drawback, and extra power on super-effective hits; it is often safer than Close Combat when both attacks achieve the same knockout. Flare Blitz benefits enormously from Orichalcum Pulse's sun but can remove large amounts of Koraidon's own HP through recoil, while Outrage traps the user for multiple turns and can end in confusion, so neither should be copied blindly from competitive sets. The 4× Fairy weakness is the central survival hazard, and unexpected Moonblast, Play Rough, Dazzling Gleam, or Fairy Tera coverage can overwhelm even Koraidon's otherwise excellent bulk. Drain Punch can trade some power for healing and Flame Charge can raise Speed while attacking, both useful when a known matchup does not require maximum force. If its Fairy weakness and recoil options are managed conservatively, Koraidon offers one of the widest combinations of speed, power, bulk, and reliable damage available in Scarlet.

pokemon.name: Koraidon
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Koraidon is a massive feathered reptilian Pokémon resembling Cyclizar, distinguished by powerful limbs, webbed feet, a large tire-like gular sac, a feathered crest, and a thick tail whose base echoes the grooved appearance of the throat structure. It can shift among five named builds: Apex Build is its full battle state, Limited Build is used while resting or weakened, Sprinting Build supports rapid land travel, Swimming Build adapts it to water, and Gliding Build spreads its head structures into aerodynamic surfaces for aerial travel. Unlike Miraidon, Koraidon does not actually use its throat and tail structures as mechanical wheels during terrestrial movement; it runs with its powerful legs. The two specimens brought to the present by Professor Sada displayed sharply different temperaments—one was curious and capable of bonding closely with humans, while the other was highly aggressive and territorial, ultimately defeating and traumatizing the first in Area Zero. The species was called the Winged King in the Scarlet Book, and its origin remains unresolved because AI Sada describes it as an ancient relative of Cyclizar while the Professor encountered at the Crystal Pool describes it as a Cyclizar counterpart from another timeline; Heath's record of a Koraidon roughly 200 years before Sada's time machine further complicates a simple time-travel explanation.

playthrough: Miraidon is a standalone Electric/Dragon Legendary Pokémon and Pokémon Violet's mascot, but the player's ride Miraidon does not become usable in ordinary battles until the climax of The Way Home, after which it can switch between ride and battle roles. A second, aggressive Miraidon remains in Area Zero after the story and can be captured, so like Koraidon its meaningful battle availability is essentially endgame and postgame rather than part of most of the badge journey. Its base 135 Special Attack and 135 Speed combine with 100/100/115 bulk, while Hadron Engine automatically creates Electric Terrain and multiplies Miraidon's Special Attack by roughly four-thirds while the terrain is active. Electro Drift is a 100-base-power, perfectly accurate signature Electric attack whose damage receives an additional roughly 33% increase when the move is super effective, and Electric Terrain further boosts grounded Electric attacks, making it devastating against vulnerable targets. Dragon Pulse provides reliable Dragon STAB, while Draco Meteor reaches far greater power at 90% accuracy and lowers Special Attack by two stages; Volt Switch and U-turn can preserve momentum, and Calm Mind or Charge can support setup. Electric/Dragon strongly resists Electric and resists Fire, Flying, Grass, Steel, and Water, but Ground, Ice, Dragon, and Fairy all threaten super-effective damage. Its five named modes—Ultimate, Low-Power, Drive, Aquatic, and Glide—describe full battle power, weakened/resting condition, and different traversal configurations; only Ultimate Mode is normally usable in battle. Timid is generally the safest Nature because its base-135 Speed tier is highly contested, while Modest makes Hadron Engine-boosted attacks even more destructive.
competitive: Miraidon is currently classified as Anything Goes in Smogon's Scarlet/Violet structure because it was ultimately banned even from Ubers, a rare distinction that separates its singles history from Koraidon's. Hadron Engine is the core of the problem: on entry it creates Electric Terrain and, while that terrain remains active, multiplies Miraidon's already base-135 Special Attack by roughly 1.333×, creating enormous immediate power without requiring a setup turn. Electro Drift is a 100-base-power perfectly accurate Electric STAB that receives another roughly 1.333× modifier when super effective, while Draco Meteor pressures Ground-types that block Electric moves and U-turn lets Miraidon escape those checks without surrendering all momentum. Choice Specs, Heavy-Duty Boots pivoting, Calm Mind, and Agility sets have all exploited different aspects of its toolkit, and Terastallization can bypass traditional Dragon or Ground counterplay or raise its STAB damage even further. Miraidon narrowly survived an Ubers suspect in March 2024, when the pro-ban vote fell short of the required threshold, but a second major suspect concluded on October 20, 2024 with 92 of 111 votes—82.9%—supporting a ban, sending Miraidon to Anything Goes. Official VGC remained a separate legal environment: Miraidon became a metagame-defining restricted Pokémon through Hadron Engine, Electro Drift, Volt Switch, Draco Meteor, Protect, and terrain support for partners such as Iron Hands. That success persisted through the 2025 World Championships, where Miraidon appeared on a Masters semifinal team and several strong Senior and Junior teams, showing that its oppressive singles power translated into elite but legally manageable doubles play.
nuzlocke: Miraidon is one of Violet's strongest possible Nuzlocke Pokémon if box Legendaries are allowed, but its battle use begins only at the end of the main story, greatly limiting how much of the run it can actually influence. Base 135 Speed is an outstanding survival tool and Electro Drift is nearly ideal for permadeath play because it is perfectly accurate, extremely strong, and becomes even stronger against super-effective targets without imposing recoil or defensive drops.
