Hadron Engine automatically strengthens Miraidon's special offense while creating Electric Terrain, so many encounters can be ended without spending a separate turn on setup. Dragon Pulse is a safer routine Dragon move than Draco Meteor when its lower power still secures the knockout, since Draco Meteor is only 90% accurate and leaves Miraidon's Special Attack two stages lower afterward. Volt Switch and U-turn provide valuable controlled repositioning, especially against Ground-types that are immune to Electro Drift, but Ground, Ice, Dragon, and Fairy coverage must still be identified before assuming Miraidon's strong overall bulk makes a matchup safe. Calm Mind can improve both damage and special durability, yet using it is often unnecessary when Miraidon's unboosted offense already overwhelms ordinary opponents. When played around its four weaknesses rather than used as a universal switch-in, Miraidon combines speed, reliable offense, useful resistances, and momentum control at an exceptional level.

pokemon.name: Miraidon
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Miraidon is a sleek mechanical reptilian Pokémon resembling Cyclizar, with glowing digital eyes, antenna-like structures, jet-equipped hindquarters, and luminous throat and tail structures that can change shape with its operating mode. Ultimate Mode is its fully powered battle state, Low-Power Mode is used while weakened or resting, Drive Mode turns the throat and tail structures into wheel-like rings for land travel, Aquatic Mode supports movement across water, and Glide Mode transforms the antennae and body posture for aerial travel. In its travel modes the rear legs fold away while built-in propulsion systems take over, making its locomotion much more machine-like than Koraidon's muscular running. The two known modern specimens also displayed contrasting temperaments, with the player's Miraidon capable of curiosity, fear, attachment, and trust while the second specimen was aggressively territorial. Its origin is deliberately unresolved: AI Turo identifies it as a future relative or descendant of Cyclizar, while the Professor encountered at the Crystal Pool describes it as a Cyclizar counterpart from another timeline, and the Violet Book's much older record again complicates a straightforward future-import explanation.

playthrough: Walking Wake is a standalone Water/Dragon Paradox Pokémon, but unlike the ordinary Area Zero Paradox species it is event-exclusive in Scarlet/Violet rather than permanently encounterable in the wild. The most recent official rerun placed Water-Tera Walking Wake in 5-star Scarlet raids from December 19, 2025 through January 4, 2026, with one catch permitted per save across the recurring event series; as of August 2026 that event has ended, so a new player needs a previously obtained specimen, trade, HOME access, or a future rerun. When available, its base 125 Special Attack and 109 Speed make it an excellent special attacker, and Water/Dragon is defensively efficient because only Dragon and Fairy are naturally super effective while Fire and Water are each resisted 4×. Its signature Hydro Steam is an 80-base-power, perfectly accurate Water attack with an extraordinary weather interaction: harsh sunlight boosts it by 50% instead of halving Water damage, allowing Walking Wake to thrive on the same sun teams that activate Protosynthesis. Dragon Pulse provides reliable secondary STAB, Draco Meteor offers much higher immediate damage at 90% accuracy and a two-stage Special Attack drop, while Flamethrower or Weather Ball benefit from sun and Flip Turn can reposition the user. Protosynthesis can increase Special Attack or Speed depending on its actual stat spread, with Speed receiving the larger 50% modifier. Timid is usually ideal for maintaining its strong Speed tier, while Modest maximizes Hydro Steam and Draco Meteor damage.
competitive: Walking Wake remains OU in Scarlet/Violet and has one of the more interesting early DLC-era tiering stories because its release immediately transformed sun offense. Hydro Steam solves the traditional contradiction between Water STAB and sun: rather than being weakened, the 80-base-power move becomes 1.5× stronger in harsh sunlight, while Protosynthesis activates at the same time and sun also strengthens Flamethrower or Weather Ball. Choice Specs sets combine Hydro Steam with Draco Meteor to pressure most conventional Water answers, while Timid or stat-manipulated Booster Energy sets can use Protosynthesis for speed and non-Choice variants can pivot with Flip Turn or disrupt switch-ins with Knock Off. Smogon formally suspect-tested Walking Wake in March 2023 after its explosive debut, but the final vote produced only about 45% support for a ban, so it remained legal and over time settled into a strong but manageable OU niche rather than becoming another immediate Paradox ban. Its main constraints are dependence on sun for maximum wallbreaking efficiency, imperfect Draco Meteor accuracy, competition for team slots and Terastallization, and defensive answers that can exploit Choice locking or force it to predict correctly. Walking Wake also translated into high-level VGC sun compositions: its Hydro Steam uniquely benefits from Koraidon's weather rather than fighting against it, and it appeared on the 2025 World Championships Junior Division runner-up team alongside Koraidon. Its sustained OU status therefore reflects a rare case where a spectacularly synergistic signature mechanic proved powerful enough to reshape an archetype without ultimately being judged broken in standard singles.
nuzlocke: Walking Wake is mechanically excellent for a Nuzlocke but practically difficult to obtain because its official Scarlet/Violet raid distributions are temporary and the latest rerun ended on January 4, 2026. If a legal specimen is available, Water/Dragon's only natural weaknesses are Fairy and Dragon, and its strong base 109 Speed plus 125 Special Attack let it avoid many hits by securing fast knockouts. Hydro Steam is one of the safest powerful Water moves in the series for this role because it is perfectly accurate and becomes stronger rather than weaker in sunlight, eliminating the normal weather conflict that would otherwise make sun dangerous for a Water attacker. Dragon Pulse is preferable to Draco Meteor when its damage is sufficient, because Draco Meteor can miss and lowers Special Attack by two stages, potentially making a continued battle unsafe. Flip Turn provides controlled repositioning, while Flamethrower offers perfectly accurate coverage and becomes stronger under the same sunlight that activates Protosynthesis. Walking Wake's bulk is respectable rather than exceptional, so physical Fairy attacks, strong Dragon moves, priority, and critical hits should still be respected despite the clean defensive typing. When availability permits, a Timid, reliability-focused set built around Hydro Steam and accurate coverage is one of the safest ways to use it under permadeath rules.

pokemon.name: Walking Wake
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Walking Wake is a huge bipedal theropod-like Paradox Pokémon resembling Suicune, with powerful hind legs, small forelimbs, two long tails, and a multicolored mane reminiscent of an aurora. It is described as ferocious and can walk directly across the surface of water while remaining upright on its hind legs. Its control of water is unusual even for a Water-type: Walking Wake can generate superheated water powerful enough to scorch opponents, the biological concept reflected directly in Hydro Steam. A creature resembling it was recorded in the Scarlet Book roughly two centuries before Professor Sada built her time machine; AI Sada later describes Walking Wake as an ancient relative of Suicune, while the Crystal Pool Professor instead calls it a Suicune counterpart from another timeline. Because those explanations conflict and its historical sighting predates the machine that supposedly imported it, its true origin remains explicitly unresolved.

playthrough: Iron Leaves is a standalone Grass/Psychic Paradox Pokémon whose Scarlet/Violet availability is also limited to special Tera Raid events rather than a permanent Area Zero encounter. The most recent official distribution placed Psychic-Tera Iron Leaves in 5-star Pokémon Violet raids from December 19, 2025 through January 4, 2026, and the event allows only one capture per save across reruns; as of August 2026 that event is over, so new access depends on an already-caught specimen, trade, HOME, or a future distribution. Its base 130 Attack, 108 Special Defense, and 104 Speed create a fast physical attacker with useful special resilience, while Quark Drive can increase Attack or Speed under Electric Terrain or after Booster Energy activates. The signature Psyblade is a perfectly accurate 80-base-power physical Psychic attack whose power becomes 120 in Electric Terrain, creating excellent synergy with Miraidon or any other terrain setter that also activates Quark Drive. Leaf Blade provides powerful perfectly accurate Grass STAB with a high critical-hit ratio, Sacred Sword and Close Combat cover Steel- and Dark-types, and Swords Dance can raise Attack by two stages when a safe setup opportunity exists. Grass/Psychic carries a severe defensive cost: Iron Leaves is weak to Flying, Poison, Ghost, Fire, Ice, and Dark and takes 4× damage from Bug, making U-turn and other Bug attacks particularly dangerous. Jolly is usually the most practical Nature for leveraging base 104 Speed, while Adamant maximizes its substantial physical power.
competitive: Iron Leaves is currently RUBL in Scarlet/Violet, meaning it is banned from RU while not possessing enough usage for a standard higher usage tier. Swords Dance is the defining singles setup option, and Booster Energy can trigger Quark Drive immediately, allowing carefully constructed sets to raise Speed and then threaten a sweep with Leaf Blade, Psyblade, and Fighting or Electric coverage. Psyblade is especially dangerous alongside Electric Terrain because its base power rises from 80 to 120 at the same time Quark Drive activates, giving Miraidon-based or dedicated terrain teams a natural way to amplify both Iron Leaves's stats and its signature Psychic attack. Its high base 130 Attack and 104 Speed are strong for lower tiers, and historical RU discussion repeatedly identified Booster Energy plus Swords Dance as too difficult for the tier to manage, helping explain its continued RUBL status. The drawbacks are equally obvious: Grass/Psychic has seven weaknesses including a 4× Bug weakness, common U-turn users can exploit it brutally, and Iron Leaves lacks the broad immediate priority or defensive utility that makes some other Paradox attackers easier to fit. Leaf Blade and Psyblade are reliable and powerful, but using Close Combat lowers both defenses and Megahorn's 85% accuracy makes it a less consistent coverage choice. Iron Leaves has had much less enduring high-level VGC prominence than Walking Wake or the box Legendaries, so its competitive history is best described through its documented singles tiering niche rather than forcing a tournament résumé it does not possess.
nuzlocke: Iron Leaves can be a strong Nuzlocke attacker if a legal event or transferred specimen is available, but like Walking Wake it is not currently a normal fresh-save encounter in Scarlet/Violet as of August 2026. Base 104 Speed, 130 Attack, and perfectly accurate Leaf Blade and Psyblade provide a reliable offensive foundation, while base 108 Special Defense lets Iron Leaves survive many neutral special attacks better than most fast physical sweepers. Psyblade becomes especially attractive under Electric Terrain because its power increases to 120 without sacrificing accuracy, and Quark Drive can simultaneously boost a key stat. Swords Dance can produce decisive sweeps against a known team, but the defensive typing makes blind setup dangerous: a 4× Bug weakness and ordinary weaknesses to Flying, Poison, Ghost, Fire, Ice, and Dark leave many common coverage moves capable of ending the run. Close Combat should be reserved for situations where the defensive drops will not matter on the following turn, while Megahorn's 85% accuracy is generally too risky when a safer move already covers the matchup. Leaf Blade's high critical-hit ratio can help break opposing defensive boosts without introducing accuracy variance, and Sacred Sword is particularly useful because it ignores the target's Defense and evasion stat changes. Iron Leaves is therefore safest as a fast, matchup-specific physical attacker rather than a Pokémon expected to absorb hits simply because its Special Defense is high.

pokemon.name: Iron Leaves
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Iron Leaves is a metallic stag-like Paradox Pokémon resembling Virizion, with glossy green armor, digital red eyes, and luminous sections along its forehead, neck leaves, and limbs. The glowing structures on its head and sides can extend into ethereal blades, and eyewitness accounts describe those blades slicing large trees and boulders into short, thin strips. When Iron Leaves sleeps, it powers itself down, causing the red energy on its head, leaves, and legs to turn black. Its origin remains unresolved in the same way as the other future Paradox species: AI Turo calls it a distant descendant of Virizion, while the Professor encountered at the Crystal Pool describes it as a Virizion counterpart from another timeline. The Violet Book records a matching creature roughly 200 years before Turo's time machine existed, leaving the mechanism by which it appeared in that era unexplained.

playthrough: Poltchageist and Sinistcha are introduced in The Teal Mask and therefore require access to Kitakami rather than appearing in the base Paldea Pokédex progression. Poltchageist has Counterfeit and rarer Artisan forms; the battle stats and Abilities are identical, but Counterfeit Form evolves with an Unremarkable Teacup while Artisan Form requires a Masterpiece Teacup, producing Unremarkable or Masterpiece Form Sinistcha respectively. Sinistcha's 121 Special Attack and 106 Defense make it a capable bulky special attacker, while Grass/Ghost grants Normal and Fighting immunities plus useful resistances to Electric, Grass, Ground, and Water. Its signature Matcha Gotcha is an 80-base-power Grass special attack that hits both opponents in doubles, restores up to half of the damage dealt, and has a 20% chance to burn, but its 90% accuracy means it is not completely reliable. Heatproof is generally the more useful singles Ability because it halves the offensive stat used for Fire damage against Sinistcha and halves burn damage, while Hospitality is designed for doubles and restores one-quarter of an ally's maximum HP when Sinistcha enters the field. Strength Sap provides excellent recovery while lowering the target's Attack, Calm Mind can build toward a sweep, and Shadow Ball or Hex supplies reliable Ghost STAB. Dark, Fire, Flying, Ghost, and Ice weaknesses prevent Sinistcha from functioning as a universal wall, and base 70 Speed means many attackers move first. Bold is particularly useful for defensive or Calm Mind sets, while Modest can emphasize immediate special damage and Calm can strengthen its weaker special-defense side.
competitive: Sinistcha is currently UU in Scarlet/Violet and has established a substantial defensive and setup niche rather than functioning as a novelty counterpart to Polteageist. High base 121 Special Attack and 106 Defense combine with Calm Mind, Strength Sap, Matcha Gotcha, and Heatproof to create a setup sweeper that can repeatedly recover while reducing the damage of physical attackers. Strength Sap restores HP based on the target's Attack and lowers that Attack by one stage, allowing Sinistcha to turn many physical Pokémon into setup opportunities, while Matcha Gotcha provides simultaneous offense and healing and can inflict burn. Heatproof is usually preferred in singles because it effectively neutralizes the normal Fire weakness and also reduces burn damage, while Heavy-Duty Boots or Leftovers improve repeated switching and long-term recovery. Its weaknesses to Dark, Flying, Ghost, and Ice remain exploitable, and Matcha Gotcha's 90% accuracy plus base 70 Speed give offensive teams ways to force progress before Sinistcha becomes too difficult to break. In doubles, Hospitality gives it a completely different identity by healing its partner for 25% of maximum HP whenever Sinistcha switches in, while Rage Powder, Life Dew, Matcha Gotcha, and its immunity to Fake Out through Ghost typing make it a legitimate redirection-and-recovery support Pokémon. The Counterfeit/Artisan and Unremarkable/Masterpiece distinctions do not change stats, types, Abilities, or competitive movesets, so their tiering history is shared rather than form-specific.
nuzlocke: The Poltchageist line can become an excellent Kitakami Nuzlocke support Pokémon, although evolution requires locating the correct teacup item for the form caught rather than simply reaching a level threshold. Counterfeit Poltchageist needs an Unremarkable Teacup and Artisan Poltchageist needs a Masterpiece Teacup; the resulting Sinistcha forms are mechanically identical after evolution, so the rarer authenticity stamp does not itself make one survivor stronger. Sinistcha's Normal and Fighting immunities provide completely safe switches against known moves, while base 106 Defense, Strength Sap, and Heatproof can make many physical matchups highly forgiving. Strength Sap is particularly valuable because it is perfectly accurate, restores HP based on the target's Attack, and simultaneously lowers that Attack, reducing both immediate and future danger. Matcha Gotcha combines damage and healing but is only 90% accurate, so Giga Drain or another perfectly accurate option may be safer when a miss could result in a death; its 20% burn chance should be treated as a bonus rather than a plan. Memento causes the user to faint and directly conflicts with conventional Nuzlocke rules, while Stun Spore's 75% accuracy creates substantial variance despite its useful speed control. With its five weaknesses checked in advance, Sinistcha's immunities, recovery, attack reduction, and good physical bulk give it an unusually strong toolkit for keeping both itself and, in doubles through Hospitality, its partner alive.

pokemon.name: Poltchageist
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Poltchageist is a Grass/Ghost Pokémon made from living matcha powder inhabiting a traditional Japanese tea caddy and carrying a small tea scoop. An old tale says it originated from the regrets of a tea-ceremony master who became so obsessed with perfecting his craft that he drove everyone around him away before dying. It is most active at night, prowling towns and their outskirts, while during the day it prefers cool, dark places such as old houses. Poltchageist scatters its powder onto people or food; anyone who touches or consumes that powder can have their life force drained into the Pokémon's body, and it is capable of draining multiple people at once. It also uses matcha to repair cracked or broken objects, filling gaps with its own powder. Counterfeit and Artisan forms differ by an authenticity stamp hidden beneath the tea caddy and by the teacup required for evolution, but canon does not establish different temperament, anatomy beyond that mark, or ecology substantial enough to justify separate biology entries.

pokemon.name: Sinistcha
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Sinistcha is a Grass/Ghost Pokémon composed of matcha inhabiting a chawan tea bowl, with a whisk-like structure on its head that it uses to stir itself and build energy before battle. It prefers cool, dark hiding places such as the backs of shelves or spaces beneath floorboards and becomes more active after sunset. Historically, Sinistcha would sneak into houses and imitate ordinary tea so that people would drink it, allowing the Pokémon to drain their life force, but the decline in use of the traditional bowls it inhabits made that tactic less effective. Modern Sinistcha therefore roam towns and suburbs in search of prey and can attack approaching creatures by splashing them with life-force-draining tea. Unremarkable and Masterpiece forms are distinguished by an authenticity stamp on the base of the bowl and derive from the corresponding Poltchageist form, but their battle statistics, Abilities, and known biological behavior are otherwise the same.

playthrough: Okidogi is a standalone Poison/Fighting Legendary Pokémon introduced in The Teal Mask. After Ogerpon has been caught and The Teal Mask's main storyline is completed, Okidogi reappears at Paradise Barrens as a fixed level-70 encounter, so it is a late DLC acquisition rather than a Pokémon that develops alongside the player. Its base 128 Attack and 115 Defense make it an excellent physical bruiser, while Poison/Fighting provides strong STAB coverage and useful resistances to Bug, Dark, Fighting, Grass, Poison, and Rock. Toxic Chain gives every damaging move a 30% chance to badly poison a susceptible target, allowing even ordinary attacks such as Drain Punch, Poison Jab, Knock Off, or Ice Punch to create long-term attrition without using Toxic separately. Drain Punch is especially valuable because it is perfectly accurate and converts Okidogi's high Attack into recovery, while Bulk Up can increase both Attack and Defense when a matchup safely allows setup. Its Hidden Ability Guard Dog prevents forced switching and turns an opposing Intimidate activation into a one-stage Attack boost instead of a drop, which can be particularly useful in doubles or against Intimidate-heavy trainers. The largest defensive flaw is a 4× Psychic weakness, joined by ordinary Ground and Flying weaknesses, and base 80 Speed means Okidogi will often need to take a hit before moving. Adamant suits straightforward physical offense, while Careful can reinforce the weaker special side for bulky Drain Punch or Bulk Up sets.
competitive: Okidogi is currently UUBL in Scarlet/Violet singles, meaning it is legal in OU but considered too strong for UU. Its main competitive strength is the combination of base 128 Attack, 88/115/86 bulk, Poison/Fighting typing, and either Toxic Chain or Guard Dog, allowing it to make progress even when it does not immediately score a knockout. Assault Vest sets use Drain Punch, Knock Off, Poison STAB, and coverage such as Ice Punch to absorb special hits while Toxic Chain threatens badly poisoned status on switch-ins, and Drain Punch offsets chip damage as Okidogi repeatedly trades blows. Bulk Up sets instead commonly use Guard Dog, turning Intimidate from a defensive answer into a potential Attack boost while also preventing phazing effects that would otherwise remove a setup Pokémon. Its Poison typing gives it useful matchups into Fairy-types and its Fighting STAB threatens Dark- and Steel-types, but Ground and Flying attacks remain dangerous and the 4× Psychic weakness can force defensive Terastallization. Okidogi has also shown that its niches translate into official doubles: it appeared on Cristhian Andrade's championship team at the 2024 São Paulo Regional, demonstrating that its bulk, physical pressure, and anti-Intimidate potential were viable at high-level VGC rather than merely theoretical. Its UUBL status accurately captures the overall picture—too potent and difficult to contain for UU, but more specialized and easier to exploit than the most consistently dominant OU staples.
nuzlocke: Okidogi can be a very strong Nuzlocke capture if Legendary encounters are allowed, although its fixed level-70 post-story availability means it contributes mainly to late Teal Mask content, The Indigo Disk, and other endgame battles. Base 115 Defense, good HP, and several useful resistances make physical damage relatively manageable, while Drain Punch offers perfectly accurate STAB and immediate healing rather than requiring a separate recovery turn. Toxic Chain is useful passive insurance because any damaging move can badly poison a susceptible opponent, but its 30% trigger rate is too inconsistent to rely on when survival depends on status occurring that turn. Guard Dog is extremely attractive when available because it removes Intimidate as an Attack-reduction risk and prevents forced switching, allowing Okidogi to maintain Bulk Up boosts or a favorable matchup. The 4× Psychic weakness is the major survival hazard: an unexpected Psychic or Psyshock can overwhelm otherwise excellent bulk, while Ground and Flying coverage must also be respected. Gunk Shot's 80% accuracy and Close Combat or Superpower's defensive or offensive drawbacks make safer moves such as Poison Jab and Drain Punch preferable whenever they already secure the necessary knockout. Used against known physical or neutral matchups rather than blind special attackers, Okidogi combines strong damage, recovery, and defensive stability very effectively.

pokemon.name: Okidogi
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Okidogi is a muscular canine Legendary Pokémon whose most distinctive feature is the toxic chain wrapped around its neck. According to the history revealed through Pecharunt, Okidogi was once smaller and weaker; its desire for strength led it to accept Pecharunt's Binding Mochi, after which the toxic chain stimulated its muscles and transformed it into its present powerful physique while binding it to Pecharunt's will. It is a short-tempered ruffian capable of swinging the chain with enough force to pulverize what it strikes. Despite its greedy and arrogant behavior toward outsiders, Okidogi maintains a genuine working relationship with Munkidori and Fezandipiti, communicating privately with them and cooperating in battle. Kitakami's people long worshipped it as one of the Loyal Three and believed reverence for Okidogi could promote kindness and harmonious relations, a heroic reputation created by the community's mistaken understanding of its ancient conflict with Ogerpon.

playthrough: Munkidori is a standalone Poison/Psychic Legendary Pokémon that becomes catchable at level 70 in Wistful Fields after the player captures Ogerpon and completes The Teal Mask's main storyline. Its stat distribution is built for special offense and speed rather than physical durability: base 130 Special Attack and 106 Speed are excellent, while base 66 Defense makes strong physical attacks a serious concern. Psychic or Psyshock and Sludge Bomb or Sludge Wave provide reliable STAB, while Shadow Ball and Focus Blast cover many opposing Psychic-, Ghost-, Dark-, and Steel-types that would otherwise complicate those attacks. Nasty Plot can raise Special Attack by two stages and turn Munkidori into a dangerous sweeper, while U-turn or Parting Shot can reposition it when a matchup is unfavorable. Toxic Chain gives every damaging move a 30% chance to badly poison a susceptible target, so even U-turn can leave lasting damage behind as Munkidori escapes. Its Hidden Ability Frisk identifies opposing held items on entry and can provide information, but Toxic Chain is usually the more directly powerful option for ordinary play. Poison/Psychic strongly resists Fighting and also resists Fairy, Grass, and Poison, but weaknesses to Dark, Ghost, and Ground pair poorly with its weak physical Defense. Timid is generally ideal for maximizing the important Speed tier, while Modest can be used when additional special damage matters more than outrunning nearby opponents.
competitive: Munkidori currently resides in SV NU, where base 130 Special Attack, base 106 Speed, Toxic Chain, and U-turn make it a strong special attacker and offensive pivot. Psychic or Psyshock pressures Fighting- and Poison-types, while Sludge Bomb or Sludge Wave punishes Fairy- and Grass-types; Focus Blast and Shadow Ball can be chosen to address Steel-, Dark-, Psychic-, or Ghost-type answers. Toxic Chain is central to its pivoting value because U-turn can both maintain momentum and carry a 30% chance to badly poison the target, gradually weakening defensive Pokémon that might otherwise absorb Munkidori's attacks. Choice Scarf sets exploit its Speed and pivoting, while Nasty Plot sets use the switches it forces to double Special Attack and attempt a sweep; Trick can cripple defensive walls that rely heavily on their held item or move flexibility. Its limitations are substantial physical frailty, vulnerability to strong Dark priority, and the fact that Steel-types are completely immune to poison and often require dedicated coverage. Frisk can provide useful information but normally gives up too much long-term pressure compared with Toxic Chain. Munkidori's NU placement therefore reflects a capable fast breaker and pivot whose offensive tools are real but whose defensive profile and reliance on coverage keep it from dominating stronger tiers.
nuzlocke: Munkidori is a useful late-game Nuzlocke attacker when Legendary encounters are allowed, but its base 66 Defense means it survives primarily by moving first rather than by absorbing physical damage. Psychic, Psyshock, Sludge Wave, and Shadow Ball provide perfectly accurate options for many matchups, while Focus Blast's 70% accuracy is a major risk and should generally be reserved for situations where no safer coverage can solve the problem. Toxic Chain can badly poison an opponent while Munkidori attacks, but the 30% chance should be treated as bonus attrition rather than a dependable defensive plan. U-turn is especially useful because base 106 Speed often lets Munkidori deal damage and leave before the opponent acts, reducing exposure to its Dark, Ghost, and Ground weaknesses. Nasty Plot can enable a sweep against a known passive or special opponent, but spending a setup turn against an unknown physical attacker creates a poor margin for error. Frisk can be a meaningful scouting Ability if an Ability Patch is available and enemy held items are relevant, although losing Toxic Chain's passive pressure is a real tradeoff. A Timid, accuracy-conscious set that prioritizes fast attacks and pivoting is much safer than attempting to use Munkidori as a general defensive switch-in.

pokemon.name: Munkidori
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Munkidori is a monkey-like Legendary Pokémon whose toxic chain is wrapped around its head like a headband and whose present intelligence is directly tied to that chain. The history surrounding Pecharunt says Munkidori was once clumsy and dim-witted; its wish for intelligence led it to consume Binding Mochi, after which the toxic chain stimulated its brain, awakened powerful Psychic abilities, and bound it to Pecharunt's control. Its enhanced mind is capable of perceiving the near future, and Munkidori prefers to remain somewhere comparatively safe while using psychic power to manipulate or torment opponents from a distance, including inducing severe dizziness. It is greedy and manipulative but nevertheless cooperates closely with Okidogi and Fezandipiti. Kitakami later revered it as one of the Loyal Three, obscuring the fact that its original arrival was connected to Pecharunt's attempt to obtain Ogerpon's masks.

playthrough: Fezandipiti is a standalone Poison/Fairy Legendary Pokémon that returns as a fixed level-70 encounter on Oni Mountain after Ogerpon is captured and The Teal Mask's storyline is completed. Its 125 Special Defense, 99 Speed, and respectable 88/82 physical bulk make it considerably more defensive than its elegant appearance suggests, while Poison/Fairy offers a Dragon immunity, very strong Bug and Fighting resistance, and additional resistances to Dark, Fairy, and Grass. Its offenses are less focused—base 91 Attack and 70 Special Attack—but Play Rough, Poison Jab or Gunk Shot, U-turn, Beat Up, and coverage moves give it several ways to contribute without relying on pure damage. Toxic Chain gives every damaging move a 30% chance to badly poison a susceptible target, and multi-hit moves check that chance independently for every hit; a six-hit Beat Up therefore has roughly an 88% chance of triggering Toxic Chain at least once when all six party members contribute and the target can be poisoned. Roost is one of Fezandipiti's most important advantages because reliable 50% recovery complements its excellent special bulk, while U-turn lets it pivot out of Ground-, Psychic-, and Steel-type threats. Its Hidden Ability Technician boosts moves with 60 or less base power, but Toxic Chain generally offers the more distinctive defensive and attrition value. Careful is particularly well suited to a bulky pivot, while Jolly can exploit base 99 Speed and Adamant can improve its moderate physical damage.
competitive: Fezandipiti currently sits in SV UU and has developed into a disruptive pivot and special wall rather than an ordinary offensive Legendary. Its base 125 Special Defense, Poison/Fairy typing, Roost, U-turn, and Toxic Chain allow it to repeatedly enter against special attackers, heal the damage, and leave while threatening badly poisoned status on anything that can be poisoned. Beat Up has a particularly unusual interaction with Toxic Chain because every hit receives an independent 30% trigger chance; with six healthy contributing party members the probability of at least one trigger is about 88%, making it a much more reliable poison-spreading tool than a single attack. Play Rough, Gunk Shot, Poison Jab, or utility moves prevent it from being completely passive, and Heavy-Duty Boots often preserve its ability to pivot throughout a long match. Smogon has even documented an OU niche in which Fezandipiti checks particular special threats such as Darkrai and Iron Valiant, illustrating that its UU usage tier does not strictly define the highest level at which its defensive toolkit can function. Its limitations are mediocre direct damage, Ground-, Psychic-, and Steel-type weaknesses, and the complete immunity Steel- and Poison-types have to Toxic Chain's bad poison. Technician can support specialized offensive sets, but the combination of Toxic Chain, Roost, and U-turn is the strategy that most clearly distinguishes Fezandipiti from other Fairy- or Poison-type pivots.
nuzlocke: Fezandipiti is one of the safer Loyal Three for a Nuzlocke because Poison/Fairy supplies a complete Dragon immunity, a 4× resistance to both Fighting and Bug, several additional resistances, and base 125 Special Defense. Roost gives it reliable repeatable recovery, allowing Fezandipiti to erase chip damage rather than depending entirely on consumable healing items. U-turn can reduce exposure by allowing it to pivot after dealing damage, while Toxic Chain may badly poison the opponent during that same escape; the status chance is valuable but should never be assumed to occur on demand. Beat Up can generate several Toxic Chain checks in one move and can therefore spread bad poison very reliably with a healthy party, but its damage depends on the available team and it should not replace a stronger safe attack when an immediate knockout is needed. Play Rough is only 90% accurate and Gunk Shot only 80%, so Poison Jab or other perfectly accurate moves may be better in high-stakes situations despite lower power. Ground, Psychic, and Steel attacks remain the main dangers, and Fezandipiti's physical bulk is good rather than exceptional despite its extraordinary special side. With Roost and conservative move choices, it works particularly well as a long-term pivot whose job is to survive and gradually reduce opposing options.

pokemon.name: Fezandipiti
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Fezandipiti is an elegant pheasant-like Legendary Pokémon whose toxic chain is wrapped around its waist and whose transformed appearance is tied directly to Pecharunt's power. According to the revealed history, it was once a Pokémon with short, dull feathers; a wish to become beautiful led it to Pecharunt's Binding Mochi, after which the chain transformed its body, improved its capabilities, and bound it to Pecharunt's will. The resulting Fezandipiti possesses glossy wings, a striking appearance, and a beautiful voice, and it can release potent pheromones by beating its wings to captivate both humans and Pokémon. It is greedy and arrogant but maintains close relations with Okidogi and Munkidori and coordinates with them against shared enemies. Kitakami's later worship of Fezandipiti as a bringer of good luck and serendipity reflects the same mistaken heroic tradition that surrounded all three Loyal Pokémon after their ancient battle with Ogerpon.

playthrough: Ogerpon is a standalone female Legendary Pokémon obtained at the climax of The Teal Mask, and unusually for a Legendary DLC encounter its level depends on when the DLC is completed: it is level 20 if caught before completing The Way Home and level 70 afterward, with the final capture guaranteed after a four-phase mask battle. Its base 120 Attack and 110 Speed already make it an excellent physical attacker, and the four masks create meaningfully different battle configurations rather than cosmetic forms. Teal Mask is pure Grass with Defiant and, because it does not require one of the three held mask items, can use ordinary items such as Heavy-Duty Boots; Wellspring becomes Grass/Water with Water Absorb, Hearthflame becomes Grass/Fire with Mold Breaker, and Cornerstone becomes Grass/Rock with Sturdy. The Wellspring, Hearthflame, and Cornerstone held masks also increase the power of Ogerpon's attacks by 20%, while locking the item slot and fixing Ogerpon's Tera Type to Water, Fire, or Rock respectively; Teal is always Grass Tera. Ivy Cudgel is the centerpiece of every form: it is a perfectly accurate 100-base-power physical move with an increased critical-hit ratio whose type becomes Grass, Water, Fire, or Rock according to the active mask. When Ogerpon Terastallizes, its Ability changes to Embody Aspect and immediately raises one stat by one stage—Speed for Teal, Special Defense for Wellspring, Attack for Hearthflame, or Defense for Cornerstone—giving every mask a distinct Tera payoff. Horn Leech provides accurate Grass damage and recovery, while Swords Dance, Knock Off, Encore, U-turn, Follow Me, Spiky Shield, Stomping Tantrum, and other moves allow Ogerpon to shift between sweeper, pivot, and support roles. Jolly is generally the safest Nature for maintaining base-110 Speed, while Adamant is excellent when the selected mask or team structure already supplies sufficient speed control.
competitive: Ogerpon is unusual because its four mask forms have genuinely different tiering histories: current Smogon data places Teal Mask and Wellspring Mask in OU, Cornerstone Mask in UUBL, and Hearthflame Mask in Uber. Hearthflame was the immediate singles outlier after The Teal Mask released and was quickbanned from SV OU on September 22, 2023 by a 7-2 council vote; Mold Breaker, the mask's 20% attack-power bonus, Swords Dance, 100-BP Fire Ivy Cudgel, base 110 Speed, and the +1 Attack from Embody Aspect after Terastallizing made defensive counterplay too unreliable. Wellspring instead became one of OU's most durable offensive pivots and wallbreakers, combining Grass/Water typing, Water Absorb, a 20%-boosted Water Ivy Cudgel, Horn Leech, Swords Dance, Encore, Knock Off, U-turn, and a +1 Special Defense Embody Aspect when it Terastallizes. Teal Mask lacks the 20% held-mask damage bonus but can use any normal item, has Defiant to punish opposing stat reduction, and gains +1 Speed from Embody Aspect, supporting flexible pivot, cleaner, or wallbreaker sets. Cornerstone uses Sturdy as built-in one-hit insurance and Rock Ivy Cudgel as strong accurate STAB, but its Grass/Rock defensive profile and mandatory mask make it less broadly consistent, resulting in UUBL rather than OU usage. Ogerpon was just as important in doubles: Follow Me and Spiky Shield let its forms provide redirection and protection while still threatening enormous Ivy Cudgel damage, with Wellspring valued especially for Water Absorb and Hearthflame for offensive pressure. Hearthflame Ogerpon reached the highest possible official result when Luca Ceribelli used it on the team that won the 2024 Pokémon World Championships Masters Division, confirming that the form banned from OU could still be a balanced but elite tool under VGC's doubles rules.
nuzlocke: Ogerpon is an exceptional Nuzlocke reward because its capture is guaranteed, it can be obtained as early as level 20 if The Teal Mask is completed before The Way Home, and the same individual can switch among four defensive and offensive configurations between battles. Ivy Cudgel is nearly ideal for permadeath play: it is 100 base power, perfectly accurate, has an increased critical-hit ratio, and changes type with the mask, giving Ogerpon powerful STAB without relying on inaccurate attacks. Wellspring is often the safest general configuration because Water Absorb converts Water attacks into both immunity and healing; Cornerstone can provide emergency insurance through Sturdy when Ogerpon enters at full HP; Teal allows defensive held items and punishes stat drops with Defiant; Hearthflame offers the greatest immediate offensive pressure through Mold Breaker and its Fire typing. Horn Leech adds perfectly accurate recovery through damage, while Spiky Shield can scout and punish contact and Encore can lock a known opponent into a harmless or setup move. Wood Hammer's recoil is much less attractive under permadeath rules when Horn Leech or another Grass attack can accomplish the same objective, and Swords Dance should be reserved for matchups where Ogerpon cannot be surprised by a lethal coverage move. Terastallization can be extremely useful, but Ogerpon cannot choose arbitrary Tera Types: each mask fixes its Tera Type and Embody Aspect boost, so the player must plan around the exact defensive change rather than treating Tera as unrestricted emergency coverage. Because the forms can be changed outside battle, careful mask selection before major fights gives Ogerpon an unusually high ability to reduce matchup risk across an entire run.

pokemon.name: Ogerpon
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Ogerpon is a female Legendary Pokémon that came to Kitakami long ago with a human partner from a distant land and lived with him in the Dreaded Den after the pair were shunned by local villagers. A sympathetic mask maker created four masks for them using crystals from the Crystal Pool, allowing the pair to conceal their faces and participate in village festivals; the Teal Mask became the mask most closely associated with Ogerpon herself. After Pecharunt and the Pokémon later called the Loyal Three attempted to steal the masks, Ogerpon's partner was killed and Ogerpon defeated the attackers, but the villagers misunderstood what had happened and remembered Ogerpon as the villain while honoring the attackers as heroes. The Teal Mask draws on Grass-type power, is associated with Ogerpon's swift movements and kicking attacks, and is said to restore life to withered plants. Ogerpon's unique Terastallization is driven by intense emotion and memories stored through the mask; in the Teal state, those memories manifest through Embody Aspect as increased Speed.

pokemon.name: Ogerpon
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: The Wellspring Mask changes Ogerpon into a Grass/Water form and carries a sorrowful expression accented by tear-like Tera crystals. Its power is associated with flowing water: Ogerpon's kicks and ivy strikes are described as unrelenting like the continuous rush of a spring, and the mask is said to give it enough Water-type power to stop the flow of a river. In battle the form possesses Water Absorb, directly converting incoming Water attacks into healing, while Terastallization changes Ogerpon defensively to pure Water and Embody Aspect raises Special Defense. The mask's emotional and defensive emphasis distinguishes it from Hearthflame's aggression and Cornerstone's physical solidity rather than representing a simple change of color.

pokemon.name: Ogerpon
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: The Hearthflame Mask gives Ogerpon Grass/Fire typing and an angry, flame-like visage whose Tera crystals and surrounding mane emphasize the mask's aggressive nature. Canon explicitly describes Ogerpon as becoming its most aggressive in this form, mercilessly spearing opponents with thorn-covered ivy and bombarding them with the intensity of a blazing hearth. The mask's Fire power is said to be capable of turning a candle flame into a raging inferno. Its Mold Breaker Ability reflects the form's ability to attack through opposing defensive Abilities, while Terastallizing into its fixed Fire Tera state activates Embody Aspect and raises Attack.

pokemon.name: Ogerpon
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: The Cornerstone Mask changes Ogerpon into a Grass/Rock form and has a craggy, broad profile associated with the solidity of stone foundations. While wearing it, Ogerpon's body becomes rock-solid and can absorb powerful impacts; the form is said to have enough force to break even extremely hard stone apart. Its natural Ability is Sturdy, mirroring that emphasis on surviving impacts, while Terastallization changes Ogerpon defensively to pure Rock and Embody Aspect raises Defense. This form therefore represents the most explicitly defensive interpretation of Ogerpon's mask powers even though its base 120 Attack and Rock-type Ivy Cudgel still allow it to attack aggressively.

playthrough: Gouging Fire is a standalone Fire/Dragon Paradox Pokémon introduced in The Indigo Disk and obtainable naturally only in Pokémon Scarlet; Violet players need trade or HOME access from a Scarlet source. It is a very late single-copy encounter: after completing Perrin's earlier photography quest and registering at least 200 species in the Blueberry Pokédex, Perrin reveals photographs that allow Gouging Fire to be found as a static encounter in Area Zero. Its 105 HP, 121 Defense, 93 Special Defense, and 115 Attack give it an unusual combination of genuine bulk and physical power, while Fire/Dragon has only three natural weaknesses—Ground, Rock, and Dragon—and resists or strongly resists several common attacking types. Dragon Dance raises Attack and Speed and can turn its merely moderate base 91 Speed into a sweeping stat, while Heat Crash is a perfectly accurate recoil-free Fire attack whose power often becomes very high because Gouging Fire is exceptionally heavy. Flare Blitz provides consistent maximum Fire power against heavy targets but carries substantial recoil, while Dragon Claw is a safer Dragon STAB than Outrage or Dragon Rush and Earthquake offers reliable coverage. Burning Bulwark is its signature defensive move, protecting against damaging attacks for the turn and burning an opponent that makes contact into the protection, making it particularly effective against physical attackers. Morning Sun gives direct recovery and becomes stronger in sunlight, while Protosynthesis can also use that same weather or Booster Energy to increase Gouging Fire's highest stat. Jolly is valuable for Dragon Dance and Speed-boosting Protosynthesis builds, while Adamant maximizes damage on bulkier or externally speed-controlled sets.
competitive: Gouging Fire is currently Uber in Scarlet/Violet after one of the generation's more unusual two-stage suspect-test histories. Its first OU suspect concluded on March 16, 2024 with only 42.34% support for a ban, leaving it legal, but metagame development exposed increasingly difficult Dragon Dance, sun, Booster Energy, and Breaking Swipe variants; a second suspect ended on September 7, 2024 with 91.14% support for a ban. Its problem in OU was not simply base 115 Attack: 105/121/93 bulk created many setup opportunities, Fire/Dragon was difficult to punish efficiently, Morning Sun supplied recovery, and Protosynthesis or sun could increase either power or Speed while also strengthening Fire attacks. Dragon Dance sets combined Flare Blitz or Heat Crash with Dragon STAB and Earthquake, while Breaking Swipe variants could lower an opponent's Attack and turn supposed physical checks into additional setup opportunities; defensive Terastallization expanded that range further. In Uber-level play it is much easier to pressure because base 91 Speed requires help and the tier's legendary attackers can overwhelm even its impressive bulk, but Dragon Dance, Loaded Dice Scale Shot, Flare Blitz, Morning Sun, and Burning Bulwark still give it a niche. Its doubles identity is notably more supportive: Breaking Swipe lowers both opponents' Attack, Howl raises its own and its ally's Attack, and Burning Bulwark punishes Fake Out or other contact attempts while Booster Energy can provide immediate Speed. That role was proven in official play during Regulation F, including a Gouging Fire on Nick Schrott's runner-up Masters team at the 2024 Dortmund Regional and additional top cuts at events such as Goiânia and Melbourne.
nuzlocke: Gouging Fire is a powerful but extremely late Scarlet Nuzlocke encounter if the run permits Paradox and Legendary-like static Pokémon, since Perrin's quest and the 200-species Blueberry Pokédex requirement place it deep into DLC progression. Its natural 105/121/93 bulk and Fire/Dragon typing provide a large survival margin against neutral damage, with only Ground, Rock, and Dragon attacks hitting it super effectively under ordinary conditions. Burning Bulwark is excellent permadeath utility because it blocks damaging attacks for the turn and guarantees a burn on susceptible opponents that make contact, cutting the physical damage they deal afterward; it does not block status moves, so it should not be treated as identical to complete immunity for the turn. Morning Sun provides repeatable recovery and becomes stronger under harsh sunlight, which can simultaneously activate Protosynthesis and strengthen Gouging Fire's Fire STAB. Heat Crash is normally safer than Flare Blitz when its weight-based damage is sufficient because it has perfect accuracy and no recoil, while Dragon Claw avoids Outrage's multi-turn lock and confusion and avoids Dragon Rush's poor accuracy. Dragon Dance can enable an easy sweep in known matchups, but critical hits and unexpected Ground, Rock, or Dragon coverage still matter and should be checked before spending a turn setting up. With conservative move selection, Gouging Fire is one of the rare setup attackers whose natural bulk, reliable recovery, and defensive signature move can make the setup process itself comparatively safe.

pokemon.name: Gouging Fire
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Gouging Fire is a massive quadrupedal Paradox Pokémon resembling Entei combined with a ceratopsian dinosaur, dominated by a huge golden, horned crest surrounding its face. Only a small number of sightings are documented, but one recorded specimen was seen rampaging while erupting pillars of flame, and reports attribute exceptionally powerful control of fire to the species. Its fur can be superheated so intensely that it both protects Gouging Fire and burns enemies that make physical contact, the biological basis of its exclusive Burning Bulwark move; rumors further claim that its roar can trigger magma eruptions. Occulture's claim that the creature is an Entei regenerated from a fossil is explicitly speculative rather than established fact. Its true origin remains unresolved: AI Sada calls Gouging Fire an ancient ancestor of Entei, while the Professor encountered at the Crystal Pool describes it as an Entei counterpart from another timeline, and Heath's Scarlet Book records a matching creature roughly two centuries before Sada's time machine existed.

playthrough: Raging Bolt is a standalone Electric/Dragon Paradox Pokémon introduced in The Indigo Disk and obtainable naturally only in Pokémon Scarlet; Violet players need trade or HOME access from a Scarlet source. It is a very late single-copy encounter: after completing Perrin's earlier quest and registering at least 200 species in the Blueberry Pokédex, Perrin provides the clue that leads to the level-75 Raging Bolt in Area Zero. Its 125 HP, 137 Special Attack, and 91 Defense give it unusual offensive bulk, while base 75 Speed is modest enough that its signature Thunderclap is central to how it handles faster opponents. Thunderclap is a 70-base-power, perfectly accurate Electric attack with +1 priority, but it succeeds only if the target has selected an attacking move and has not yet acted, so it is powerful priority rather than guaranteed priority. Thunderbolt and Dragon Pulse provide perfectly accurate routine STAB, Volt Switch gives controlled repositioning, and Draco Meteor supplies much greater Dragon damage at the cost of 90% accuracy and a two-stage Special Attack drop. Calm Mind can improve both damage and special durability, while Protosynthesis can boost Raging Bolt's highest stat under harsh sunlight or after Booster Energy activates; sun is especially convenient in Scarlet teams built around Koraidon. Electric/Dragon resists Electric especially strongly and also resists Fire, Flying, Grass, Steel, and Water, but Ground, Ice, Dragon, and Fairy attacks remain dangerous. Modest emphasizes its enormous Special Attack, while Timid can be useful when base 75 Speed needs every possible advantage outside Thunderclap.
competitive: Raging Bolt remains OU in Scarlet/Violet singles and has become one of the format's defining bulky special attackers and setup threats. Calm Mind sets exploit 125 HP and strong physical bulk to accumulate Special Attack and Special Defense, while Thunderclap compensates for base 75 Speed by threatening faster attackers with +1-priority Electric damage. Dragon Pulse or Draco Meteor supplies complementary Dragon STAB, and Volt Switch lets Raging Bolt function as a bulky offensive pivot on sets that do not commit entirely to sweeping. Booster Energy and sun both activate Protosynthesis, allowing teams to emphasize immediate Special Attack or manipulate the stat spread for other boosts, while defensive Terastallization can remove troublesome Ground, Ice, Dragon, or Fairy weaknesses. Thunderclap's conditional nature creates real counterplay because it fails into status moves, setup, switching, and some priority interactions, while Ground-types are immune to the move entirely and can force Raging Bolt to use Dragon or coverage attacks instead. Its official doubles résumé is also substantial: Thunderclap, Assault Vest or Calm Mind variants, Electric pressure, and strong bulk made it a recurring VGC threat, and Giovanni Cischke used Raging Bolt on the team that won the 2025 Pokémon World Championships Masters Division. That combination of top-level singles viability and a World Championship-winning doubles role makes Raging Bolt one of the most competitively successful late additions from The Indigo Disk.
nuzlocke: Raging Bolt can be an exceptional late-game Scarlet Nuzlocke encounter if Paradox static encounters are permitted, though the Perrin and Blueberry Pokédex requirements mean it arrives very late. Its 125 HP and 91 Defense give it far more physical margin for error than many special attackers, while its resistances create useful opportunities to enter safely against known Electric, Fire, Flying, Grass, Steel, or Water moves. Thunderbolt and Dragon Pulse are ideal routine attacks because both are perfectly accurate, and Volt Switch provides one of the safest ways to deal damage while leaving an unfavorable matchup. Thunderclap can rescue Raging Bolt against a faster attacker, but the move should never be treated as guaranteed emergency priority because it fails if the opponent does not choose an attacking move. Calm Mind is relatively safe against known special attackers because it raises Special Defense while increasing damage, but critical hits and physical Ground, Ice, Dragon, or Fairy coverage can still punish careless setup. Draco Meteor is better reserved for a deliberate finishing blow because its 90% accuracy and two-stage Special Attack drop both create additional risk in a continued battle. A conservative set built around accurate STAB, Volt Switch, and selective Calm Mind use gives Raging Bolt excellent survival prospects despite its relatively low natural Speed.

pokemon.name: Raging Bolt
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Raging Bolt is an enormous long-necked Paradox Pokémon resembling Raikou combined with a sauropod dinosaur, with its face surrounded by a dense mane shaped like dark storm clouds. It can spread those cloud-like structures across the sky and call down lightning by extending its neck, and reports claim that electricity released from its fur can be powerful enough to disintegrate objects. Its towering neck lets the relatively compact head remain high above the ground while the heavy body moves on four legs, giving it a radically different body plan from modern Raikou. As with the other ancient Paradox Pokémon, its actual origin is unresolved: AI Sada presents it as an ancient ancestor of Raikou, while the Professor encountered at the Crystal Pool describes it as a Raikou counterpart from another timeline. A matching creature was recorded in the Scarlet Book long before Sada's time machine was constructed, further preventing a simple time-travel explanation from being treated as settled fact.

playthrough: Iron Boulder is a standalone Rock/Psychic Paradox Pokémon introduced in The Indigo Disk and obtainable naturally only in Pokémon Violet; Scarlet players require trade or HOME access from Violet. Like the other Perrin Paradox encounters, it is a single level-75 static Pokémon found only after completing the prerequisite Perrin quest and registering at least 200 species in the Blueberry Pokédex. Its base 120 Attack and exceptional base 124 Speed make it a fast physical attacker, while base 108 Special Defense gives it meaningful resilience against special attacks despite only base 80 Defense. Its signature Mighty Cleave is a 95-base-power, perfectly accurate Rock attack that can strike through moves such as Protect, Detect, Spiky Shield, King's Shield, Baneful Bunker, Silk Trap, and Burning Bulwark, making defensive scouting much less effective against it. Psycho Cut offers perfectly accurate Psychic STAB with an increased critical-hit ratio, while Earthquake, Close Combat, and other coverage can address Steel-, Dark-, Ground-, and opposing Rock-type targets. Swords Dance doubles Attack if Iron Boulder receives a safe turn, and Quark Drive can strengthen a key stat in Electric Terrain or through Booster Energy, with Speed receiving the larger multiplier if it is the boosted stat. Rock/Psychic has a difficult defensive profile with weaknesses to Bug, Dark, Ghost, Grass, Ground, Steel, and Water, so Iron Boulder's high Speed is often more valuable for survival than attempting repeated switches. Jolly is usually ideal to preserve its elite Speed tier, while Adamant can be justified when Booster Energy or outside speed control already handles faster threats.
competitive: Iron Boulder is currently UUBL in Scarlet/Violet: it is legal in OU but considered too strong for UU, where it was banned shortly after dropping into the tier in April 2024. Its core offensive package combines base 120 Attack, base 124 Speed, Swords Dance, Booster Energy, and Mighty Cleave, giving it a reliable Rock STAB that also bypasses common protection moves. Earthquake and Close Combat provide exceptionally broad coverage alongside Mighty Cleave, while Psycho Cut or Zen Headbutt can supply secondary STAB depending on whether reliability or power is preferred. The Speed tier is especially valuable in lower-powered environments because Iron Boulder can threaten offense without a Choice Scarf, while Booster Energy can push it beyond most revenge killers or amplify another key stat. During its UU stint, all-out-attacking and Expert Belt variants also proved difficult to handle because prospective checks could be removed by the correct coverage move rather than merely being forced to survive a single predictable Swords Dance set. Its weaknesses explain why it is not an automatic OU staple: seven exploitable defensive weaknesses, only moderate physical bulk, vulnerability to priority, and competition from stronger or more defensively useful offensive Pokémon all reduce its consistency. Iron Boulder's UUBL placement therefore reflects a Pokémon with an oppressive speed-and-coverage package for UU but a more matchup-dependent role at OU power levels.
nuzlocke: Iron Boulder is a strong late-game Violet Nuzlocke attacker when its static encounter is permitted, but its defensive typing makes careful matchup selection essential. Base 124 Speed is its greatest survival asset because it can remove many opponents before taking damage, and Mighty Cleave is particularly safe because it combines high power, perfect accuracy, and the ability to ignore most conventional protection moves. Psycho Cut is also perfectly accurate and has a high critical-hit ratio, making it a lower-variance Psychic option than Zen Headbutt when the reduced power is sufficient. Close Combat should be used selectively because lowering both defenses can leave Iron Boulder exposed on the following turn, while Swords Dance should be attempted only against known opponents that cannot exploit its seven weaknesses. Booster Energy can make Speed-based sweeps especially secure, but the one-use activation does not protect against priority attacks or eliminate the danger of super-effective coverage. Its base 108 Special Defense can absorb many neutral special hits, yet only base 80 Defense and weaknesses to Bug, Dark, Ghost, Grass, Ground, Steel, and Water mean blind physical matchups remain risky. A Jolly set emphasizing Mighty Cleave, accurate coverage, and immediate knockouts is generally safer than attempting to reproduce every aggressive competitive setup.

pokemon.name: Iron Boulder
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Iron Boulder is a robotic bull-like Paradox Pokémon resembling Terrakion, with metallic armor and a pair of large blade-like horns mounted around its head. Those horns can rotate and extend into broad axe-like cutting structures, and Iron Boulder stores concentrated light or laser-like energy in the head before charging through obstacles. It can also imbue the horn blades with psychic power, linking its mechanical weaponry directly to its Psychic typing. When sleeping, Iron Boulder powers down and the orange energy visible across its body and horns goes dark. Its relationship to Terrakion is unresolved: AI Turo describes future Paradox Pokémon as distant descendants, while the Crystal Pool Professor calls them counterparts from other timelines, and the Violet Book records a matching creature long before Turo's machine existed.

playthrough: Iron Crown is a standalone Steel/Psychic Paradox Pokémon introduced in The Indigo Disk and obtainable naturally only in Pokémon Violet; Scarlet players need trade or HOME access from Violet. It is a single level-75 static encounter unlocked through Perrin after the player has completed her earlier quest and registered at least 200 species in the Blueberry Pokédex. Its base 122 Special Attack, 98 Speed, 100 Defense, and 108 Special Defense create a balanced fast special attacker that is considerably sturdier than many offensive Pokémon. Its signature Tachyon Cutter is a 50-base-power Steel special move that always hits and strikes exactly twice, effectively delivering 100 base power while breaking Focus Sash, Substitute-like barriers, and other effects that are vulnerable to repeated hits. Psychic, Psyshock, and Psychic Noise provide Psychic STAB options with different targets, while Volt Switch gives momentum and Focus Blast offers strong coverage at the significant cost of only 70% accuracy. Calm Mind raises both Special Attack and Special Defense, and Quark Drive can boost a key stat under Electric Terrain or through Booster Energy, allowing Iron Crown to function as either an immediate attacker or a setup threat. Steel/Psychic grants a Poison immunity and a large collection of resistances, but Dark, Fire, Ghost, and Ground attacks remain important weaknesses and base 98 Speed is useful rather than elite. Timid is generally the safest offensive Nature, while Modest emphasizes damage and Bold or Calm can suit more defensive Calm Mind approaches.
competitive: Iron Crown is currently UUBL in Scarlet/Violet, remaining legal in OU while sitting above the power level allowed in UU. Booster Energy Calm Mind sets are among its defining singles strategies: Quark Drive can provide immediate Speed, Calm Mind increases Special Attack and Special Defense, and Tachyon Cutter supplies reliable two-hit Steel STAB that punishes Focus Sash and Substitute-based counterplay. Psyshock can pressure specially defensive targets through their Defense stat, while Psychic Noise can prevent recovery and Focus Blast threatens Dark- and Steel-types that would otherwise resist its primary attacks. Its 90/100/108 natural bulk and Steel/Psychic typing give it more setup opportunities than a typical fast special attacker, and defensive Terastallization can remove Ground, Ghost, Dark, or Fire weaknesses when a sweep requires it. The drawbacks are a merely good base 98 Speed before Quark Drive, reliance on Booster Energy or setup for its most explosive roles, and the poor reliability of Focus Blast when coverage is essential. Iron Crown also has a documented doubles niche beside Psychic Terrain and Indeedee, where Expanding Force can become spread Psychic offense while Tachyon Cutter retains its reliable Steel pressure. Its UUBL status reflects strong setup and coverage potential without the universal splashability or immediate speed of the most entrenched OU special attackers.
nuzlocke: Iron Crown can be one of the safer offensive Paradox Pokémon in a late-game Violet Nuzlocke because its defensive stats are balanced and Steel/Psychic supplies numerous resistances plus a Poison immunity. Tachyon Cutter is excellent under permadeath rules because it never misses and strikes twice, reducing the danger of Focus Sash or similar one-hit survival effects without imposing recoil or stat drops. Psychic and Psyshock offer accurate secondary STAB, while Volt Switch allows Iron Crown to deal damage and leave before an unfavorable opponent can exploit its Dark, Fire, Ghost, or Ground weaknesses. Calm Mind is relatively safe against known special attackers because it raises Special Defense at the same time as Special Attack, but it offers no protection from a powerful physical Earthquake or other Ground move. Focus Blast's 70% accuracy is difficult to justify in a Nuzlocke unless the coverage is indispensable, and safer alternatives should be preferred whenever they achieve the same knockout. Booster Energy can turn a carefully built Iron Crown into a much faster attacker, but it should not replace checks for opposing priority or super-effective moves. A Timid or bulk-conscious set centered on Tachyon Cutter, accurate Psychic STAB, Volt Switch, and selective Calm Mind use gives it an excellent combination of reliability and flexibility.

pokemon.name: Iron Crown
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Iron Crown is a robotic goat- or antelope-like Paradox Pokémon resembling Cobalion, with a metallic blue body and luminous structures across its head and armor. Its head can rotate independently, and the glowing horn structures can extend into long energy blades or fire particle-like blades capable of slicing extremely hard material. Reports describe Iron Crown destroying everything around it with these weapons, giving the otherwise elegant machine a highly destructive combat profile. When it sleeps, it powers down and the normally luminous sections of its body go dark. Its true relationship to Cobalion remains uncertain because AI Turo presents it as a future descendant while the Crystal Pool Professor describes it as a Cobalion counterpart from another timeline, and the Violet Book records a matching creature well before Turo's time machine was created.

playthrough: Terapagos is a standalone Normal-type Legendary Pokémon obtained near the climax of The Indigo Disk in the Area Zero Underdepths, where its level-85 capture is guaranteed and it becomes the player's principal source of the Stellar Tera Type. Outside battle it is normally in Normal Form, but Tera Shift automatically changes it into Terastal Form whenever it enters battle, so the small 450-BST form is essentially not a sustained battle state in Scarlet/Violet. Terastal Form has 95 HP, 95 Attack, 110 Defense, 105 Special Attack, 110 Special Defense, and 85 Speed, and Tera Shell causes damaging moves used against a full-HP Terapagos to be treated as not very effective unless they would deal no damage at all. If Terapagos Terastallizes, it changes into Stellar Form with 160 HP, 105 Attack, 110 Defense, 130 Special Attack, 110 Special Defense, and 85 Speed; its fixed Tera Type is Stellar and cannot be replaced with an ordinary alternative. Teraform Zero activates when Stellar Form appears and immediately removes the current weather and terrain, potentially shutting down opposing sun, rain, snow, sand, Electric Terrain, Psychic Terrain, Grassy Terrain, or Misty Terrain strategies. Tera Starstorm is a perfectly accurate 120-base-power signature attack that is normally Normal-type, but in Stellar Form becomes Stellar-type and hits both opponents in Double Battles, giving Terapagos an unusually reliable high-powered centerpiece move. Calm Mind, Rapid Spin, Stealth Rock, Earth Power, Ice Beam, Flamethrower, Thunderbolt, and other coverage or utility options let it function as a setup attacker, spinner, or bulky support Pokémon rather than relying on one fixed set. Modest and Timid are natural special-offense Natures, while more defensive Natures can support utility sets that exploit Tera Shell and Terapagos's strong Terastal/Stellar bulk.
competitive: Terapagos was quickbanned from Scarlet/Violet OU on December 16, 2023 almost immediately after The Indigo Disk released and remains Uber in current SV play. The core problem for OU was that Tera Shift automatically gave it the much stronger Terastal Form, Tera Shell made the first damaging hit at full HP effectively not very effective, and Terastallization then unlocked a 700-BST Stellar Form with base 160 HP and 130 Special Attack. Calm Mind sets could exploit that initial protection to begin boosting, while Tera Starstorm supplied a perfectly accurate 120-base-power attack and broad coverage such as Earth Power or Ice Beam prevented many defensive Pokémon from answering it cleanly. In current Ubers, Terapagos also fills bulky utility roles with combinations of Rapid Spin, Stealth Rock, Tera Starstorm, Toxic, Roar, and Heavy-Duty Boots, using Tera Shell to create a predictable first-hit buffer while controlling hazards. Stellar Form carries an important team-building cost because reaching it consumes the team's Terastallization, and Tera Shell only functions at full HP, so entry hazards or prior chip can remove one of Terapagos's most valuable defensive mechanics before it acts. In doubles, Teraform Zero can erase weather and terrain at the moment Terapagos enters Stellar Form, directly disrupting teams dependent on sun, rain, Electric Terrain, Psychic Terrain, or similar field conditions, while Stellar Tera Starstorm becomes spread damage. Terapagos also reached major official competition during the Scarlet/Violet era, including a Masters Division quarterfinal appearance at the 2024 World Championships, showing that its restricted-format value extended beyond its immediate singles quickban.
nuzlocke: Terapagos is an extraordinarily safe late-game Nuzlocke reward if Legendary encounters are permitted because its capture is guaranteed and Tera Shift automatically brings the much stronger Terastal Form into battle. Tera Shell is one of the strongest forms of first-hit insurance available: at full HP, essentially any damaging move that can hit Terapagos is treated as not very effective for that attack, creating a predictable cushion against unexpected coverage. That protection disappears after Terapagos has taken chip damage, however, so entry hazards, weather damage, status, or earlier attacks can materially reduce its safety; Rapid Spin is therefore valuable for preserving both team health and future Tera Shell activations. Tera Starstorm is perfectly accurate and powerful, making it a much safer centerpiece than high-powered moves that depend on imperfect accuracy or recoil. Calm Mind can be used relatively safely when Tera Shell has guaranteed a weak first damaging hit, though critical hits, status moves, and multi-turn battle dynamics still prevent setup from being completely risk free. Terastallizing into Stellar Form gives enormous HP and Special Attack and clears weather and terrain through Teraform Zero, but it also consumes the team's Tera and cannot be changed to a different defensive Tera Type for a specific boss. Used with full-HP management and accurate coverage, Terapagos provides exceptional survivability, but the player should not mistake the automatic first-hit protection for permanent resistance to every attack.

pokemon.name: Terapagos
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Normal Form Terapagos is a small cyan turtle-like Pokémon with a compact crystalline shell and a comparatively delicate body, representing its dormant or low-energy state outside battle. When endangered or entering extremely long dormancy it can withdraw into a jewel-like form, protecting itself behind crystal and remaining inactive for immense periods. Terapagos can create green crystalline barriers around itself, and the enormous crystal formations throughout Area Zero are directly connected to the species' Terastal energy. The known Scarlet/Violet specimen appears to be the last known member of a species that once lived in Paldea millions of years ago before environmental changes drove it into deep hibernation beneath Area Zero. Animated canon further depicts Terapagos as capable of sharing Terastal energy with other Pokémon, reinforcing that its small resting body contains far more energy than its appearance suggests.

pokemon.name: Terapagos
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Terastal Form is the larger battle state Terapagos assumes automatically through Tera Shift, becoming a floating indigo sea-turtle-like creature surrounded by fur-like structures and a crystalline shell. The shell contains patterns representing all eighteen Pokémon types and stores tremendous Terastal energy, allowing Terapagos to influence or distort ordinary type interactions. It floats rather than walking in this form and uses the energy concentrated in its shell both defensively and offensively. Tera Shell reflects that structure's protective function by weakening the first damaging hit received while Terapagos is at full HP, making the crystallized shell more than a visual transformation. This form is still only an intermediate expression of Terapagos's power; direct Terastallization causes it to expand into the much larger Stellar Form.

pokemon.name: Terapagos
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Stellar Form is Terapagos's fully Terastallized state, produced when Terastal Form receives energy through the Tera Orb and expands into a massive crystalline dome-like body surrounded by eighteen orbiting gems representing the Pokémon types. The transformation releases so much Terastal power that Terapagos can cancel existing weather and terrain, represented mechanically by Teraform Zero, and can absorb or interfere with Terastal energy used by other Pokémon. Its signature Tera Starstorm changes into Stellar type in this state and can strike multiple opponents at once, while the enormous transformation raises Terapagos's base-stat total to 700. Animated depictions show that full-power Terapagos can resonate with all eighteen Pokémon types and distribute enough energy to Terastallize numerous Pokémon, but using such tremendous power can exhaust it and force another period of dormancy. The destructive potential of uncontrolled Stellar Form is significant enough that its release beneath Area Zero is portrayed as a threat not merely to opponents but to the surrounding environment.

playthrough: Pecharunt is a standalone Poison/Ghost Mythical Pokémon encountered through the Mochi Mayhem epilogue after the player has progressed through the required Scarlet/Violet and Hidden Treasure of Area Zero content and obtained the Mythical Pecha Berry. The event item was distributed beginning in January 2024 without a normal fixed end date and remains claimable, allowing eligible players to trigger the epilogue and eventually receive a guaranteed level-88 Pecharunt at Loyalty Plaza. Its stat spread is highly unusual: every base stat is 88 except Defense, which is an enormous 160, making Pecharunt exceptionally sturdy against physical attacks but only moderately durable on the special side. Its signature Malignant Chain is a perfectly accurate 100-base-power Poison special attack with a 50% chance to badly poison the target, and Poison Puppeteer additionally confuses opponents that become poisoned or badly poisoned specifically because of one of Pecharunt's moves. Shadow Ball or Hex supplies Ghost STAB, with Hex becoming much stronger against statused targets, while Recover provides direct healing and Parting Shot can lower an opponent's Attack and Special Attack before safely bringing in a teammate. Nasty Plot offers offensive setup, while Foul Play can punish high-Attack physical opponents without depending on Pecharunt's own Attack stat. Poison/Ghost grants Normal and Fighting immunities plus useful resistances, but Dark, Ghost, Ground, and Psychic attacks remain important weaknesses and strong special moves can exploit the gap between base 160 Defense and base 88 Special Defense. Bold is excellent for maximizing its defining physical-wall role, while Calm can balance special durability and Timid can support faster offensive or pivot-oriented sets.
competitive: Pecharunt remains OU in Scarlet/Violet and has established itself primarily as a physically defensive pivot and status-oriented disruptor rather than as a conventional Mythical wallbreaker. Base 160 Defense lets it check or annoy a wide range of physical attackers, while Recover gives reliable longevity and Parting Shot both reduces an opponent's Attack and Special Attack and preserves momentum for the rest of the team. Malignant Chain is central to its offensive pressure because the move is 100 base power, perfectly accurate, and has a 50% chance to badly poison; when that poison is caused by Pecharunt's move, Poison Puppeteer also confuses the target. That combination can create extremely punishing turns for physical attackers such as Zamazenta, Ogerpon-Wellspring, Dragonite, or Rillaboom, especially when Pecharunt uses Rocky Helmet, Heavy-Duty Boots, or Air Balloon to tailor its defensive role. Shadow Ball provides consistent Ghost damage, while Hex can capitalize on poison and Foul Play punishes targets whose own Attack is much higher than Pecharunt's. Its weaknesses prevent it from being an unconditional wall: strong special Ground, Psychic, Ghost, or Dark attacks can exploit base 88 Special Defense, and Steel- and Poison-type Pokémon cannot be poisoned by ordinary Poison effects. Poison Puppeteer also does not activate merely because Toxic Spikes poisoned an opponent, so successful competitive use depends on Pecharunt actually causing the poison with its own move rather than treating field hazards as automatic confusion support.
nuzlocke: Pecharunt can be an extremely safe late-game Nuzlocke Pokémon if Mythical encounters and the Mochi Mayhem epilogue are permitted, particularly because its story capture is guaranteed rather than dependent on a low catch rate. Base 160 Defense creates an enormous buffer against physical attacks, while Normal and Fighting immunities provide completely safe switches against known moves and Recover can erase accumulated damage without consuming a limited healing item. Malignant Chain is unusually reliable for a status-inflicting signature move because it is perfectly accurate while still carrying a 50% chance to badly poison, and Poison Puppeteer can add confusion when that status is successfully inflicted by Pecharunt itself. Confusion should nevertheless be treated only as bonus variance rather than a defensive plan, because the opponent can still act successfully and poison-immune Steel or Poison Pokémon bypass the interaction entirely. Parting Shot is excellent permadeath utility because it reduces both offensive stats before switching Pecharunt out, often making the incoming teammate substantially safer. Strong special Ground, Psychic, Ghost, or Dark attacks remain dangerous despite the enormous Defense stat, and a Nuzlocke player should not mistake physical invulnerability for overall bulk. Memento causes the user to faint and is normally incompatible with conventional Nuzlocke rules, so Recover, Parting Shot, Malignant Chain, and reliable Ghost damage are much more appropriate survival-focused tools.

pokemon.name: Pecharunt
pokemon.biologyAndBehavior: Pecharunt is a small Mythical Pokémon that normally hides inside a peach-shaped poisonous shell, where it stores and ferments toxins that can be formed into mochi and long purple chains. Its Binding Mochi draws out the deepest desires of whoever eats it, strengthening or transforming the victim while also allowing Pecharunt to bind that individual to its will through toxic chains; it can control many affected humans or Pokémon at the same time. Long ago, an elderly childless couple cared for Pecharunt, and it used its mochi to make them increasingly attached to it; their growing desires eventually led Pecharunt to seek Ogerpon's treasured masks and recruit Okidogi, Munkidori, and Fezandipiti by granting each one's wish. Ogerpon defeated Pecharunt during that conflict, after which it remained dormant for centuries and became known in Kitakami as the Never-Rotting Peach before awakening again during Mochi Mayhem. Despite its capacity for manipulation, Pecharunt is portrayed as cowardly and dependent on others to fight for it, and it may feign helplessness or cry like a baby to gain sympathy. Its pleasant sweet scent and innocuous peach-like shell therefore function as part of a deceptive survival strategy built around controlling stronger companions rather than confronting danger directly.
